Listing 2.3, the <samp class="listingcharacter">main(...)</samp> method contains the following:

```
System.out.println( 
                "Arrest the usual suspects!" );
System.out.println( 
                true );
System.out.println( 
                -273 );
System.out.println( 
                1.6180339887498948 ); 
```

The arguments for <samp class="listingcharacter">println(...)</samp> such as the string, the truth value, or the numbers, are expressions. In this example, the expression comes from a literal, but operators can be used to form more complex expressions such as <samp class="listingcharacter">(1 + 2) * 1.19</samp> , as in the following example:

```
System.out.println( 
                (1 + 2) * 1.19 ); 
```

The value of an expression is also referred to as its result. Expressions always have a value, which isn’t true for statements (such as a loop). For this reason, an expression can exist in all places where a value is needed, for example, as an argument of <samp class="listingcharacter">println(...)</samp>. This value is either a numeric value (from arithmetic expressions), a truth value ( <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp>), or a reference (such as from an object creation).

### 2.2.9    Expression Statements

A program is made out of statements. Certain expressions and method calls can also be used as statements if they are terminated with a semicolon, which is called an expres sion statement . For example, each method call with a semicolon forms an expression statement. Whether the method itself returns a return value or not doesn’t matter.

```
System.out.println();        // println() has no return value (void)
Math.random();               // random() returns a float 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.random()</samp> method returns, as its result, a random value between 0 (inclusively so 0 is included) and 1 (exclusively, so 1 is never a selected value). Since nothing is done with the result of the expression, the return value is simply discarded. In the case of the random method, discarding the return value doesn’t make sense because the method itself doesn’t do anything else except for the calculation.

Besides method calls with terminating semicolons, other types of expression statements include assignments, for example. What all expression statements have in common is the final semicolon. [[ 41 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_09)

###### [»]  Note

Not every expression can be an expression statement. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">1+2</samp> is an expression, but <samp class="listingcharacter">1+2;</samp> (with the expression terminated with a semicolon) isn’t a valid statement. In JavaScript, these things are allowed, but not in Java.

### 2.2.10    First Insights into Object Orientation

In an OOP language, all methods are bound to specific objects (hence the term object-oriented). For example, let’s consider the object <samp class="listingcharacter">radio</samp>: A radio plays music when the power switch is turned on and a station and volume are set. Thus, a radio provides certain services (operations), like <samp class="listingcharacter">music on</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">off</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">louder</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">softer</samp>. In addition, an object has a state, for example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">volume</samp> or the <samp class="listingcharacter">year of construction</samp> .

Note that, in OO languages, without exception, operations and states are always bound to objects or classes (more on this distinction follows in [Chapter 3](#03_001.html_h3) and in [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6)). Calling a method on an object directs the request exactly to that particular object. If only the call <samp class="listingcharacter">louder</samp> exists in a Java program, the compiler doesn’t know who to ask if there are, say, three <samp class="listingcharacter">radio</samp> objects. What if there’s also a TV with the same operation? For this reason, you associate the object that can do something with an operation. A dot separates the object from its operation or state. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">println(...)</samp> belongs to an <samp class="listingcharacter">out</samp> object, which takes care of the screen output. The <samp class="listingcharacter">out</samp> object in turn belongs to the <samp class="listingcharacter">System</samp> class.

The runtime system provides two output channels: one for normal output and one to which you can direct errors. One advantage of this subdivision is that it enables you to separate errors from conventional outputs. The standard output goes to <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out</samp> , while the error output is directed to <samp class="listingcharacter">System.err</samp> . The <samp class="listingcharacter">print*(...)</samp> methods are the same for both <samp class="listingcharacter">out</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">err</samp> , which are of the same data type, as in the following example:

```
System.
                out.println( "This is a normal output" );
System.
                err.println( "This is an error output" ); 
```

**Listing 2.5**     src/main/java/SystemOutErr.java, main()

In this case, the object orientation becomes particularly clear once again. The <samp class="listingcharacter">out</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">err</samp> objects are two objects that can do the same thing, namely, output something via <samp class="listingcharacter">print*(...)</samp>. But you cannot call the <samp class="listingcharacter">println()</samp> method without an explicit object referenced and expect the runtime environment to know whether the request goes to <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out</samp> or to <samp class="listingcharacter">System.err</samp> .

[![IntelliJ Displays Normal Outputs and Error Outputs in Different Colors to Easily Distinguish Each Channel. The System.err Object Shouldn’t Be Used to Turn Everything Red on the Screen!](bilderklein/klein02_003.png)](img-f2.3.html)

**Figure 2.3**     IntelliJ Displays Normal Outputs and Error Outputs in Different Colors to Easily Distinguish Each Channel. The System.err Object Shouldn’t Be Used to Turn Everything Red on the Screen!

### 2.2.11    Modifiers

The declaration of a class or method can contain one or several modifiers that may, for example, restrict its usage or synchronize parallel access.

###### [eg]  Example

In the following program, two different modifiers occur in three places, which are set in bold:

```
 public class Application {

                    public static void main( String[] args ) {
    System.out.println( "Hello World" );
  }
}
```

The keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> is a visibility modifier that determines whether or not the class or method is visible to the program code of other classes.

The keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> allows you to call the method without forming an object of the class. In other words, without <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp>, an object must be formed, and the method must be called via the concrete object. We’ll only use static methods in the first two chapters of this book before introducing you to non-static methods starting in [Chapter 3](#03_001.html_h3) .

### 2.2.12    Grouping Statements with Blocks

A block summarizes a group of statements that are executed one after the other. Thus, a block is a statement that combines a sequence of statements into a new statement within curly brackets <samp class="listingcharacter">{ }</samp> . In other words, the sequence of statements becomes a new statement when placed within curly brackets, thus combining multiple statements into a single block, as the following:

```
{

                Statement1;

                Statement2;
  …
} 
```

A block can be used wherever a single statement can be located. However, the new block has a special feature with regard to variables since it forms a local area for the statements located within it, including its (local) variables.

###### [»]  Code with Style

Lines enclosed in curly brackets are usually indented with whitespace. Usually, two whitespaces are used (as in this book) or four spaces. Many authors place the curly brackets on separate lines. A wealth of other code style advice focuses on ease of reading and understanding for humans. For instance, lines shouldn’t be too long (80 to 100 characters is a good size), deep nesting should be avoided, and individual thematical units should be created using blank lines. The “Google Java Style Guide” at [https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html](https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html) provides some useful suggestions.

#### Empty Blocks

A block <samp class="listingcharacter">{}</samp> without a statement is referred to as an empty block . It behaves like an empty statement, that is, like a semicolon. In some cases, the empty block is indeed interchangeable with the semicolon, whereas in other cases the Java language forces a block to be empty if there are no instructions, instead of allowing a semicolon there as well.

#### Nested Blocks

Blocks can be as nested as you like, which results in inner blocks and outer blocks, as in the following example:

```
 {             // Start outer block
  {           // Start inner block
  }           // End inner block
}             // End outer block 
```

With empty blocks, the following code is fine in the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">main(...)</samp> :

```
public static void main( String[] args ) {

                    { System.out.println( "Hello Javanese" ); 
                    {{}}{{}{}}}
} 
```

Blocks play an important role in grouping statements that are executed once or several times depending on conditions. In [Section 2.5](#02_005.html_h2.5) and in [Section 2.6](#02_006.html_h2.6) , we’ll come back to this topic in practice.

## 2.3    Data Types, Typing, Variables, and Assignments

As is typical for imperative programming languages, Java uses variables to store data. A variable is a reserved memory area and—depending on the content—occupies a fixed number of bytes. All variables (and also expressions) have a type that is known at translation time. The type is also called a data type because a variable contains a data value. Examples of simple data types are integers , floats , truth values, and characters . The type also determines the allowed operations because truth values can’t be added, for example, whereas integers can. In contrast, floats can be added, but not linked via XOR. Since each variable has a fixed data type specified by the programmer, which is known at translation time and can’t be changed subsequently, and since Java is quite careful about which operations are allowed and also knows the type of each expression at runtime at the latest, Java is considered both a statically typed and strictly (strongly) typed programming language. [[ 42 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_10)

###### [»]  Note

In Java, the data type of a variable must be known at translation time. This requirement is referred to as statically typed. The opposite is dynamic typing , which is what JavaScript uses. In dynamic typing, the type of a variable can change at runtime, depending on what the variable contains.

Data types in Java fall into two categories:

*   Primitive types : The primitive (simple) types are hard-coded data types in the Java language for numbers, Unicode characters, and truth values.

*   Reference types : This data type can be used to manage object references to strings, data structures, or players' objects in a computer game, for example.

At the time, Sun decided on this categorization for a simple reason: Java was designed as a programming language to support small, weak devices. On these devices, the Java software, which was still interpreted at the beginning, had to run as quickly as possible. If the compiler distinguishes between primitive types and reference types, it can generate bytecode relatively easily that also distinguishes between those two types. This distinction also allows the runtime environment to execute the program code much more quickly and with a relatively simple compiler. This criterion was more important in the early days and is no longer important today because the runtime environment performs various optimizations.

###### [»]  Language Comparison with Smalltalk and .NET*

In Smalltalk, everything is an object, including the built-in language data types. For numbers, the base type <samp class="listingcharacter">Number</samp> has <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Fraction</samp> subtypes. Then, arithmetic operators, like <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">//</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">\\</samp>, (to list them all) exist, but these operators are only methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Number</samp> class. [[ 43 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_11) For Java developers, method names like <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> are unusual, but in Smalltalk, they aren’t. Syntactically, a <samp class="listingcharacter">1 + 2</samp> doesn’t differ in Java and Smalltalk, but in Smalltalk, the addition is a message call of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> object <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> and of the <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> method with the argument <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp>, which in turn is an <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> object as well—the compiler builds the objects independently from the literals. An <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> class for integers has other methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">asCharacter</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">floor</samp>. [[ 44 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_12) Note that this difference only impacts the semantic model on the language side; it has nothing to do with how later the runtime environment optimizes these particular message calls. By dividing Java into primitive data types and reference types, the language’s creators accepted a break from the OO principle to optimize the interpreted runtime in the early 1990s—an optimization that is unnecessary from today’s perspective.

.NET is more like Java: The compiler knows the built-in data types and gives them special treatment; they aren’t method calls. Statements such as addition and subtraction can also be found in the bytecode (called the Common Intermediate Language, or CIL in .NET). But there’s one more difference to Java: The compiler maps data types of .NET languages to .NET classes, and these classes have methods. In C#, the built-in <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> data type is identical to the <samp class="listingcharacter">Single</samp> data type (from the .NET <samp class="listingcharacter">System</samp> package), and whether developers write <samp class="listingcharacter">float f</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Single f</samp> doesn’t matter. However, <samp class="listingcharacter">Single</samp> (or <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>) has no mathematical operations compared to Smalltalk but does have a few methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">ToString()</samp>. [[ 45 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_13) Consequently, in .NET, the built-in data types behave like objects: They have methods but have the same value semantics (for example, in method calls) as in Java and also look similar in bytecode, which gives them the same good performance.

The following sections deal with primitive data types. References are only used when objects come into play. We’ll look at references in detail in [Chapter 3](#03_001.html_h3), [Section 3.7.1](#03_007.html_h3.7.1) .

### 2.3.1    Overview of Primitive Data Types

In Java, two types of built-in primitive data types exist:

*   Arithmetic types , for integers, such as integral types , floats, and Unicode characters

*   Truth values for the states true and false

[Table 2.5](#02_003.html_t2.5) provides an overview of these data types. We’ll look at each data type in greater detail.

| Type | Assignment (Value Range) |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> | 16-bit Unicode character (0x0000 ... 0xFFFF) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> | –2 ⁷ to 2 ⁷ – 1 (–128 … 127) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> | –2 ^(15) to 2 ^(15) – 1 (–32,768 … 32,767) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> | –2 ^(31) to 2 ^(31) – 1 (–2,147,483,648 … 2,147,483,647) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> | –2 ^(63) to 2 ^(63) – 1 (–9,223,372,036,854,775,808 … 9,223,372,036,854,775,807) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> | 1.4 × 10 ^(-45) … 3.4 × 10 ^(38) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> | 4.9 × 10 ^(-324) … 1.7 × 10 ^(308) |

**Table 2.5**     Java Data Types and Their Value Ranges

Concerning integers, note that there’s one positive number “less” than negative ones. This is due to the coding of two’s complement.

For <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, the display is somewhat abbreviated, and the sign is not specified since the smallest and largest numbers that can be represented can be both positive and negative. In other words, the value ranges don’t differ—unlike with <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, for example—depending on the sign. [[ 46 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_14) [Table 2.6](#02_003.html_t2.6) shows a slightly different representation.

[![](bilderklein/klein02_003_01.png)](img-f_none_02_05.html)

###### [»]   Detailed Knowledge

Strictly speaking, the grammar of the Java language doesn’t provide for negative number literals. For a number like <samp class="listingcharacter">-1.2</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">-1</samp> , the minus is the unary operator and doesn’t belong to the number. In the bytecode itself, the negative numbers are mapped again.

| Type | Size | Format |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Integers |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> | 8-bit | Two’s complement |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> | 16-bit | Two’s complement |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> | 32-bit | Two’s complement |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> | 64-bit | Two’s complement |
| Floats |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> | 32-bit | IEEE 754 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> | 64-bit | IEEE 754 |
| Other data types |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> | 1-bit | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> | 16-bit | 16-bit Unicode |

**Table 2.6**     Java Data Types and Their Sizes and Formats

###### [»]   Note

Strings are treated preferentially but are merely references to objects and not a primitive data type.

Two main aspects distinguish the primitive data types:

*   All data types have a fixed length that doesn’t change under any circumstances. The disadvantage that the length of a data type can change in some high-level languages doesn’t exist in Java. In C(++), this length always remains uncertain, and the move to 64-bit machines entails a lot of problems. The <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> data type is 16 bits long.

*   The numeric data types <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> are signed, floating point values of type <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. Unfortunately, their usage is not always practical, yet you should keep this fact in mind at all times. Problems arise when assigning the value 240 to a byte, for example, because 240 is outside the range of values that extends from –128 to 127\. A <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> is basically an unsigned integer type.

To sort the numeric data types by size (let’s leave <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> out of this scenario), you could build two lines for integers and floats, as in the following example:

```
byte < short < int < long
float < double 
```

###### [»]  Note

The classes <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Character</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp> declare the constants <samp class="listingcharacter">MAX_VALUE</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">MIN_VALUE</samp> , which specify the largest and smallest permissible values of the value range or the limits of the value ranges of each data type:

```
System.out.println( Byte.MIN_VALUE );       // -128
System.out.println( Byte.MAX_VALUE );       // 127
System.out.println( Character.MIN_VALUE );  // '\u0000'
System.out.println( Character.MAX_VALUE );  // '\uFFFF'
System.out.println( Double.MIN_VALUE );     // 4.9E-324
System.out.println( Double.MAX_VALUE );     // 1.7976931348623157E308
```

A separate class for each primitive data type with helper methods exists around that data type. For more information on these special classes, refer to [Chapter 11](#11_001.html_h11), [Section 11.5](#11_005.html_h11.5) .

### 2.3.2    Variable Declarations

Variables can be used to store data that can be read and written by the program. To use variables, they must first be declared (defined [[ 47 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_15)). The notation of a variable declaration is always the same: The type name is followed by the name of the variable. The declaration is a statement and must therefore end with a semicolon. In Java, the compiler knows exactly the type of each variable and expression.

Let’s declare a few (local) variables in the <samp class="listingcharacter">main(...)</samp> method to store the properties common to candies.

```
public class FirstVariable {

  public static void main( String[] args ) {

                String  name; 
    int     quantity;

                    double  price;

                    boolean sticky;
    boolean chewy;
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.6**     src/main/java/FirstVariable.java

On the left, either a primitive type (like <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>) or a reference type (like <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>) is used. A declaration is not much more difficult since cryptic specifications common in C don’t exist in Java. [[ 48 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_16) A variable name (which is then an identifier) can contain all the letters and digits of the Unicode character set, except no digit should start the identifier. Also, the identifier name cannot be identical to any reserved keyword.

#### Declaring Multiple Variables Compactly

In the preceding listing, two variables ( <samp class="listingcharacter">sticky</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">chewy</samp> ) are of the same type. Whenever the variable type is the same, the declaration can be shortened with the variables separated by commas, as in the following example:

```
boolean sticky
                    , chewy; 
```

#### Variable Declaration with Value Initialization

In a declaration, a variable can be initialized with an initial value. The equal sign is followed by the value, which is often a literal.

```
public class Lollipop {

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    String  name     = "Lollipop";
    int     quantity = 12;
    double  price    = 0.99;

                        boolean sticky   = false;
    boolean chewy    = false;
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.7**     src/main/java/Lollipop.java

As before, note that, when multiple variables of the same type are declared, a comma separates the identifiers. How you declare these variables also affects the initialization. For example, consider the following code:

```
boolean sticky     = true,
        chewy      = true;
String  person1    = "Silvio",
        person2    = "Ruby";
double  x, y,
        bodyHeight = 165 /* cm */; 
```

The lines declare several variables at once. The variables <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> at the end remain uninitialized.

#### Calculating Interest: An Example of Variable Declaration, Initialization, and Output

Using the console output, we can now program a simple interest calculator. This program is supposed to output the interest on a given principal, at a given interest rate, after 1 year.

```
public class InterestRates {
  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    double capital      = 20000 /* Euro */;
    double interestRate = 3.6   /* percent */;
    double totalInterestRate = capital * interestRate / 100; // Year 1
    System.out.print( "Interest: " );
    System.out.println( totalInterestRate );  // 720.0
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.8**     src/main/java/InterestRates.java

###### [+]  Tip

Strings can be attached to each other with a plus sign. If a segment isn’t a string, it will be converted to a string and then appended.

```
System.out.println( "Interest: " + totalInterestRate );   // Interest: 720.0
```

More examples follow in [Section 2.4.11](#02_004.html_h2.4.11) .

### 2.3.3     Automatic Type Detection with var

When variables are declared, the variable type can be replaced by <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> in some cases.

```
var name = "Lollipop";
var quantity = 12;
var price = 1;
var sticky = false;
var chewy = false; 
```

**Listing 2.9**     src/main/java/VarLollipop.java (Snippet)

Note that, unlike our previous example, variable types such as <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> are no longer explicit in the code when declaring variables, only <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp>. However, this omission doesn’t mean that the compiler leaves the types open! The compiler absolutely needs information to the right of the equal sign to determine the type. This scenario is called local-variable type inference .

For this reason, a discrepancy exists in our program, namely, at <samp class="listingcharacter">var price = 1</samp>, which clearly demonstrates a problem with <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp>. The variable is no longer a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> as before, but <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> is an integer literal, so the Java compiler gives the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">price</samp> the type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> .

The use of <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> is intended to help developers write shorter code, especially when the variable name already clearly indicates the type. If we find a <samp class="listingcharacter">text</samp> variable, the <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> type is obvious, just as <samp class="listingcharacter">length</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">size</samp> is an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or a prefix like <samp class="listingcharacter">is</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">has</samp> indicates a <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> variable.

But if <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> is used at the expense of comprehensibility, the abbreviation should not be used. The Java compiler also provides the following barriers:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> is only possible if an initialization specifies a type. A declaration of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">var age;</samp> without initialization is not possible and leads to a compiler error.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> can only be used with local variables. But variables can be declared in Java in other places, for instance, where using <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> isn’t possible.

###### [»]  Language Comparison

Java is relatively late with <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp>. [[ 49 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_17) Other statically typed languages have provided this option for a long time, for example, C++ with <samp class="listingcharacter">auto</samp> or C# with <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp>. JavaScript also uses <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp>, but in a completely different context: In JavaScript, variables aren’t typed until runtime, and all operations aren’t checked until execution time, whereas Java doesn’t abandon type safety with <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> .

### 2.3.4     Final Variables and the final Modifier

Variables can be declared with the <samp class="listingcharacter">final</samp> modifier so that exactly one assignment is possible. This additional keyword consequently prohibits further assignment to this variable, so that it can no longer be changed. A common use case for this modifier is to define constants, as in the following example:

```
int width = 40, height = 12;

                final int area = width * height;

                final int perimeter;

                final var random = Math.random() * 100;
perimeter = width * 2 + height * 2;
area = 200;         // 

                 Compiler error
perimeter = 100;    // 

                 Compiler error 
```

In the case of an attempted second assignment, compiler errors will occur.

Java allows deferred initialization for final values . Thus, assigning a value at the time of variable declaration isn’t mandatory, as shown in our example, with the <samp class="listingcharacter">perimeter</samp> variable.

If variables are declared and initialized, <samp class="listingcharacter">final</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">var</samp> can be used together. Some programming languages provide their own keyword for this case (e.g., <samp class="listingcharacter">val</samp> ), but Java doesn’t.

###### [»]  Outlook

Object variables and class variables can also be final. However, the variables must then either be assigned in the declaration or in a deferred initialization in the constructor. We’ll cover this topic in more detail in [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6), [Section 6.4.1](#06_004.html_h6.4.1) . If final variables are inherited, subclasses can no longer overwrite this value either (which could be a problem, but perhaps also an advantage, for some constants).

The <samp class="listingcharacter">final</samp> keyword has additional meanings in the context of inheritance. We’ll look at that later in [Section 2.7.2](#02_007.html_h2.7.2) as well.

### 2.3.5    Console Inputs

So far, you’ve learned about methods for output and <samp class="listingcharacter">random()</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">println(...)</samp> methods “hang” on the <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">System.err</samp> object, and <samp class="listingcharacter">random()</samp> “hangs” on the <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> object.

The counterpart to <samp class="listingcharacter">print*(...)</samp> is a console input, with several different variants. The simplest variant involves the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.Scanner</samp> class. In [Chapter 5](#05_001.html_h5), [Section 5.10.2](#05_010.html_h5.10.2) , we’ll examine this class in much more detail. However, at this point, we just want to emphasize how strings, integers, and floats are read.

| Reading Input of Type | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">String s = new java.util.Scanner(System.in).nextLine();</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int i = new java.util.Scanner(System.in).nextInt();</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">double d = new java.util.Scanner(System.in).nextDouble();</samp> |

**Table 2.7**     Reading a String or Integer and Float from the Console

Let’s combine the three possibilities into one example. The next program will first read a string, then an integer, and finally a float.

```
public class SmallConversation {
  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    System.out.println( "Hey! What’s your favorite candy?" );
    String name = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextLine();

    System.out.printf( "How many %s candy can you eat?%n", name );
    int quantity = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextInt();

    System.out.printf( "I see, %s. And how much did that cost?%n", quantity );
    double value = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextDouble();

    System.out.printf( "%s? I see, I was guessing %s.%n",
                       value, value * 2 / 3 );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.10**     src/main/java/SmallConversation.java

The conversation thus looks something like this:

```
Hey! What's your favorite candy?
Tootsie Roll
How many Tootsie Roll candy can you eat?
9
I see, 9\. And how much did that cost?
6.90
6.9? I see, I was guessing 4.6000000000000005 
```

The float must be entered in a localized manner. Floats often can’t be represented quite precisely, hence the strange output.

The output via <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(...)</samp> can also write localized floats, with the format specifier <samp class="listingcharacter">%f</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">%g</samp> .

###### [+]   Dialog Input

If the input doesn’t originate from the console, but from a separate dialog instead, a class from the <samp class="listingcharacter">Swing</samp> package can be helpful, as shown in the following example:

```
String input = javax.swing.JOptionPane.showInputDialog( "Input" );
```

### 2.3.6    Truth Values

The <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> data type describes a truth value that’s either <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. The strings <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> are reserved words and form literals along with constant strings and primitive data types. No other value is possible for truth values; in particular, numeric values aren’t interpreted as truth values.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> type is needed for conditions, branches, and loops, for example. As a rule, a truth value results from comparisons.

### 2.3.7    Integer Data Types

Java provides five integer data types: <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> , with <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp>fixed lengths of 1, 2, 4, and 8 bytes, respectively, which is an essential feature of Java. Integer types are always signed in Java (with the exception of <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>); no <samp class="listingcharacter">unsigned</samp> modifier exists, as in C(++). [[ 50 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_18) Negative numbers are formed by prefixing them with a minus sign. A plus sign for positive characters is possible. <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> are the preferred types. <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> rarely occurs, and <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> only in really rare cases, such as arrays with image data.

#### Integers Are by Default of the int Type

Looking at following code line, no error is seen on first sight:

```
System.out.println( 123456789012345 );      // 
```

Nevertheless, the compiler won’t translate the line because it assumes an integer literal without explicit size specification as a 32-bit <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. The line therefore results in a compiler error since our number isn’t within the valid <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> value range of –2,147,483,648 to +2,147,483,647, but instead far outside (2,147,483,647 < 123,456,789,012,345). Thus, Java doesn’t reserve as many bits as needed and doesn’t automatically select the appropriate range of values.

#### Larger Integer Values with long

The Java compiler automatically considers any integer literal as <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. If the value range of about +/–2 billion isn’t sufficient, developers resort to the next higher data type, the <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> data type. The fact that a number is <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> must be explicitly stated. For this purpose, an <samp class="listingcharacter">l</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">L</samp> is placed at the end of integer literals of the <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> type. To make the output of the number <samp class="listingcharacter">123456789012345</samp> valid, you must write the following:

```
System.out.println( 123456789012345
                    L ); 
```

###### [+]  Tip

The lowercase “l” looks similar to the number one. For this reason, an uppercase “L” should always be used in length specifications.

###### [»]  Question

What will the following statement output?

```
System.out.println( 123456789 + 5432l );
```

#### The byte Data Type

A <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> is a data type with a value range from –128 to +127\. An initialization like

```
byte b = 200;                 // 
```

is therefore not allowed, since 200 > 127\. Thus, all numbers from 128 to 255 (hexadecimal <samp class="listingcharacter">0x80</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">0xFF</samp>) are dropped. In data processing, the Java <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> isn’t really useful because it has a sign, and especially in file processing, value ranges from 0 to 255 are required.

Java doesn’t permit unsigned integers, but with an explicit type conversion number like 200 can be stored in a <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> , for example, in the following code:

```
byte b = 
                    (byte) 200; 
```

The Java compiler simply takes the bit assignment of 200 ( <samp class="listingcharacter">0b00000000_00000000_00000000_</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">1001000</samp> ), cuts off the upper 3 bytes during type conversion and interprets the uppermost bit then set as a sign bit, as shown in the following output:

```
byte b = (byte) 200;
System.out.println( b );      // -56 
```

More information about type conversion will follow in [Section 2.4.10](#02_004.html_h2.4.10) .

#### The short * Data Type

The <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> data type is rarely encountered. With its 2 bytes, this data type can represent a value range from –32,768 to +32,767\. The sign “costs” 1 bit as with the other integers. Thus, this data type has 16 bits, but only 15 bits are available for numbers. However, as with <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>, an unsigned <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> can also be initialized in two ways:

```
short s = 
                    (short) 33000;
System.out.println( s );      // -32536 
```

### 2.3.8    Underscores in Numbers

In some areas of application, numbers can get large rather quickly, for example, in the context of conversions. For instance, the <samp class="listingcharacter">System.currentTimeMillis()</samp> method returns the milliseconds that have passed since 1/1/1970, 00:00 according to the system clock. At 12:26:40 (UTC) on September 13, 2020, that’s 1,600,000,000,000 milliseconds. How can we convert this number to days?

To convert a number of milliseconds into days, a division operation can be made. To convert milliseconds to seconds, we’ll divide by 1,000; from seconds to minutes, divide by 60; from minutes to hours, divide by 60; and then for hours to days, the final division by 24\. The product of 24 * 60 * 1,000 is 86,400,000\. Let’s write that down to make a calculation from the current time with the following code:

```
long currentMillis = System.currentTimeMillis();
long days = currentMillis / 86400000L;
System.out.println( days );   // 18530 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">86400000L</samp> is not particularly readable. Java provides the solution to make numeric literals more readable by means of an underscore. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">86400000L</samp> , we can write:

```
long days = currentMillis / 86_400_000L; 
```

The underscores make the blocks of 1,000 easy to read. [[ 51 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_19)

Another solution is avoid using such a number at all and build it up by <samp class="listingcharacter">24 * 60 * 60 * 1000L</samp> —this approach doesn’t cost more runtime since this constant expression is fixed at translation time. In this case, building up the number is the better approach.

###### [eg]  Example

The underscore notation is also helpful for literals in binary and hexadecimal representation since the underscores can also set off blocks, as in the following examples:

```
int  i = 0b01101001_01001101_11100101_01011110;
long l = 0x7fff_ffff_ffff_ffffL;
```

A literal starts with <samp class="listingcharacter">0b</samp> in binary notation, with <samp class="listingcharacter">0x</samp> in hexadecimal notation. More details follow in [Chapter 21](#21_001.html_h21), [Section 21.1.3](#21_001.html_h21.1.3) .

The underscore can be used in any numeric literal, but two consecutive underscores aren’t allowed, and it must not be located at the beginning.

###### [»]  Note

The underscores in literals are just an aid like spaces for indentation and won’t be translated into the bytecode. In the class file, <samp class="listingcharacter">0b01101001_01001101_11100101_01011110</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">0b01101001010011011110010101011110</samp> look identical, especially because they are stored as the integer <samp class="listingcharacter">1766712670</samp> anyway.

### 2.3.9    Alphanumeric Characters

The alphanumeric data type <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> (from character) is 2 bytes in size and holds one Unicode character. A <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> is unsigned. The literals for characters are placed in single quotation marks. Language beginners often confuse the single quotation marks with the quotation marks of strings. The simple mnemonic rule is: one character—one quotation mark; several characters—two quotation marks.

###### [eg]  Example

The correct quotation marks for characters and strings are shown in the following examples:

```
char   c = 
                    'a
                    ';
String s = 
                    "Already barked today?
                    ";
```

Since the compiler can automatically convert a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">int c = 'a';</samp> is also valid.

### 2.3.10    The float and double Data Types

For floats (also called floating point numbers) of simple and increased precision, Java provides the data types <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. These data types are described in the IEEE-754 standard and have a length of 4 bytes for <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> and 8 bytes for <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> . Float literals can have a pre-decimal part and a post-decimal part separated by a decimal point (no comma). A float literal doesn’t require any digits before or after the decimal point, so the following code is also valid:

```
double d = 10.0 + 20\. + .11; 
```

Using only the dot is of course nonsense, whereas <samp class="listingcharacter">.0</samp> is certainly allowed.

###### [»]  Note

The <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> data type is a bad joke with 4 bytes (i.e., 32 bits). The <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> data type is just fine with 64 bits. The IA32, x86-64, and Itanium processors support a “double extended” mode with 80 bits and thus offer better precision.

###### [»]   Note

The compiler doesn’t report an error if a float can’t be read precisely. No mistake exists in writing the following:

```
double pi = 3.141592653589793238462643383279502884197169399375105820974944592;
```

#### The float * Data Type

By default, float literals are of the <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> type. A trailing <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp> (or <samp class="listingcharacter">F</samp>) indicates to the compiler that the value is a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

Valid assignments for floats of the <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> types include the following:

```
double pi = 3.1415, delta = .001;
float  ratio  = 4.33F;
```

A <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> (or <samp class="listingcharacter">D</samp>) can also be added for the <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> data type, but this addition isn’t necessary if literals for decimal numbers are in the source code; numbers like <samp class="listingcharacter">3.1415</samp> are automatically of the <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> type. However, while <samp class="listingcharacter">1 + 2 + 4.0</samp> first adds <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp> as <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, then converts the event to <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and then adds <samp class="listingcharacter">4.0</samp>, the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">1D + 2 + 4.0</samp> would start right away with the float <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp>. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">1D</samp> is also equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">1.</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">1.0</samp>. [[ 52 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_20)

###### [»]  Question

What’s the resulting output of the following lines of code?

```
System.out.println( 20000000000F == 20000000000F+1 );
System.out.println( 20000000000D == 20000000000D+1 );
```

###### [+]  Tip

What are the value ranges of <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>? [[ 53 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_21)

#### Even More Precise Resolution for Floats*

No higher resolution or more precise data type for floats exists than <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. The standard library provides the <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> class for this task in <samp class="listingcharacter">java.math</samp>, which is described in more detail in [Chapter 21](#21_001.html_h21), [Section 21.6](#21_006.html_h21.6). This class is useful for data that should have particularly good accuracy, such as currencies. [[ 54 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_22)

###### [»]  Language Comparison

In C#, the <samp class="listingcharacter">decimal</samp> data type has 128 bits (i.e., 16 bytes) and thus also offers enough precision to express a number like 0.000000000000000000000000001.

### 2.3.11    Good Names, Bad Names

For optimal readability and comprehensibility in the code, developers should consider some points when writing code:

*   A consistent naming schema is important Is a numerator called <samp class="listingcharacter">nu</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">num</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">nur</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">numerator</samp>? Also, we should write correct text and pay attention to spelling mistakes; otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter">necessaryConnection</samp> easily becomes <samp class="listingcharacter">nesesarryConnection</samp>. Variables of similar notation, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">counter</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">counters</samp> , should be avoided.

*   Abstract identifiers should also be avoided The declaration <samp class="listingcharacter">int TEN = 10;</samp> is absurd. A nonsensical idea is also the following: <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean FALSE = true, TRUE = false;</samp>. The program code would then work with <samp class="listingcharacter">FALSE</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">TRUE</samp> . Code written in this way would win top place in a contest for the most botched Java program.

*   Some Unicode characters can be included in identifiers, but they should be avoided The statements <samp class="listingcharacter">int Ⅳ = 4; int Ⅴ = 5; double λ = Ⅳ + Ⅴ;</samp> are however correct.

*   0 and O and 1 and l are easily confused The combination “rn” is difficult to read and, depending on the character set, easily confused with “m.” [[ 55 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_23) Also valid—but bad—is: <samp class="listingcharacter">int ínt, ìnt, înt; boolean bôõleañ</samp> ;.

###### [»]  Remark

Using unique names for your variables is vital. When vague names like <samp class="listingcharacter">temp1</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">temp2</samp> , etc. are used, how can you tell the difference between them?

If a designator name is chosen in an unfortunate way ( <samp class="listingcharacter">pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis</samp> is indeed a bit long), consistent renaming is still possible. Select Refactor • Rename… or press (Shift)+ (F6) ; the cursor must be on the identifier. At the same time, all references to the variable will change along with it.

### 2.3.12    No Automatic Initialization of Local Variables

The runtime environment—or the compiler—doesn’t automatically initialize local variables with a null value or truth variants with <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. Before reading, local variables must be initialized manually; otherwise, a compiler error will occur. [[ 56 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_24)

In the following example, the two local variables <samp class="listingcharacter">quantity</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">chewy</samp> aren’t automatically initialized, and so a compiler error occurs when <samp class="listingcharacter">quantity</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">chewy</samp> are attempted to be output. The reason is that initialization is necessary prior to the read access.

```
int     
                quantity;
boolean 
                chewy;
System.out.println( 
                quantity );    // 

// variable quantity might not have been initialized
quantity = 18;
if ( 
                quantity >= 10 )              // case distinction: if-then

                chewy = true;
System.out.println( 
                chewy );  // 

// variable chewy might not have been initialized 
```

Because assignments in conditional statements might not be executed, the compiler also reports an error with <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println(chewy)</samp> because it determines a program flow without an assignment. Since <samp class="listingcharacter">chewy</samp> is only set to the value <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> after the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> query, write access to <samp class="listingcharacter">chewy</samp> would only occur, and subsequent read access would only be possible under the condition that <samp class="listingcharacter">quantity</samp> is greater than or equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">10</samp> . But since the compiler assumes that other cases might exist, accessing an uninitialized variable would be an error.

[![IntelliJ Displaying Hints and Suggestions for Improvement When a Local Variable Isn’t Initialized but Is Accessed](bilderklein/klein02_004.png)](img-f2.4.html)

**Figure 2.4**     IntelliJ Displaying Hints and Suggestions for Improvement When a Local Variable Isn’t Initialized but Is Accessed

## 2.4     Expressions, Operands, and Operators

Let’s start with some mathematical expressions and then illustrate how they are written in Java. A mathematical formula, such as the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">-27 * 9</samp>, consists of operands and operators . For example, an operand is a variable, a literal, or the return of a method call. In the case of a variable, the value is read from the variable and the calculation is performed with it.

The operators link the operands. Depending on the number of operands, the following types of operators are distinguished:

*   An operator defined on exactly one operand is referred to as a unary operator (or monadic operator ). The minus (negative sign ) before an operand is a unary operator since it applies to exactly the following operand.

*   The usual operators (plus, minus, multiply, and divide) by are binary ( dyadic) operators .

*   A question mark operator is used for conditional expressions, which have 3 characters.

Operators allow the connection of individual expressions to new expressions. Some operators are familiar from school, such as addition, comparison, assignment, and others. C(++) programmers will recognize many old friends.

### 2.4.1    Assignment Operator

In Java, the equal sign <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> is used for an assignment . [[ 57 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_25) The assignment operator is a binary operator with the variable to be assigned on the left and an expression on the right.

###### [eg]  Example

Let’s look at some expressions with assignments:

```
int quantity = 12, total;
total = quantity * 2;
```

The multiplication calculates the product of 12 and 2 and stores the result in <samp class="listingcharacter">total</samp>. From all primitive variables that occur in the expression, the value is read and inserted into the expression. [[ 58 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_26) This process is also called a value operation because the value of the variable is considered (and not its location or even its variable name).

Only after the expression has been evaluated does the assignment operator copy the result into the variable. If runtime errors occur, for example, due to a division by zero, no write access to the variable is possible.

###### [»]  Language Comparison

The simple equals sign <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> is only used for assignment in Java, which is also the case in almost all programming languages. Rarely, a programming language uses a different symbol for the assignment, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">:=</samp> in Pascal or <samp class="listingcharacter"><-</samp> in F# and R. To separate assignments from comparisons, Java follows the C(++) tradition and defines a binary comparison operator <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> with two equal signs. The comparison operator always returns the <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> result type, as in the following code:

```
int 
                    quantity = 1;
System.out.println( 
                    quantity == 1 );   // "true": Expression with comparison
System.out.println( 
                    quantity = 2 );    // "2": Expression with assignment
```

#### Assignments Are Also Expressions

Although assignments are often found as expression statements , assignments can be found anywhere an expression is allowed, for example, in a method call like <samp class="listingcharacter">print*(...)</samp> :

```
int 
                    quantity = 1;                    // Declaration with initialization

                    quantity = 2;                        // Statement with assignment
System.out.println( 
                    quantity = 3 );  // Expression with assignment. Delivers 3.
```

#### Multiple Assignments in One Step

Assignments of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">a = b = c = 0;</samp> are allowed and are equivalent to the three statements <samp class="listingcharacter">c = 0; b = c; a = b;</samp> .

The explicit parentheses <samp class="listingcharacter">a = (b = (c = 0))</samp> make it clear once again that assignments can be nested, and assignments like <samp class="listingcharacter">c = 0</samp> are expressions that return a value. However, consider the following:

```
a = (b = c + d) + e; 
```

This is a good simplification compared to the following:

```
b = c + d;
a = b + e; 
```

In general, you should get by with one assignment per line .

The order of evaluation is shown in the following example:

```
int quantity = 10;
System.out.println( (quantity = 2) * quantity );  // 4
System.out.println( quantity );                   // 2 
```

Nevertheless, code like this shouldn’t occur in production.

### 2.4.2    Arithmetic Operators

An arithmetic operator links the operands with the operators addition ( <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> ), subtraction (- ), multiplication ( <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> ), and division ( <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp> ). In addition, the remainder operator ( <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp> ) considers the remainder left when dividing. All operators are defined for integer values as well as for float values. The arithmetic operators are binary, and on the left and right sides, the types are numeric. The result type is also numeric.

#### Numeric Promotion

For expressions with different numeric data types, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, the compiler sets all operands to the more comprehensive type before applying the operation. Thus, before evaluating <samp class="listingcharacter">1 + 2.0</samp>, the integer <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> is converted to a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and then the addition operation is performed—the result has the <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> type again. This feature is called numeric promotion . For <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, a special rule applies in that they are first converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. [[ 59 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_27) (Also, in Java bytecode, no arithmetic operations can occur on <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> ). Then, the operation is executed, and the result type corresponds to the more comprehensive type.

#### The Division Operator

The binary operator <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp> forms the quotient of the dividend and divisor . On its left is the dividend, and on the right, the divisor. Division operations are defined for integers and for floats. Integer division rounds to zero, and the result is not a float, so <samp class="listingcharacter">1/3</samp> provides the result <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> and not 0.333.... The data type of the result is determined by the operands and not the operator. If the result should be of the <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> type, at least one operand must also be a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> .

```
System.out.println( 1.0 / 3 );          // 0.3333333333333333
System.out.println( 1   / 3.0 );        // 0.3333333333333333
System.out.println( 1   / 3 );          // 0 
```

#### Division by Zero Penalty

In school, mathematics taught us that division by zero is not allowed. If we perform an integer division with the divisor 0 in Java, Java punishes us with an <samp class="listingcharacter">ArithmeticException</samp>. If the <samp class="listingcharacter">ArithmeticException</samp> isn’t handled, the executing thread will end, and if the unchecked exception takes place in the <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> thread and isn’t caught, the program will end. For floats, division by zero doesn’t yield an exception, but +/– infinity instead, and <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0/0.0</samp> results in the special value, not a number NaN (described in more detail in [Chapter 21](#21_001.html_h21), [Section 21.2.1](#21_002.html_h21.2.1)). Sometimes called a “non-number ,” NaN is generated by the processor when it cannot perform certain mathematical operations, such as division by zero.

###### [»]  Anecdote

On the guided missile cruiser USS Yorktown , a crew member accidentally entered the number zero. This attempt at division by zero resulted in an error propagated to the point where the software crashed, and the drive system stopped. The ship drifted in the water for several hours without propulsion.

#### The Remainder Operator %*

An integer division operator doesn’t necessarily always tally smoothly, as in the case of 9 / 2\. In this case, there is the remainder 1\. This remainder is provided by the remainder operator (% ) , often also referred to as modulo . [[ 60 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_28) The operands can also be negative.

###### [eg]  Example

```
System.out.println( 9 % 2 );            // 1
```

The division and the remainder are based on a simple formula in Java: (int)( a/ b) × b + ( a% b) = a .

###### [eg]  Example

The equation is satisfied if we choose, say, <samp class="listingcharacter">a = 10</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b = 3</samp>. The following applies: <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)(10/3) = 3</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">10 % 3</samp> results in <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp>. Then, <samp class="listingcharacter">3 * 3 + 1 = 10</samp> .

As shown in this equation, with the remainder, the result is negative only if the dividend is negative; the result is positive only if the dividend is positive. It’s easy to see that the result of the residual operation is always genuinely smaller than the value of the divisor. We have the same case as with integer division, that a divisor with the value 0 throws an <samp class="listingcharacter">ArithmeticException</samp> and leads to the result NaN for floats.

```
System.out.println( "+5 % +3 = " + (+5 % +3) );  //  2
System.out.println( "+5 / +3 = " + (+5 / +3) );  //  1
System.out.println( "+5 % -3 = " + (+5 % -3) );  //  2

                    System.out.println( "+5 / -3 = " + (+5 / -3) );  // -1

System.out.println( "-5 % +3 = " + (-5 % +3) );  // -2
System.out.println( "-5 / +3 = " + (-5 / +3) );  // -1

System.out.println( "-5 % -3 = " + (-5 % -3) );  // -2
System.out.println( "-5 / -3 = " + (-5 / -3) );  //  1 
```

**Listing 2.11**     src/main/java/RemainderAndDivDemo.java, main()

The fact that the first operand ( dividend ) defines the sign of the remainder and the second one ( divisor ) never does requires getting used to. In [Chapter 21](#21_001.html_h21), [Section 21.3.6](#21_003.html_h21.3.6), you’ll learn about the <samp class="listingcharacter">floorMod(...)</samp> method, which works a little differently.

###### [»]  Note

If you want to use <samp class="listingcharacter">value % 2 == 1</samp> to test whether <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> is an odd number, <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> must be positive because Java calculates <samp class="listingcharacter">-3 % 2</samp> as <samp class="listingcharacter">-1</samp>. The test for odd numbers is only correct again with <samp class="listingcharacter">value % 2 != 0</samp> .

#### Remainder for Floats

The remainder operator is also applicable to floats, and the operands can again be negative.

###### [eg]  Example

Test whether a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> number is an integer after all: <samp class="listingcharacter">(d % 1) == 0</samp> .

If this expression is too crazy for you, you can alternatively use <samp class="listingcharacter">d == Math.rint(d)</samp> .

#### Remainder for Floats and Math.IEEEremainder( )*

Using the formula mentioned earlier, you can easily calculate the result of a remainder operation even for floats. Note that the operator doesn’t behave as it does under IEEE 754 because this standard specifies that the remainder operation calculates the remainder from a rounding division and not from a truncating one. Thus, the behavior wouldn’t be analogous to the remainder for integers. However, Java defines the remainder for floats in the same way as it defines the remainder for integers. If you want remainder behavior as prescribed by IEEE 754, you can use the static library method <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.IEEEremainder(...)</samp>. [[ 61 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_29)

You should also never expect an exception for the remainder operation on floats. Any errors are indicated with NaN, as described in the IEEE standard. Overflow or underflow may occur but can’t be tested.

### 2.4.3    Unary Minus and Plus

Binary operators sit between two operands, while a unary operator takes on exactly one operand. The unary minus (operator for sign reversal ), for example, reverses the sign of the operand. Thus, a positive value becomes negative, and a negative value becomes positive.

###### [eg]  Example

Reverse the sign of a number: <samp class="listingcharacter">a = -a;</samp>

An alternative is: <samp class="listingcharacter">a = -1 * a;</samp>

The unary plus is actually unnecessary; however, the Sun team included it to establish symmetry. [[ 62 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_30)

###### [eg]  Example

Minus and plus sit directly in front of the operand, and the compiler knows independently whether this is a unary or binary operator. The compiler also recognizes the following construction:

```
int i = - - - 2 + - + 3;
```

This expression results in the value <samp class="listingcharacter">-5</samp>. It’s easier to understand the compiler if we include the operator order and mentally set the parentheses: <samp class="listingcharacter">-(-(-2)) + (-(+3))</samp>. On the other hand, the compiler doesn’t recognize an expression like <samp class="listingcharacter">---2+-+3</samp> because the connected minus signs are interpreted as a decrement and not as a unary operator. So, the separators (spaces in this case) are significant.

### 2.4.4    Prefix or Postfix Increment and Decrement

Incrementing and decrementing variables is a common operation, for which the developers in the predecessor language C had also provided an operator. The practical operators <samp class="listingcharacter">++</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">--</samp> abbreviate the program lines for increments and decrements:

```
 quantity++;            // Abbreviation for quantity = quantity + 1

                quantity--;            //               quantity = quantity - 1 
```

However, a local variable must be initialized upfront since a read access takes place before a write access. The <samp class="listingcharacter">++</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">––</samp> thus fulfills two tasks: Besides returning the value, it changes variables.

###### [»]  Note

Notice the post-increment in the name of the C++ programming language. The ++ is supposed to express that C++ is “C-with-one-up” (i.e., an improved C). Knowing about the postfix operator, however, this increase occurs only after being used—so C++ is also just C and the advantage follows later. One of the developers of Java, Bill Joy, once described Java as C++-- by which he meant C++ without the hard-to-maintain features.

#### Before or after?

The two operators return an expression and therefore return a value. However, subtle differences occur depending on where this operator is placed. In fact, the operator comes in two varieties: It can be placed before the variable, as in <samp class="listingcharacter">++i</samp> (prefix notation), or after it, as in <samp class="listingcharacter">i++</samp> (postfix notation). The prefix operator changes the variable before the expression is evaluated, while the postfix operator changes it after the expression is evaluated. In other words, if you use a prefix operator, the variable is first incremented or decremented, and then the value is supplied.

###### [eg]  Example

Consider the following uses of prefix/postfix in an output statement:

| Prefix Increment and Decrement | Postfix Increment and Decrement |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int i = 10, j = 20;</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println( ++i ); // 11</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println( --j ); // 19</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println( i ); // 11</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println( j ); // 19</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int i = 10, j = 20;</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println( i++ ); // 10</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println( j-- ); // 20</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println( i ); // 11</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println( j ); // 19</samp> |

**Table 2.8**     Prefixes and Postfixes in an output statement

The possibility of increasing and decreasing variables can result in the following four variants:

|  | Prefix | Postfix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Increment | Pre-increment , <samp class="listingcharacter">++i</samp> | Post-increment , <samp class="listingcharacter">i++</samp> |
| Decrement | Pre-decrement , <samp class="listingcharacter">--i</samp> | Post-decrement , <samp class="listingcharacter">i--</samp> |

**Table 2.9**     Prefixes and Postfixes for Incrementing and Decrementing

###### [»]   Note

In Java, increment ( <samp class="listingcharacter">++</samp>) and decrement ( <samp class="listingcharacter">--</samp> ) are allowed for all numeric data types, including float values:

```
double price = 12;
System.out.println( --price );              // 11.0
price = 12.456;
System.out.println( --price );              // 11.456
```

#### Some Oddities*

Finally, let’s deal with a peculiarity of post-increment and pre-increment that shouldn’t be imitated. Consider the following cases:

```
int i = 1;

                    i = ++i;
System.out.println( i ); // 2
int j = 1;

                    j = j++;
System.out.println( j ); // 1 
```

The first case is not surprising because <samp class="listingcharacter">i = ++i</samp> increases the value 1 by 1, and then, 2 is assigned to the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp>. The situation with <samp class="listingcharacter">j</samp> is more sophisticated: The value of <samp class="listingcharacter">j</samp> is 1, and this value is remembered internally. Then, <samp class="listingcharacter">j++</samp> increments the variable by 1\. But the assignment sets <samp class="listingcharacter">j</samp> to the remembered value, which was 1. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">j = 1</samp> .

### 2.4.5    Assignment with Operation (Compound Assignment Operator)

In Java, assignments can be combined with numeric operators. For a binary operator (symbolically called <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp>) in the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">a = a # (b)</samp>, the compound assignment operator truncates the expression to <samp class="listingcharacter">a #= b</samp>. [[ 63 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_31) Let’s look at some examples.

| Detailed Notation | Notation with Compound Assignment Operator |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">a = a + 2</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a += 2</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">a = a - 10</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a -= 10</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">a = a * –1</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a *= –1</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">a = a / 10</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a /= 10</samp> |

**Table 2.10**     Detailed Variant and Short Notation with the Compound Assignment Operator

While the prefix/postfix increment/decrement only increases/decreases by 1, compound operations in a relatively compact notation also allow larger increments/decrements, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">a+=2</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">a-=10</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

An assignment is always an expression, as in the following examples:

```
int a = 0;
System.out.println( a );        // 0
System.out.println( 
                    a = 2 );    // 2
System.out.println( 
                    a += 1 );   // 3
System.out.println( a );        // 3
```

Pay special attention to the automatic addition of parentheses for expressions like <samp class="listingcharacter">a *= 3 + 5</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">a = a * (3 + 5)</samp> and not, of course, the dot-before-dash rule <samp class="listingcharacter">a = a * 3 + 5</samp> .

###### [»]  Pun: A New Operator?

The “sleepy operator” <samp class="listingcharacter">-=-</samp> is rarely used. Consider, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">i -=- i</samp> . What is exactly happening here?

#### One-Time Evaluation for Array Access*

If the left side in the compound assignment operator is an array access (see [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.1](#04_001.html_h4.1)), the index calculation will be performed only once. This fact is important when using the prefix/postfix operator or method calls that have side effects, such as changing states like an enumerator. [[ 64 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_32)

###### [eg]  Example

You can benefit from the compound assignment operator in array access because, first, the notation is short and, second, because the evaluation of the index occurs only once. Consider the following example:

```
int[] array1 = { 10, 90, 0 };
int i = 0;
array1[++i] = array1[++i] + 10;
System.out.println( Arrays.toString( array1 ) );  // [10, 10, 0]
int[] array2 = { 0, 90, 0 };
int j = 0;
array2[++j] += 10;
System.out.println( Arrays.toString( array2 ) );  // [0, 100, 0]
```

### 2.4.6     Relational Operators and Equality Operators

Relational operators are comparison operators that compare expressions with each other, and the result is a truth value of the <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> type. The operators provided by Java for numerical comparisons include the following:

*   Greater than ( <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> )

*   Less than ( <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> )

*   Greater than or equal to ( <samp class="listingcharacter">⩾</samp> )

*   Less than or equal to ( <samp class="listingcharacter">⩽</samp> )

The special operator <samp class="listingcharacter">instanceof</samp> is for testing type relationships.

In addition, two comparison operators , called equality operators , are available in Java:

*   Test for equality ( <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> )

*   Test for inequality ( <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> )

The fact that Java makes a distinction between equality operators and comparison operators is due to a slightly different precedence, but this order of precedence shouldn’t concern you any further.

Like arithmetic operators, relational operators match their operands to a common type. If the types are reference types, only the comparison operators <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> are allowed. An exception is <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> is also allowed.

#### Confusion Caused by == and =

The use of the relational operator <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> and the assignment operator <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> often causes problems for beginners because mathematics always knows only one equal sign for comparisons and assignments. Fortunately, the problem in Java isn’t as drastic as in C(++), for example, because the types of the operators are different. The comparison operator always returns only the <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> value. However, assignments of numeric types result in a numeric type again. Thus, the following problem cannot occur:

```
int a = 10, b = 11;
boolean result1 = ( 
                    a = b );        // 

                     Compiler error
boolean result2 = ( 
                    a == b ); 
```

###### [eg]  Example

For example, let’s say the truth variable <samp class="listingcharacter">isExpensive</samp> should be <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the price is above 10:

```
int price = 12;
boolean isExpensive = price > 10;
```

The evaluation sequence is as follows: First, the result of the comparison is calculated, and this truth value is then copied to <samp class="listingcharacter">isExpensive</samp>. Commonly, the expression on the right is placed in parentheses, which can improve readability, as in the following example:

```
boolean isExpensive = (price > 10);
```

###### [»]  (Anti-)Style

In a comparison with <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> , both operands can be swapped—if the two sides don’t produce influencing side effects, such as state changes, for example. The result doesn’t change because the comparison operator is commutative. Consequently, the following lines are semantically the same:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">if ( worldExpoShanghaiCostInUSD == 58000000000L )</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">if ( 58000000000L == worldExpoShanghaiCostInUSD )</samp>

In an equality comparison between a variable and a literal, many developers with experience in the C programming language will put the constant on the left and the variable on the right. The reason for this style (called the Yoda style [[ 65 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_33)) is to avoid mistakes. If an equal sign is missing in C, then <samp class="listingcharacter">if(worldExpoShanghaiCostInUSD = 58000000000L)</samp> can still be compiled as an assignment (although with a warning), whereas <samp class="listingcharacter">if(58000000000L = worldExpoShanghaiCostInUSD)</samp> cannot. The first incorrect version initializes a variable and always jumps to the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement because in C every expression (here from the assignment, which is an expression) not equal to 0 is interpreted as true. This error is a logical error that the second notation prevents because it leads to a compiler error. In Java, this error can’t happen unless the variable type is <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp>, and then comparisons are also usually not written with <samp class="listingcharacter">== false</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">== true</samp> . In a nutshell, the Yoda notation shouldn’t be used in Java.

### 2.4.7    Logical Operators: NOT, AND, OR, and XOR

The processing of program code is often linked to conditions. These conditions are often complex in their structure, with three operators being the most commonly used ones:

*   NOT (negation): Turns the statement around; true becomes false, and false becomes true .

*   AND (conjunction) : Both statements must be true for the overall statement to be true.

*   OR (disjunction) : One of the two statements must be true for the overall statement to be true.

###### [»]  Note

More than these three logical operators are actually not necessary to realize all possible logical operations. In mathematics, this is called Boolean algebra .

Logical operators are used to link truth values according to defined patterns. Logical operators operate only on <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> types, other types lead to compiler errors. Java provides the operators NOT ( <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp>) , AND ( <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> ), OR ( <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp> ), and XOR ( <samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp> ). XOR is an operation that returns true only if exactly one of the two operands is <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>.
