If both operands are equal (i.e., either <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>), the result is <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. XOR is also referred to as exclusive OR . The phrase “either ... or” captures this pretty well: It’s either one or the other, but not both together. Example: “Do you want to either go to the movies or watch a DVD?” <samp class="listingcharacter">a ^ b</samp> is an abbreviation for <samp class="listingcharacter">(a && !b) || (!a && b)</samp> .

| <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean a</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">! a</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a && b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a &#124;&#124; b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">a ^ b</samp> |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |

**Table 2.11**     Links of the Logical Operators NOT, AND, OR, and XOR

The logical operators always work on the <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> type. In [Chapter 22](#22_001.html_h22), [Section 22.1.1](#22_001.html_h22.1.1) , we’ll see that the same operations can be performed on any bit of an integer.

###### [»]  Outlook on Propositional Logic*

Links of this kind are rather important in propositional logic or Boolean algebra. The terms AND, OR, and XOR, which are common for us, might also be known under different names. The AND link is called a conjunction , the OR link is called a disjunction , and the exclusive OR is called a contravalence . The three binary operators AND, OR, and XOR cover certain linkages, not all of which are possible. Propositional logic also features implication (if-then linkage) and equivalence .

### 2.4.8    Short-Circuit Operators

A logical expression only needs to be evaluated further if the final result can still change. If the result is already irrefutably fixed before the evaluation of all parts, the compiler shortens the program flow. The two operators <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> (AND) and <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp> (OR) are useful for optimizing expressions:

*   AND : If one of the two expressions is false, the expression can’t be true. The result is false.

*   OR : If at least one of the expressions is true, then the entire expression is also true.

Take, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">true || Math.random() > 0.5</samp>. In this case, the method won’t be called because the two operators <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp> are short-circuit operators . [[ 66 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_34) Thus, the characteristic of short-circuit operators is that they serve as shortcuts when the result of an expression is fixed; the remaining expressions are not evaluated.

#### Non-Short-Circuit Operators*

In some cases, a useful approach is for the runtime environment to evaluate all subexpressions. Perhaps, a method is intended to have side effects, such as state changes. For this reason, Java additionally provides the operators <samp class="listingcharacter">|</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> , which don’t work via a short-circuit and force an evaluation of all partial expressions. The result of the evaluation is the same as before.

The operation is documented by the following program, where you can easily see that a variable is incremented only when the non-short-circuit operator performs an evaluation.

```
int a = 0, b = 0, c = 0 , d = 0;
System.out.println( true || a++ == 0 );  // true, a not incremented
System.out.println( a );                 // 0
System.out.println( true | b++ == 0 );   // true, b incremented
System.out.println( b );                 // 1
System.out.println( false && c++ == 0 ); // false, c not incremented
System.out.println( c );                 // 0
System.out.println( false & d++ == 0 );  // false, d incremented 
```

**Listing 2.12**     src/main/java/CircuitNotCircuitOperator.java, main()

No short-circuit operator can be used for XOR since both operands must always be evaluated before the result is fixed.

###### [»]  Note

Under certain conditions, omitting the short-circuit operator can be more performant because the compiler can avoid branches and jumps.

### 2.4.9     The Rank of Operators in Evaluation Order

The rule that multiplication and division operations take precedence over addition and subtraction operations is well known. Thus, the expression 1 + 2 × 3 results in 7 and not in 9.

###### Example

Even though expressions like <samp class="listingcharacter">a() + b() * c()</samp> form the product first, the evaluation order of binary operators dictates that the left operand must be evaluated first, which means that Java calls the <samp class="listingcharacter">a()</samp> method first.

Beyond addition and multiplication, a multitude of operators each have their own precedence rules. [[ 67 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_35) For example, the multiplication operator has a higher priority and thus a different evaluation order than the plus operator.

The ranking of the operators (or operator precedence) is listed in [Table 2.12](#02_004.html_t2.12), where the lambda arrow <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp> is omitted. The arithmetic type represents integers and floats, the integral type stands for <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> and integers, and the entry “primitive” stands for any primitive data types (i.e., also <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> ).

| Operator | Ranking | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">++</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">--</samp> | 1 | arithmetic | Increment and decrement |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> | 1 | arithmetic | Unary plus and minus |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">~</samp> | 1 | integral | Bitwise complement |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> | 1 | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> | Logical complement |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(Type)</samp> | 1 | any | Cast |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">/</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp> | 2 | arithmetic | Multiplication, division, and remainder |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> | 3 | arithmetic | Binary operator for addition and subtraction |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> | 3 | <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> | String concatenation |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><<</samp> | 4 | integral | Shift to the left |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> | 4 | integral | Right shift with sign extension |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">>>></samp> | 4 | integral | Right shift without sign extension |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp> | 5 | arithmetic | Numerical comparisons |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">instanceof</samp> | 5 | object | Type comparison |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> | 6 | primitive | Equality/inequality of values |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> | 6 | object | Equal/inequal references |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> | 7 | integral | Bitwise AND |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp> | 7 | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> | Logical AND |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp> | 8 | integral | Bitwise XOR |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">^</samp> | 8 | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> | Logical XOR |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&#124;</samp> | 9 | integral | Bitwise OR |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&#124;</samp> | 9 | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> | Logical OR |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> | 10 | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> | Logical conditional AND, short-circuit |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">&#124;&#124;</samp> | 11 | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> | Logical conditional OR, short-circuit |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">? :</samp> | 12 | any | Condition operator |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp> | 13 | any | Assignment |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">*=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">/=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">%=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">+=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><<=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">>>=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">>>>=</samp>,
<samp class="listingcharacter">&=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">^=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">&#124;=</samp> | 14 | arithmetic | Assignment with operation |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">+=</samp> | 14 | <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> | Assignment with string concatenation |

**Table 2.12**     Operators with Ranking Order in Java (Operator Ranking Order )

The rule that multiplication and division operations take precedence over addition and subtraction operations is easy to remember. Also, note that the typical arithmetic operators (such as for addition and multiplication) by have a higher priority than comparison operations. But the evaluation becomes more complicated for numerous operators that may occur less frequently in the program.

###### [eg]  Example

What is the evaluation for the next expression?

```
boolean sticky = false,
        chewy  = false,
        hard   = true;
System.out.println( sticky && chewy || hard );
```

The result could be <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> depending on the ranking. But Table 2.11 shows that, in this example, the AND binds more strongly than the OR. Thus, the expression is read as <samp class="listingcharacter">(sticky && chewy) || hard</samp> and not as <samp class="listingcharacter">sticky && (chewy || hard)</samp> and thus evaluates to <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> .

Presumably, programmers implicitly know this order of precedence or have the table with rankings stuck to the monitor. But when reading through other people’s code, it’s inconvenient to need to consult the table that reveals whether the binary XOR or the binary AND binds more strongly.

###### [+]  Tip

All expressions that go beyond the simple rule about multiplication/division taking precedence over addition/subtraction should be placed in parentheses. Since unary operators also bind rather strongly, parentheses can be omitted in their cases.

#### Left and Right Associativity*

Mathematical commutativity and associativity apply to the operators <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>. In other words, operands can basically be rearranged without affecting the result. In division, you can additionally distinguish between left and right associativity , which is clearly illustrated by the example <samp class="listingcharacter">A / B / C</samp>. In this case, Java evaluates the expression from left to right, as <samp class="listingcharacter">(A / B) / C</samp>. Therefore, the division operator is left-associative. Parentheses are useful in this context because, if the compiler evaluates the expression to <samp class="listingcharacter">A / (B / C)</samp>, this evaluation would be equivalent to <samp class="listingcharacter">A * C / B</samp>. In Java, most operators are left-associative, with some exceptions, such as assignments of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">A = B = C</samp>, which the compiler evaluates to <samp class="listingcharacter">A = (B = C)</samp> .

###### [»]  Note

Mathematical associativity is of course endangered if calculation errors are involved due to overflows or non-representability. Consider, for example, the following code:

```
float a = -16777217F;
float b =  16777216F;
float c =  1F;
System.out.println( a + b + c );    // 1.0
System.out.println( a + (b + c) );  // 0.0
```

Mathematically, –16,777,217 + 16,777,216 equals –1, and –1 plus +1 equals 0\. In the second case, –16.777.217 + (16.777.216 + 1) = –16.777.217 + 16.777.217 = 0\. But Java evaluates <samp class="listingcharacter">a + b</samp> to 0 by constraining <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, and thus, for 0 plus <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> , the output is 1 instead of 0.

### 2.4.10     Typecasting (Casting )

Java is a statically typed language, but the language isn’t so strongly typed that it is obstructive. Thus, the compiler translates the following lines without any problem:

```
int  anInt = 1;
long long1 = 
                1;
long long2 = 
                anInt; 
```

Strictly speaking, a compiler could reject the last two lines if the typing is strong because the literal <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and not <samp class="listingcharacter">1L</samp> (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>). Furthermore, in <samp class="listingcharacter">long2 = anInt</samp>, the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">anInt</samp> is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> instead of the desired data type <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> .

#### Types of Casting

So, in practice, data types must be converted, which is referred to as typecasting (or casting for short). Java distinguishes between two types of typecasting:

*   Automatic (implicit) typecasting
    Data of a smaller data type is automatically (implicitly) matched to the larger one. The compiler makes this adjustment independently. For this reason, our first example works with something like <samp class="listingcharacter">long2 = anInt</samp> .

*   Explicit typecasting
    A larger type can be assigned to a smaller type, with possible loss of information.

Typecasting exists for primitive data types and for reference types. While the following paragraphs describe some adaptations for simple data types, [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6), [Section 6.1.4](#06_001.html_h6.1.4) , covers type compatibility for references.

#### Automatic Adjustment of the Size

Values of the <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> data types are automatically converted to the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> data type during arithmetic operations. If an operand is of data type <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, then all operands are extended to <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>. However, if <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> is required as the result, then you must specify this data type change with an explicit typecast. Only the least significant bits of the result value are passed. Java generally performs typecasting automatically.

| From Type | To Type |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> |

**Table 2.13**     Implicit Typecasting

[![Graphical Representation of Automatic Typecasting](bilderklein/klein02_005.png)](img-f2.5.html)

**Figure 2.5**     Graphical Representation of Automatic Typecasting

The adjustment is called a widening conversion because it automatically expands the range of values. The <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> type doesn’t appear in this list since it cannot be converted to any other primitive type.

###### [»]  Note

The fact that a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> can be converted to a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, which also applies to a conversion from <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> might be regarded as a bug in the Java language because information is lost during this shortening process. A <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> can’t use the 64 bits for integers as “efficiently” as a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> . Consider, for example, the following code:

```
System.out.println( Long.MAX_VALUE ); // 9223372036854775807
double d = Long.MAX_VALUE;
System.out.printf( "%.0f%n", d );     // 922337203685477
                        6000
System.out.println( (long) d );       // 922337203685477
                        5807
```

However, the implicit type conversion should be entirely without loss.

###### [»]  Note

Although in terms of data type size, a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> (16 bit) lies between <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> (8 bit) and <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> (32 bit), the type doesn’t appear anywhere in the right-hand column of [Table 2.13](#02_004.html_t2.13) because <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> can’t store a sign. The other data types ( <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> ) all have a sign. For this reason, the following code can’t work:

```
byte b = 'b';
char c = b;    // 

                         Type mismatch: cannot convert from byte to char
```

#### Explicit Typecasting

The explicit conversion narrows a type, so this operation is referred to as a narrowing conversion . The desired type for typecasting is placed in parentheses before the data type to be converted. You must be clear that information can be lost with any explicit typecasting.

###### [eg]  Example

When converting a float into an integer, the entire decimal part disappears, as in the following code:

```
int n = 
                        (int) 3.1415;                  // n = 3
```

Typecasting has a very high priority. Therefore, the expression may need to be parenthesized.

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, the assignment to <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> misses the mark:

```
int n = 
                        (int) 1.0315 + 2.1;
int m = (int)(1.0315 + 2.1);            // that is correct
```

[![If the Type of an Expression Doesn’t Fit, Press Ctrl+1](bilderklein/klein02_006.png)](img-f2.6.html)

**Figure 2.6**     If the Type of an Expression Doesn’t Fit, Press Ctrl+1

#### Typecasting from Floats to Integers

Explicit typecasting from <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> to an integer type can, of course, result in a loss of precision as well as a limitation of the value range. When converting floats, Java uses rounding to zero, so it simply truncates the decimal part.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example shows explicit typecasting from a float to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> :

```
System.out.println( (int) +12.34 );     //  12
System.out.println( (int) +67.89 );     //  67
System.out.println( (int) -12.34 );     // -12
System.out.println( (int) -67.89 );     // -67
int r = 
                        (int)(Math.random() * 5 );      // 0 <= r <= 4
```

#### Automatic Typecasting for Calculations with byte and short to int*

An operation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> type with <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> returns the result type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> .

```
int   int1  = 1, int2 = 2;
int   int3  = int1 + int2;
long  long1 = 1, long2 = 2;
long  long3 = long1 + long2; 
```

**Listing 2.13**     src/main/java/AutoConvert.java, main()

These lines will be compiled by the compiler as expected. And so, it seems intuitive that the same is true for the data types <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> . The following code still works:

```
short short1 = 1, short2 = 2;
byte  byte1  = 1, byte2  = 2; 
```

However, the following code does not:

```
short short3 = short1 + short2;  // 

// Type mismatch: cannot convert from int to short
byte  byte3 = byte1 + byte2;     // 

// Type mismatch: cannot convert from int to byte 
```

You cannot add two <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> numbers without explicit typecasting. The correct version of the code is the following:

```
 short short3 = 
                    (short)( short1 + short2 );

                    byte  byte3  = 
                    (byte)( byte1 + byte2 ); 
```

The reason for this limitation can be found in the Java compiler. When integer expressions of type less than <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> are bound to an operator, the compiler arbitrarily adjusts the type to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. The addition of the two numbers in the example thus doesn’t work with <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> values, but with <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> values; internally in the bytecode it is realized in the same way.

Consequently, all integer operations with <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> automatically lead to the result type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. And this leads to a problem with the assignment from the example because if the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> type is on the right-hand side and the smaller type <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> is on the left-hand side, the compiler must report an error. We can enforce this conversion using explicit typecasting.

We simply must accept that the compiler makes this adjustment. <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> remain <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>; <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> remain <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>. When an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> dances with a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, the result type becomes <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>. If the operator works on a <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>, the result is automatically <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> .

###### [+]   Tip

Small types like <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> often lead to problems. If not intentionally used in large arrays and memory space is not an absolute criterion, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> turns out to be the best choice because Java doesn’t excel in particularly intuitive type conversions. For example, consider what happens with the unary minus and plus signs in the following code:

```
byte b = 0;
b = -b;             // 

                         Cannot convert from int to byte
b = +b;             // 

                         Cannot convert from int to byte
```

The compiler reports an error because the expression on the right is converted to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> by the unary operator, which is always true for the types <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>. [[ 68 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_36)

#### No Typecasting between Simple Types and Reference Types

General conversions between simple types and reference types don’t exist. For example, the following statements are false.

```
String s = (String) 1;      // 

                     Cannot cast from int to String
int i = (int) “1”;          // 

                     Cannot cast from String to int 
```

**Listing 2.14**     src/main/java/TypecastPrimRef.java, main() (Snippet)

###### [»]  Trickery with Boxing*

Sometimes, things look like typecasting when actually a technique called autoboxing is being used. [Chapter 11](#11_001.html_h11), [Section 11.5](#11_005.html_h11.5) , goes into more detail, but for now, consider the following code:

```
Long lông = (Long) 2L;      // Alternative: Long lông = 2L;
System.out.println( (Boolean) true );
((Integer)2).toString();
```

**Listing 2.15**     src/main/java/TypecastPrimRef.java, main() (Snippet)

#### Typecasting Methods

In the case of explicit typecasting of integers, Java truncates the higher-order bytes. When converting from <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> (8 bytes) to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> (4 bytes), the upper 4 bytes are dropped. If these four upper bytes are <samp class="listingcharacter">0x00</samp>—we consider only the positive integers—then there’s no loss of information. If we want to convert from <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, but the loss of information should be reported, the static <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">int toIntExact(long value)</samp> can be used. With this method, an exception will be raised if the conversion entails data loss.

When converting floats to integers, the truncation of decimal places always occurs. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class has methods that can also round numbers, such as the two static <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> methods <samp class="listingcharacter">int round(float)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long round(double)</samp>. [Chapter 21](#21_001.html_h21), [Section 21.3.4](#21_003.html_h21.3.4), provides detailed information about the <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class.

#### Typecasting with the Compound Assignment Operator*

The compound assignment operator does a little more than resolve <samp class="listingcharacter">E1 #= E2</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">E1 = (E1) # (E2)</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp> represents a binary operator. Interestingly, the type of <samp class="listingcharacter">E1</samp> also comes into play because the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">E1 # E2</samp> is set to the data type of <samp class="listingcharacter">E1</samp> before the assignment, so the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">E1 #= E2</samp>, will become <samp class="listingcharacter">E1 = (</samp> type of E1 <samp class="listingcharacter">)((E1) # (E2))</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

The compound assignment operator is supposed to add an integer to a float, as in the following example:

```
int total = 1973;
total += 30.2;
```

The use of the compound assignment operator is fine because the interpreter carries out an implicit typecasting, so the meaning is <samp class="listingcharacter">total = (int)(total + 30.2)</samp> . So much for Java being an intuitive and simple programming language.

### 2.4.11    Overloaded Plus for Strings

Although in Java nearly all operators refer to primitive data types, the plus operator is also used in another area. This overloaded plus sign was introduced in Java because the concatenation of strings is often needed. Objects of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> type can be connected to other strings and data types by the plus operator. If contiguous parts do not all take the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> data type, they will automatically be converted to a string. The result type is always <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

Let’s put five pieces together to make a string:

```
String s = '"' + "Extreme Salt Liquorice" + '"' + " above the age of " + 18;
//         char  String                     char    String               int
System.out.println( s ); // "Extreme Salt Liquorice" above the age of 18 
```

String concatenation is strictly from left to right and is of course not commutative like numeric addition.

If an expression consists of several parts, the evaluation order must be observed; otherwise, unwanted compositions will occur. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">"The song: " + 90 + 9 + " Bottles of</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Beer"</samp> ends up with “The song: 909 Bottles of Beer” because the compiler starts the conversion to strings when it has recognized an expression as a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object. In other words, the compiler switches from “+ adds numbers” to “+ concatenates strings.”

Let’s look at the evaluation sequence of the plus operator with an example.

```
System.out.println( 1 + 2 );                     // 3
System.out.println( "1" + 2 + 3 );               // 123
System.out.println( 1 + 2 + "3" );               // 33
System.out.println( 1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5 );       // 3345
System.out.println( 1 + 2 + "3" + (4 + 5) );     // 339
System.out.println( 1 + 2 + "3" + (4 + 5) + 6 ); // 3396 
```

**Listing 2.16**     src/main/java/PlusString.java, main()

###### [»]  Note

The plus operator for strings proceeds strictly from left to right and sometimes causes problems with embedded arithmetic expressions. In this context, parenthesizing can help, as in the following example:

```
int quantity = 10;
String s = "You have " + (quantity == 12 ? "a dozen" : quantity);
System.out.println( s ); // You have 10
```

If the expression around the condition operator were not parenthesized, then the plus operator would append the 1 to the string, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> operator would occur. That operator, however, expects compatible data types, which aren’t given in our case as the string would be on the left and the integer 2 on the right.

#### char Character in Concatenation

Only a string in double quotes is a string, and only then does the plus operator unfold its special effect. Java converts a single character in single quotes to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> according to the rules of typecasting in calculations, and additions are integer additions.

```
System.out.println( '0' + 2 );     // 50, because the ASCII value of '0' is 48
System.out.println( 'A' + 'a' );   // 162, because 'A'=65, 'a'=97 
```

### 2.4.12    Operators Missing*

Some programming languages have a power operator (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">**</samp>), which doesn’t exist in Java. Since no pointer operations exist in Java, the operator characters known in C(++) for referencing ( <samp class="listingcharacter">&</samp>) and de-referencing ( <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp>) don’t exist. Likewise, a <samp class="listingcharacter">sizeof</samp> is unnecessary since the runtime system and the compiler always know the size of classes and the primitive data types always have a fixed length.

Script languages like Perl or Python not only offer simple data types; they also define lists or associative memories, for example. Operators are automatically associated, for example, to query the data structures for values or to insert elements. In addition, many scripting languages allow you to check strings against regular expressions, such as Perl with the <samp class="listingcharacter">=~</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">!~</samp> operators.

For testing references for identity, Java provides the <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> operator. Some programming languages additionally provide a <samp class="listingcharacter">===</samp> operator so that with one operator a test for equality and with the other a test for identity is possible. We’ll look at identity and the <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> operator in more detail in [Chapter 3](#03_001.html_h3), [Section 3.7.1](#03_007.html_h3.7.1) .

## 2.5    Conditional Statements or Case Distinctions

Control structures are used in a programming language to execute specific program parts under certain conditions. Java provides the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> statements as well as the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement for executing various parts of the program. Besides branching, loops are used to execute program parts multiple times. The significant part in the phrase “control structures” is the word “structure” because the structure should be obvious by just looking at it. Without loops and “high-level” control structures, only if/thens and jumps, the logic of the program was not obvious, and the result was called spaghetti code. Although a general jump via <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> isn’t possible in Java, the language still has a special jump variant. In loops, <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> allow defined jump destinations.

### 2.5.1    Branching with the if Statement

The <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement consists of the keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>, which is necessarily followed by an expression of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> in parentheses. This expression is followed by a statement, which is often a block statement.

For example, let’s use an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement to test if a user has guessed a random number correctly:

```
public class WhatsYourNumber {

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    int number = (int) (Math.random() * 5 + 1);

    System.out.println( "What number do I have in mind between 1 and 5?" );
    int guess = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextInt();

                if ( number == guess ) {
      System.out.println( "Good guess!" );
    }

                    System.out.println( "Restart the program and guess again!" );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.17**     src/main/java/WhatsYourNumber.java

The processing of the output statement depends on the expression in <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> , in the following ways:

*   If the result of the expression is true ( <samp class="listingcharacter">number == guess</samp> evaluates to <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>), the following statement (i.e., the console output with <samp class="listingcharacter">"Good guess!"</samp> ) is executed.

*   If the result of the expression is false ( <samp class="listingcharacter">number == guess</samp> evaluates to <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>), the statement is skipped, and the program continues with the first statement after the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement.

###### [»]  Comparison of Programming Languages

In Java, the test expression for the condition of the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement must always be of the <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> type. The same applies to loop conditions. Other programming languages such as JavaScript, C(++), or PHP evaluate a numeric expression to true if the result of the expression is not 0\. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">if (10)</samp> is also valid in those languages, which would correspond to <samp class="listingcharacter">if (true)</samp> in Java. In PHP or JavaScript, an empty string or array is also “falsy.”

#### if Queries and Blocks

After the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> and the condition, the compiler expects a statement. A <samp class="listingcharacter">{}</samp> block is a special statement, as in our example. If only one statement is to be executed depending on the condition, the statement can be set directly without a block. The following variants are therefore identical:

| Explicit Parenthesizing of the Statement | Without Parenthesizing the Statement |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">if ( number == guess ) {</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println( "Super!" );</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">if ( number == guess )</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println( "Super!" );</samp> |

A program error occurs when the <samp class="listingcharacter">{}</samp> block is missing, but several statements still need to be evaluated depending on the condition. Let’s look at an example: An <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement is supposed to test whether the guessed number was equal to the random number, and then if it was, assign a new random number to the <samp class="listingcharacter">number</samp> variable and return an output. First, let’s consider the semantically incorrect variant:

```
if ( number == guess )
  number = (int)(Math.random()*5 + 1); System.out.println( "Good guess!" ); 
```

The implementation is semantically incorrect since the output always appears regardless of the test. The compiler assigns only the next statement to the case distinction, even if the appearance suggests otherwise. [[ 69 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_37) This is a great risk for programmers who want to visually create relationships that don’t exist in reality. The compiler interprets the statements in the following context, where the indentation reflects the actual execution:

```
if ( number == guess )
  number = (int) (Math.random() * 5 + 1);
System.out.println( "Good guess!" ); 
```

For our desired logic of executing both statements together depending on the condition, you’ll need to use a block, as in the following example:

```
if ( number == guess ) 
                    {
  number = (int) (Math.random() * 5 + 1);
  System.out.println( "Good guess!" );

                    } 
```

Basically, putting statements in blocks—even if there is only one statement in the block—is therefore not wrong.

###### [+]  Tip

Indentations don’t change the semantics of the program! Indentations can only severely disrupt comprehension. For the program to be correct, you must use a block and put the statements together. Developers should consistently use indentation to clarify dependencies, and furthermore, only one statement should exist in a line.

#### Compound Conditions

The previous queries were quite simple, but much more complex conditions will occur in practice. Commonly used logical operators include <samp class="listingcharacter">&&</samp> (AND), <samp class="listingcharacter">||</samp> (OR), and <samp class="listingcharacter">!</samp> (NOT).

For example, to test whether

*   a guessed number is either equal to the random number <samp class="listingcharacter">guess</samp> OR

*   a certain number of trials has already been exceeded ( <samp class="listingcharacter">trials</samp> greater than 10),

then we would write the compound condition in the following way:

```
if ( number == guess || trials > 10 ) 
```

If the logically linked expressions are more complex, the individual conditions should be placed in parentheses to support readability since not everyone immediately has access to the precedence rules for the operators found in Table 2.11.

### 2.5.2     Choosing the Alternative with an if-else Statement

If the condition is met, the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> branch is run through. But how can it be programmed that, in the reverse case (i.e., if the condition isn’t true), program code is also executed?

One solution is to write a second <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement with a negated condition:

```
if ( 
                number == guess )
  System.out.println( "Good guess!" );
if ( 
                number != guess )
  System.out.printf( "Well, not true, I thought %s!", number ); 
```

However, a better solution is available: In addition to the one-sided alternative, a two-sided approach can be used. The optional keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> with the appended statement causes the alternative to be executed if the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> test is false.

If the user in our little game doesn’t guess the number correctly, we want to output the random number to the user.

```
public class GuessTheNumber {

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    int number = (int) (Math.random() * 5 + 1);

    System.out.println( "What number do I have in mind between 1 and 5?" );
    int guess = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextInt();

                if ( number == guess )
      System.out.println( "Good guess!" );

                else
      System.out.printf( "Well, not true, I thought %d!", number );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.18**     src/main/java/GuessTheNumber.java

If the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">number == guess</samp> is true, the first statement is executed; otherwise, the second statement is executed. In this way, you can assure that a statement will be executed in every case.

#### The Dangling else Problem

For branches with <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp>, a well-known problem is called the dangling-else problem. Which statement does the <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> belong to?

```
if ( 
                    expression1 )
  if ( 
                    expression2 )

                    statement1;

                    else

                    statement2; 
```

The indentation suggests that <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> is the alternative to the first <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement, which is, however, incorrect. The semantics of Java (and also almost all other programming languages) is defined in such a way that <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> belongs to the innermost <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>. Therefore, the only programming tip for this case is to parenthesize the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statements:

```
if ( 
                    expression1 ) {
  if ( 
                    expression2 ) {

                    statement1;
  }
}
else {

                    statement2;
} 
```

These parentheses prevent confusion from arising in the first place. If <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> always belongs to the innermost <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> but this is not what you want, use curly brackets as shown earlier or add an empty statement in the <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> branch:

```
if ( x >= 0 )
  if ( x != 0 )
    System.out.println( "x really greater than zero" );
  else
    ; // x is equal to zero
else
  System.out.println( "x really less than zero" ); 
```

[![Pressing Ctrl+Space after the if Allows You to Create an if Statement with a Block](bilderklein/klein02_007.png)](img-f2.7.html)

**Figure 2.7**     Pressing Ctrl+Space after the if Allows You to Create an if Statement with a Block

#### The Evil Semicolon

At this point, note that a novice programmer will probably write a semicolon after the closing parenthesis of the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement. However, doing so results in a completely different execution sequence. Consider the following example:

```
 int age = 29;
if ( age < 0 ) ;              // 

                     logical error
  System.out.println( "Alright, still in the womb" );
if ( age > 150 ) ;            // 

                     logical error
  System.out.println( "I see, a new Moses" ); 
```

The semicolon causes the empty statement to be executed depending on the condition and always produces the output “Alright, still in the womb” and “I see, a new Moses” regardless of the content of the <samp class="listingcharacter">age</samp> variable. This result is certainly not our intention. The example should be regarded as a caution against writing only more than one statement in each line; the empty statement with the semicolon is a statement in itself.

If an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement is followed by two statements that aren’t combined by a block statement, then the one following <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> statement is reported as an error because the associated <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> branch is missing because the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> branch ends after the first statement without <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> . Consider the following example:

```
int age = 29;
if ( age < 0 )
  ;
System.out.println( "Alright, still in the womb" );
else if ( age > 150 ) ;       // 

                     Compiler error message: 'else' without 'if'
  System.out.println( "I see, a new Moses" ); 
```

#### Multiple Branching or Nested Alternatives

<samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statements for program guidance occur quite often in programs, even more often than for checking a variable for a certain value. For this purpose, <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> statements are often nested (cascaded). If a variable matches a value, then a statement is executed; otherwise, the variable is tested with a different value, and so on.

###### [eg]  Example

Cascaded <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statements help you assign, for example, a <samp class="listingcharacter">days</samp> variable matching the month (preassigned <samp class="listingcharacter">month</samp> variable) and the information if the year is a leap year (preassigned <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> variable <samp class="listingcharacter">isLeapYear</samp> ):

```
int month = 2; boolean isLeapYear = false; int days;
if ( month == 4 )
  days = 30;
else if ( month == 6 )
  days = 30;
else if ( month == 9 )
  days = 30;
else if ( month == 11 )
  days = 30;

                        else if ( month == 2 )
  if ( isLeapYear )      // Special treatment in case of leap year
    days = 29;
  else
    days = 28;
else
  days = 31;
```

In this small program, semantic indentations are used; actually, the statements would move further and further to the right with each <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> .

The indented branches are also called accumulated if statements (or an if cascade ) because each <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> statement in turn contains other <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statements until all queries have been made.

Let’s apply this principle to our number guessing game. Perhaps, we want to give the user a hint whether the entered number was smaller or larger than the target number.

```
public class GuessTheNumber2 {

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    int number = (int) (Math.random() * 5 + 1);

    System.out.println( "What number do I have in mind between 1 and 5?" );
    int guess = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextInt();

    if ( number == guess )
      System.out.println( "Good guess!" );

                    else if ( number > guess )
      System.out.println( "Nope, my number is larger than yours!" );
    else // number < guess
      System.out.println( "Nope, my number is smaller than yours!" );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.19**     src/main/java/GuessTheNumber2.java

### 2.5.3    The Condition Operator

In Java, a single operator can use three operands, called the conditional operator . This operator allows you to make the value of an expression dependent on a condition without the use of an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement. Operands are separated by <samp class="listingcharacter">?</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp> and use the following syntax:

```
 Condition 
                ? 
                Expression if condition is true 
                : 
                Expression if condition is false 
```

###### [eg]   Example

Determining the maximum is a good way to illustrate the use of the condition operator:

```
max = ( a > b ) 
                    ? a 
                    : b;
```

The value of the <samp class="listingcharacter">max</samp> variable is set depending on the condition <samp class="listingcharacter">a > b</samp>. The expression corresponds to the following <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement:

```
if ( a > b ) max = a; else max = b;
```

Three expressions occur in the conditional operator, which makes it a ternary operator —from the Latin ternarius (“consisting of three”). [[ 70 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_38) The first expression (in our case, the comparison <samp class="listingcharacter">a > b</samp>) must be of the <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> type. If the condition is met, then the variable is assigned the value of the second expression; otherwise, the <samp class="listingcharacter">max</samp> variable will be assigned the value of the third expression.

The condition operator can be used if the second and third operands are of a numeric type, Boolean type, or reference type. Calling methods that return <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp> isn’t allowed. So, it’s not a compact syntax to simply call any two methods depending on a condition without <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> because there’s always a result with the condition operator. We can do all sorts of things with it, such as outputting it directly.

###### [eg]  Example

To output the maximum of <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> directly, you would use the following code:

```
System.out.println( ( a > b ) ? a : b );
```

With <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp>, this case is only possible with temporary variables or with two <samp class="listingcharacter">println(...)</samp> statements.

#### Examples

*   The maximum or minimum of two numbers is given by the expressions <samp class="listingcharacter">a > b ? a : b</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">a < b ? a : b</samp> , respectively.

*   The absolute value of a number returns <samp class="listingcharacter">x >= 0 ? x : -x</samp>. [[ 71 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_39)

*   An expression is supposed to convert a number <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp>, which lies between 0 and 15, into a hexadecimal number: <samp class="listingcharacter">(char)((n < 10) ? ('0' + n) : ('a'</samp> – <samp class="listingcharacter">10 + n ))</samp> .

#### Nested Application of the Condition Operator*

Using the condition operator can quickly lead to unreadable programs, and therefore, you should use it with care. [[ 72 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_40) You must use sufficient parenthesizing to make sure that the expressions are also evaluated in the intended order. Unlike most operators, the condition operator is right-associative (the assignment is also right-associative).

The following two expressions are therefore equivalent:

```
b1 ? a1 : b2 ? a2 : a3
b1 ? a1 : ( b2 ? a2 : a3 ) 
```

###### [eg]  Example

To write an expression that returns –1, 0, or 1 for a number <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> depending on the sign, you can use a nested condition operator, for example, in the following code:

```
int sign = 
                        (n < 0) ? -
                        1 : 
                        (n > 0) ? 1 : 0;
```

However, line breaks after the colons make sense and clarify the nested conditional expressions:

```
int sign = (n < 0) ? -1 :
           (n > 0) ? 1 :
            0;
```

#### The Condition Operator Is Not an L-Value*

The condition operator returns an expression as a result, which can be then used on the right side of an assignment. Since the resulting expression occurs on the right, it’s called the R-Value. It can’t be used on the left-hand side of an assignment (L-Value) in such a way that it selects a variable to which a value is assigned. [[ 73 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_41)

###### [eg]  Example

The following application of the condition operator isn’t possible in Java:

```
boolean up = false, down = false;
int direction = 12;
((direction >= 0) ? up : down) = true; // 

                         Compiler error
```

However, the condition operator can select a reference, and then a method call is valid.

### 2.5.4     The Switch Statement Provides an Alternative

A shorthand form for specially constructed, accumulated <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statements is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp>. In a <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> block, a number of different jump targets are each marked with <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement allows the selection of the following elements:

*   Integers

*   Wrapper types (for more information, refer to [Chapter 11](#11_001.html_h11), [Section 11.5](#11_005.html_h11.5) )

*   Enumerations ( <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp> )

*   Strings

###### [»]  Internal Affairs

The bytecode contains only one <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> variant for integers. For strings, enumerations, and wrapper objects, the compiler applies tricks to reduce them to integer-based <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> constructions.

#### switch for Integers (and Also chars)

A simple calculator for four binary operators can be quickly implemented with <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp>. We’ll use the <samp class="listingcharacter">charAt(0)</samp> method to access the first character from a string input to get a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> .

```
public class Calculator {

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    double x = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextDouble();
    char operator = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextLine().charAt( 0 );
    double y = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextDouble();

                    switch ( operator ) {
      case '+':
        System.out.println( x + y );
        break;
      case '-':
        System.out.println( x - y );
        break;
      case '*':
        System.out.println( x * y );
        break;
      case '/':
        System.out.println( x / y );
        break;
    }

                      }
} 
```

**Listing 2.20**     src/main/java/Calculator.java

The runtime environment searches for a jump label (also called a jump target ), which is a constant that matches the expression specified in <samp class="listingcharacter">switch.</samp> If a hit is made, all statements following <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> are executed until an (optional) <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> terminates the execution. (Without <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>, the execution continues automatically in the next <samp class="listingcharacter">case block</samp>; more on this topic later in this section, when we discuss fall-through without a break.) If no constant of a <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> block matches the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> expression, no statements in the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> block will be executed for the time being. The <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> constants must be different; otherwise, a compiler error will arise.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement has some limitations, such as the following:

*   The JVM can execute <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> only on expressions of the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> data type. Elements of data type <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> are thus allowed since the compiler automatically adjusts the type to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. Likewise, the enumerations and the wrapper objects <samp class="listingcharacter">Character</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> are possible since Java automatically takes the values. More on this topic will follow in [Chapter 11](#11_001.html_h11), [Section 11.5](#11_005.html_h11.5). The data types <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> can’t be used. Although enumerations and strings are also possible as <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> expression types, internally, they are mapped to integers. Apart from that, general objects aren’t allowed.

*   The values listed after <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> must be constant. Dynamic expressions, such as returns from method calls, aren’t possible.

*   No range specifications are possible, which would be useful for ages, for example, to define the ranges 0-18, 19-60, 61-99\. The only solution in this context would be accumulated <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statements.

###### [»]  Note

The specification for <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> must be constant but may well come from a constant (final variable):

```
final char 
                        PLUS = '+';
switch ( operator ) {
   case 
                        PLUS:
   …
}
```

#### Covering Everything Else with default

If a program part should be processed only when no match with any other <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> constant is made, you can use the special jump label <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> . For example, in the case of an unknown operator, if your program should output an error message, you would write the following code:

```
switch ( operator ) {
  case '+':
    System.out.println( x + y );
    break;
  case '-':
    System.out.println( x - y );
    break;
  case '*':
    System.out.println( x * y );
    break;
  case '/':
    System.out.println( x / y );
    break;

                    default:
    System.err.println( "Unknown operator " + operator );
} 
```

The use of <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> is to detect incorrectly entered operators because the statements after <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> are always executed if no <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> constant was equal to the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> expression. <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> can also appear between the <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> blocks, but this is less clear and thus not recommended for general applications. Thus, the <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> program part would be processed even if a <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> part preceding the <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> has no <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>. Only one <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> is allowed.

###### [»]  Note

Of course, the compiler can’t know whether all the values you use are covered by a <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> block. A <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> can help to find errors faster if a number arrives at <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> for which the program doesn’t store any operations. If you don’t use <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> , an unhandled value will otherwise remain without consequences.

With enumerations, the situation is different again because, in this case, the quantity is countable. Code analysis can determine if as many <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> blocks exist as constants. IntelliJ, for example, can report on this metric.

#### switch Has Fall-Through without a Break

Up to now, we’ve put a <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> statement in the last line. Without a <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>, all subsequent statements would be executed after a match. They would thus run into a new section until a <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> or the end of <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> has been reached. This scenario is comparable to a toy ball falling through from top to bottom and this thus referred to as fall-through . A com mon programming error is to forget the <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> , which is why an intended fall-through should always be specified as a comment.

This fall-through enables you to always execute the same instruction for different values. The following example implements a small parser for simple date values. The parser should handle three different dates, for example:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">"18 12"</samp> : Year in short form and month

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">"2018 12"</samp> : Year and month

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">"12"</samp> : Month only (The current year should be applied implicitly.)

```
public class SimpleYearMonthParser {

  public static void main( String[] args ) {

    String date = "17 12";

    int month = 0, year = 0;
    java.util.Scanner scanner = new java.util.Scanner( date );

    switch ( date.length() ) {

                    case 5:  // YY MM
        year = 2000;
        // Fall-through

                    case 7: // YYYY MM
        year += scanner.nextInt();
        // Fall-through

                    case 2: // MM
        month = scanner.nextInt();
        if ( year == 0 )
          year = java.time.Year.now().getValue();
        break;
      default : 
        System.err.println( "Wrong format" );
    }

    System.out.println( "month=" + month + ", year=" + year );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.21**     src/main/java/SimpleYearMonthParser.java

In this example, a <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> statement determines the structure via the length. If the length is 5, the year is shortened, and we initialize the year with <samp class="listingcharacter">2000</samp> to read the year in the following step with the help of the <samp class="listingcharacter">scanner</samp>. We also would come to this step directly if the length of the input had been 7 (i.e., if the year had been 4 digits long). This section of code clarifies the year portion, but we still need to parse the months. If we come directly over a string of length 2, and no year is set before, we’ll retrieve the current year via <samp class="listingcharacter">java.time.Year.now().getValue()</samp> ; otherwise, we won’t overwrite the variable.

What should the reader take away from this example? Actually, nothing but shake your head because the solution is hard to understand. Fall-through is really only useful for summarizing multiple <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> blocks.

###### [»]  Language Comparison*

Although a missing <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> can lead to annoying programming errors, the developers of Java adopted this behavior from its syntactic predecessor, C. An interesting alternative solution would be to turn the behavior around exactly and explicitly require the fall-through, for example, with a keyword. An interesting development in this regard is available: Java inherits this property from C(++), and C(++) in turn inherits fall-through from the programming language B. One of the “inventors” of B is Ken Thompson, who now works at Google and is involved in the new programming language Go. In Go, developers must explicitly use a <samp class="listingcharacter">fallthrough</samp> statement when forwarding one <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> block to the next. The same applies to the new Swift programming language; in this case, too, you can find <samp class="listingcharacter">fallthrough</samp> statements. Even in C++, since the C++17 standard, the standard <samp class="listingcharacter">[[fallthrough]]</samp> attribute [[ 74 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_42) instructs a compiler not to display a warning if fall-through occurs.

#### Stack Case Labels

If several <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> blocks are placed one below the other to map areas, we call them stack case labels . Let’s say a variable <samp class="listingcharacter">hour</samp> stands for an hour in the day, and we want to determine if it’s now afternoon rest time, evening rest time, or working time. Consider the following example:

```
int hour = 12;

switch ( hour ) {
  // Night rest from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.

                    case 10:
  case 11:
  case 12: case 0:
  case 1: 
  case 2: 
  case 3: 
  case 4:
  case 5: 

                        System.out.println( "Night rest" );
    break;

  // Afternoon rest from 1 to 3 p.m.

                    case 1:
  case 2: 
    System.out.println( "Afternoon rest" );
    break;

  default :
    System.out.println( "Work" );
    break;
} 
```

**Listing 2.22**     src/main/java/RestOrWork.java (Snippet)

<samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> blocks can be summarized even more compactly and separated with commas. For instance, the example can be rewritten in the following way:

```
int hour = 12;
switch ( hour ) {
  // Night rest from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.
  case 10, 11, 12, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5:
    System.out.println( "Night rest" );
    break;

  // Afternoon rest from 1 to 3 p.m.
  case 1, 2:
    System.out.println( "Afternoon rest" );
    break;

  default:
    System.out.println( "Work" );
    break;
} 
```

Single or multiple range specifications, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">22 - 24</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">22 - 24, 0 - 5</samp> , are not permitted in Java!

#### switch on Strings

Besides the option to use <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> on integers, a <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement on <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> objects is also possible.

```
 String input = javax.swing.JOptionPane.showInputDialog( "Input" );

switch ( input.toLowerCase() ) {
  case "cookies":
    System.out.println( "I like cookies." );
    break;
  case "cake":
    System.out.println( "I like cake." );
    break;
  case "chocolate":
  case "liquorice":
    System.out.println( "Hm. Yummy too." );
    break;
  default:
    System.out.printf( "Can you really eat %s?", input );
    break;
} 
```

**Listing 2.23**     src/main/java/SweetsLover.java, main()

Although direct string comparisons are possible, regular expression checks unfortunately aren’t, something that’s provided in particular by scripting languages like Ruby or Perl.

As with <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> with integers, the strings in the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> branch can come from final variables. For example, if <samp class="listingcharacter">string COOKIES = "cookies";</samp> is predefined, <samp class="listingcharacter">case COOKIES</samp> is allowed.

### 2.5.5    Switch Expressions

The <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> keyword can be used in Java for statements and expressions. In total, <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> can appear in four forms.

| Statement/Expression | Java Version | Syntax | Fall-Through | Complete Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Statement | 1.0 | <samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp> | Yes | No |
| Statement | 14 | <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp> | No | No |
| Expression | 14 | <samp class="listingcharacter">:</samp> | Yes | Yes |
| Expression | 14 | <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp> | No | Yes |

**Table 2.14**     Four Types of Switch

We’ve already looked at the first type extensively, so let’s look at the other variants now.

#### Simplified switch Statement, No Fall-Through, No Full Coverage

In the simplified <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement, no colon exists after the label or <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp>, but instead, you would use a <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp>. This use of <samp class="listingcharacter">-></samp> has nothing to do with lambda expressions, even if the symbols are the same. The arrow is either followed by an expression, a block in curly brackets, or a <samp class="listingcharacter">throw</samp> statement that throws an exception. Implicitly, a <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> terminates each branch, so no more fall-through occurs.

###### [eg]  Example

A variable <samp class="listingcharacter">operator</samp> is assigned with an operator character. A <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement with arrow notation is to give an output for <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> .

```
String operator = "+";
switch ( operator ) {
  case "+" -> System.out.println( "Plus" );
  case "-" -> { String minus = "Minus"; System.out.println( minus ); }
}
```

Because blocks must always be set for multiple statements, a local variable also doesn’t step out of scope. A <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> can be set but isn’t mandatory. The <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> doesn’t need to cover every possibility, which doesn’t work for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> -numbers and strings anyway.

###### [eg]  Example

A variable <samp class="listingcharacter">operator</samp> is assigned with an operator character. A <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement with arrow notation should always provide an output.

```
String operator = "+";
switch ( operator ) {
  case "+" -> System.out.println( "Plus" );
  case "-" -> System.out.println( "Minus" );
  default  -> System.out.println( "Unknown operator" );
}
```

With simplified <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statements, multiple labels that have the same handling are possible. Commas separate the labels.

###### [eg]  Example

The operators <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">×</samp> are treated in the same way:

```
String operator = "+";
switch ( operator ) {
  case "+"      -> System.out.println( "Plus" );

                        case "*", "×" -> System.out.println( "Multiplied by" );
}
```

#### Switch Expressions, No Fall-Through, Full Coverage

Traditionally, case distinctions are found with <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> as a statement, and statements return nothing.

###### [eg]  Example

A string <samp class="listingcharacter">writtenOperator</samp> will be initialized directly with an expression determined by the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> expression.

```
String operator = "+";
String writtenOperator = (switch ( operator ) {
  case "+" -> "Plus";
  case "-" -> "Minus";
  default  -> "Unknown operator";
} ).toUpperCase();
System.out.println( writtenOperator );
```

Expressions must always return results, and consequently, <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> must always make a path to a value. The usual case is <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> as shown, but in some special cases (e.g., with enumerations), the compiler can check that all possibilities have been covered.

###### [eg]  Example

In the case of enumerations, such as the days of the week in the <samp class="listingcharacter">DayOfWeek enum</samp> , the compiler can check for complete coverage:

```
DayOfWeek today = LocalDate.now().getDayOfWeek();
System.out.println( switch ( today ) {
  case MONDAY, TUESDAY, WEDNESDAY, THURSDAY, FRIDAY -> "Work";
  case SATURDAY, SUNDAY -> "Party";
} );
```

If no simple expression exists to the right of the arrow, but instead you write a block, this block must also return a result. For this purpose, the new keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">yield</samp> is used, followed by an expression. A block must have a <samp class="listingcharacter">yield</samp> or throw an unchecked exception.

###### [eg]  Example

In a block, <samp class="listingcharacter">yield</samp> returns an expression for the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> expression:

```
String operator = "+";
System.out.println( switch ( operator ) {
  case "+" -> "Plus";
  case "-" -> { String minus = "Minus"; 
                        yield minus; }
  default  -> throw new IllegalArgumentException( "Unknown operator" );
} );
```

#### Switch Expression with the Colon Syntax, with Fall-Through, Full Coverage

The colon syntax can also be used as an expression. With a colon, fall-through is also possible again. A <samp class="listingcharacter">yield</samp> is mandatory; otherwise, an unchecked exception must be triggered. The syntax contains a source of error with fall-through, so this variant is perhaps the worst.

###### [eg]  Example

Traditional colon <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> syntax as an expression with <samp class="listingcharacter">yield</samp> .

```
String operator = "+";
System.out.println( switch ( operator ) {
  case "+" : yield "Plus";
  case "*" : System.out.println( "Asterisk" );
  case "×" : yield "Multiplied by";
  default  : throw new IllegalArgumentException( "Unknown operator" );
} );
```

## 2.6    Always the Same with Loops

Loops are used to process certain statements over and over again. A loop includes a loop condition and the loop’s body. The loop condition, a Boolean expression, decides under which condition the repetition is executed. Depending on the loop condition, the body can be executed several times. For this purpose, the loop condition is checked in each loop pass. The result decides whether the body is traversed another time ( <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>) or the loop is terminated ( <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> ). Java provides four types of loops.

| Loop Type | Syntax |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop | <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">(</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">condition</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">statement</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop | <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">statement</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">(</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">condition</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">);</samp> |
| Simple <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop | <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">(</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">initialization</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">condition</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">for-statement</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">  statement</samp> |
| extended <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop (also referred to as for-each loop ) | <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">(</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">variable type</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">variable :</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">collection</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">  statement</samp> |

**Table 2.15**     Four Loop Types in Java

The first three types of loops will be described in the following sections, while the extended <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop is necessary only for collections and therefore is described later in the context of arrays (see [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.2](#04_002.html_h4.2)) and dynamic data structures (see [Chapter 18](#18_001.html_h18), [Section 18.1.6](#18_001.html_h18.1.6) ).

### 2.6.1     The while Loop

The <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop is a rejecting loop that checks the loop condition before each loop entry. If a condition is true, the program executes the body; otherwise, it terminates the loop. As with <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp>, the type of the condition for <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loops must be <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp>. [[ 75 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_43)

Before each loop pass, the expression is re-evaluated, and if the result is <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>, the body will be executed. The loop is finished when the result is <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> . If the condition isn’t true even before the first entry into the body, the body won’t be traversed at all.

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, an integer should be divided by 2 until the division results in 0:

```
int number = 1234;
while ( number > 0 ) {
  number /= 2;
  System.out.println( number );
}
```

**Listing 2.24**     src/main/java/WhileLoop.java, main()

###### [»]  Note

If everything interesting is performed within the loop header, a statement must still follow. This scenario is the appropriate use of the empty statement <samp class="listingcharacter">;</samp> or the empty block <samp class="listingcharacter">{}</samp> .

```
while ( Files.notExists( Paths.get( "dump.bin" ) ) )
  ;
```

If the file doesn’t exist, <samp class="listingcharacter">notExists(...)</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>, the loop continues and is immediately followed by a new existence test. If the file exists, the return is <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> , which initiates the end of the loop. A quick tip at this point: Instead of going directly to the next file test, you should implement a short delay.

#### Endless Loops

If the condition of a <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop is always true, then the loop is endless. As a consequence, the loop is repeated endlessly, as in the following example:

```
public class WhileTrue {
  public static void main( String[] args ) {

                    while ( true ) {

                              // over and over again
    }
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.25**     src/main/java/WhileTrue.java

Endless loops usually mean the end for a program. But help is available! You can escape from this endless loop with <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>, which we’ll describe in more detail in [Section 2.6.5](#02_006.html_h2.6.5).
