Strictly speaking, however, uncaught exceptions or <samp class="listingcharacter">System.exit(int)</samp> also terminate a program.

[![Console View with the Red Button for Terminating Programs](bilderklein/klein02_008.png)](img-f2.8.html)

**Figure 2.8**     Console View with the Red Button for Terminating Programs

[![In the Development Environment, Programs Can Be Terminated from the Outside. IntelliJ Provides a Square Red Button to Terminate Any Running Program after Activation.](bilderklein/klein02_009.png)](img-f2.9.html)

**Figure 2.9**     In the Development Environment, Programs Can Be Terminated from the Outside. IntelliJ Provides a Square Red Button to Terminate Any Running Program after Activation.

###### [»]  Fun

If a variable is decremented in a loop, the special “operator” <samp class="listingcharacter">--></samp> can be used. For example, if the numbers from 12 to 1 are to be listed, this “goes-down-to operator” can be used:

```
int month = 12;
while ( month  -->  0 )
  System.out.println( month + 1 );
```

What’s behind this? [[ 76 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_44)

### 2.6.2     The do-while Loop

This loop type is an assuming loop because <samp class="listingcharacter">do-while</samp> doesn’t check the loop condition until after each loop pass. Before it comes to the first test, the body has already been run through once. The loop type helps perfectly with our number guessing game because there is at least one pass with an input, and only if the user enters a wrong number should the body be traversed again.

```
public class TheFinalGuess {

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    int number = (int) (Math.random() * 5 + 1);
    int guess;

                do {
      System.out.println( "What number do I have in mind between 1 and 5?" );
      guess = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextInt();

      if ( number == guess )
        System.out.println( "Good guess!" );
      else if ( number > guess )
        System.out.println( "Nope, my number is larger than yours!" );
      else // number < guess
        System.out.println( "Nope, my number is smaller than yours!" );

                }
    while ( number != guess );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.26**     src/main/java/TheFinalGuess.java

Make sure you pay attention to the semicolon after the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> statement. If the condition returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>, the body will be executed again. [[ 77 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_45) Otherwise, the loop is terminated, and the program continues with the next statement after the loop. One interesting detail is that you now must declare the <samp class="listingcharacter">guess</samp> variable outside the <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> block because a variable declared in the loop block isn’t visible to the retest in <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp>. Also, the compiler knows that the <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> block is run at least once, and <samp class="listingcharacter">guess</samp> will be initialized in any case; accessing uninitialized variables is forbidden and considered an error by the compiler.

#### Equivalence of a while and a do-while loop*

The <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop is used less often than the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop. Nevertheless, the two can be merged. Let’s look at the first case by replacing a <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop with a <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop, as in the following syntax:

```
while ( 
                    expression )

                    Statement 
```

Let’s look at what’s happening: Depending on the <samp class="listingcharacter">expression</samp>, the body will be executed. Since a test comes first, the <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop would already be one block execution further. Thus, in a first step, you’ll query whether the condition is true or not via an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement. If yes, then the program code will run in a <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop. The equivalent <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop uses the following syntax:

```
if ( 
                    expression )
  do

                    Statement
  while ( 
                    expression ) ; 
```

Let’s consider the second case by replacing the <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop with a <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop, as in the following syntax:

```
do

                    Statement
while ( 
                    expression ) ; 
```

Since the statements are executed first and then the test, for the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> variant, you’ll simply write the expressions before the test. In this way, you can ensure that they are processed at least once:

```
 Statement
while ( 
                    expression )

                    Statement 
```

### 2.6.3    The for Loop

The <samp class="listingcharacter">for loop</samp> is a special variant of a <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop and is typically used for counting. Just like <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loops, <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops are dismissive: The body won’t be executed until the condition is true.

###### [eg]  Example

You can output the numbers from 1 to 10 on the screen.

```
for ( int i = 1; i <= 10; i++ )            // i is loop counter
  System.out.println( i );
```

**Listing 2.27**     src/main/java/ForLoop.java, main()

A closer look at the loop shows various segments:

*   Initialization of the loop
    The first part of the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop is an expression like <samp class="listingcharacter">i = 1</samp>, which is executed exactly once before the loop is executed. The expression initializes the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp>, but the result then is discarded. If an error occurs in the evaluation, the processing is interrupted, and the loop can’t be executed completely. The first part can declare and initialize local variables. This count variable is then no longer valid outside of the block. [[ 78 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_46) No local variable should share the same name. The first part can also be empty.

*   Loop test/loop condition
    The middle part, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">i <= 10</samp>, is tested before passing through the loop body (i.e., before each loop entry). If the expression returns <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>, the loop won’t be executed, or it won’t be executed again and will be terminated instead. The result must be of type <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp>, as in a <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop. The middle test part can be missing in the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop, which makes it like an implicit <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> .

*   Loop increment through a for-statement
    The last part, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">i++</samp>, is always executed at the end of each loop pass, but before the next loop entry. The result isn’t used any further. If the condition of the test returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> , then the next time the body is entered, the changed value is in the body. The last part may also be missing.

Looking at our earlier example, the following evaluation sequence is performed:

1.  Initialize <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> with 1.

2.  Test whether <samp class="listingcharacter">i <= 10</samp> is true.

3.  If the result is <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> , then execute the block; otherwise, the end of the loop has been reached.

4.  Increase <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> by 1.

5.  Go to step 2.

#### Loop Counter

If the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop is used to run through a variable, the loop counter is called either a count variable or run variable .

The initialization and the correct query at the end are important. The loop can run through once too often, leading to incorrect results. This kind of error in a query is also called an off-by-one error . For example, if instead of <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp> you use the operator <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, then the loop runs only to 9\. Another name for the loop error is fencepost-error . Consider the number of posts needed for a 100-meter fence so that all posts are spaced apart by 10 meters: Do you need 9, 10, or 11 fence posts?

#### When to Use a for and When to Use a while Loop?

Since the <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops are similar, you may wonder when to use one over the other. Unfortunately, the compact <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop can tempt you to overload. Some programmers like to pack everything into the loop head, and the body is just an empty statement. This bad style should be avoided.

<samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops should be used whenever a variable is increased by a constant amount. If no loop variable occurs in the loop that’s incremented or decremented, a <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop should be used. A <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop should be used if the termination condition can’t be evaluated until the end of a loop pass. Also, the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop should be used where all three expressions in the loop head refer to the same variable. Disjointed expressions in the loop header should be avoided.

Using write access to the loop variable in the body is a bad idea if the variable also modified in the head at the same time—this approach is hard to comprehend and can easily lead to endless loops.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop isn’t fixed to a particular type, even though using <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops for incrementing suggests the implicit type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. The initialization part can preassign anything, whether <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, or a reference variable. The condition can test anything imaginable, but the result must be a <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> .

#### A for Loop Doesn’t Have to Be a Counting Loop

The <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop shows compactly all essential information in the loop head but isn’t limited to counting up values. Rather, a good option is a variable whose state is changed in each iteration and with the termination somehow dependent on the variable.

#### An Endless Loop with for

Since all three expressions in the head of the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop are optional, they can be omitted. If no loop condition is specified in the <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop, the expression is always true. For instance, the notation

```
for ( ; ; ); 
```

is equivalent to

```
for ( ; true; ); 
```

The separating semicolons in <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> are required. No initialization and no evaluation of the update expression follows, which in turn is semantically equivalent to the following statement:

```
 while ( true ); 
```

All three variables declare an endless loop.

###### [+]  Tip

The Motor Industry Software Reliability Association (MISRA) guidelines for the C programming language recommend the notation <samp class="listingcharacter">for(;;)</samp> for endless loops.

#### Nested Loops

Loops, especially for <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops, can be nested. Syntactically, this nesting is logical since any statements can reside within the loop body. To output five lines of asterisks, with one extra asterisk appearing in each subsequent line, you can write the following code.

```
for ( int i = 1; i <= 5; i++ ) {
  for ( int j = 1; j <= 
                    i; j++ )
    System.out.print( '*' );
  System.out.println();
} 
```

**Listing 2.28**     src/main/java/Superstar.java, main()

A special element in this example is the dependence of the loop counter <samp class="listingcharacter">j</samp> on <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> . The code produces the following output:

```
*
**
***
****
***** 
```

The parent loop is called the outer loop , and the child is the inner loop . In our example, the outer loop with <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> counts the rows, and the inner loop outputs the asterisks to a line, so it’s responsible for the column.

Since loops can be nested arbitrarily deep, you must pay special attention to the runtime. The inner loops are always executed with their passes as often as the outer loop is passed through.

#### Positioning for Loops and Expression Statements behind Each Other with a Comma*

A comma can be inserted in the first and last part of a <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop to place several expression statements one after the other. In this way, you can declare either several variables of the same type, as we’ve already done, or you can write several expressions next to each other, but no arbitrary statements or even other loops.

Using the variables <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">j</samp> , you can build a small multiplication table in the following way:

```
for ( int i = 1
                    , j = 9; i <= j; i++
                    , j-- )
  System.out.printf( "%d * %d = %d%n", i, j, i*j ); 
```

The following output should result:

```
1 * 9 = 9
2 * 8 = 16
3 * 7 = 21
4 * 6 = 24
5 * 5 = 25 
```

Another example with a more complex condition would be initializing starting value for the variables <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> before the loop is run. Then, we want the program to increment <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> and execute the loop as long as <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp> remains less than 10:

```
double x, y;
for ( x = Math.random(), y = Math.random(), x++, y++;
      x < 10 || y < 10;
      x += Math.random(), y += Math.random() ) {
  // …
} 
```

###### [+]  Tip

Complicated <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops become more readable by placing the three <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> parts on separate lines.

### 2.6.4    Loop Conditions and Comparisons with ==*

Loop termination conditions can look quite different from each other. In counting, the loop termination condition is often the comparison to a final value. Often at this point, an absolute comparison is written with <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> , which can become problematic for two reasons.

###### [»]  Question

The following program counts to 10, right?

```
int input = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextInt();
for ( int i = input; 
                    i != 11; i++ ) 
  System.out.println( i );
```

If the value of the variable <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> is smaller than 11, no problem occurs when counting because then the loop ends at 11 at the latest, and the loop terminates. However, if the value comes from an unknown source and is genuinely greater than 11, the condition is equally true, and the loop body will run through for quite a long time—to be precise, until you start again at 0 due to an overflow and then also end up at 11 on termination. Our intention was certainly different. The loop should only count as long as <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> is less than 11 and not simply not equal to 11\. Therefore, the following code is a better fit:

```
int input = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextInt();
for ( int i = input; 
                i < 11; i++ )  // Counts always only up to 10 or not at all
  System.out.println( i ); 
```

Now, the interpreter doesn’t run on endlessly for numbers greater than 11 but instead stops the loop immediately without a pass.

#### Calculation Inaccuracies Aren’t the Programmer’s Friend

The second problem arises with floats. Demanding real comparisons can be quite problematic, as in the following example:

```
double d = 0.0;
while ( d != 1.0 ) {           // Warning! Problematic comparison!
  d += 0.1;
  System.out.println( d );
} 
```

If you let the program segment run, you’ll see the loop quickly overshoots the target, as in the following output:

```
0.1
0.2
0.30000000000000004
0.4
0.5
0.6
0.7
0.7999999999999999
0.8999999999999999
0.9999999999999999
1.0999999999999999
1.2
1.3 
```

And so on to infinity.

The reason for this problem is that the number <samp class="listingcharacter">0.1</samp> can’t be exactly represented, and each addition operation leads to an accumulation of small inaccuracies.

For float values, therefore, a good idea is to always work with the relational operators <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp> .

A second possibility (besides the true less than/greater than comparison) is to define an allowed deviation (a delta ). Mathematicians denote the deviation of two values with the Greek lowercase letter epsilon. To compare two floats while considering a tolerance in an equality comparison, you can simply write the following code:

```
if ( Math.abs(x - y) <= epsilon )
  … 
```

The epsilon is the allowed deviation. <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.abs(x)</samp> calculates the absolute value of a number <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> .

#### How to Write Range Specifications*

For range specifications of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">a >= 23 && a <= 42</samp>, we recommend including the lower value in the comparison, but not the value for the upper limit (that is, including lower limits and excluding upper limits). For our example, where <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> is to remain in the interval , the following is better: <samp class="listingcharacter">a >= 23 && a < 43</samp> . This recommendation applies to both floats and integers. The reasoning behind this approach is plausible when you consider the following points:

*   The size of the interval is the difference of the limits.

*   If the interval is empty, the interval limits are the same.

*   The left lower limit is never greater than the right upper limit.

###### [»]  Note

The standard library also uses this convention throughout, for example, in the case of <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(...)</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> objects or <samp class="listingcharacter">subList(...)</samp> for lists or when specifying array index values.

Our suggestions can be adopted for normal loops with comparisons. Thus, a loop with ten passes looks better when written in the following way:

```
for ( i = 0; i < 10; i++ )              // Better 
```

In contrast, the following code, although semantically equivalent, is not recommended:

```
for ( i = 0; i <= 9; i++ )              // Not so good
for ( i = 1; i <= 10; i++ )             // Not so good either 
```

### 2.6.5     Loop Termination with break and back to Test with continue

A <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> statement within a <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop terminates the loop pass, and processing continues at the first statement after the loop. The fact that an endless loop can be terminated via <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> is useful when a condition occurs that determines the end of the loop. Let’s apply this principle to our number guessing game next.

```
public class GuessWhat {

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    int number = (int) (Math.random() * 5 + 1);

                while ( true ) {
     System.out.println( "What number do I have in mind between 1 and 5?" );
      int guess = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextInt();

      if ( number == guess ) {
        System.out.println( "Good guess!" );

                break;                   // End of loop
      }
      else if ( number > guess )
        System.out.println( "Nope, my number is larger than yours!" );
      else if ( number < guess )
        System.out.println( "Nope, my number is smaller than yours!" );

                }
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.29**     src/main/java/GuessWhat.java

The case distinction determines whether the user must guess again in another loop pass or whether the guess was correct; then, the <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> statement will end the loop.

###### [+]  Tip

Since a small <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> quickly disappears in the program text, but its significance is great, a small note should be placed on this statement.

#### Flags or break

<samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> can be used easily to break out of a loop prematurely without using flags:

```
boolean endFlag = false;
do {
  if ( 
                    condition ) {
    …

                        endFlag = true;
  }
} while ( 
                    OtherCondition && ! endFlag ); 
```

Instead, you should simply follow this syntax:

```
do {
  if ( 
                    condition ) {
    …
    break;
  }
} while ( 
                    OtherCondition ); 
```

The second alternative is no longer semantically identical with the first one if there are additional statements in the loop body after the <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> statement.

#### New Run with continue

Within a <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">do</samp>- <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop, you can use a <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> statement, which doesn’t end the loop like <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> but instead returns to the loop head. After evaluating the continuation <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> statement, the next step is to check again whether the loop should be run through further. A frequent use of <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> is in loops, which repeatedly fetch and test values in the body until they are suitable for further processing.

Let’s look again at our guessing game example. So far, the user has been told to enter only numbers between 1 and 5 (inclusive), but if he enters -1234567, nothing different occurs. Let’s change this by prepending a test that returns to the input prompt if the value range is wrong. In this case, <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> helps you get back to the beginning of the block, which starts with a new prompt.

```
public class GuessRight {

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    int number = (int) (Math.random() * 5 + 1);
    while ( true ) {
      System.out.println( "What number do I have in mind between 1 and 5?" );
      int guess = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).nextInt();

      if ( guess < 1 || guess > 5 ) {
        System.out.println( "Only numbers between 1 and 5!" );

                    continue;
      }

      if ( number == guess ) {
        System.out.println( "Good guess!" );
        break;                   // End of loop

                          }
      else if ( number > guess )
        System.out.println( "Nope, my number is larger than yours!" );
      else if ( number < guess )
        System.out.println( "Nope, my number is smaller than yours!" );
    }
  }
} 
```

**Listing 2.30**     src/main/java/GuessRight.java

[![](bilderklein/klein02_009_01.png)](img-f_none_02_12.html)

However, some program sections are more readable without <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> . A <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> at the end of an <samp class="listingcharacter">if</samp> query can be made much clearer by an <samp class="listingcharacter">else</samp> part. The following syntax is a bad example:

```
while ( 
                    condition ) {       // Sweetened by continue
  if ( 
                    OtherCondition ) {
    // Code, Code, Code
    continue;
  }
  // More beautiful code
} 
```

A much clearer example would follow this syntax:

```
while ( 
                    condition ) {
  if ( 
                    OtherCondition ) {
    // Code, Code, Code

                      }
  else {
    // More beautiful code
  }
} 
```

### 2.6.6     break and continue with Labels*

Although the keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> appears in the list of reserved words, Java doesn’t allow arbitrary jumps, and <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> lacks functionality. However, in Java, statements (or a block, which represents a special statement) can be labeled. One reason for introducing labels is that <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> can be ambiguous. Consider the following points:

*   If you have two nested loops, a <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> in the inner loop would only terminate the inner loop. However, what if the outer loop also should be terminated? The same applies to <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> if the outer loop is to be continued, but not the inner loop.

*   Not only do loops use the <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> keyword, but also the <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement. What if a loop contains a <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement, but the local <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> branch shouldn’t be terminated via <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp>, while the entire loop should be terminated with <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> ?

Java language designers decided to introduce labels so that <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> can either leave or pass through the labeled statement again. Used incorrectly, you might get spaghetti code as from the world of unstructured programming languages. But as responsible Java programmers, you shouldn’t misuse this feature, of course.

#### break with a Label for loops

Let’s look at a first example with a label, in which <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> not only breaks out of the inner devil’s loop, but out of the outer one as well. Labels are defined by ending an identifier with a colon and placing it before a statement, thus labeling the statement like a loop.

```
 heaven:
while ( true ) {

                    hell:
  while ( true )

                    break /* continue */ heaven;
  // System.out.println( "hell" );
}
System.out.println( "heaven" ); 
```

**Listing 2.31**     src/main/java/BreakAndContinueWithLabels.java, main()

A <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> without a label in the inner <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop only terminates the inner repetition, and a <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> would lead to the continuation of this inner <samp class="listingcharacter">while</samp> loop. Our example shows the use of a label after the keywords <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp>. The example doesn’t use the <samp class="listingcharacter">hell</samp> label, and the line with the output “hell” is deliberately commented out, because it isn’t accessible and would otherwise lead to a compiler error. The fact that the statement isn’t reachable is clear because, with <samp class="listingcharacter">break heaven</samp> , the program would never get to the next statement after the inner loop, and thus a console output wouldn’t be reachable.

If we put <samp class="listingcharacter">break hell</samp> in the inner loop instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">break heaven</samp> , things change:

```
 heaven:
while ( true ) {

                    hell:
  while ( true )

                    break /* continue */ hell;
  System.out.println( "hell" );
}
// System.out.println( "heaven" ); 
```

In this scenario, the “heaven” output is not attainable and must be commented out. The <samp class="listingcharacter">break hell</samp> in the inner loop acts like a simple <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> without a label, and the running program continuously results in screen outputs of the text “hell.”

###### [»]  Note

Labels can be defined before all statements (including before blocks). In our first case, we’ve put the label before the <samp class="listingcharacter">while(true)</samp> loop. Interestingly, a <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> with a label can exit not only a loop and <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> , but also a exit a simple block, as in the following:

```
label:
{
  …
  break label;
  …
}
```

Thus, the <samp class="listingcharacter">break label</samp> corresponds to a <samp class="listingcharacter">goto</samp> to the end of the block. A <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> cannot be replaced by <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> because <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> needs a loop in any case. Furthermore, a normal <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> without a label wouldn’t be valid and couldn’t leave the block.

Why does the compiler interpret the following without complaint?

```
class WithoutComplaint {
  static void main( String[] args ) {
    http://www.tutego.de/
    System.out.print( "IT training institute" );
  }
}
```

**Listing 2.32**     src/main/java/WithoutComplaint.java

#### Terminating switch with break and a Label

Since <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> has multiple functions in the Java language, ambiguity occurs when <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> is used in the <samp class="listingcharacter">case</samp> block of a <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement.

In the following example, a loop passes through a string. The access to a character in the string is realized by the <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> object method <samp class="listingcharacter">charAt(int)</samp>; the length of a string is returned by <samp class="listingcharacter">length()</samp>. C, G, A, and T are the allowed characters in the string. To create statistics about the number of individual letters, a <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement increments the correct variables <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">g</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp> by <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> each time a hit occurs. If an unallowed character exists in the string, the loop will be terminated. This scenario is where the label takes center stage.

```
// cytosine [C], guanine [G], adenine [A] or thymine [T]
String dnaBases = "CGCAGTTCTTCGGXAC";
int a = 0, g = 0, c = 0, t = 0;

loop:
for ( int i = 0; i < dnaBases.length(); i++ ) {
  switch ( dnaBases.charAt( i ) ) {
    case 'A', 'a':
      a++;
      break;
    case 'C', 'c':
      c++;
      break;
    case 'G', 'g':
      g++;
      break;
    case 'T', 't':
      t++;
      break;
    default:
      System.err.println( "Unknown nucleotide " + dnaBases.charAt( i ) );
      break loop;
  }
}

System.out.printf( "Total: A=%d, G=%d, C=%d, T=%d%n", a, g, c, t ); 
```

switch ( val ) {
  case 1:
    System.out.println( 1 );

## 2.7    Methods of a Class

In OOP, objects interact with each other at runtime and send messages to each other as requests to do something. These requests result in a method call containing statements that are then executed. In Java, the offer of an object with regard to what it “can do” is expressed by means of methods.

You’ve already learned about several methods with the frequently used <samp class="listingcharacter">println(...)</samp> in our examples. This method is a method of the <samp class="listingcharacter">out</samp> object. Another program section now sends a message to the <samp class="listingcharacter">out</samp> object to execute the <samp class="listingcharacter">println(...)</samp> method. In the following descriptions, we won’t look further into the active part of the message sending process; we’ll simply say that a method is “called.”

Three reasons exist for declaring methods:

*   Recurring program parts shouldn’t be programmed again and again but instead provided in one place. Changes to functionality can then be made more easily if the code is grouped together locally.

*   Complex programs are broken down into small subprograms so that the complexity of the program is broken down as well. This organization makes it easier to see the control flow.

*   The operations of a class, that is, the offerings of an object, are the reasons for method declarations in an OOP language. However, other reasons also speak in favor of methods, which we’ll describe in this section.

### 2.7.1    Components of a Method

A method is composed of several components: the method head ( head for short ) and the method body ( body for short ). The head consists of a return type (also called a result type ), the method name, and an optional parameter list .

Let’s consider the well-known static <samp class="listingcharacter">main(String[])</samp> method in the following example:

```
public static void main( String[] args ) {
  System.out.println( "What happened to you? Did you run here?" );
} 
```

This code has the following components:

*   The static method doesn’t return anything, so the “return type” is <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp>. At this point, note that <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp> is not a type in Java; <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp> simply means “free,” “the void,” or “cavity.”

*   The method name is <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp> .

*   The parameter list is <samp class="listingcharacter">String[] args</samp> .

*   The body consists only of the screen output.

###### [»]  Naming Conventions

Like variable names, method names start with lowercase letters and are written in mixed case. Identifiers should not be named like keywords. [[ 79 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_47)

#### The Signature of a Method

The method name and the parameter list determine the signature of a method; the return type and exceptions are not part of a method signature. [[ 80 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn02_48) The parameter list is described by the number, order, and types of parameters. Only one method of the same signature can exist in a class; otherwise, the compiler will report an error. Since the methods <samp class="listingcharacter">void main(String[] args)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">String main(String[] arguments)</samp> have the same signature ( <samp class="listingcharacter">main</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">String[]</samp> )—the names of the parameters don’t matter—they can’t be declared together in one class. (Later in this section, we’ll show you how subclasses do allow certain special cases.)

###### [»]  Duck Typing

Scripting languages in particular (such as JavaScript, Python, or Ruby) allow for method declarations without a parameter type, so methods can be called with different argument types, as in the following code:

```
printSum( a, b ) print a + b
```

Due to the unspecified parameter type, the method can be called with integers, floats, or strings. The runtime environment is tasked with recognizing this dynamic type and with executing the addition on the concrete type. This approach isn’t possible in Java where the type must be known to the compiler. Programming languages that check the presence of methods or operators on the type only at runtime use what’s called duck typing. The term comes from a poem by James Whitcomb Riley: “When I see a bird that walks like a duck and swims like a duck and quacks like a duck, I call that bird a duck.” Applied to our case, if the parameters <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> support the operation “add,” then the values can be added.

### 2.7.2    Signature Description in the Java Application Programming Interface Documentation

In the Java API documentation, all methods with their return values and parameters (including possible exceptions) are exactly defined. Let’s look at the documentation of the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">max(int, int)</samp> of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class.

[![The Online API Documentation for Math.max()](bilderklein/klein02_010.png)](img-f2.10.html)

**Figure 2.10**     The Online API Documentation for Math.max()

The help information shown in [Figure 2.10](#02_007.html_f2.10) provides details about the complete signature of the method. The return type is an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, the static method is called <samp class="listingcharacter">max</samp>, and it expects exactly two <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> numbers. We’ve concealed the keywords <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> (which are called modifiers ). The keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> specifies the visibility and who can use this method. Let’s look a bit more closely at these keywords:

*   In the case of <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp>, anyone can use this method. The opposite is <samp class="listingcharacter">private</samp> in which only the object itself can use this method. This distinction is useful when methods are intended to reduce complexity and solve sub-problems. Private methods are usually not displayed in the help because they are an implementation detail.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> keyword indicates that the method can be used with the class name, that is, no instance of an object is required.

#### Other Modifiers and Exceptions*

Many methods that have other modifiers and an extended signature. Another example from the API documentation is shown in [Figure 2.11](#02_007.html_f2.11). The visibility of this method is <samp class="listingcharacter">protected</samp>, which means that only derived classes and classes in the same directory (the same package) can use this method. An additional modifier is <samp class="listingcharacter">final</samp>, which in inheritance doesn’t allow the subclass to overwrite the method and give it new program code. Finally, the <samp class="listingcharacter">throws</samp> keyword is followed by an exception. This exception tells you something about errors that might be caused by the method and what the programmer must take care of. In connection with inheritance, we’ll discuss <samp class="listingcharacter">protected</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">final</samp> later. [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9) is devoted to exceptions. Based on “Since: 1.1” in the documentation, we can note that the method has existed since Java 1.1\. The information can also be bound to the class.
