To find out if a string has no characters, the method <samp class="listingcharacter">isEmpty()</samp> can be used instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">length() == 0</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">isBlank()</samp> method tests whether a string is empty or consists only of whitespace. In the context of this method, whitespace is any character where <samp class="listingcharacter">Character.isWhitespace(int)</samp> returns as true.

| Statement | Result |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">"".length()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">"".isEmpty()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">" ".length()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">" ".isEmpty()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">" ".isBlank()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">String s = null; s.length();</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> |

**Table 5.7**     Results of the length(...), isEmpty(...), and isBlank(...) Methods

###### [»]   Note

From arrays, recall that <samp class="listingcharacter">length</samp> is an object variable. For <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">length()</samp> is an object method and thus requires parentheses.

#### A Handy Helper Method: isNullOrEmpty(String)

For example, while the .NET framework provides the static member function <samp class="listingcharacter">IsNullOrEmpty(String)</samp>, which tests whether the passed reference is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> or the string is empty, in Java, this evaluation must be tested separately. A separate static utility method comes in handy, as in the following example:

```
/**
 * Checks if a String is {@code null} or empty ({@code ""}).
 *
 * <pre>
 * StringUtils.isNullOrEmpty(null) == true
 * StringUtils.isNullOrEmpty(&quot;&quot;) == true
 * StringUtils.isNullOrEmpty(&quot; &quot;) == false
 * StringUtils.isNullOrEmpty(&quot;bob&quot;) == false
 * StringUtils.isNullOrEmpty(&quot; bob &quot;) == false
 * </pre>
 *
 * @param str The String to check, may be {@code null}.
 * @return {@code true} if the String is empty or {@code null}, {@code false}
 * otherwise.
 */
public static boolean isNullOrEmpty( String str ) {
  return str == null || str.isEmpty();
} 
```

**Listing 5.3**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/string/LengthAndEmptyDemo.java (Snippet)

This method, however, doesn’t test whether the string consists of whitespace only.

### 5.5.5    Accessing a Specific Character with charAt(int)

Perhaps the most important method of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class is <samp class="listingcharacter">charAt(int index)</samp>. [[ 116 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn05_06) This method returns the corresponding character in a place called index. This method thus provides a way to traverse the characters of a string (along with the <samp class="listingcharacter">length()</samp> method). If the index is less than zero or greater than or equal to the number of characters in the string, the method throws a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringIndexOutOfBoundsException</samp> [[ 117 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn05_07) with the error location.

###### [eg]  Example

The following code returns the first and last characters in the string <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> :

```
String s = "I'm not fat, just well-covered!";
char first = s.
                    charAt( 0 );                          // 'I'
char last  = s.
                    charAt( s.length() - 1 );             // '!'
```

You must remember that the count starts from 0\. Therefore, you must subtract one digit from the length of the string. Since the comparison to the correct range occurs each time <samp class="listingcharacter">charAt(int)</samp> is accessed, you should consider whether the string should be copied once into its own character array instead (in case multiple access is expected).

###### [»]  Note*

Since Unicode characters can also be composed of 2 Java <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>s (the surrogate pair), an alternative method is available: <samp class="listingcharacter">int codePointAt(int index)</samp>. This method is slower than <samp class="listingcharacter">charAt(...)</samp> because a linear search must be performed. It isn’t known in advance at which position a Unicode character is located from exactly one <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> or from two <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>s. In this book, we always assume Unicode characters that can be encoded in a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> .

### 5.5.6    Searching for Contained Characters and Strings

The object method <samp class="listingcharacter">contains(CharSequence)</samp> tests whether a substring occurs in the string and returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if it does. Case sensitivity is relevant. In the following program, we’ll test whether a string contains one of the allowed names of candy:

```
static boolean containsCandyName( String text ) {
  text = text.toLowerCase();
  String[] candyNames = {
      "starburst", "snackers", "n&n", "cold tamales" 
  };
  for ( String candyName : candyNames )
    if ( text.contains( candyName ) )
      return true;
  return false;

                }

public static void main( String[] args ) {
  String msg1 = "Starburst is so delicious.";
  System.out.println( containsCandyName( msg1 ) );  // true
  String msg2 = "I only like warm milk.";
  System.out.println( containsCandyName( msg2 ) );  // false
} 
```

**Listing 5.4**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/string/ContainsCandyName.java (Snippet)

#### Returning Found Locations with indexOf(...)

The <samp class="listingcharacter">contains(...)</samp> method is not overloaded with a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>, so we can’t search for a single character unless the string consisted of only 1 character. However, this search is possible with the <samp class="listingcharacter">indexOf(...)</samp> method, which returns the location of a character or substring. If <samp class="listingcharacter">indexOf(...)</samp> finds nothing, it returns -1.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example searches a character with <samp class="listingcharacter">indexOf(...)</samp> :

```
String s = "Ernest Gräfenberg";
int index1 = s.
                        indexOf( 'e' );                     // 3
int index2 = s.
                        indexOf( 'e', index1 + 1 );         // 11
int index3 = s.
                        indexOf( 'e', 69696969 );           // -1 
```

The assignment of <samp class="listingcharacter">index1</samp> is 3 because, at code point 3, an <samp class="listingcharacter">'e'</samp> occurs for the first time. The second method <samp class="listingcharacter">indexOf(...)</samp> continues searching with the second expression <samp class="listingcharacter">index1 + 1</samp> (that is, starting at code point 4). The result is 11.

Like <samp class="listingcharacter">contains(...)</samp> , the search is case sensitive. The characters in a string are numbered like array elements starting from 0\. If the index argument is less than 0, this number is ignored, and the index is automatically set to 0.

###### [eg]  Example

If the character <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> describes an escape character, for example, a tab or a return, then processing can continue in the following way:

```
if ( "\b\t\n\f\r\"\\".
                        indexOf(c) >= 0 ) {
  …
} 
```

We couldn’t use <samp class="listingcharacter">contains(...)</samp> because the parameter type is only <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp>, not <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> .

The <samp class="listingcharacter">indexOf(...)</samp> method is parameterized not only with <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>, but also with <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>, [[ 118 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn05_08) to search for entire strings and return the starting point.

###### [eg]  Example

Call <samp class="listingcharacter">indexOf(String, int)</samp> with the search for a partial string:

```
String str = "I'll be ill if you remove the apostrophe.";
//            0123456789
String s = "ll";
int index = str.
                        indexOf( s, str.indexOf(s) + 1 );       // 9 
```

The next search position is calculated from the old finder position. The result is 9 because the substring “ll” appears there for the second time.

#### Searching from the End

Just as you can search a string starting at the beginning, you can also start at the end.

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">lastIndexOf(...)</samp>method is used for this purpose :

```
String str = "May the F
                        orce be with y
                        ou.";
int index  = str.
                        lastIndexOf( 'o' );                 // 23 
```

As with <samp class="listingcharacter">indexOf(...)</samp> , an overloaded version can search backwards from a certain position for the next occurrence of “o.” In this case, you would write the following code:

```
index = str.lastIndexOf( 'o', index - 1 );          // 9 
```

The parameters of the <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>-oriented methods <samp class="listingcharacter">indexOf(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">lastIndexOf(...)</samp> are all of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and not, as one might expect, of type <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. The character to be searched is passed as the first <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> argument. The conversion of <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> is done automatically by the Java compiler, so this change isn’t noticeable. Unfortunately, however, confusion in the order of arguments may occur: With <samp class="listingcharacter">s.indexOf(start, c)</samp> the first parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">start</samp> is interpreted as a character, and the desired character <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> is interpreted as the start position of the search.

#### Number of Substrings of a String*

So far, the Java library doesn’t provide a direct method to determine the number of substrings in a string. However, such a method can be written quickly in the following way:

```
 public class CountMatches {

  public static int frequency( String source, String part ) {
    if ( source == null || source.isEmpty() || part == null || part.isEmpty() )
      return 0;

    int count = 0;

    for ( int pos = 0; (pos = source.indexOf( part, pos )) != -1; count++ )
      pos += part.length();

    return count;
  }

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    System.out.println( frequency( "cherry schnaps, schnitzel", "sch" ) );  // 2
    System.out.println( frequency( "cherry schnaps, schnitzel", "zel" ) );  // 1
    System.out.println( frequency( "cherry schnaps, schnitzel", "" ) );     // 0
  }
} 
```

**Listing 5.5**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/string/CountMatches.java (Snippet)

The chosen implementation returns the number of non-overlapping substrings. The implementation would return the result “2” when calling <samp class="listingcharacter">frequency("aaaa", "aa")</samp> because, with <samp class="listingcharacter">pos += part.length()</samp> , the implementation always moves as many steps further to the right as the substring is long. Depending on the interpretation of the task—and other algorithms—the value “3” would also be a permitted return, but then the loop would always have to go only one position to the right.

### 5.5.7    The Hangman Game

The methods you’ve learned so far can solve an estimated 90% of all tasks in daily programming practice. In summary, so far, we covered the following methods:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int charAt(int)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int length()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean equals(Object)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean contains(CharSequence)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int indexOf(char)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int indexOf(String)</samp>

Let’s now use these methods to make a little game, the famous Hangman game. The aim is to guess all the letters of a word. At the beginning, each letter is made unrecognizable by an underscore. The user starts guessing and gradually fills in the individual placeholders. If the player fails to guess the word after a fixed number of rounds, he has lost.

```
String hangmanWord = "alligatoralley";
String usedChars = "";

String guessedWord = "";
for ( int i = 0; i < hangmanWord.length(); i++ )
  guessedWord += "_";

for ( int guesses = 0; ; guesses++ ) {
  if ( guesses == 10 ) {
    System.out.printf(
     "Sorry, game over after 10 attempts! Speaking of which, the word was '%s'.",
     hangmanWord );
    break;
  }

  System.out.printf(
      "Round %d. Previous guess: '%s'. What character do you choose?%n",
      guesses, guessedWord );
  char guessedChar = new java.util.Scanner( System.in ).next().charAt( 0 );

  if ( usedChars.indexOf( guessedChar ) >= 0 )
    System.out.printf( "'%c' you have entered before!%n", guessedChar );
  else {  //Character has not been used yet
     usedChars += guessedChar;
    �� hangmanWord.indexOf( c ) == -1
    if ( hangmanWord.indexOf( guessedChar ) >= 0 ) {
      guessedWord = "";
      for ( int i = 0; i < hangmanWord.length(); i++ )
        guessedWord += usedChars.indexOf( hangmanWord.charAt( i ) ) >= 0 ?
                         hangmanWord.charAt( i ) : "_";

      if ( guessedWord.contains( "_" ) )
        System.out.printf( "Good guess, |%s| can be found in the word. " +
                           "But there’s something missing!%n", guessedChar );
      else {
        System.out.printf( "Congratulations, you have guessed the word '%s'!",
                           hangmanWord );
        break;
      }
    }

                    else
      System.out.printf( "Bad luck, %c does not occur in the word!%n",
                         guessedChar );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 5.6**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/string/Hangman1.java, main(…)

The game starts with the following output:

```
Round 0\. Previous guess: '______________'. What character do you choose? 
```

The player types in a letter, such as “e,” and then presses (Enter) . In turn, the program responds in the following way:

```
e
Good guess, 'e' can be found in the word. But there's something missing!
Round 1\. Previous guess: '____________e_'. What character do you choose?
a
Good guess, 'a' can be found in the word. But there's something missing!
Round 2\. Previous guess: 'a____a___a__e_'. What character do you choose? 
```

This gameplay loop continues until the end of the game.

### 5.5.8    Good That We Have Compared

To compare strings, many possibilities and options are available, such as the following:

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class searches for absolute matches.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">equalsIgnoreCase(...)</samp> method of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class can be used for case-insensitive comparisons.

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">switch</samp> statement allows you to compare <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects with a list of jump targets. Internally, <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> performs the comparison.

*   Whether a string starts or ends with a word is indicated by the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> methods <samp class="listingcharacter">startsWith(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">endsWith(...)</samp> .

*   For comparing individual sections, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">regionMatches(...)</samp> , a method that can also work case insensitively.

*   If a match to a regular expression is desired, the <samp class="listingcharacter">matches(...)</samp> method of <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> and the special classes <samp class="listingcharacter">Pattern</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Matcher</samp> , which are specific to regular expressions, will help.

###### [»]  Note

While the vast majority of scripting languages and also C# allow string comparisons via <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, the semantics for Java is unique: Comparison with <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> is only true if the two references are identical (i.e., two <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects are identical). <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> doesn’t test equivalence.

#### The equals(...) Method

The <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class overrides the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method inherited from the <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> class to compare two strings. The method returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the strings are of equal length and if all characters match.

When comparing identities via <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, the result is usually different for strings than when comparing via <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> . Consider the following example:

```
String input = javax.swing.JOptionPane.showInputDialog( "Password" );
String expected = "qwerty123";
System.out.println( input == expected );                 // (1)
System.out.println( input.equals( expected ) );          // (2.1)
System.out.println( expected.equals( input ) );          // (2.2)
System.out.println( Objects.equals( expected, input ) ); // (3) 
```

Assuming that <samp class="listingcharacter">input</samp> references the string <samp class="listingcharacter">qwerty123</samp>, the comparison (line 1) via <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> yields the value <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> since the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object returned by <samp class="listingcharacter">showInputDialog(...)</samp> is a completely different one than the present password <samp class="listingcharacter">qwerty123</samp>. Only the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> comparison (lines 2.1 and 2.2) is correct in this case because the pure characters are compared, and they are equal. Basically, the variants (in lines 2.1 and 2.2) are the same since <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> is symmetric. But an advantage exists with line 2.2 because <samp class="listingcharacter">input</samp> can also be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, and so a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> won’t be thrown, as with line 2.1\. <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects.equals(...)</samp> is useful in this context because the method internally checks for <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> .

###### [»]  Note

In the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> comparison, all characters play a role, even if they aren’t visible. Thus, the following comparisons lead to <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> :

```
System.out.println( 
                        "\t".equals( 
                        "\n" ) );                // false
System.out.println( 
                        "\t".equals( 
                        "\t " ) );               // false
System.out.println( 
                        "\u0000".equals( 
                        "\u0000\u0000" ) );  // false
```

#### The equalsIgnoreCase(...) Method

When you perform comparisons, <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> is case sensitive. With <samp class="listingcharacter">equalsIgnoreCase(...)</samp> , the Java library provides an additional method that compares strings case insensitively; the test is done character by character.

###### [eg]  Example

Let’s compare two strings, one case sensitive and the other case-insensitive:

```
String str = "BOOMERANG";
boolean result1 = str.
                        equals( "boomerang" );             // false
boolean result2 = str.
                        equalsIgnoreCase( "BOOMerang" );   // true
```

###### [»]   Comparison of Methods

Let’s assume we want to compare two strings regardless of case (ß is a letter only used in German).

```
String s = "Spaß", t = "SPASS";
System.out.println( s.toUpperCase().equals( t.toUpperCase() ) ); // true
System.out.println( t.toUpperCase().equals( s.toUpperCase() ) ); // true
System.out.println( s.toLowerCase().equals( t.toLowerCase() ) ); // false
System.out.println( t.toLowerCase().equals( s.toLowerCase() ) ); // false
System.out.println( s.equalsIgnoreCase( t ) );                   // false
System.out.println( t.equalsIgnoreCase( s ) );                   // false
```

With <samp class="listingcharacter">equalsIgnoreCase(...)</samp>, length is compared at the beginning. It’s unequal, so the result is quickly determined. If the lengths are equal, all characters will be compared individually. <samp class="listingcharacter">Character.toUpperCase('ß')</samp> is also “ß” so far.

#### Lexicographic Comparisons with Greater/Less Relation

Like <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">equalsIgnoreCase(String)</samp>, the methods <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(String)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">compareToIgnoreCase(String)</samp> compare the current string with another string. Note, however, that the return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(String)</samp> isn’t a <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp>, but an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. The result signals whether the argument is lexicographically less than, greater than, or equal to the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object. These distinctions are important in a sorting method, for example. The sorting algorithm must know how to sort two strings when comparing them.

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, we’ll compare three strings in their lexicographic order. All comparisons show <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> :

```
System.out.println( "Justus".compareTo( "Bob" )    > 0 );
System.out.println( "Justus".compareTo( "Justus" ) == 0 );
System.out.println( "Justus".compareTo( "Peter" )  < 0 );
```

In the first case, since “Justus” is lexicographically greater than “Bob,” the numeric return of the <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(String)</samp> method is greater than 0.

The comparison made by <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(String)</samp> is based only on the internal numeric encoding of the Unicode characters. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp> does not take into account specific regional features, such as the usual treatment of German umlauts. For this purpose, we’d need to use <samp class="listingcharacter">Collator</samp> classes.

<samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">compareToIgnoreCase(...)</samp> is for ordering (greater than, less than, equal to) while <samp class="listingcharacter">equalsIgnoreCase(...)</samp> is for testing the string equivalence: for both methods, case is irrelevant.

###### [»]  Note

The OpenJDK implements <samp class="listingcharacter">compareToIgnoreCase(...)</samp> with a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator<String></samp>, which puts any two strings in order. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator<String></samp> is also accessible as a static variable named <samp class="listingcharacter">CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER</samp>, which is, for example, convenient for sorted sets where case isn’t important. Comparators are introduced in more detail in [Chapter 11](#11_001.html_h11), [Section 11.4](#11_004.html_h11.4) .

#### If the String Ends with ..., Does It Start with ...?

To determine whether a string starts with a certain string (let’s call this a prefix ), you can call the <samp class="listingcharacter">startsWith(...)</samp> method. A similar method exists for suffixes : <samp class="listingcharacter">endsWith(...) , which</samp> checks if a string ends with a specific string of characters.

###### [eg]  Example

The following code tests a filename extension with <samp class="listingcharacter">endsWith(String)</samp> and tests a salutation with <samp class="listingcharacter">startsWith(String)</samp> :

```
String   filename   = "The best openings for beginners (in chess).TXT";
boolean  isTxt      = filename.toLowerCase().endsWith( ".txt" );   // true
String   email      = "Very honoured P. Ennis,\nThank you for your offer.";
boolean  isHonoured = email.toLowerCase().startsWith( "Dear" );   // false
```

The string is converted to lowercase before the request because no method of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">endsWithIgnoreCase(...)</samp> exists.

#### Comparing String Sections with regionMatches(...) *

An extension of the whole-or-nothing comparison methods is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter">regionMatches(...)</samp> , which compares individual sections of one string with sections of another. If the first argument of <samp class="listingcharacter">regionMatches(...)</samp> assumes the truth value <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>, then case doesn’t matter. As with <samp class="listingcharacter">equals*(...)</samp>, the return value is a <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, the call of <samp class="listingcharacter">regionMatches(...)</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> :

```
String  s = "She's a straight lemonhead! ";
// Position: 0                17
boolean b = s.regionMatches( 17, "Make life! Take the lemons back!", 20, 5 );
// Position:                     0                    20
```

The method starts the comparison at the 17th character, that is, at the “l” in the string <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>, and at the 20th letters in the comparison string , which is also an “l.” The counting of the characters starts again at 0\. Five characters are compared from these two positions. In this example, comparing “lemon” and “lemon” returns as <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, if the comparison should be case insensitive , the first argument of the overloaded method is <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> :

```
String  s = "She's a straight LEMONhead! ";
// Position: 0                17
boolean b = s.regionMatches( true, 17, "Make life! Take the LemOns back!", 20, 5 );
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class can’t perform a case-insensitive comparison for the <samp class="listingcharacter">startsWith(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">endsWith(...)</samp> methods. Instead, you would use <samp class="listingcharacter">regionMatches(...)</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

To test if an email starts with a certain salutation, regardless of capitalization:

```
String startWith = "Dear ";
String email = "DEAR HAROLD, when is it time for sports again?";
boolean niceOpening = email.regionMatches( true,
                          0, startWith, 0, startWith.length() ); // true
```

### 5.5.9    Extracting String Sections

At this point, you’ve already used the most important method of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class several times, namely, <samp class="listingcharacter">charAt(int index)</samp> . However, this method is not the only method for accessing certain sections of a string.

#### Using substring(...) to Retrieve Sections of a String as a String

To retrieve a substring from a string, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(...)</samp> method . This method exists in two variants, both of which return a new <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object that corresponds to the desired section of the original.

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(int)</samp> returns a substring starting from an index to the end. The result is a new <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object:

```
 String s1 = "I think I am, therefore, I am. I think.";
// Position: 0                              31
String s2 = s1.
                        substring( 31 );          // I think.
```

[![](bilderklein/klein05_002_03.png)](img-f_none_05_02.html)

The index of <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(int)</samp> specifies the starting position (zero-based) from which characters are copied into the new substring. <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(int)</samp> returns the part from this character to the end of the original string. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">s.substring(0)</samp> is equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> for any <samp class="listingcharacter">non-zero</samp> string <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> .

To specify a substring more precisely, you would use the second variant, <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(int, int)</samp> . Your arguments indicate the beginning and the end of the desired section.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example cuts out a section of the string:

```
String twitter = "Instagram is just Twitter for people who go outside.";
//                0                 18     25
System.out.println( twitter.substring( 18, 25 ) );   // Twitter
```

While the start position is inclusive, the end position is exclusive. This specification is common in Java. In other words, at the end position, the character no longer belongs to the substring.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(int)</samp> method is nothing more than a specialization of <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(int, int)</samp> because the first variant with the starting index can also be written as <samp class="listingcharacter">s.substring(beginIndex, s.length())</samp> .

###### [eg]   Example

The following example converts the first character of a text to uppercase:

```
public static String firstToUpper( String ){
  if ( string.isEmpty() ) return "";
  return string.substring( 0, 1 ).toUpperCase().concat( string.substring( 1 ) );
}
```

Note there is another solution, namely, the following:

```
return Character.toUpperCase( string.charAt( 0 ) ) + string.substring( 1 );
```

Of course, various index checks are now added—a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringIndexOutOfBoundsException</samp> [[ 119 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn05_09) reports incorrect positional information as with <samp class="listingcharacter">charAt(int)</samp> .

#### String before/after a Delimiter String*

The <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class doesn’t provide a simple library method for the case where a delimiter is given and a substring is requested before or after that delimiter. [[ 120 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn05_10) Such a method would be useful, for example, for files where the dot separates the filename from the suffix. You can write two static utility methods, <samp class="listingcharacter">substringBefore(String string, String delimiter)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">substringAfter(String string, String delimiter)</samp> , which do exactly that. When applied, they look like this (ignore for a moment that the filename itself can also contain a dot):

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">substringBefore( "index.html", "." )</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">"index"</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">substringAfter( "index.html", "." )</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">"html"</samp> .

The implementation of these methods is simple: In the first step, the methods search for the delimiter via <samp class="listingcharacter">indexOf(...)</samp>. Then, they return the substring before or after this found delimiter string via <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(...)</samp>. A few agreements: The delimiter isn’t part of the return. And if the delimiter doesn’t appear in the string, <samp class="listingcharacter">substringBefore(...)</samp> returns the entire string, while <samp class="listingcharacter">substringAfter(...)</samp> returns the empty string. String and delimiter must not be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. If so, a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> will follow, indicating the programming error. Programmed out, the two methods look as follows:

```
 public class StringUtils {

  /�**
   * Returns the substring before the first occurrence of a delimiter.
   * The delimiter is not part of the result.
   *
   * @param string    to get a substring from.
   * @param delimiter String to search for.
   * @return          Substring before the first occurrence of the delimiter.
   */
  public static 
                    String substringBefore( String, String delimiter ) {
    int pos = string.indexOf( delimiter );

    return pos >= 0 ? string.substring( 0, pos ) : string;
  }

  /**
   * Returns the substring after the first occurrence of a delimiter. 
   * The delimiter is not part of the result.
   *
   * @param string    to get a substring from.
   * @param delimiter String to search for.
   * @return          Substring after the first occurrence of the delimiter.
   */
  public static 
                    String substringAfter( String string, String delimiter ) {
    int pos = string.indexOf( delimiter );

    return pos >= 0 ? string.substring( pos + delimiter.length() ) : "";
  }
} 
```

**Listing 5.7**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/string/StringUtils.java (Snippet)

#### Extracting Strings as an Array from the String via getChars(...)*

While <samp class="listingcharacter">charAt(int)</samp> returns only one character from the string, <samp class="listingcharacter">getChars(int srcBegin, int srcEnd, char[] dest, int dstBegin)</samp> copies multiple characters from a specified range of the string into a passed array.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example copies parts of the string into an array:

```
String s = "Blessing of the Throats";
char[] chars = new char[ 5 ];
int srcBegin = 7;

                        s.
                        getChars( srcBegin, srcBegin + 5, chars, 0 );
System.out.println( new String(chars) );  // blessing 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">s.getChars(...)</samp> copies five characters from position 7 of the string <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> into the elements of the array <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>. The first character from the section is then in <samp class="listingcharacter">chars[0]</samp> .

The method <samp class="listingcharacter">getChars(...)</samp> must of course again test whether the specified arguments are in the green range, that is, whether the start value isn’t < 0 and whether the end value doesn’t exceed the size of the string. If the arguments don’t fit, the method throws a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringIndexOutOfBoundsException</samp>. In addition, if the start value is behind the end value, a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringIndexOutOfBoundsException</samp> will arise, which indicates how big a difference between the positions exists. The best approach is to calculate the end position from the start position, as was done in the earlier example. If all characters fit into the array, the implementation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">getChars(...)</samp> method uses <samp class="listingcharacter">System.arraycopy(...)</samp> to copy the characters from the internal array of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object to the destination you’ve specified.

For accessing the complete contents of a string as an array of characters, you can use the <samp class="listingcharacter">toCharArray()</samp> method. Internally, the method also works with <samp class="listingcharacter">getChars(...)</samp>. As a destination array, <samp class="listingcharacter">toCharArray()</samp> just creates a new array, which we then get back.

###### [»]  Note

The following code can be used to iterate over a string:

```
String string = "Clones are people two.";
for ( char c : string.toCharArray() )
  System.out.println( c );
```

This solution comes at a price, however, because simply creating a new <samp class="listingcharacter">char[]</samp> object for the pass costs memory and computation time for memory allocation and garbage collection. Therefore, this variant isn’t recommended. Alternatively, <samp class="listingcharacter">chars()</samp> can be used, which returns a stream of characters for the string, but then works without an explicit <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop; we’ll describe the Stream API in [Chapter 18](#18_001.html_h18), [Section 18.4](#18_004.html_h18.4) .

#### Other Options for Decomposition

Two other ways exist for extracting certain parts from a string. One option is <samp class="listingcharacter">split (...)</samp>, which allows you to split a string using a regular expression. You could also use the <samp class="listingcharacter">lines()</samp> method, which returns a stream of lines that were separated by line breaks.

###### [eg]  Example

A string consists of several lines. The following example cuts off the whitespace at the beginning and end of each line and then output all lines:

```
 String text = “ I wouldn’t lie to you. \n Well...that’s a lie. \t “;
text.lines().forEach( line -> System.out.println( line.trim() ) ); 
```

This example draws on lambda expressions, which are the subject of [Chapter 13](#13_001.html_h13) .

### 5.5.10    Appending Strings, Merging Strings, Case Sensitivity, and Whitespace

Although <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects themselves are immutable, the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class provides methods that take out or add parts of a string. Of course, these changes aren’t made to the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object itself on which the method is called, but the method returns a reference to a new <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object with modified contents.

#### Appending to Strings

To append another string to a string, two obvious possibilities are available:

*   Using the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">concat(String)</samp>

*   Using the plus operator (which is more flexible since non-strings are first converted to strings)

Later, we’ll show you how the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder/StringBuffer</samp> classes can take it even further and provide overloaded <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> methods for different data types.

###### [eg]  Example

The following code appends the current time (with deleted nanoseconds) to the end of a string:

```
String s1 = "Current time: ";
String s2 = LocalTime.now().withNano(0).toString();
String s3 = s1.concat( s2 ); // Current time: 12:53:14 
```

Similarly, you can write the following code:

```
String s4 = "Current time: " + LocalTime.now().withNano(0).toString(); 
```

This code can even shortened because the plus operator automatically calls <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> on objects:

```
String s5 = "Current time: " + LocalTime.now().withNano(0); 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">concat(String)</samp> creates an internal array, copies the two strings into it via <samp class="listingcharacter">getChars(...)</samp>, and returns the resulting string with a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> constructor.

#### Merging Multiple Strings

Two overloaded class methods related to <samp class="listingcharacter">join(...)</samp> can join multiple strings and put a separator string between the links. These methods differ in terms of their parameter lists: One receives the links directly via a vararg, while the other receives them via <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterable</samp> :

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String join(CharSequence delimiter, CharSequence... elements)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String join(CharSequence delimiter, Iterable<? extends CharSequence></samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">elements)</samp>

The arguments must be strings and can’t be common objects that are automatically converted to strings. In addition, the links must not be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

The following example puts words together with a space to form a sentence:

```
String[] words = { "I", "programmed", "you", "to", "believe", "that." };
String s = String.join( " ", words ); 
```

The delimiter string must not be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> but can be empty.

No comparable method exists in <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder/StringBuffer</samp>, but a small <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner</samp> class can do the actual work of <samp class="listingcharacter">join(...)</samp> .

#### Case Sensitivity

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Character</samp> class declares some static methods that convert single characters to uppercase/lowercase. We can save the loop that does this for each character using the methods <samp class="listingcharacter">toUpperCase(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">toLowerCase(...)</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class.

What’s interesting about both methods is that they observe some language-dependent subtleties. For example, that there is not really a capital “ß” in German, because “ß” becomes “SS.” To take country-specific features into account, the <samp class="listingcharacter">to*Case(...)</samp> methods can additionally be fed with a <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> object (which represent a linguistic region).

###### [»]  Note

Some conversions to uppercase/lowercase may result in different strings depending on the local language.

The specification of a <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> for the two <samp class="listingcharacter">to****Case(...)</samp> methods is especially important for Turkish-language applications, as in the following example:

```
System.out.println( "TITANIK".toLowerCase()  );                    // t
                        itan
                        ik
System.out.println( "TITANIK".toLowerCase( new Locale( "tr" ) )  ); // t
                        ıtan
                        ık
```

Note the subtle difference: In the second result string, the “i” has no dot!

###### [»]   Note

The parameterless methods <samp class="listingcharacter">toUpperCase()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">toLowerCase()</samp> can select a locale according to the locale settings of the operating system. In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter">toLowerCase()</samp> is modified by a locale:

```
public String toLowerCase() {
  return toLowerCase( Locale.getDefault() );
} 
```

Thus, you should keep in mind that the default setting isn’t necessarily the best.

#### Removing Whitespace

In a user input or in a configuration file, commonly whitespace (such as spaces or tabs) may exist before or after the important part of a text.

These whitespaces should be removed before processing. The <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class provides <samp class="listingcharacter">trim()</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">strip()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">stripLeading()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">stripTrailing()</samp> for this purpose. Let’s look at their differences.

| Method | Removes... |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">trim()</samp> | All code points less than or equal to the space U+0020 at the beginning and at the end of the string. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">strip()</samp> | All characters at the beginning and at the end of the string that are whitespace characters according to the definition of <samp class="listingcharacter">Character.isWhitespace(int)</samp> . |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stripLeading()</samp> | Like <samp class="listingcharacter">strip()</samp> , but only at the beginning of the string. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">stripTrailing()</samp> | Like <samp class="listingcharacter">strip()</samp> , but only at the end of the string. |

**Table 5.8**     Differences between trim() and strip*()

None of these four methods can remove whitespace in the middle of a string.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example removes spaces and similar fill characters at the beginning and end of a string:

```
String s = " \tTalk to the hand.\n  \t ";
System.out.println( "'" + 
                        s.trim() + "'" ); // 'Talk to the hand.' 
```

###### [eg]   Example

The following example tests if a string is empty with all whitespace subtracted:

```
boolean isBlank = "".equals( s.
                        trim() );
```

An alternative is to write the following:

```
boolean isBlank = s.
                        trim().isEmpty();
```

### 5.5.11    Searched, Found, and Replaced

Since <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects are immutable, a change method can only return a new string with the changes.

```
final class java.lang.
                String
implements Serializable, Comparable<String>, CharSequence 
```

In Java, four methods can perform search and replace actions:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String replace(char oldChar, char newChar)</samp>
    Replaces all occurrences of the <samp class="listingcharacter">oldChar</samp> character with <samp class="listingcharacter">newChar</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String replace(CharSequence target, CharSequence replacement)</samp>
    One character string is replaced with another character string.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String replaceAll(String regex, String replacement)</samp>
    Replaces all strings described by a regular expression.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String replaceFirst(String regex, String replacement)</samp>
    Replaces the first string described by a regular expression.

#### Replacing without Regular Expressions

The <samp class="listingcharacter">replace(char, char)</samp> method replaces single characters.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example changes the letter “o” occurring in a string to “u”:

```
String s1 = "H
                        on
                        olulu";
String s2 = s1.
                        replace( 'o', 'u' );          // s2 = "H
                        un
                        ululu" 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object named <samp class="listingcharacter">s1</samp> doesn’t get changed. Only a new <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object with the content <samp class="listingcharacter">Hunululu</samp> is created and returned by <samp class="listingcharacter">replace(...)</samp> .

If something must be replaced, <samp class="listingcharacter">replace(...)</samp> internally creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> array, performs the replacements, and converts the internal character array to a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object that represents the return. If there’s nothing to replace, we’ll get back the same <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object that made the request. The <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">replace(...)</samp> method always replaces all characters. We must write ourselves a variant that replaces only the first character.

A second overloaded variant, <samp class="listingcharacter">replace(CharSequence, CharSequence)</samp> , searches for all occurring strings and replaces them with another string. The replacement string can also be empty, in which case the characters in the result will be deleted.

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, for the string <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> , “wristwatches” should be replaced by “watches”:

```
String s = "Which wristwatches are Swiss wristwatches?";
System.out.println( s.replace( "wristwatches", "watches" ) );
```

The result is: “Which watches are Swiss watches?”

#### Searching and Replacing with Regular Expressions*

The methods <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceAll(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceFirst(...)</samp> search in strings using regular expressions and make replacements. <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceFirst(...)</samp> , as the name suggests, replaces only the first occurrence.

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, more than two spaces in a row should be compressed to one space:

```
String s = "A  proper  copper    coffee pot.";
System.out.println( s.replaceAll( " +", " " ) );  
// A proper copper coffee pot.
System.out.println( s.replaceFirst( " +", " " ) );
// A proper  copper    coffee pot. 
```

Because the search string is always a regular expression and special characters like “.” or “+” have a special role, <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceAll(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceFirst(...)</samp> aren’t directly suitable for general replacement tasks; instead, the <samp class="listingcharacter">replace(...)</samp> method is more suitable and also faster.

###### [eg]  Example

For string replacement, you can juxtapose <samp class="listingcharacter">replace(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceAll(...)</samp> , as in the following example:

```
String s = """
    I’m Watt. \
    What’s your name? \

                            Watt’s my name. \
    Yes, what’s your name?""";
System.out.println( s.replace( ".", "!" ) );
```

The call replaces all dots with exclamation marks, so the result would be the following:

```
I’m Watt! What’s your name? Watt’s my name! Yes, what’s your name?
```

Using <samp class="listingcharacter">s.replaceAll(".", "!")</samp> won’t be successful, since the following string will be the result:

```
!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
```

The dot (.) stands for any character in regular expressions. Only when a backslash ( <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp>) masks out the dot (since the backslash is used in escape sequences in strings, this character itself must also be masked out), a statement like <samp class="listingcharacter">s.replaceAll("\\.", "!")</samp> returns the desired result. The static method <samp class="listingcharacter">Pattern.quote(String)</samp> masks out the pattern special characters for you, so that <samp class="listingcharacter">s.replaceAll(Pattern.quote("."), "!")</samp> works fine. The API documentation [https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/util/regex/Pattern.html](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/util/regex/Pattern.html) provides some small examples in addition to the full documentation.

### 5.5.12    Creating String Objects with Constructors and from Repeats*

The <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class has various methods that build new <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects, especially because <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects are immutable. These methods include <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">join(</samp>...), and <samp class="listingcharacter">format(</samp> ...).

#### Building New String Objects with Constructors

If the string isn’t present as a string literal, new <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects can be built using the various constructors of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class. Most constructors are intended for special cases and don’t occur in normal Java programs. With a quick overview, the function is self-explanatory:

```
final class java.lang
                    .String
implements CharSequence, Comparable<String>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String()</samp>
    Creates a new object without characters (the empty string <samp class="listingcharacter">""</samp> ).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String(String string)</samp>
    Creates a new object with a copy of <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>. Basically, the constructor is unnecessary since <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects are immutable .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String(char[] value)</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">String(char[] value, int offset, int length)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">String(int[] codePoints, int offset, int count)</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">String(byte[] bytes)</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">String(byte[] bytes, int offset, int length)</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">String(byte[] bytes, String charsetName) throws UnsupportedEncodingException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String(byte[] bytes, Charset charset)</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">String(byte[] bytes, int offset, int length, String charsetName)</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">throws UnsupportedEncodingException</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">String(byte[] bytes, int offset, int length, Charset charset)</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">String(StringBuffer buffer)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String(StringBuilder builder)</samp>

In particular, the constructors are only necessary if a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object is to be built from a foreign representation such as a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">char[]</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">byte[]</samp> or parts (substring or sub-array) of them.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example tests whether two strings—regardless of case—represent anagrams, that is, the two strings have the same letters:

```
String a1 = "iPad", a2 = "Paid";
char[] a1chars = a1.toCharArray();
char[] a2chars = a2.toCharArray();
Arrays.sort( a1chars );
Arrays.sort( a2chars );
boolean isAnangram = 
                        new String(a1chars).equalsIgnoreCase(
                        new String(a2chars));
System.out.println( isAnangram );       // true 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.sort(...)</samp> method sorts an array, in this case, the <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> array. If case sensitivity is relevant, <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.equals(char[], char[])</samp> can be used.

#### On the Constructor Call New String(String)

One constructor easily leads to confusion—the constructor that adopts another string. Thus, the following two lines result in the reference to a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object:

```
String rudi = "There is no spoon";
String rudi = new String( "There is no spoon" ); 
```

The second solution unnecessarily creates an additional <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object because the literal is already a full-fledged <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object. The constructor is basically unnecessary.

#### Strings in the Constant Pool

The JVM automatically creates a corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object for each string literal. This creation happens once at most for each constant string, no matter how often the JVM uses it in the course of the program and which classes reference the string. This <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object “lives” in an area called the constant pool . [[ 121 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn05_11)

###### [»]  Note

Let’s assume that the following statement is contained in one class <samp class="listingcharacter">A</samp> and in another class <samp class="listingcharacter">B</samp> :

```
System.out.println( 
                        "tutego" );
```

We can execute the following code:

```
int len = "tutego".length();
```

Then, the string “tutego” exists as a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object only once in the runtime environment.

For constant values, the compiler performs optimizations, such as computing constant expressions the same way. Not only does it insert the result <samp class="listingcharacter">3</samp> for expressions like <samp class="listingcharacter">1 + 2</samp> , but the compiler also joins broken constant string parts concatenated with plus to form a string.

###### [eg]  Example

The first and second declarations look the same in the bytecode:

```
String s =
 "Operating systems are like underwear-nobody really wants to look at them.";
String s = "Operating systems are like underwear" 
                        +
           '-' 
                        + "nobody really wants to look at them."; 
```

The compiler automatically merges the strings [[ 122 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn05_12) into one large string, so no concatenation is necessary at runtime. The compiler always “calculates” constant expressions directly itself.

#### Empty Strings or Null Strings

The statements both reference <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects that don’t contain any characters:

```
String s = "";
String s = new String(); 
```

However, the second notation creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object, while in the first case the string literal is in the constant pool.

We call a string without characters an empty string or a null string . Unfortunately, the last term is chosen somewhat unfortunately, so we won’t use it in the book because the term null string can easily be confused with the term <samp class="listingcharacter">null reference</samp>. But while access to a null string might be unproblematic, de-references on the <samp class="listingcharacter">null reference</samp> inevitably lead to a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> , as in the following example:

```
String s = null;
System.out.println( s );         // Output: null
s.length();                      // 

                     NullPointerException 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">print*(null)</samp> results in the console output “null,” and no exception arises because the case distinction in <samp class="listingcharacter">print*(Object)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">print*(String)</samp> consider the <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> reference as a special case. [[ 123 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn05_13) Accessing <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> via <samp class="listingcharacter">s.length()</samp>, on the other hand, leads to the unpopular <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> .

#### Generating Strings from Repetitions

The useful object method <samp class="listingcharacter">repeat(int count)</samp> multiplies a string.

###### [eg]  Example

The following code repeats the string <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> three times:

```
String s = "tu";
System.out.println( s.repeat( 3 ) );    // tututu 
```

## 5.6    Mutable Strings with StringBuilder and StringBuffer

Strings stored in <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects in the Java virtual machine share a property in that their contents can’t be modified. The object of the classes <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> , to which changes can be made, behave differently. The changes subsequently affect the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> object itself, and no newly created object is returned as a result, as for example with the plus operator and the <samp class="listingcharacter">concat(String)</samp> method for conventional <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects. But apart from that difference, the implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> objects is similar. In both cases, the classes use an internal character array.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> class provides the same methods as <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> but isn’t synchronized. In concurrent programs, the internal data structure of the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> object can therefore become inconsistent. <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> works a bit more quickly because the implementation doesn’t need to take care of concurrent access. Nowadays, however, the difference is no longer significant; that is, non-parallel access to a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> is equally fast.

<samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> can be quickly explained: A constructor builds the objects and modification methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp>, and the <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> method returns the result as a string.

###### [»]  Note

Because of the symmetrical API of <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>, we’ll only refer to the methods of <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> in the following sections.

### 5.6.1    Creating StringBuilder Objects

You can use various constructors to build <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects:

```
final class java.lang.
                StringBuilder
implements Appendable, CharSequence, Comparable<StringBuilder>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder()</samp>
    Creates a new object that contains the empty character line and has space for (initially) up to 16 characters. Subsequent insert operations fill in the buffer and automatically increase it further.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder(int length)</samp>
    Similar to the previous constructor, but the initial capacity of the object is sufficient for the specified number of characters. Ideally, you should set the size so that it’s close to the final size of the dynamic string.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder(String str)</samp>
    Builds an object that contains a copy of the characters from <samp class="listingcharacter">str</samp> . In addition, the constructor already plans space for 16 more characters.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder(CharSequence seq)</samp>
    Creates a new object from a <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp>. Thus, the strings of other <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects can also become the basis of this object.

Since only <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects are supported directly by the language, you can only use the explicit call of a constructor to create <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects. All string literals in quotes are already instances of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class.

###### [»]  Note

Neither in the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class nor in <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> does a constructor exist that explicitly allows a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> as a parameter to build a string from the given character. Nevertheless, <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> has a constructor that accepts an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, where the passed integer speci fies the internal starting size of the buffer. If we call the constructor with a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>—for example, a <samp class="listingcharacter">'*'</samp>—the compiler automatically converts the character to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. The resulting object doesn’t contain any character but has only an initial capacity of 42 characters, since 42 is the ASCII code of the asterisk. Consequently, the only correct way to build a mutable string filled with the starting character <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">new StringBuilder(Character.toString(c))</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">new StringBuilder().append(c)</samp> .

### 5.6.2    Converting StringBuilder to Other String Formats

<samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> is usually used internally in methods but rarely appears as a parameter or return type. From the constructors of the classes, notice how a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> is built for a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> parameter type, for example, but the way back is missing.

```
final class java.lang.
                StringBuilder
implements Appendable, CharSequence, Comparable<StringBuilder>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String toString()</samp>
    Creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object from the current string.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void getChars(int srcBegin, int srcEnd, char[] dst, int dstBegin)</samp>
    Copies a desired section into a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> array.

### 5.6.3    Requesting Characters or Strings

The familiar request methods from <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> can also be found in <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">charAt(int)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">getChars(...)</samp> behave identically for instances of both classes. Also, <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(int start)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(int start, int end)</samp> are known from the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class as well. If only these methods are necessary, a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> is also unnecessary, and a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object is sufficient.

### 5.6.4    Appending Data

The most common use of <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects is to join texts from data of different types. For this purpose, the classes declare a number of <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> methods that are overloaded with different data types. The <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> methods of <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> return a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> methods always append data to the end and increase the internal space—an internal array—if necessary. They don’t create a new <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> object. Let’s use this information for a custom <samp class="listingcharacter">enumerate(...)</samp> method that traverses a string array and generates a screen enumeration.

```
public static String enumerate( String... lines ) {
  if ( lines == null || lines.length == 0 )
    return "";

                StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();

 for ( int i = 0; i < lines.length; i++ ) {

                sb.append( i + 1 
                );
    sb.append( ". " 
                );
    sb.append( lines[i] 
                ).append( System.lineSeparator() 
                );
  }

  return 
                sb.toString().trim();
} 
```

**Listing 5.8**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/string/Enumerator.java, enumerate(…)

A call of <samp class="listingcharacter">enumerate("It's your choice to take this personally.", "Life is effort. I'll stop when I die!")</samp> returns a string that looks like the following output:

```
1\. It’s your choice to take this personally.
2\. Life is effort. I'll stop when I die! 
```

The summary lists all <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> methods:

```
final class java.lang.
                StringBuilder
implements Appendable, CharSequence, Comparable<StringBuilder>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(boolean b)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(char c)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(char[] str)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(char[] str, int offset, int len)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(CharSequence s)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(CharSequence s, int start, int end)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(double d)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(float f)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(long lng)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(Object obj)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(String str)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder append(StringBuilder sb)</samp>

The methods <samp class="listingcharacter">append(char)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">append(CharSequence)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">append(CharSequence, int, int)</samp> are required by the interface <samp class="listingcharacter">Appendable</samp> .

Particularly useful in practice is <samp class="listingcharacter">append(CharSequence, int, int)</samp>, which allows you to append parts of <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> objects.

###### [»]  Note

Each <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> method modifies the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> and returns a reference to it. This scenario has a great advantage in that calls of the <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> methods can be easily cascaded, as in the following example:

```
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder( "George Peppard" )
                    .append('
                    ,'
                    );
sb.append(" Mr. T, ").append("Dirk Benedict, ").append("Dwight Schultz");
```

The evaluation is from left to right, so the result is “George Peppard, Mr. T, Dirk Benedict, Dwight Schultz”.

###### [+]  Tip

Using the plus operator inside <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> strings is counterproductive. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">sb.append(", " + value)</samp> would be better written as <samp class="listingcharacter">sb.append(", ").append(value)</samp> .

### 5.6.5    Setting, Deleting, and Reversing Characters and Strings

Since characters can be modified in a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>, other modification methods besides the <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> methods can be used that are missing in the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class.

#### Setting Individual Characters

```
final class java.lang.
                    StringBuilder
implements Appendable, CharSequence, Comparable<StringBuilder>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void setCharAt(int index, char ch)</samp>
    Replaces <samp class="listingcharacter">index</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter">ch</samp> character and overrides the old character.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example changes the first character in the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> to an uppercase letter:

```
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder( "save water, shower together" );
char upperCharacter = Character.toUpperCase( sb.charAt(0) );
sb.
                        setCharAt( 0, upperCharacter );
```

The first argument <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">setCharAt(int, char)</samp> represents the position of the character to be set.

#### Inserting Strings

Various <samp class="listingcharacter">insert (...)</samp> methods insert the string representation of a value in a specific position, which is similar to the overloaded <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> method:

```
final class java.lang.
                    StringBuilder
implements Appendable, CharSequence, Comparable<StringBuilder>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int offset, boolean b)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int offset, char c)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int offset, char[] str)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int index, char[] str, int offset, int len)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int dstOffset, CharSequence s)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int dstOffset, CharSequence s, int start, int end)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int offset, double d)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int offset, float f)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int offset, int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int offset, long l)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int offset, Object obj)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder insert(int offset, String str)</samp>

For <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> arrays, <samp class="listingcharacter">insert(...)</samp> is available in a modified way: <samp class="listingcharacter">insert(int index, char[] str, int offset, int len)</samp>. In this case, the method doesn’t transfer the complete array into the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> , only a section.

#### Deleting Single Characters and Character Ranges

A sequence of characters can be deleted via <samp class="listingcharacter">delete(int start, int end)</samp>. Similarly, <samp class="listingcharacter">deleteCharAt(int index)</samp> deletes only one character. In both cases, an incorrect index is penalized by a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringIndexOutOfBoundsException</samp> .

#### Replacing Character Ranges

The <samp class="listingcharacter">replace(int start, int end, String str)</samp> method first deletes the characters between <samp class="listingcharacter">start</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">end</samp> and then inserts the new string <samp class="listingcharacter">str</samp> starting from <samp class="listingcharacter">start</samp> . As always, the end positions are exclusive; that is, they specify the first character after the section to be changed.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example replaces the substring at positions 4 and 5 (that is, up to and excluding 6):

```
 StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder( "Sub-XX-Sens-O-Matic" );
//                                     0123456
System.out.println( sb.
                        replace( 4, 6, "Etha" ) ) ;  // Sub-Etha-Sens-O-Matic 
```

#### Reversing Strings

Another method, <samp class="listingcharacter">reverse()</samp> , reverses the string.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example tests whether <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> string is a palindrome, regardless of case. Palindromes read the same from the beginning as from the end, such as “racecar”:

```
boolean isPalindrome =
  new StringBuilder( s ).
                        reverse().toString().equalsIgnoreCase( s );
```

### 5.6.6    Length and Capacity of a StringBuilder Object*

As with a string, the length and the number of characters contained can be queried via the <samp class="listingcharacter">length ()</samp> method. However, <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects also have an internal buffer size, which can be queried via <samp class="listingcharacter">capacity()</samp> and is set in the constructor as described. In this buffer, which is rather an array of type <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>, changes, such as cutting or appending characters, are made. While <samp class="listingcharacter">length()</samp> specifies the number of characters, <samp class="listingcharacter">capacity()</samp> is always greater than or equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">length()</samp> and tells us something about how many more characters the buffer can store without needing a new, larger internal array.

###### [eg]  Example

```
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder( "www.tutego.de" );
System.out.println( sb.
                    length() );                      // 13
System.out.println( sb.
                    capacity() );                    // 29 
```

For the length query, <samp class="listingcharacter">sb.length()</samp> returns 13, but <samp class="listingcharacter">sb.capacity()</samp> returns 13 + 16 = 29.

The start size should be initialized with the expected size to avoid internal zooming later, which costs more computing time. If the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> has a large internal buffer, but is short on characters in the long run, it can be shrunk to a smaller size with <samp class="listingcharacter">trimToSize()</samp> .

#### Changing the Length

If the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> is supposed to store more data, <samp class="listingcharacter">setLength(int)</samp> changes the length to a specified number of characters. The parameter is the new length. If it’s smaller than <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">length()</samp> , the rest of the string will simply be truncated, but this approach doesn’t change the size of the internal buffer.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example concatenates all strings in an array with a separator and truncates the last separator at the end:

```
String[] elements = { "Manila", "Cebu", "Ipil" };
String separator = ", ";
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for ( String elem : elements )
  sb.append( elem ).append( separator );

                        sb.setLength( sb.length() - separator.length() );
System.out.println( sb );          // Manila, Cebu, Ipil 
```

If <samp class="listingcharacter">setLength(int)</samp> is greater, the buffer increases, and the method fills the remaining characters with null characters <samp class="listingcharacter">\0000</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">ensureCapacity(int)</samp> method requires that the internal buffer is sufficient for a certain number of characters. If necessary, the method creates a new, enlarged <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> array but doesn’t change the string represented by the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> object.

### 5.6.7    Comparison of StringBuilder Instances and Strings with StringBuilder

The well-known <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method can be used to compare <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>s. However, this method is not implemented in <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> as expected. In addition, other methods can make comparisons without regard to case.

#### equals(...) for the String Class

The <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class implements the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp> method so that a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> can be compared to another <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp>. However, <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> compares only <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> pairs. The method doesn’t start the comparison until the argument is also of type <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>.
