Thus, the compiler allows all passes also of type <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> at <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp>, but at runtime the result is always <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>, because a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> simply isn’t of type <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> . Whether the strings are the same or not is irrelevant.

#### contentEquals(...) for the String

A common method for comparing one string with either another string or with <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">contentEquals(CharSequence)</samp>. This method returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> and the <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> have the same character content. (Recall that <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> are classes of type <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp>.) The internal length of the buffer doesn’t matter. If the argument is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> gets thrown.

###### [eg]   Example

The following example compares a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> with a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> :

```
String        s  = "Cognition Amplifier";
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder( "Cognition Amplifier" );
System.out.println( s.
                        equals(sb) );                   // false
System.out.println( s.
                        equals(sb.toString()) );        // true
System.out.println( s.
                        contentEquals(sb) );            // true 
```

#### No Own equals(...) for StringBuilder

To compare two <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects with each other, you cannot use the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method. For the usual method inherited from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>, only object references are compared. In other words, <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> doesn’t override the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method. Thus, if two different <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects with the same content are compared with <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>, the result is always <samp class="listingcharacter">false.</samp>

###### [eg]  Example

To implement the content comparison of two <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects, you can first convert them to strings with <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> and then compare them using <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> methods, as in the following example:

```
StringBuilder sb1 = new StringBuilder( "The Ocean Cleanup" );
StringBuilder sb2 = new StringBuilder( "The Ocean Cleanup" ); 
System.out.println( 
                        sb1.equals( sb2 ) );                        // false
System.out.println( 
                        sb1.toString().equals( sb2.toString() ) );  // true
System.out.println( 
                        sb1.toString().contentEquals( sb2 ) );      // true 
```

You’ll learn about another option in the following section.

#### Lexicographic Comparisons (StringBuilder is Comparable)

<samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> allows lexicographic comparisons via the <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(StringBuilder another)</samp> method. ( <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> implements the interface <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable<StringBuilder></samp>.) Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> both realize an ordering (see the section on lexicographic comparisons in [Section 5.5.8](#05_005.html_h5.5.8) ).

One side effect is that, for equal strings, the return of <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp> is 0\. This approach, however, is much better than converting the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> to a string first.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp> method of <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> performs the comparison only with other <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects. The static method <samp class="listingcharacter">compare(CharSequence, CharSequence)</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> is more flexible in this respect. With this method, a lexicographic comparison of all conceivable <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> instances is possible.

###### [eg]   Example

These are proper ways to compare two <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> instances:

```
StringBuilder sb1 = new StringBuilder( "The Ocean Cleanup" );
StringBuilder sb2 = new StringBuilder( "The Ocean Cleanup" ); 
System.out.println( 
                        sb1.compareTo( sb2 ) == 0 );                // true
System.out.println( 
                        CharSequence.compare( sb1, sb2 ) == 0 );    // true 
```

### 5.6.8    hashCode() with StringBuilder*

Our previous discussion shows that an <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method that compares the content of <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects wouldn’t be bad. Nevertheless, a problem exists regarding when exactly <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects should be considered equal. This question is interesting because <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> objects are not only determined by their content, but also by the sizes of their internal buffers, that is, by their capacities. Should <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> return <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the contents are equal, or only if the contents and buffer size are equal? Since every developer has different views on equivalence, the default test for identical object references remains the only one. A similar reasoning applies to the <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method, which returns the same, ideally unique, numeric value for all objects with the same content. The <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class has a <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method, but <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> inherits the implementation from the <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> class unchanged. In other words, the classes themselves don’t provide an implementation.

## 5.7    CharSequence as Base Type

So far, you’ve learned how the classes <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> can store and pass strings. A <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> is a value object and an important tool in programs since immutable string values are represented by it, while <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> comprise mutable strings.

But what happens when a substring is required where it shouldn’t matter whether the original is a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> object? And what if read-only access is to be allowed so that changes are excluded? One solution is to expect everything to be a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object (and the Java library does this). But then the program parts that use <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> internally must first construct a new <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> , and that costs resources.

Fortunately, the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> classes have a common base type: <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> . This type represents an immutable, read-only sequence of characters. (Interfaces, base types, and their implementation are described further in [Chapter 8](#08_001.html_h8), [Section 8.1](#08_001.html_h8.1).) Methods therefore no longer must decide on concrete classes but can simply accept a <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> object as an argument or pass it on as a return. As a return, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> isn’t especially useful; in this context, <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> is more practical. A <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> and a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> object have many more methods than <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp>, but as a parameter type, <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> is well suited if more functionality isn’t needed.

[![Some Implementing Classes of the CharSequence Interface](bilderklein/klein05_003.png)](img-f5.3.html)

**Figure 5.3**     Some Implementing Classes of the CharSequence Interface

###### [eg]  Example

If a method is to obtain a string and the type doesn’t matter, you can implement something like the following example:

```
void process( CharSequence s ) {
  …
}
```

In this way, you can avoid the use of these two methods:

```
void process( String s ) { … }
void process( StringBuilder sb ) {
  process( sb.toString() );
}
```

### 5.7.1    Basic Operations of the Interface

The <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> interface makes three methods mandatory for the implementing classes:

```
interface java.lang.
                CharSequence 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">char charAt(int index)</samp>
    Returns the character at the <samp class="listingcharacter">index</samp> position.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int length()</samp>
    Returns the length of the character string.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default boolean isEmpty()</samp>
    Abbreviation for the test <samp class="listingcharacter">length() == 0</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence subSequence(int start, int end)</samp>
    Returns a new <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">start</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">end</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">subSequence(...)</samp> returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> object. The effect is the same as calling <samp class="listingcharacter">substring(begin, end)</samp> on a <samp class="listingcharacter">string</samp> ; only the return type is different.

The following method already present anyway via the absolute superclass <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Object</samp> :

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String toString()</samp>
    Returns a string of the sequence. The length of the <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> string is exactly the length of the sequence.

Among others, <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> are implementing classes of the <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> interface and implement these methods:

```
class java.lang.String implements CharSequence, …
class java.lang.StringBuilder implements CharSequence, …
class java.lang.StringBuffer implements CharSequence, … 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence subSequence(int beginIndex, int endIndex)</samp>
    Returns a read-only substring.

### 5.7.2    Static compare(...) Method in CharSequence

<samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> has the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">compare(...)</samp>, which compares two <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> objects lexicographically:

```
interface java.lang.
                CharSequence 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int compare(CharSequence cs1, CharSequence cs2)</samp>
    Compares the two strings lexicographically.

This static method has an advantage in that now all combinations of <samp class="listingcharacter">CharBuffer</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Segment</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> can be checked with this one method. Furthermore, if the comparison results in 0, you also know that the strings contain the same characters.

### 5.7.3     Default Methods in the CharSequence Interface*

This interface has two default methods:

```
interface java.lang.
                CharSequence 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default IntStream chars()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default IntStream codePoints()</samp>

The importance of <samp class="listingcharacter">default</samp> and interfaces in general is discussed in [Chapter 7](#07_001.html_h7). At this point, we just want to emphasize the advantage that <samp class="listingcharacter">chars()</samp> can be used to run over the characters. However, this method has nothing to do with the extended <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> , but with a different programming idiom.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example runs over a string and outputs each character:

```
"Drama is life with the dull bits left out.".chars().forEach( c ->
  System.out.print( (char) c )
 );
```

Syntactically, this example uses lambda expressions, which are introduced in detail in [Chapter 13](#13_001.html_h13) .

## 5.8    Converting Primitives and Strings

Before a data type can be output to the screen, sent to the printer, or stored in an ASCII file, the Java program must convert it to a string. For example, if we output the number 7 without conversion, we wouldn’t see a “7” on the screen, but your computer may beep, depending on the implementation. Conversion is also important the other way round: If a user specifies his or her age in a dialog, this value is always a string at first. In a second step, the application must convert this value to an integer to implement an age query, for example.

### 5.8.1    Converting Different Types to String Representations

Overloaded static <samp class="listingcharacter">String.valueOf(...)</samp> methods return the string representation of a primitive value or object.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example shows some conversions of data types to strings:

```
 String s1 = String.valueOf( 10 );                // 10
String s2 = String.valueOf( Math.PI );           // 3.141592653589793
String s3 = String.valueOf( 1 < 2 );             // true 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(...)</samp> method is overloaded, and in total, an implementation exists for each primitive data type:

```
final class java.lang
                .String
implements CharSequence, Comparable<String>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String valueOf(boolean b)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String valueOf(char c)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String valueOf(double d)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String valueOf(float f)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String valueOf(int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String valueOf(long l)</samp>
    Returns the string representation of the primitive elements.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String valueOf(char[] data)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String valueOf(char[] data, int offset, int count)</samp>
    Returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object from the <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> array or a section of the <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> array.

#### The valueOf(Object) Method

You can pass any object to the <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(Object)</samp> method.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example shows some conversions of objects to strings:

```
String r = String.valueOf( new java.awt.Point() );  // java.awt.Point[x=0,y=0]
String s = String.valueOf( java.nio.file.Paths.get( "." ) ); // .
String t = String.valueOf( java.time.LocalTime.now() ); // 09:48:28.047834 
```

Since each object has a <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> method, <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(Object)</samp> simply delegates to it.

```
public static String valueOf( Object obj ) {
  return (obj == null) ? "null" : obj.toString();} 
```

**Listing 5.9**     java/lang/String.java, valueOf()

The implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(Object obj)</samp> simply asks the <samp class="listingcharacter">obj</samp> object itself for the string conversion. The special handling tests whether <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> was passed and then returns a valid string with the content <samp class="listingcharacter">"null"</samp>. Since <samp class="listingcharacter">String.valueOf(null)</samp> returns “null,” an output like <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println(null)</samp> also outputs the string <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> to the console because <samp class="listingcharacter">println(Object)</samp> internally calls <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(…)</samp>. Likewise, <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out. println(null + "0")</samp> produces the output <samp class="listingcharacter">"null0"</samp> since <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> is a link in the addition chain.

```
final class java.lang
                    .String
implements CharSequence, Comparable<String>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String valueOf(Object obj)</samp>
    If <samp class="listingcharacter">obj</samp> is not equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">bull</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">obj.toString()</samp> method returns, otherwise it returns “null.”

### 5.8.2    Converting String Contents to a Primitive Value

Parsing a string—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">"123"</samp> from a user input for the integer 123—isn’t the responsibility of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class, but of special classes that exist for each primitive data type. The classes listed in [Table 5.9](#05_008.html_t5.9) declare static <samp class="listingcharacter">parse*(string)</samp> methods.

| Class | Conversion Method | Return Type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Boolean</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">parseBoolean( String s )</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Byte</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">parseByte( String s )</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Short</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">parseShort( String s )</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Integer</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt( String s )</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">parseLong( String s )</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Double</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">parseDouble( String s )</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Float</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">parseFloat( String s )</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> |

**Table 5.9**     Methods for Converting a String to a Primitive Type

For each primitive type, what’s called a wrapper class is available with <samp class="listingcharacter">parse*(string)</samp> conversion methods. [Chapter 11](#11_001.html_h11), [Section 11.5](#11_005.html_h11.5) , explains the meaning of these classes in more detail. At this point, we only briefly consider the conversion functionality.

#### Example with Double.parseDouble(String)

Let’s use the <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.parseDouble(String)</samp> method in an example. The user is asked for a float in a graphical dialog box, and the sine and cosine of this number should then be output to the screen.

```
 String s = javax.swing.JOptionPane.showInputDialog( "Input floating decimal" );
double value = Double.parseDouble( s );
System.out.println( "Sine:   " + Math.sin( value ) );
System.out.println( "Cosine: " + Math.cos( value ) ); 
```

**Listing 5.10**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/string/SineAndCosine.java (Snippet)

#### parse*(String) and Potential NumberFormatException Errors

If a <samp class="listingcharacter">parse*(String)</samp> method can’t perform a conversion because a string like <samp class="listingcharacter">"1lala2lö"</samp> cannot be converted, it throws a <samp class="listingcharacter">NumberFormatException</samp>. This problem also arises when <samp class="listingcharacter">parseDouble(String)</samp> receives a comma instead of a period as decimal separator. For the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">parseBoolean(String)</samp> , case is irrelevant.

###### [»]  Note

This <samp class="listingcharacter">NumberFormatException</samp> error can serve as a test to determine whether a string contains a number or not, because no check method like <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.isInteger(String)</samp> is available. An alternative is to use a regular expression and test against it, for instance, in the following example:

```
stringWithNumber.matches("\\p{Digit}+")
```

#### parse*(...) and the Behavior with Plus, Minus, and Space Characters

If a string represents negative numbers, the string starts with a “-”; positive numbers may also start with a “+.” The static conversion method <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.parseInt(String)</samp> doesn’t truncate spaces and would report a parser error if, for example, the string ended with a space. (The creator of the Java library, however, thought differently with <samp class="listingcharacter">Float.parseFloat(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.parseDouble(...)</samp> , because the string is automatically trimmed before parsing.)

###### [eg]  Example

The following example truncates spaces from the string and converts it to an integer:

```
String s = " 1234    ".
                        trim();            // s = "1234"
int i = Integer.parseInt( s );            // i = 1234 
```

What appears as the result in a <samp class="listingcharacter">String.valueOf(...)</samp>—and this is also what <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.print*(...)</samp> is based on, for example—can <samp class="listingcharacter">parse*(...)</samp> back into the same value.

#### Localized parse*(String)

The <samp class="listingcharacter">parse*(...)</samp> methods aren’t localized, so they can only convert English formatted strings into primitive values. With integers, this method is no problem, but with floats, a big problem arises because <samp class="listingcharacter">parseDouble("1,3")</samp> leads to <samp class="listingcharacter">NumberFormatException</samp>, while <samp class="listingcharacter">parseDouble("1.3")</samp> doesn’t. Two approaches to solving this problem are available. One is to convert the decimal separator to a point beforehand, as in the following example:

```
String s = "3,1";
double d = Double.parseDouble( 
                    s.replace( ',', '.' ) );               // 3.1 
```

However, this solution isn’t good. Rather, a much better approach is to draw on classes that allow localized parsing, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">scanners</samp> (we’ll return to this class in [Section 5.10.2](#05_010.html_h5.10.2) ):

```
String s = "3,1";
double d = 
                    new Scanner( s ).useLocale( Locale.GERMANY ).nextDouble(); // 3.1 
```

### 5.8.3    String Representation in Binary, Hex, and Octal Formats*

In addition to the overloaded static <samp class="listingcharacter">String.valueOf(primitive)</samp> methods, which return a number from a string representation in the familiar decimal system, and the reverse <samp class="listingcharacter">parse*(...)</samp> methods of the wrapper classes, other methods can convert and parse strings into the following number systems:

*   Binary (base 2)

*   Octals (base 8)

*   Hexadecimal (base 16)

*   Any base (up to 36)

The methods aren’t found in the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class, but together with methods for parsing in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> classes.

#### Building String Representations

On one hand, general class methods <samp class="listingcharacter">toString(int i, int radix)</samp> are available for any radix in the classes <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> . On the other hand, special methods exist for the radixes 2, 8, and 16.

```
final class java.lang.
                    Integer
extends Number
implements Comparable<Integer>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toBinaryString(int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toOctalString(int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toHexString(int i)</samp>
    Creates a binary representation (base 2), octal number representation (base 8), or hexadecimal representation (base 16) of the unsigned number.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toString(int i, int radix)</samp>
    Creates a string representation of the number to the specified base.

```
 final class java.lang.
                    Long
extends Number
implements Comparable<Long>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toBinaryString(long i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toOctalString(long i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toHexString(long i)</samp>
    Creates a binary representation (base 2), octal number representation (base 8), or hexadecimal representation (base 16) of the unsigned number.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toString(long i, int radix)</samp>
    Creates a string representation of the number to the specified base.

Negative numbers get a negative sign with the <samp class="listingcharacter">toString(...)</samp> methods, which isn’t true for the other methods mentioned.

The parameter type is <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> and not <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> , which leads to outputs that must be taken into consideration. In the same way, leading zeros aren’t output.

| Statement | Result |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.toHexString(15)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.toHexString(16)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">10</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.toHexString(127)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">7f</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.toHexString(128)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">80</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.toHexString(255)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ff</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.toHexString(256)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">100</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.toHexString(-1)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ffffffff</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Long.toHexString(-1)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">ffffffffffffffff</samp> |

**Table 5.10**     Examples of the toHexString() Method

If the number is negative, it’s treated unsigned, and 2 ^(32) (for <samp class="listingcharacter">integer</samp>) and 2 ^(64) (for <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> ) are added.

Output with <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(...)</samp>—or formatting with <samp class="listingcharacter">String.format(...)</samp>—provides an alternative, as described in detail in [Section 5.11.1](#05_011.html_h5.11.1) .

###### [»]  Note

A conversion with <samp class="listingcharacter">toHexString(x)</samp> isn’t the same with negative numbers as with <samp class="listingcharacter">toString(x, 16)</samp> , as shown in the following example:

```
 System.out.println( Integer.toHexString( -10 ) );  // fffffff6
System.out.println( Integer.toString( -10, 16 ) ); // -a 
```

In this case, <samp class="listingcharacter">toHexString(...)</samp> applies what is given as a remark in the Java documentation, namely, that for negative numbers the unsigned number is taken (i.e., 10) and then 2 ^(32) is added, which isn’t the case with <samp class="listingcharacter">toString(...)</samp> and an arbitrary radix.

#### Parsing Strings with radix

A method for converting a string to an integer for a given base can be found in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> classes. Only the <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> classes contain support for a base that is also not equal to 10:

```
final class java.lang.
                    Integer
extends Number
implements Comparable<Integer>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int parseInt(String s)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int parseInt(String s, int radix)</samp>

```
final class java.lang.
                    Long
extends Number
implements Comparable<Long>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long parseLong(String s)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long parseLong(String s, int radix)</samp>

Some use cases include the following:

| Conversion Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt("0", 10)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt("473", 10)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">473</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt("-0", 10)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt("-FF", 16)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">-255</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt("1100110", 2)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">102</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt("2147483647", 10)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">2147483647</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt("-2147483648", 10)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">-2147483648</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt("2147483648", 10)</samp> | ![inline image](bilder/totenkopf.png)<samp class="listingcharacter"> throws NumberFormatException</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt("99", 8)</samp> | ![inline image](bilder/totenkopf.png)<samp class="listingcharacter"> throws NumberFormatException</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt("Papa", 10)</samp> | ![inline image](bilder/totenkopf.png)<samp class="listingcharacter"> throws NumberFormatException</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt("Papa", 27)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">500050</samp> |

**Table 5.11**     Examples of Integer.parseInt(...) with Different Number Bases

###### [eg]  Example

The radix goes up to 36 (that is, 10 digits and 26 lowercase letters). With radix 36, for example, integer IDs can be represented more compactly as text than if they were decimal. Consider the following example:

```
String string = Long.toString( 2656437647773L, 36 );
System.out.println( string );   // xwcmdz8d
long l = 
                        Long.parseLong( string, 36 );
System.out.println( l ); // 2656437647773 
```

###### [»]  Puzzle

What is the result of the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">Long.parseLong( "" + 1 / 0., 35 )</samp> ?

#### Parsing Binary, Octal, and Hexadecimal Numbers

In the case of string conversions, special methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">toHexString(...)</samp> exist for the standard bases 2, 8, and 16, but they don’t exist for parsing. A hexadecimal number is processed by <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt(s, 16)</samp> because a method like <samp class="listingcharacter">parseHex(String)</samp> isn’t available.

###### [»]  Note

The <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">parseLong(...)</samp> methods don’t behave as expected with string representations of negative numbers. Consider the following example:

```
int i = Integer.parseInt( "7fffffff", 16 ); // 2147483647
int j = Integer.parseInt( "80000000", 16 ); // 

                         NumberFormatException 
```

0x7fffffff is the largest positive <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> number that can be represented. However, instead of returning the value -2,147,483,648 at 0x80000000, it returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">NumberFormatException</samp>. The Java API documentation also provides this example but doesn’t make this behavior particularly clear. With negative numbers and <samp class="listingcharacter">parseInt(…)</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">parseLong(…)</samp>, a minus must also be specified as a sign. So, the <samp class="listingcharacter">parse*(...)</samp> methods aren’t reverse methods to, say, <samp class="listingcharacter">toHexString(...)</samp>, but always to <samp class="listingcharacter">toString(</samp> ...). Consider the following example:

```
 System.out.println( Integer.toString( -2147483648, 16 ) ); // -80000000
System.out.println( Integer.parseInt( "-80000000", 16 ) ); // -2147483648 
```

### 5.8.4    parse*(...) and print*() Methods in DatatypeConverter*

The <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.HexFormat</samp> class helps with the task of producing and parsing hexadecimal strings.

###### [eg]  Example

Convert a byte array to a hexadecimal string representation.

```
byte[] bytes = { 1, 2, 3, (byte) 254, (byte) 255 };
HexFormat = HexFormat.ofDelimiter( " " ).withPrefix( "#" );
String hex = hexFormat.formatHex( bytes );
System.out.println( hex );
```

## 5.9    Concatenating Strings

To generate a new string from partial strings, Java provides the following options:

*   The plus operator for involved <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">concat(String)</samp> method of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> classes with their <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> methods

*   A <samp class="listingcharacter">join(...)</samp> method for the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class or the helper class <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.StringJoiner</samp> for joining parts with a common separator

*   Using <samp class="listingcharacter">format(...)</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> or the helper class <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.Formatter</samp>

In addition, a few methods and types can also be referred to as concatenations:

*   Two special <samp class="listingcharacter">append*(...)</samp> methods for appending strings in the course of a replacement in the context of regular expressions

*   A special <samp class="listingcharacter">StringWriter</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">write(</samp> ...) methods

###### [+]  Tip

The newly built <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> should ideally get the appropriate buffer size in the constructor right away. However, the JVM itself also tries to optimize concatenation.

### 5.9.1    Concatenating Strings with StringJoiner

To concatenate strings into one large result using a common separator, <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> provides the convenient helper method <samp class="listingcharacter">join(...)</samp>. This method is based on a small class named <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner</samp> , which can also be used directly.

###### [eg]   Example

Let’s say we have an array that contains prices that should be concatenated into one large string. The segments should be separated with semicolons and spaces, “USD” should be placed in front of each price, and prices should use 2 decimal places with a dot as the decimal separator. Consider the following example:

```
double[] prices = { 1.90, 2.49 };
StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner( "; " );
for ( double price : prices )
  joiner.add( String.format( Locale.ENGLISH, "USD %.2f", price ) );
System.out.println( joiner );                    // USD 1.90; USD 2.49 
```

Note that the static <samp class="listingcharacter">format(...)</samp> method is localized with English formatting.

The delimiter (which can of course also be an empty string <samp class="listingcharacter">""</samp>) is placed between each element that has been added. The <samp class="listingcharacter">add(CharSequence)</samp> method used in the example accepts a join string of type <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp> and returns the current <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner</samp>, so that the <samp class="listingcharacter">add(...)</samp> calls can be cascaded. The <samp class="listingcharacter">merge(StringJoiner)</samp> method can be used to integrate the content of another <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner</samp> .

#### Concatenating with Infixes, Prefixes, and Suffixes

Not only the separator itself can be specified, but also a start character and end character.

###### [eg]  Example

The output should start with a “{” and end with a “}” as in the following example:

```
StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner( ", ", 
                        "{", "}" );
```

#### Nothing Given to Concatenate

Sometimes, the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner</samp> isn’t given anything to join. In this case, it will still use a prefix and suffix, as in the following example:

```
StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner( ", ", "{", "}" );
System.out.println( joiner.toString() ); // {} 
```

If this behavior isn’t desirable, <samp class="listingcharacter">setEmptyValue(CharSequence)</samp> specifies a substitute that comes into play exactly when no <samp class="listingcharacter">add(...)</samp> has added anything to the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner</samp> , as in the following example:

```
StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner( ", ", "{", "}" ).setEmptyValue("-");
System.out.println( joiner.toString() ); // - 
```

In summary, the class provides two constructors and five methods:

```
class java.util.
                    StringJoiner 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner(CharSequence delimiter)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner(CharSequence delimiter, CharSequence prefix, CharSequence suffix)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner add(CharSequence newElement)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner merge(StringJoiner other)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner setEmptyValue(CharSequence emptyValue)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int length()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String toString()</samp>

###### [»]  Note

Actually, the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner</samp> class is quite weak, and even <samp class="listingcharacter">String.join(...)</samp> allows to accept strings as a collection of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterable</samp>, which <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner</samp>, the implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">String.join(…)</samp> , does not allow itself.

## 5.10    Decomposing Strings

The Java library provides some classes and methods that allow us to break large strings into smaller ones according to certain patterns. In this context, the terms token and delimiter are worth mentioning: A token is a part of a string which is separated from other tokens by certain delimiters . Let’s take the sentence “Modern music is playing instruments according to notes” (Peter Sellers) as an example. If we choose spaces as separators, the individual tokens will be “Modern,” “Music,” etc.

The Java library provides a number of options for string decomposition. The first two from this list are presented in the following sections:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">split(…)</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> : Splits using a delimiter described by a regular expression.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">lines()</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>: Returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<String></samp> of lines.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> : nice class to traverse an input, also line by line.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">StringTokenizer</samp> : Delimiters are only single characters.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BreakIterator</samp> : Finds character, word, line, or sentence boundaries.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Matcher</samp>: In connection with the <samp class="listingcharacter">Pattern</samp> class, <samp class="listingcharacter">Matcher</samp> decomposes strings using regular expressions.

The methods and classes are, generally speaking, the counterparts of the concatenation options. For instance, <samp class="listingcharacter">split(...)</samp> is opposed to <samp class="listingcharacter">join(...)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringTokenizer</samp> is opposed to <samp class="listingcharacter">StringJoiner</samp> .

### 5.10.1     Splitting Strings via split(...)

The object method split <samp class="listingcharacter">(...)</samp> of a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object splits its own string into substrings. The separators are completely arbitrary and described as a regular expression. The return is an array or an <samp class="listingcharacter">iterable</samp> with substrings.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example decomposes a domain name into its component parts:

```
String path = "www.tutego.com";
String[] segs = 
                    path.split( Pattern.quote( "." ) );
System.out.println( Arrays.toString(segs) ); // [www, tutego, com] 
```

Since the dot as a separator is a special character for regular expressions, it must be appropriately commented out with the backslash. This is done by the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">Pattern.quote(String)</samp>, which returns a “disarmed” regex string. Otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter">split(".")</samp> returns an array of length 0 on each string.

A common separator is <samp class="listingcharacter">\s</samp> , which is whitespace.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example counts the number of words in a sentence:

```
String = "So just listen now to my musical doodle.";
int wordCount = string.split( "(\\s|\\p{Punct})+" ).length;
System.out.println( wordCount );       // 8
```

The separator is either whitespace or a punctuation mark. Alternatively, the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">"[\\s\\p{Punct}]+"</samp> can be used.

```
final class java.lang.
                String
implements CharSequence, Comparable<String>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String[] split(String regex)</samp>
    Splits the current string with the regular expression.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String[] split(String regex, int limit)</samp>
    Splits the current string with the regular expression but returns a maximum limited number of substrings.

### 5.10.2    Yes We Can, Yes We Scan: The Scanner Class

The <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.Scanner</samp> class can split a string into tokens and read simple files line by line. In the decomposition, a regular expression can describe the delimiter. This feature makes <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> more flexible than a <samp class="listingcharacter">StringTokenizer</samp> , which only allows single characters as separators.

#### Building a Scanner

To build a <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> object, the class provides several constructors that take the strings to be parsed from various sources, such as a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>, a data stream (when reading from the command line, this data stream is <samp class="listingcharacter">System.in</samp>), a <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> object, or various other input sources. If the source is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Closeable</samp>, like a <samp class="listingcharacter">Writer</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> should be closed via <samp class="listingcharacter">close()</samp>, which forwards the <samp class="listingcharacter">close()</samp> to the <samp class="listingcharacter">Closeable</samp> object. You do not need to call <samp class="listingcharacter">close()</samp> when the source is a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> .

```
final class java.util.
                    Scanner
implements Iterator<String>, Closeable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(String source)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(Path source) throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(Path source, String charsetName) throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(Path source, Charset charset) throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(File source) throws FileNotFoundException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(File source, String charsetName) throws FileNotFoundException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(File source, Charset charset) throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(InputStream source)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(InputStream source, String charsetName)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(InputStream source, Charset charset)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(Readable source)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(ReadableByteChannel source)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(ReadableByteChannel source, String charsetName)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner(ReadableByteChannel source, Charset charset)</samp>

#### Reading a File Line by Line

Once the <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> object has been created, the pair <samp class="listingcharacter">hasNextLine()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">nextLine()</samp> can be used to easily read a file line by line.

A program is supposed to read a file and reverse the lines in such a way that the last line of the file is at the top and the first line of the file is at the bottom. The result on the console should be a string with no whitespace at the beginning and end.

```
InputStream resource = ReverseFile.class.getResourceAsStream( "EastOfJava.txt" );
try ( Scanner input = new Scanner( resource ) ) {

                    StringBuilder result = new StringBuilder();
  while ( input.hasNextLine() )

                    result.insert( 0, input.nextLine() + System.lineSeparator() );
  System.out.println( 
                    result.toString().trim() );
} 
```

**Listing 5.11**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/string/ReverseFile.java (Snippet)

The construction with <samp class="listingcharacter">try (...) { ... }</samp> is called try with resources and automatically closes the file after its use. The handling of exceptions and the special use of <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> are both explained in more detail in [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.6](#09_006.html_h9.6). Also, the encoding should always be specified, which in our case is ISO 8859-1 (i.e., Latin-1). The encoding string necessary for the <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> constructor comes from a constant from <samp class="listingcharacter">StandardCharsets</samp> .

```
final class java.util.
                    Scanner
implements Iterator<String>, Closeable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean hasNextLine()</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if a next line can be read.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String nextLine()</samp>
    Returns the next line.

###### [+]  Tip

If we initialize a <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> with a string, this string can be decomposed line by line by the scanner. The string method <samp class="listingcharacter">lines()</samp> is an alternative; the result is a stream of lines. We’ll discuss streams in more detail in [Chapter 16](#16_001.html_h16) .

#### Next, Please

After creating the <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> object, the <samp class="listingcharacter">next()</samp> method returns the next string if a <samp class="listingcharacter">hasNext()</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>. (These methods are then also methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator</samp> interface, where <samp class="listingcharacter">remove()</samp> isn’t implemented.)

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, a <samp class="listingcharacter">String s</samp> will be read from the standard input:

```
Scanner scanner = new Scanner( System.in );
String s = scanner.next();
```

Important: The <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> shouldn’t be closed in this case!

In addition to the <samp class="listingcharacter">next()</samp> method, which returns only a string, <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> provides various <samp class="listingcharacter">next<type>()</samp> methods, which read the next token and convert it into a desired format, for example, into a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">nextDouble()</samp>. With the same number of <samp class="listingcharacter">hasNext<type>()</samp> methods, you can query whether another token of this type follows.

###### [eg]  Example

Let’s look at the individual <samp class="listingcharacter">next*()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">hasNext*()</samp> methods with the following example:

```
Scanner scanner = new Scanner( "tutego 12 1973 12,03 True 123456789000" );
System.out.println( scanner.
                        hasNext() );        // true
System.out.println( scanner.
                        next() );           // tutego
System.out.println( scanner.
                        hasNextByte() );    // true
System.out.println( scanner.
                        nextByte() );       // 12
System.out.println( scanner.
                        hasNextInt() );     // true
System.out.println( scanner.
                        nextInt() );        // 1973
System.out.println( scanner.
                        hasNextDouble() );  // true
System.out.println( scanner.
                        nextDouble() );     // 12.03
System.out.println( scanner.
                        hasNextBoolean() ); // true
System.out.println( scanner.
                        nextBoolean() );    // true
System.out.println( scanner.
                        hasNextLong() );    // true
System.out.println( scanner.
                        nextLong() );       // 123456789000
System.out.println( scanner.
                        hasNext() );        // false 
```

## 5.11    Formatting Outputs

Again and again, numbers, dates, and text must be formatted in a variety of ways. Java provides various solutions for formatting, such as the following:

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">format(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(...)</samp> methods enable formatted outputs.

*   Formatting via <samp class="listingcharacter">Format</samp> classes: General formatting behavior is fixed in an abstract <samp class="listingcharacter">Format</samp> class. Concrete subclasses, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">NumberFormat</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">DateFormat</samp> , take care of specific data formats.

*   Conversion of a string according to a given mask with a <samp class="listingcharacter">MaskFormatter</samp>

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Format</samp> classes not only provide country- and language-dependent output via <samp class="listingcharacter">format(...)</samp>, but also the reverse way to split strings back into types like <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">date</samp>. Any string generated by the <samp class="listingcharacter">Format</samp> object can also be read again with the parser.

### 5.11.1     Formatting and Outputting via format()

The <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class provides a way to format strings according to a default with the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">format(...)</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

Build the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> “Hey Patrick, I thought of something funnier than 24… 25!”:

```
String s = 
                    String.format( "Hey %s, I thought of something funnier than %d… %d!",
                          "Patrick", 24, 24+1 );
System.out.println( s ); 
```

The first string passed to <samp class="listingcharacter">format(...)</samp> is called the format string . In addition to characters to be output, it contains additional format specifiers to tell the formatter how to format the argument. <samp class="listingcharacter">%s</samp> stands for an unformatted output of a string. The format string is followed by a vararg (or alternatively the array directly) containing the values referred to by the format specifiers.

| Specifier | Stands for ... | Specifier | Stands for ... |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%n</samp> | New line | <samp class="listingcharacter">%b</samp> | Boolean |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%%</samp> | Percentage sign | <samp class="listingcharacter">%s</samp> | String |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%c</samp> | Unicode character | <samp class="listingcharacter">%d</samp> | Decimal number |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%x</samp> | Hexadecimal notation | <samp class="listingcharacter">%t</samp> | Date and time |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%f</samp> | Float | <samp class="listingcharacter">%e</samp> | Scientific notation |

**Table 5.12**     The Most Important Format Specifiers

###### [+]  Tip

The line feed is dependent on the operating system, but <samp class="listingcharacter">%n</samp> is a good means of obtaining this line feed character (or string). However, instead of using <samp class="listingcharacter">String.format("%n")</samp> to query the separator, <samp class="listingcharacter">System.lineSeparator()</samp> is a better solution.

```
final class java.lang.
                String
implements CharSequence, Comparable<String>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String format(String format, Object… args)</samp>
    Returns a formatted string from the string and arguments.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">static String format(Locale l, String format, Object... args)</samp>
    Returns a formatted string consisting of the desired language, the string, and the arguments.

Internally, <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.Formatter</samp> (no <samp class="listingcharacter">java.text.Format</samp> objects exist) are at work, which can also be used directly; the documentation is also placed there.

#### System.out.printf(…)

If a string formatted with <samp class="listingcharacter">String.format(...)</samp> should be output immediately, <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.print(String.format(format, args));</samp> doesn’t need to be used. Conveniently, the <samp class="listingcharacter">format(...)</samp> method known from <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> is also contained in the <samp class="listingcharacter">PrintWriter</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">PrintStream</samp> classes for formatting and for outputs. (The <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out</samp> object is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">PrintStream</samp>.) However, since the method name <samp class="listingcharacter">format(...)</samp> isn’t really consistent with the other <samp class="listingcharacter">print*(...)</samp> methods, the developers have made the <samp class="listingcharacter">format(...)</samp> methods also available under the name <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(...)</samp> . (The implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(...)</samp> is a simple redirect to the <samp class="listingcharacter">format(...)</samp> method.) Also, with <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(...)</samp> a <samp class="listingcharacter">locale</samp> is possible as first argument.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example outputs the numbers from 0 to 15 in hexadecimal format:

```
for ( int i = 0x0; i <= 0xf; i++ )

                        System.out.printf( "%x%n", i );  // 0 1 2 … e f 
```

#### Pimp My String with Format Specifiers*

The number of format specifiers is so large and their further parameterization so diverse that a look into the API documentation is definitely necessary. The most important specifiers are:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">%n</samp> results in the line feed character(s), each related to the current platform. This notation is preferable to a hard <samp class="listingcharacter">\n</samp> , which may or may not be the line feed character of the current platform.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">%%</samp> returns the percentage sign itself, just as <samp class="listingcharacter">\\</samp> masks out the backslash in a string.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">%s</samp> returns a string, where <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> leads to the output “null.” <samp class="listingcharacter">%S</samp> capitalizes the output.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">%b</samp> writes a <samp class="listingcharacter">Boolean</samp>, namely, the value <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">false.</samp> The output is always <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> for other types like <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">%B</samp> capitalizes the string.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">%c</samp> writes a character, where the types wrapper types <samp class="listingcharacter">Character</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp> are allowed. <samp class="listingcharacter">%C</samp> writes the character in uppercase.

*   For numeric integer outputs with <samp class="listingcharacter">%d</samp> (decimal), <samp class="listingcharacter">%x</samp> (hexadecimal), and <samp class="listingcharacter">%o</samp> (octal), the wrapper types <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> are allowed; <samp class="listingcharacter">%X</samp> capitalizes the hexadecimal letters.

*   For floats with <samp class="listingcharacter">%f</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">%e</samp> ( <samp class="listingcharacter">%E</samp>), <samp class="listingcharacter">%g</samp> ( <samp class="listingcharacter">%G</samp>), and <samp class="listingcharacter">%a</samp> ( <samp class="listingcharacter">%A</samp>), the wrapper types <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> are additionally allowed. The standard precision for <samp class="listingcharacter">%e</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">%E</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">%f</samp> is six decimal places.

*   In case of date/time specifications with <samp class="listingcharacter">%t</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">%T</samp>, the following are allowed: <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Calendar</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Date</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">%t</samp> requires additional information, as you’ll see in the next example.

*   The hash code is written by <samp class="listingcharacter">%h</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">%H</samp>. If the value is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> , the result is also the string with the content “null.”

Additional flags, for example, for length specifications and the number of decimal places, are possible, as shown in the following example:

```
PrintStream o = System.out;

int i = 123;
o.printf( "|%d|%d|%n" ,       i, -i );      // |123|-123|
o.printf( "|%5d|%5d|%n" ,     i, -i );      // |  123| -123|
o.printf( "|%-5d|%-5d|%n" ,   i, -i );      // |123  |-123 |
o.printf( "|%+-5d|%+-5d|%n" , i, -i );      // |+123 |-123 |
o.printf( "|%05d|%05d|%n%n",  i, -i );      // |00123|-0123|

o.printf( "|%X|%x|%X|%n", 0xabc, 0xabc, -0xabc ); // |ABC|abc|FFFFF544| 
o.printf( "|%04x|%#x|%n%n", 0xabc, 0xabc ); // |0abc|0xabc|

double d = 12345.678;
o.printf( "|%f|%f|%n" ,         d, -d );    // |12345,678000|-12345,678000|
o.printf( "|%+f|%+f|%n" ,       d, -d );    // |+12345,678000|-12345,678000|
o.printf( "|% f|% f|%n" ,       d, -d );    // | 12345,678000|-12345,678000|
o.printf( "|%.2f|%.2f|%n" ,     d, -d );    // |12345,68|-12345,68|
o.printf( "|%,.2f|%,.2f|%n" ,   d, -d );    // |12.345,68|-12.345,68|
o.printf( "|%(.2f|%(.2f|%n",    d, -d );    // |12345,68|(12345,68)|
o.printf( "|%10.2f|%10.2f|%n" , d, -d );    // |  12345,68| -12345,68|
o.printf( "|%010.2f|%010.2f|%n%n",d,-d);    // |0012345,68|-012345,68|

String s = "Gobbledygook";
o.printf( "|%s|%n", s );                    // |Gobbledygook|
o.printf( "|%S|%n", s );                    // |GOBBLEDYGOOK|
o.printf( "|%20s|%n", s );                  // |        Gobbledygook|
o.printf( "|%-20s|%n", s );                 // |Gobbledygook        |
o.printf( "|%7s|%n", s );                   // |Gobbledygook|
o.printf( "|%.7s|%n", s );                  // |Gobbled|
o.printf( "|%20.7s|%n%n", s );              // |             Gobbled|

                    Date t = new Date();
o.printf( "%tT%n", t );                     // 18:19:20
o.printf( "%tD%n", t );                     // 09/13/21 
```

**Listing 5.13**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/string/PrintfDemo.java, main()

In the case of floats, these values are rounded according to the <samp class="listingcharacter">RoundingMode.HALF_UP</samp>. Thus, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.printf("%.1f", 0.45);</samp> returns the output “0.5.”

Some flags can be read from the examples, especially for floats. A comma controls whether the thousands separators are used. A <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> indicates whether a sign always appears, and a space indicates whether a space is then left empty for positive characters. An opening parenthesis doesn’t place a minus for negative numbers, but places instead negative numbers in parentheses.

###### [+]  Tip

If <samp class="listingcharacter">format(...)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(...)</samp> is called without a <samp class="listingcharacter">locale</samp> , the default language of the operating system is used. Compare the following examples:

```
double bitcoinPrice = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble( 50_000 );
System.out.printf( "%.2f%n", bitcoinPrice );
System.out.printf( Locale.ENGLISH, "%.2f%n", bitcoinPrice );
```

The following outputs would result:

46714,42
46714.42

#### Format Specifier for Date Values

From our earlier example, note that <samp class="listingcharacter">%t</samp> doesn’t simply output the time but always expects another suffix that specifies exactly which date/time part is actually desired. [Table 5.13](#05_011.html_t5.13) contains the most important suffixes, and more can be found in the API documentation. All outputs take into account the given <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> environment.

| Symbol | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tA</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">%ta</samp> | Full/abbreviated name of the day of the week |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tB</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">%tb</samp> | Full/abbreviated name of the name of the month |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tC</samp> | 2-digit century (00–99) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%te</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">%td</samp> | Numeric day of the month without or with leading zeros (1–31 or 01–31) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tk</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">%tl</samp> | Hour specification related to 24 or 12 hours (0–23, 1–12) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tH</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">%tI</samp> | 2-digit hour information related to 24 or 12 hours (00–23, 01–12) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tj</samp> | Day of the year (001–366) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tM</samp> | 2-digit minute specification (00–59) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tm</samp> | 2-digit month specification (usually 01–12) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tS</samp> | 2-digit second specification (00–59) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tY</samp> | 4-digit year specification |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%ty</samp> | The last 2 digits of the year (00–99) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tZ</samp> | Abbreviated time zone |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tz</samp> | Time zone with shift related to GMT |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tR</samp> | Hours and minutes in the <samp class="listingcharacter">%tH:%tM</samp> format |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tT</samp> | Hours/minutes/seconds in the <samp class="listingcharacter">%tH:%tM:%tS</samp> format |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tD</samp> | Date in the <samp class="listingcharacter">%tm/%td/%ty</samp> format |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tF</samp> | ISO-8601 format <samp class="listingcharacter">%tY-%tm-%td</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">%tc</samp> | Complete date with time in the format <samp class="listingcharacter">%ta %tb %td %tT %tZ %tY</samp> |

**Table 5.13**     Suffixes for Date Values

Allowed data types are <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Calendar</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Date</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp>and implementations of <samp class="listingcharacter">TemporalAccessor</samp> include <samp class="listingcharacter">DayOfWeek</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Instant</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">LocalDate</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">LocalDateTime</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">LocalTime</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Month</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">MonthDay</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">OffsetDateTime</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">OffsetTime</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Year</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">YearMonth</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ZonedDateTime</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">ZoneOffset</samp> .

#### Position Specifications

The formatting string can contain a position specification of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">Position</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">$</samp>, where then <samp class="listingcharacter">1$</samp> refers to the first argument, <samp class="listingcharacter">2$</samp> to the second and so on. (Note here that the numbering doesn’t start at zero).

###### [eg]  Example

Output the day and month of March 12, 2025:

```
LocalDate date = LocalDate.of( 2022, Month.MARCH, 12 );
System.out.printf( Locale.ENGLISH, "%te. %1$tb%n", date );  // 12\. Mar
System.out.printf( Locale.FRENCH, "%te. %1$tb%n", date );   // 12\. mars 
```

The first statement creates a date object from year, month, and day.

The position specification in the format string enables two things:

*   If, as in the example, the same argument is used more than once, you don’t need to specify it more than once. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">printf("</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">%te</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">.</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">%tb</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">%n",</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> repeats the argument <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp>, which avoids specifying a position. Instead of this solution, you could also write <samp class="listingcharacter">%te. %</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">1$</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">tb%n</samp> , thus explicitly prescribing the position 1 for the second argument as well.

*   The order of the passed arguments usually always remains the same, but the format string can put the arguments in different positions.

The second point is important for localized editions. Let’s look at an example: A screen output is supposed to output the first and last name in different languages. However, the order of the parts of the name can be different, and the first name doesn’t always precede the last name in every language. In English, the welcome text would read “Hello Christian Ullenboom,” but in another language it could be “nuqneH Ullenboom Christian.”

```
Object[] formatArgs = { "Christian", "Ullenboom" };

String germanFormat = "Hello %
                    1$s %
                    2$s";
System.out.printf( englishFormat, formatArgs );
System.out.println();

String bwatutiFormat = "nuqneH %
                    2$s %
                    1$s";
System.out.printf( bwatutiFormat, formatArgs ); 
```

**Listing 5.14**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/string/FormatPosition.java, main()

The calling order for first name/last name is always the same, but the format string, which comes from an external configuration file or database, for example, can change this order to match the local language.

###### [+]  Tip

If a subsequent format element references the preceding argument, a <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp> can be set:

```
LocalDate d1 = LocalDate.of( 1973, Month.MARCH, 1 );
LocalDate d2 = LocalDate.of( 1966, 4, 23 );
System.out.printf( Locale.ENGLISH,
                   "%te. %<tb %<ty  -  %2$te. %<tb %<ty%n", d1, d2 );
//                       1\. Mar 73  -  23\. Apr 66 
```

The specifications for month and year reference the preceding items in each case. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">d1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">d2</samp> need to be specified only once.

## 5.12     Further Reading

For more information, take a look at the API documentation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Formatter</samp> classes and also explore regular expressions ( <samp class="listingcharacter">Pattern</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Matcher</samp> classes), which can be used to elegantly answer questions about matching as well as about the position of substrings.

When large amounts of data are processed as strings, the question of optimization is quite relevant. The default implementation of the JDK only uses a simple search algorithm, which is rather inefficient for large patterns and search strings. In the field of search algorithms, however, computer science has produced interesting approaches in recent decades, for example, the optimal mismatch algorithm. However, the complete Unicode standard with 32 bits poses a certain problem. Enterprise libraries, for example, for parsing XML or JSON, don’t necessarily support the current Unicode standard with its hundreds of thousands of characters.

# 6     Writing Custom Classes

“The law is the abstract expression of the general will being in and of itself.”
—Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770–1831)

In the preceding chapters, you learned a lot about object orientation, but our discussion was more from the user point of view. You’ve seen how objects can be built, and we’ve also implemented simple classes with static methods. Now is the time to round out your knowledge of object-oriented programming (OOP) and build your own custom data types .

###### [»]  Note

We’ll illustrate the concepts of object orientation with a program based on the Drug Wars game. John Dell developed this MS-DOS-based game in the early 1980s to demonstrate a core principle of economics: buy low and sell high. With easy-to-understand rules, Drug Wars can be played in a web browser at the following websites:

*   [https://classicreload.com/drug-wars.html](https://classicreload.com/drug-wars.html) (first version)

*   [https://archive.org/details/DruglordV2.0SW1992FantasyWareInc.Simulation](https://archive.org/details/DruglordV2.0SW1992FantasyWareInc.Simulation) (extended version)

In our examples, we’ll switch from hard drugs to soft drugs and use candy. We’ll call our game Jawbreaker .

## 6.1    Declaring Custom Classes with Members

The declaration of a class is introduced by the <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> keyword . In the body of the class, you can declare the following elements:

*   Object and class variables

*   Methods

*   Constructors

*   Class initializers as well as instance initializers

*   Nested types, such as classes, records, interfaces, and enumerations

### 6.1.1     Minimum Class

Our focus on candy is represented by the <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp> class.

```
package com.tutego.insel.game.c.v1
class Candy { } 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp> class has a constructor generated by the compiler, and <samp class="listingcharacter">new Candy()</samp> creates a instance from this blueprint. We’ll omit visibility modifiers (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp>) for now and then focus on them more closely in [Section 6.2](#06_002.html_h6.2) .

### 6.1.2    Declaring Object Variables

This <samp class="listingcharacter">class Candy { }</samp> class has no object variables and therefore can’t store any states. Let’s give the candy three object variables: one for the name (type <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>), a second for the price (type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>), and a third for the number of candies (type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> ).

```
class Candy {

                String name;
  int    price;
  int    quantity;
} 
```

**Listing 6.2**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/game/c/v2/Candy.java (Snippet)

                lollipop.name = "Lollipop";

###### [»]   Note

No special naming convention exist for object variables. Thus, although you can prefix local variables (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">f</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">_</samp> ) to distinguish them, even Eclipse has moved away from this convention. Basically, object variables can also be named like methods, but this approach is unusual because variable names are generally nouns, while methods are verbs. Furthermore, identifiers cannot be identical to keywords.

#### Initializing Object Variables

Unlike local variables, the JVM initializes all object variables with a default value—the same is true for class variables, which we’ll describe in [Section 6.3](#06_003.html_h6.3) . The following values are the defaults:

*   0 for numeric values and <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> for reference variables

If you don’t like these default values, your variables can be assigned values, as in the following example:

```
class Candy {
  String name;
  int    price;
  int    quantity 
                    = 1;
} 
```

The expression <samp class="listingcharacter">new Candy().quantity == 1</samp> would therefore return <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> .

###### [+]  Design Tip

You may find yourself walking a tightrope when using simple data types or when referencing other objects. If <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp> stores the price, an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> (or <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>) is problematic because <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp> would also have to perform a validation so that the price never becomes negative; however, this behavior does not fit in with the definition of what candy is or what it does! The general OOP rule is: For data that needs to be validated and may also be related to other object variables, create a new data type.

#### Validity Range, Visibility, and Lifetime

Local variables begin their lifecycles the moment they are declared and initialized. If the block ends, the local variable is no longer valid, and it can no longer be used because it has disappeared from the visibility area. This lifecycle is different for object variables. An object variable lives from the moment the object has been built via <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> and contin ues living until the garbage collector clears the object away. However, the variable is always visible and valid in the entire object and in all blocks. [[ 124 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn06_01)

### 6.1.3    Declaring Methods

Object variables are joined by methods that usually operate on object variables. Let’s give the candy two methods:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">totalPrice()</samp> : Calculates the total price as the product of quantity and price.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">resetQuantity()</samp> : Resets the quantity to 1.

Unlike our previous static methods, these three methods for <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp> will be object methods, so they will not carry the <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> modifier.

```
class Candy {
  String name;
  int    price;
  int    quantity = 1;

                int totalPrice() {
    return price * quantity;
  }

  void resetQuantity() {
    quantity = 1;
  }
} 
```

**Figure 6.4**     UML Class Diagram of Candy with Three Object Variables and Two Methods

The <samp class="listingcharacter">totalPrice()</samp> method builds the price as a product of price and quantity and returns the result. <samp class="listingcharacter">resetQuantity()</samp> resets the product quantity to 1.

Let’s test our methods by creating some candy.

```
Candy lollipop = new Candy();
lollipop.name = "Lollipop";
lollipop.price = 12;
lollipop.quantity = 2;
System.out.println( 
                lollipop.totalPrice() ); // 24

                lollipop.resetQuantity();
System.out.println( 
                lollipop.totalPrice() ); // 12 
```
