## 10.3     Non-Static Nested Types

A non-static nested type is an inner type that is comparable to an object property. Let’s declare an inner class named <samp class="listingcharacter">Room</samp> in <samp class="listingcharacter">House</samp> with the following example code:

```
class AlmondJoy {

  String name = "Almond Joy";
  private int introduced = 1946;

  class Coconut {
    void print() {
      System.out.println( name );
      System.out.println( introduced );
    }
  }
} 
```

**Listing 10.3**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/AlmondJoy.java (Snippet)

An instance of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Coconut</samp> class has access to all members of <samp class="listingcharacter">AlmondJoy</samp> , including its private members.

### 10.3.1    Creating Instances of Inner Classes

To create an instance of <samp class="listingcharacter">Coconut</samp>, an instance of the outer class must exist first. One important difference in this regard relates to the static nested classes: Static nested types can exist even without an object of the outer class, as discussed in [Section 10.2](#10_002.html_h10.2) .

In a constructor or in an object method of the outer class, an instance of the inner class can be created simply via the <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> keyword. If you are coming from outside the outer class (or from a static block of the outer class) and you want to create instances of the inner class, for non-static nested classes, you must ensure that an instance of the outer class is available. Java prescribes a special form for the creation via <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> , which has the following general format:

```
 reference.
                new InnerClass(…) 
```

In this syntax, <samp class="listingcharacter">reference</samp> is a reference of the type of the outer class. To create an object in the static <samp class="listingcharacter">main(String[])</samp> method of the house, you can write the following code:

```
AlmondJoy almondJoy = new AlmondJoy();
Coconut coconut = almondJoy.new Coconut(); 
```

**Listing 10.4**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/AlmondJoy.java, main()

This code can even be reduced to one line:

```
Coconut coconut = new AlmondJoy().new Coconut(); 
```

### 10.3.2    The this Reference

If an inner class <samp class="listingcharacter">In</samp> wants to access the <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> reference of its surrounding class <samp class="listingcharacter">Out</samp>, you must write <samp class="listingcharacter">Out.this</samp>. If variables of the inner class overlap variables of the outer class, you would write <samp class="listingcharacter">Out.this.property</samp> to access the members of the outer class <samp class="listingcharacter">Out</samp> .

```
class FurnishedHouse {

  String s = "House";

  class Room {
    String s = "Room";

    class Chair {
      String s = "Chair";

      void print() {
        System.out.println( s );                      // Chair
        System.out.println( 
                this.s );                 // Chair
        System.out.println( 
                Chair.this.s );           // Chair
        System.out.println( 
                Room.this.s );            // Room
        System.out.println( 
                FurnishedHouse.this.s );  // House
      }
    }
  }

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    new FurnishedHouse().new Room().new Chair().print();
  }
} 
```

**Listing 10.5**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/FurnishedHouse.java, FurnishedHouse

###### [»]  Note

Non-static nested classes can be nested arbitrarily, but since the name is unique, you can always get to the particular property via <samp class="listingcharacter">classname.this</samp> .

Considering our earlier examples, objects for the inner classes <samp class="listingcharacter">Room</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Chair</samp> can be created in the following ways:

```
 FurnishedHouse h            = new FurnishedHouse();  // Instance of FurnishedHouse
FurnishedHouse.Room r       = h.new Room();          // Instance of Room in h
FurnishedHouse.Room.Chair c = r.new Chair();         // Instance of Chair in r
c.print();                                           // Method of Chair 
```

The qualification with the dot in <samp class="listingcharacter">FurnishedHouse.Room.Chair</samp> doesn’t automatically mean that <samp class="listingcharacter">FurnishedHouse</samp> is a package with the <samp class="listingcharacter">Room</samp> subpackage in which the <samp class="listingcharacter">Chair</samp> class exists. The double use of the dot doesn’t really improve readability, and you risk creating confusion between inner classes and packages. For this reason, a naming convention should be followed: Class names should start with uppercase letters; package names, with lowercase letters.

### 10.3.3    Class Files Generated by the Compiler*

For our <samp class="listingcharacter">House</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Room</samp> example, the compiler creates the House.class and House$Room.class files. For the inner class to access the object variables of the outer class, the compiler automatically generates a reference to the associated object of the outer class in each instance of the inner class. As a result, the inner class can also access object variables of the outer class. For the inner class, you’ll have the House$Room.class file with the following code:

```
class House$Room {

  final 
                House this$0;

                House$Room( House house ) {
    this$0 = house;
  }
  …
} 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">this$0</samp> variable references the <samp class="listingcharacter">House.this</samp> instance (i.e., the associated outer class). The constructors of the inner class get an additional parameter of type <samp class="listingcharacter">House</samp> to initialize the <samp class="listingcharacter">this$0 variable</samp> . Since you don’t get to see the constructors anyway, it’s irrelevant.

## 10.4    Local Classes

Local classes are also inner classes, but these classes aren’t simply set like a property in the body of a class. Instead, you’ll directly define local classes in statement blocks consisting of methods, constructors, and initialization blocks. Local interfaces aren’t possible.

### 10.4.1     Example with a Custom Declaration

In the following example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">main(...)</samp> method declares an inner class named <samp class="listingcharacter">Snowden</samp> with a constructor that accesses the final variable <samp class="listingcharacter">PRISM</samp> :

```
public class NSA {

  public static void main( String[] args ) {

                final int PRISM = 1;
    int tempora = 2;
    tempora++;                          // (*)

                class Snowden {
      Snowden() {
        System.out.println( PRISM );
//        System.out.println( tempora ); // 
                     Commented out a compiler error
      }
    }
    new Snowden();
  }
} 
```

**Listing 10.6**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/NSA.java, NSA

In this case, the declaration of the local class <samp class="listingcharacter">Snowden</samp> is used like a statement. A visibility modifier is invalid for local classes, and the class must not declare class methods and general static variables. (Final constants are permitted.)

Any local class can access methods of the outer class. Additionally, a local class can access local variables and parameters, but only if the variables are <samp class="listingcharacter">final</samp>. In this context, final variables don’t necessarily require the presence of the <samp class="listingcharacter">final</samp> modifier to be final. If no write access is available to variables, they are effectively final . The <samp class="listingcharacter">PRISM</samp> variable is explicitly marked with the <samp class="listingcharacter">final</samp> modifier, so the inner class can access it. <samp class="listingcharacter">tempora</samp> isn’t final ( <samp class="listingcharacter">tempora++</samp> is a write access), and therefore, a read access in the inner class at <samp class="listingcharacter">println(tempora)</samp> leads to a compiler error. This scenario is tested in the example: If the line <samp class="listingcharacter">(*)</samp> is commented out with <samp class="listingcharacter">tempora++;</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter">tempora</samp> is effectively final, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Snowden</samp> can access <samp class="listingcharacter">tempora</samp> .

If the inner class is in a static method, the inner class cannot call object methods of the outer class.

### 10.4.2    Using a Local Class for a Timer

To make these examples a bit more concrete for real-life situations, let’s look at how a timer can perform repetitive tasks. The Java library already provides everything you need. Our task is to create an instance of <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.Timer()</samp> and to pass an instance of the <samp class="listingcharacter">TimerTask</samp> type to the <samp class="listingcharacter">scheduleAtFixedRate(...)</samp> object method. The <samp class="listingcharacter">TimerTask</samp> class prescribes an abstract method <samp class="listingcharacter">run()</samp> , in which the concurrent program code to be processed regularly is placed.

Let’s use this feature for a program that reminds us, immediately and then at regular intervals, to exercise.

```
public class SportReminder {
  public static void main( String[] args ) {

                class SportReminderTask extends TimerTask {
      @Override public void run() {
        System.out.println( "Come on, you candy-ass!" );
      }
    }
    new Timer().scheduleAtFixedRate( 
                new SportReminderTask(), 
                                     0 /* ms delay */, 
                                     1000 /* ms period */ );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 10.7**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/SportReminder.java, SportReminder

Our <samp class="listingcharacter">SportReminderTask</samp> class, which extends <samp class="listingcharacter">TimerTask</samp>, is declared directly in <samp class="listingcharacter">main(...)</samp>. The generated object follows later in <samp class="listingcharacter">scheduleAtFixedRate(...)</samp>, and the timer runs to remind us every second of the importance of exercise. The advantage of the local class declaration is that no one else can see the local class except <samp class="listingcharacter">main(...)</samp> .

## 10.5    Anonymous Inner Classes

Anonymous classes go one step further than local classes: These inner classes have no names and always automatically create an object; class declaration and object creation are combined into one language construct. The general notation is as follows:

```
new 
            ClassOrInterface() { /* Members of the inner class */ } 
```

New methods and object variables can be declared, and methods can be overridden in the block of curly brackets. <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> is followed by the name of a class or interface, with the following options:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> Class name <samp class="listingcharacter">(</samp> Optional Arguments <samp class="listingcharacter">) { ... }</samp>: If <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> is followed by a class type, then the anonymous class is a subclass of <samp class="listingcharacter">Class name</samp> . Possible arguments for the constructor of the base class can be specified (which might be necessary, for example, if the superclass doesn’t declare a parameterless constructor).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> Interface name <samp class="listingcharacter">() { ... }</samp>: If <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> is followed by the name of an interface, then the anonymous class inherits from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> and implements the given interface. If the anonymous class doesn’t implement the operations of the interface, then you have an error. This situation wouldn’t help us at all because then you’d have an abstract inner class from which no object can be created.

For anonymous inner classes, one restriction is that no additional <samp class="listingcharacter">extends</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">implements</samp> specifications are possible. Likewise, custom constructors are not possible (but instance initializers are), and only object methods and final static variables are allowed.

### 10.5.1    Using an Anonymous Inner Class for the Timer

In [Listing 10.7](#10_004.html_l10.7), we declared a new local class for the timer, but strictly speaking, we only had to use the class once, namely, to create an instance and pass <samp class="listingcharacter">scheduleAtFixedRate(...)</samp> . This scenario is perfect for anonymous inner classes. For instance, you could write the following code:

```
class SportReminderTask extends TimerTask {
  @Override public void run() { … }
}
new Timer().scheduleAtFixedRate( new SportReminderTask(), … ); 
```

These statements would be changed into the following code:

```
new Timer().scheduleAtFixedRate( new TimerTask() {
                                   @Override public void run() {
                                     System.out.println( "Come on, you candy-ass" );
                                   }
                                 },
                                 0 /* ms delay */,
                                 1000 /* ms period */); 
```

**Listing 10.8**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/ShorterSportReminder.java, main()

So, in essence, we’ve converted <samp class="listingcharacter">new SportReminderTask()</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">new TimerTask() { ... }</samp>. Nothing is left of the <samp class="listingcharacter">SportReminderTask</samp> class name; the object is anonymous.

###### [»]  Note

An anonymous class can override methods of the superclass, implement operations from interfaces, and even provide new members. Consider the following example:

```
String s = new Object() {
  String quote( String s ) {
    return String.format( "'%s'", s );
  }
}.quote( "Cora" );
System.out.println( s );  // 'Cora' 
```

**Listing 10.9**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/ObjectWithQuote.java, main()

The newly declared anonymous type has a <samp class="listingcharacter">quote(String)</samp> method that can be called directly. Without this direct call, however, the <samp class="listingcharacter">quote(...)</samp> method is invisible because the type is anonymous, and so only the methods of the superclass ( <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> , in our case) or the interface are known.

### 10.5.2    Implementing Anonymous Inner Classes*

The compiler also generates a normal class file for anonymous inner classes. As you’ve seen for a “normal” nested class, the Java compiler chooses the notation <samp class="listingcharacter">OuterClass$InnerClass</samp>. Of course, this notation doesn’t work for anonymous inner classes because we lack the name of the inner class. The compiler therefore chooses the following notation for class names: <samp class="listingcharacter">InnerToStringDate$1</samp>. If you have more than one inner class, <samp class="listingcharacter">$2</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">$3</samp> , and so on will follow accordingly.

#### Exceptions in Anonymous Inner Classes

In a stack trace, the generated class name appears in case of an exception. Let’s say, for example, that the declaration is embedded in a <samp class="listingcharacter">main(...)</samp> method of class <samp class="listingcharacter">T</samp> :

```
new Object() { String nuro() { throw new IllegalStateException(); } }.nuro(); 
```

Thus, in the execution, you’ll see the following output:

```
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalStateException
  at T$1.nuro(T.java:6)
  at T.main(T.java:6) 
```

### 10.5.3    Constructors of Anonymous Inner Classes

The compiler converts anonymous classes into normal class files. Each class can declare its own constructor, and even for anonymous classes, you should be able to put initialization code in there.

Let’s write an inner class that is a subclass of <samp class="listingcharacter">java.awt.Point</samp>. This inner class is supposed to override the <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> method.

```
Point p = new Point( 10, 12 ) {

                @Override public String toString() {
    return "(" + x + "," + y + ")";
  }
};

System.out.println( p );    // (10,12) 
```

**Listing 10.10**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/InnerToStringPoint.java, main()

Thus, the anonymous subclass is initialized by the normal constructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> .

#### Instance Initialization Blocks for Anonymous Inner Classes

However, since anonymous classes have no name, we’ll need to find some way for constructors to address them. In this case, instance initialization blocks (i.e., blocks in curly brackets directly within a class) can help, as described in [Chapter 6](#06_001.html_h6), [Section 6.6.5](#06_006.html_h6.6.5) . Instance initializers don’t actually exist in the bytecode, but the compiler automatically puts the program code into each constructor. Although anonymous classes can’t have a direct constructor, program code does get into the constructor of the bytecode file via the instance initializer.

Let’s look at an example: The anonymous class is a subclass of <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> and initializes a point with random coordinates in the constructor. From this special point object, we can then read the coordinates again.

```
java.awt.Point p = new java.awt.Point() {

                    {
    x = (int)(Math.random() * 1000); y = (int)(Math.random() * 1000);
  }
};

System.out.println( p.getLocation() );  // java.awt.Point[…}

System.out.println( new java.awt.Point( -1, 0 ) {{
  y = (int)(Math.random() * 1000);
}}.getLocation() );                     // java.awt.Point[x=-1,y=…] 
```

**Listing 10.11**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/AnonymousAndInside.java, main()

###### [»]  Language

Because of the two curly brackets, this variant is also called double brace initialization .

The double brace initialization is compact if, for example, data structures or hierarchical objects are to be initialized.

###### [eg]  Example*

Let’s create a nested <samp class="listingcharacter">map</samp> —that’s an associative memory. This map again contains another associative memory at one point, as shown in the following example:

```
Map<String,Object> map = new HashMap<String,Object>() {{
  put( "name", "Donald" );
  put( "address", new HashMap<String,Object>() {{
    put( "street", "1313 Webfoot Street" );

                            put( "city", "
                        Duckburg" );
  }} );
}};
```

###### [ ! ]  Warning

The double brace initialization is not quite “cheap” since an additional class file is generated in the file system for the subclass. In addition, the inner class holds a reference to the outer class. Furthermore, some problems may arise with <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> because, with the double brace initialization, you’re creating a subclass that may no longer be validly compared with <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> objects are now no longer identical.) All in all, this rather speaks against using this design. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> type provides a better option with the use of static <samp class="listingcharacter">of(…)</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">entry(…)</samp> methods.

#### Not at All super()*

Inside an “anonymous constructor,” <samp class="listingcharacter">super(...)</samp> can’t be used to call the superclass constructor. This limitation is because a <samp class="listingcharacter">super(...)</samp> is automatically inserted into the initialization block. The parameters for the desired variant of the (overloaded) superclass constructor are specified at the beginning of the declaration of the anonymous class, as demonstrated by the following example:

```
System.out.println( new java.awt.Point( -1, 0 ) {{
  y = (int)(Math.random() * 1000);
}}.getLocation() );                     // java.awt.Point[x=-1,y=…] 
```

###### [eg]  Example

Let’s initialize a <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> object that can store integers of any size. In the constructor of the anonymous subclass, you can then output the value using the inherited <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> method, as shown in the following example:

```
new java.math.BigDecimal( "12345678901234567890" ) {{
  System.out.println( toString() );
}};
```

### 10.5.4    Accessing Local Variables from Local and Anonymous Classes*

Local and anonymous classes can have read access to the local variables and parameters of the enclosing method, but only if the variable is <samp class="listingcharacter">final</samp>. Of course, local and inner classes can’t change these variables because <samp class="listingcharacter">final</samp> prohibits a second write access.

If a change is necessary, two tricks might be pretty useful:

*   Using a final array of length 1 to store the result

*   Using <samp class="listingcharacter">Atomic*</samp> classes from the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.concurrent.atomic</samp> package to store elements of a primitive type or a reference

Consider the following example:

```
public static void main( String[] args ) {

                final int[] result1 = { 0 };
  final String[] result2 = { null };
  final AtomicInteger result3 = new AtomicInteger();
  final AtomicReference<String> result4 = new AtomicReference<>();

  System.out.println( result1[0] );     // 0
  System.out.println( result2[0] );     // null
  System.out.println( result3.get() );  // 0
  System.out.println( result4.get() );  // null

  new Object() {{
      result1[0] = 1;
      result2[0] = "snort wasabi hot sauce";
      result3.set( 1 );
      result4.set( "skateboard in bowling lanes" );
  }};

  System.out.println( result1[0] );     // 1
  System.out.println( result2[0] );     // snort wasabi hot sauce
  System.out.println( result3.get() );  // 1
  System.out.println( result4.get() );  // skateboard in bowling lanes
} 
```

**Listing 10.12**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/ModifyLocalVariable.java, main()

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Atomic*</samp> classes are actually designed for performing atomic write and change operations but can be useful in this scenario.

### 10.5.5    Nested Classes Access Private Members

The outer enclosing class can access private members of the nested class, as shown in the following example:

```
public class NotSoPrivate {

  private static class Family { 
                private String dad, mom; }

                  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    class Node { 
                private Node next; }

    Node n = new Node();
    n.next = new Node();

    Family ullenboom = new Family();
    ullenboom.dad = "Heinz";
    ullenboom.mom = "Eva";
  }
} 
```

**Listing 10.13**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/NotSoPrivate.java, NotSoPrivate

An <samp class="listingcharacter">Outsider</samp> class defined in the same compilation unit (i.e., the same file) can’t access <samp class="listingcharacter">NotSoPrivate.Family</samp> , and of course, no class from another compilation unit has access either.

## 10.6    Nests

Nested classes have a special feature for private members, namely, that the outer type can access private members of the nested class. Similarly, the nested class can access private members of the outer class. This scenario leads to a special type of implementation in Java bytecode, which must share private members with other classes because, at the virtual machine level, only top-level classes exist.

Java provides nests [[ 171 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn10_01) to enable the mapping of nesting in the resulting bytecode. Three new object methods are available in the library for <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp>: <samp class="listingcharacter">getNestHost()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">isNestmateOf(Class)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">getNestMembers()</samp> .

```
package com.tutego.insel.nested;

public class OuterNest {

  public static class In1 {
    private void intern1() {
      new OuterNest().new In2().intern2();
    }
  }

  public class In2 {
    private void intern2() {
      new In1().intern1w();

                }
  }

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    for ( Class<?> clazz : 
            OuterNest.class.getNestMembers() ) {
      System.out.printf( "%s %b%n", clazz, 
            clazz.isNestmateOf( OuterNest.class ) );
    }
  }
} 
```

**Listing 10.14**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nested/OuterNest.java

The following output is shown on the console:

```
class com.tutego.insel.nested.OuterNest true
class com.tutego.insel.nested.OuterNest$In1 true
class com.tutego.insel.nested.OuterNest$In2 true 
```

## 10.7    Conclusion

Nested types, especially anonymous inner classes, for implementing functional interfaces have become less important with the introduction of lambda expressions. [Chapter 13](#13_001.html_h13) goes into further detail on this topic.

# 11     Special Types of Java SE

“Following advice means shifting responsibility.”
– Johannes Urzidil (1896–1970)

When we program with Java Platform, Standard Edition (Java SE), we often unconsciously use types from the standard library. This connection often goes entirely unnoticed because, for instance, the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang</samp> package is imported automatically—and thus types like <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> are always included. On the other hand, some things happen behind the scenes, such as the following behaviors:

*   If a superclass doesn’t extend its own class, it automatically inherits from <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Object</samp> .

*   If a primitive data type is given but an object type is desired, the compiler converts the simple data type to a wrapper object in a process is referred to as boxing .

*   If you concatenate strings using <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp>, the compiler—at least up to Java 8—automatically creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.StringBuilder</samp>, concatenates the segments using <samp class="listingcharacter">append(...)</samp>, and then returns a new <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp>. With no other reference type does the compiler allow “addition,” only comparisons with <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> .

*   With extended <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loops, the compiler expects either an array or something of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterable</samp>. From these objects, the compiler queries the <samp class="listingcharacter">iterator</samp> and independently walks through the collection.

*   For <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> with resources, the compiler expects an <samp class="listingcharacter">AutoCloseable</samp> and calls the <samp class="listingcharacter">close()</samp> method on these objects in the <samp class="listingcharacter">finally</samp> block.

*   When declaring an enumeration type with <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp>, the compiler generates a class derived from <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Enum</samp>. For records, the Java compiler automatically extends a <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Record</samp> superclass. You aren’t allowed to create subclasses of <samp class="listingcharacter">Enum</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Record</samp> since the compiler forbids it.

This chapter introduces different types that are favored in some way or have a special position in Java because they are ubiquitous, such as the following:

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> base class

*   Comparison objects

*   Wrapper classes

*   Enumerations and the <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterable</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator</samp> interfaces

*   Enumeration types ( <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp>) and the special class <samp class="listingcharacter">Enum</samp>

Some types are included in the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang</samp> package since these types are so elementary.

## 11.1     Object Is the Mother of All Classes

As shown in [Figure 11.1](#11_001.html_f11.1), <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Object</samp> is the topmost of all parent classes. Consequently, this class plays a special role since all other classes are automatically subclasses and inherit or overwrite the methods.

[![Unified Modeling Language (UML) Diagram of Object, the Absolute Base Class](bilderklein/klein11_001.png)](img-f11.1.html)

**Figure 11.1**     Unified Modeling Language (UML) Diagram of Object, the Absolute Base Class

### 11.1.1    Class Objects

While it’s true that every object is an instance of a class, what is a class really? In a language like C++, classes don’t exist at runtime, and the compiler translates the class structure into an executable program. An absolute contrast to this approach is Smalltalk: This runtime environment manages classes as objects. The idea of representing classes as objects is also adopted by Java—classes are objects of type <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Class</samp> .

```
class java.lang.
                Object 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final Class<? extends Object> getClass()</samp>
    Returns the reference to the class object that created the object. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object is always unique in the Java virtual machine (JVM). Thus, a call of <samp class="listingcharacter">x.getClass()</samp> from different instances <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> of type <samp class="listingcharacter">X</samp> always returns the same <samp class="listingcharacter">Class<X></samp> object, and the instance of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> can be safely checked using <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

The <samp class="listingcharacter">getName()</samp> object method of a <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object returns the name of the class, as in the following example:

```
System.out.println( "Klaviklack".getClass().getName() ); // java.lang.String
```

#### Class Literals

A class literal is an expression with the structure <samp class="listingcharacter">datatype</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">.class</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">datatype</samp> is a class, interface, array, or primitive type. Consider the following examples:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">String.class</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.class</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int.class</samp> (which isn’t identical to <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.class</samp> )

The type of the expression is always <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp>. For primitive types, writing <samp class="listingcharacter">primitiveType</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">.class</samp> returns the same result as <samp class="listingcharacter">wrapperType</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">.TYPE</samp>. For instance, <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.TYPE</samp> is therefore identical with <samp class="listingcharacter">int.class</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> objects play a role especially in dynamic queries via reflection . At runtime, any classes can be loaded, objects can be created, and methods can be called.

### 11.1.2     Object Identification with toString()

Each object should identify itself with a string via the <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> method and return the content of the relevant object variable as a string.

###### [eg]  Example

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> class implements <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> so that the return string contains the coordinates. Consider the following example:

```
System.out.println( new java.awt.Point() );  // java.awt.Point[x=0,y=0] 
```

One nice thing is that <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> is automatically called when the <samp class="listingcharacter">print*(...)</samp> methods are called with an object reference as argument. Similarly, this is also true for the string operator <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> with an object reference as operand, as in the following example:

```
public class Player {
  String name;
  int    age;

                @Override
  public String toString() {
    return getClass().getName() + "[name=" + name + ",age=" + age + "]";
  }
} 
```

**Listing 11.1**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/tostring/Player.java, Player

The result is the following output:

```
Player tinkerbelle = new Player();
tinkerbelle.name   = "Tinkerbelle";
tinkerbelle.age    = 32;
System.out.println( tinkerbelle.toString() );
System.out.println( tinkerbelle ); 
```

**Listing 11.2**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/tostring/PlayerToStringDemo.java, main()

is thus:

```
com.tutego.insel.object.tostring.Player[name=Tinkerbelle,age=32]
com.tutego.insel.object.tostring.Player[name=Tinkerbelle,age=32] 
```

In your own implementations, you must ensure that the visibility is <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> because <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> is publicly specified in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> superclass and you can’t restrict visibility in the subclass. Although the specification doesn’t clearly state that <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> must not return <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, the empty string <samp class="listingcharacter">""</samp> is definitely better. The <samp class="listingcharacter">@Override</samp> annotation makes the override clear.

###### [ ! ]  Warning

Some creative programmers use the <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> representation for object comparisons. For instance, if you have two <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> objects ( <samp class="listingcharacter">p</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">q</samp>) and <samp class="listingcharacter">p.toString().equals(q.toString())</samp>, then both points are equal. But relying on the return of <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> for this comparison is highly dangerous for several reasons: Obviously, <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> doesn’t need to be overridden. Second, <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> doesn’t necessarily need to represent all elements, and the output could be abbreviated. Third, of course, objects can be equal even if their string representations aren’t equal, which is the case with <samp class="listingcharacter">URL</samp> objects, for example. The only permitted case for such a construction would be <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">CharSequence</samp>, which explicitly deals with strings. In addition to erroneous behavior, often a massive performance problem arises. <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> usually takes shortcuts, so that, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">obj.equals(obj)</samp> immediately returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> or that, in the case of data structures, the objects are first tested for the same length before elements are compared.

#### JDK Standard Implementation

New classes should override <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp>. If not, the program will arrive at the default implementation in <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> , where only the class name and the less meaningful hash value are bound together hexadecimally, as in the following example:

```
public String toString() {
  return getClass().getName() + "@" + Integer.toHexString(hashCode());
} 
```

Let’s learn more about the method:

```
class java.lang.
                    Object 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String toString()</samp>
    Returns a string representation of the object consisting of class name and hash value.

While the hash value itself says little, for classes that don’t override <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> methods, a difference in the hash value is a first indication that the two references aren’t identical.

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, an object of <samp class="listingcharacter">class A {}</samp> is created, and <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> returns its ID:

```
class A {}
A a = new A();
System.out.println( "1\. " + a + ", 2\. " + a + ", 3\. " + new A() );
```

The output could be as follows:

```
1\. Main$1A@
                        4554617c, 2\. Main$1A@
                        4554617c, 3\. Main$1A@
                        74a14482 
```

With multiple calls of <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> on one instance (output 1 and 2), the return remains constant. When the program is restarted, the hash value may look different.

#### Having the toString() Method Generated

While the <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> method is good for debugging, typing the methods manually is rather annoying. Two solutions simplify the implementation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> method:

*   By default, IntelliJ can generate a <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> method for selected object variables via the context menu. By the way, the same is true for <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> .

*   The states are read automatically via reflection. In this case, Apache Commons Lang ([https://commons.apache.org/proper/commons-lang/](https://commons.apache.org/proper/commons-lang/)) leads onto the right path.

### 11.1.3     Object Equivalence with equals(...) and Identity

Whether two references represent the same object is determined by the comparison operator <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> , while <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> checks the opposite. The operators test against identity but know nothing of possible content equivalence. Our earlier example with strings illustrates this fact quite well: A comparison with <samp class="listingcharacter">firstname == "Christian"</samp> generally has an incorrect, unintended effect, although the expression is syntactically correct. At this point, the comparison of content should take place, evaluating whether all characters of the string match. An <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method should check objects for equivalence. Thus, the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object has an implementation that compares strings character by character, as in the following example:

```
String firstname = "Christian";
if ( "Christian".equals( firstname ) )
  …
class java.lang.
                Object 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">boolean equals(Object o)</samp>
    Tests if the other object is the same as your own. Equivalence is defined differently by each class, but the base class compares only the references <samp class="listingcharacter">o == this</samp> .

#### equals(...) Implementation from Object and Subclasses

The default implementation from the absolute superclass <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> can’t know anything about the equivalence of special objects and only tests the references.

```
public boolean equals( Object obj ) {
  return  this == obj;
} 
```

**Listing 11.3**     java/lang/Object.java, equals()

If a class doesn’t override <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp>, the result of <samp class="listingcharacter">o1.equals(o2)</samp> is equivalent to <samp class="listingcharacter">o1 == o2</samp> . Subclasses override this method to make a content comparison with their states. The method is well-served in subclasses because each class needs different logic to determine when an object is equal to another object.

Not every class implements its own <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp> method, so the runtime environment may inadvertently end up with <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> and its reference comparison. This scenario has unexpected consequences, and this misconception unfortunately occurs with instances of the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp> classes that don’t implement their own <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>. (We described this issue in detail in [Chapter 5](#05_001.html_h5), [Section 5.5.8](#05_005.html_h5.5.8) .)

#### Overriding the equals(…) Method

You must be careful when using self-declared methods because the signature is important in this context. The method must accept an <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> and return <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp>. If this signature is used incorrectly, overloading will occur (instead of the overriding of the method), and if the return isn’t equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp>, a second method with the same signature will be created, which isn’t permitted in Java (because Java doesn’t permit covariant parameter types yet). To minimize the problem, the <samp class="listingcharacter">@Override</samp> annotation should be appended to <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp> .

The use of the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp> method has some requirements, such as the following:

*   If the comparison is called <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(null)</samp>, the result is always <samp class="listingcharacter">false.</samp>

*   If a <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> is involved, a shortcut can be used, and <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> can be returned.

*   The argument may be of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>, but nevertheless, we’re always comparing concrete types. The <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp> method of a class <samp class="listingcharacter">X</samp> will therefore only compare objects of type <samp class="listingcharacter">X</samp>. An intriguing question is whether <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp> in class <samp class="listingcharacter">X</samp> should also take subclasses of <samp class="listingcharacter">X</samp> into consideration.

*   An implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp> should always involve an implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> because if two objects are equal according to <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>, the hash values must also be equal. However, with an inherited <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> this is not fulfilled in all cases, since presumably with equal objects <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> nevertheless returns different results.

###### [»]  Note

The data type for the parameter in the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp> method is always <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> and never anything else; otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> won’t be overridden but instead overloaded. Thus, the following notation for a class named <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp> is incorrect:

```
public class Candy {
  public int price;
  public boolean equals( 
                        Candy that ) { return this.price == that.price; }
}
```

In the words of computer scientists, Java doesn’t yet support covariant parameter types, but it does support covariant return types. For this reason, a good practice is to set the <samp class="listingcharacter">@Override</samp> annotation because it raises an alarm if we think we’re overriding a method but actually aren’t.

#### Basic Structure of the equals(...) Method

The previous list only captures the preliminary work until the actual comparison starts. Then, the comparison is a matter of comparing the state of one’s own object with the state of another object. In general, we can distinguish between tests of primitive values, tests of arrays, and tests of reference types :

*   For <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> and all primitive integer values, a simple <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> comparison is possible. In a <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> comparison of floats, a problem occurs due to the special value: not a number (NaN). This value bypasses the conversion to an integer bit pattern. Basically, a test using the static <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp> methods in the wrapper classes could also help in this case, in which <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...) == 0</samp> is used to check for equality.

*   For the comparison of arrays, <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.equals(array1, array2)</samp> is a good choice.

*   For the comparison of references, the comparison is passed to the objects, making sure that the reference variables are <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. The useful helper method <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects.equals(obj1, obj2)</samp> takes care of this comparison.

###### [+]  Tip

Of course, you could fall back on the object method <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> from the numeric wrapper classes, but doing so would involve the constant creation of new objects for each primitive comparison. This approach costs an unnecessary amount of time because <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> and also <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> methods must be fast since they are often called during operations in data structures.

#### Example of a custom equals(...) Method

The first two requirements are easy to meet, and an example of <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp> with the object variables <samp class="listingcharacter">price</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">quantity</samp> can be quickly implemented:

```
@Override
public boolean equals( Object o ) {
  if ( o == null )
    return false;

  if ( o == this )
    return true;

  Candy that = (Candy) o;

  return    this.price == that.price
         && this.quantity == that.quantity;
} 
```

This solution seems obvious but leads to a <samp class="listingcharacter">ClassCastException</samp> at least for a non- <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp> object. The problem can be solved quickly in the following way:

```
if ( ! (o instanceof Candy) )
  return false; 
```

Now, we are on the safe side, but has the goal been achieved?

###### [»]  Note

The <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method always returns <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> for non-matching types and doesn’t throw an exception.

#### The Problem of Symmetry *

While the listed implementation works well for final classes, the symmetry is broken for subclasses. Why? Quite simply, <samp class="listingcharacter">instanceof</samp> tests types in the hierarchy and will return <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> even if the argument passed to <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> is a subclass of <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp>. This subclass will have the same object variables as the superclass; thus, from the point of view of <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp>, everything is fine. Let’s assume two variables ( <samp class="listingcharacter">candy</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">toxicWaste</samp>) have the types <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">ToxicWaste</samp> (a fictitious subclass of <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp>), respectively. If both objects are equal, <samp class="listingcharacter">candy.equals(toxicWaste)</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>. Let’s turn the tables and ask what <samp class="listingcharacter">toxicWaste.equals(candy)</samp> will return. While we haven’t implemented <samp class="listingcharacter">ToxicWaste</samp>, we assume that there’s an <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method there, implemented using the same <samp class="listingcharacter">instanceof</samp> schema as <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp>. Then, a test will run <samp class="listingcharacter">o instanceof ToxicWaste</samp> and result in <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. However, this terminates the case distinction with <samp class="listingcharacter">return false</samp> . Let’s summarize:

```
 candy.equals( toxicWaste ) == true
toxicWaste.equals( candy ) == false 
```

This inconsistency is not acceptable, and to resolve it, you must not use <samp class="listingcharacter">instanceof</samp> but instead should ask if the type is exact. This check can be done via <samp class="listingcharacter">getClass()</samp> and a simple reference comparison. [[ 172 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn11_01) As a result, the following code is correct:

```
public class Candy {

  int price;
  int quantity;

  @Override
  public boolean equals( Object o ) {
    if ( o == null )
      return false;

    if ( o == this )
      return true;

    if ( o.getClass() != getClass() )
      return false;

    Candy that = (Candy) o;

    return    this.price == that.price
           && this.quantity == that.quantity;
  }

  @Override
  public int hashCode() {
    return 31 * price + quantity;
  }
} 
```

**Listing 11.4**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/Candy.java, Candy

You’ll learn more about the <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method in [Section 11.1.5](#11_001.html_h11.1.5). We’ve only included it here for the sake of completeness since <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> should always go hand in hand.

Specifying a new <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> for extended classes makes sense so that the new object variables will also be included in the test. For <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> methods, you’ll need to use a similar strategy.

#### Records and equals(…)/hashCode()

Records have an automatically implemented <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method. Primitive elements are implemented using the static <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> methods of the appropriate wrapper classes, and for references, the automatic implementation falls back on <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects.equals(...)</samp>. For <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp>, the vararg method <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects.hash(...)</samp> returns the hashcode across all record components.

#### Once the Same, Always the Same*

Another aspect of <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> [[ 173 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn11_02) should be noted: If the object is never changed, the result must remain the same throughout the lifecycle of the object. One small problem arises in <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> of the <samp class="listingcharacter">URL</samp> class, which compares whether two URL addresses that point to the same resource. According to the documentation:

> “Two URL objects are equal if they have the same protocol, reference equivalent hosts, have the same port number on the host, and the same file and fragment of the file.”

Host names are considered equal if either both point to the same IP address or, if an IP address can’t be resolved, both host names are equal (case-insensitive) or <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. However, since behind the URLs [http://tutego.com/](http://tutego.com/) and [http://www.tutego.com/](http://www.tutego.com/) ultimately exists [http://www.tutego.de/](http://www.tutego.de/), <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> will return <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> in the following example:

```
URL url1 = new URL( "http://tutego.com/" );
URL url2 = new URL( "http://www.tutego.com/" );
System.out.println( url1.equals( url2 ) );               // true 
```

**Listing 11.5**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/UrlEquals.java, main()

Dynamically mapping host names to IP address of computers can be problematic for several reasons:

*   The (human) reader intuitively expects something else.

*   If no network connection is available, no name resolution can be performed, and the comparison will return <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> . However, the return shouldn’t depend on whether or not a network connection exists.

*   The fact that the two URLs point to the same server could change at runtime.

### 11.1.4     Cloning an Object Using clone()*

Two ways to replicate an object are available:

*   A constructor (also called a copy constructor ) that takes an existing object as a template, creates a new object, and copies the states

*   A public <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> method

The application programming interface (API) documentation describes what each class can provide.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> object and then clones it:

```
java.awt.Point p = new java.awt.Point( 12, 23 );
java.awt.Point q = (java.awt.Point) 
                    p.clone();
System.out.println( q );                // java.awt.Point[x=12,y=23] 
```

More than 300 classes in the Java library support a <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> method that returns a new instance with the same state. An overridden method can customize the return type thanks to covariant return types. However, the <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> method at <samp class="listingcharacter">java.awt.Point</samp> use just the return type <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> .

Array objects provide <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> by default. However, if the arrays store non-primitive values, <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> will return only a flat copy, which means that the new array object (the clone) references the exact same objects as the original and doesn’t clone the entries themselves.

#### clone() from java.lang.Object

Since <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> isn’t automatically supported, the question is how you can implement <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> for your classes with the least effort. Simply calling <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> doesn’t work, however, because the method is <samp class="listingcharacter">protected</samp> , so the method is not visible for now.

```
class java.lang.
                    Object 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException</samp>
    Returns a copy of the object.

#### A Custom clone() Method

Custom classes override the <samp class="listingcharacter">protected</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> superclass and make it <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> . Two options can be considered for implementation:

*   You could manually create a new object, copy all object variables, and return the reference to the new object.

*   The runtime system should create a copy by itself, and we return that copy. The second solution shortens development time and is also more exciting.

To get the system to clone an object, two tasks must be performed:

*   A <samp class="listingcharacter">super.clone()</samp> call triggers the <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> method from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>, causing the runtime environment to create a new object and copy the object variables. The method copies the data of the current object element by element into the new one. The method is <samp class="listingcharacter">protected</samp> in the superclass, but that’s the trick: Only subclasses can call <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> ; classes outside the inheritance hierarchy cannot.

*   The class implements the marker interface <samp class="listingcharacter">Cloneable</samp>. If a <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> is called externally on an object whose class doesn’t implement <samp class="listingcharacter">Cloneable</samp> , the result is a <samp class="listingcharacter">CloneNotSupportedException</samp> . Of course, <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> does not implement the <samp class="listingcharacter">Cloneable</samp> interface itself because otherwise classes would already have this type automatically, which would be pointless.

<samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> returns a reference to the new object, but if no free memory is available, an <samp class="listingcharacter">OutOfMemoryError</samp> is thrown.

Let’s say that <samp class="listingcharacter">players</samp> need to be cloned for a game. You could write the following code:

```
package com.tutego.insel.object;

public class Player 
                    implements Cloneable {

  public String name;
  public int    age;

                    @Override
  public Player clone() {
    try {
      return (Player) super.clone();
    }
    catch ( CloneNotSupportedException e ) {
      // Can't really happen due to Cloneable
      throw new InternalError();
    }
  }
} 
```

**Listing 11.6**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/Player.java

Since covariant return types are possible in Java, <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> returns not just <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>, but the <samp class="listingcharacter">Player</samp> subtype, as shown in [Figure 11.2](#11_001.html_f11.2) . Let’s test the class in the following way:

```
 Player susi = new Player();
susi.age  = 29;
susi.name = "Susi";
Player dolly = 
                    susi.clone();
System.out.println( dolly.name + " is " + dolly.age ); // Susi is 29 
```

**Listing 11.7**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/PlayerCloneDemo.java, main()

[![Player Extends Object and Implements Cloneable](bilderklein/klein11_002.png)](img-f11.2.html)

**Figure 11.2**     Player Extends Object and Implements Cloneable

###### [»]  Note

If you inherit from a class with an implemented <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> method, which itself works with <samp class="listingcharacter">super.clone()</samp> , you’ll also get your own states copied.

#### clone() and equals(...)

The <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> method and the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method are related, as are the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> methods. If the <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> method is overridden, <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> should also be adjusted because, without an overridden <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>, the following code will be inherited from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> :

```
public boolean equals( Object obj ) {
  return  this == obj;
} 
```

**Listing 11.8**     java/lang/Object.java, equals()

However, as a result, a cloned object, which in general is a new object, is no longer <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>-equal to its creator because of its new object identity. Formally, this results in <samp class="listingcharacter">o.clone().equals(o) == false</samp> . These semantics are probably undesirable.

#### Shallow or Deep?

By default, the <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> method of the system creates a shallow copy . For child objects, only the references are copied, and the original object and the copy subsequently refer to the same child objects (they actually share them). For example, if an employee has an object variable for an employer and a copy of an employee is created, the clone will reference the same employer. With an employer, this copying may still be coherent, but for data structures, a deep copy is sometimes preferred. In this variant, all subobjects are also cloned recursively. The library implementation behind <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> can’t do that.

#### No Clones, Please!

If you don’t want either a shallow or a deep copy, but instead want to inherit a <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> implementation from the superclass, you can prevent cloning. In this case, you would override <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> but throw a <samp class="listingcharacter">CloneNotSupportedException</samp> signaling that you don’t want the object to be cloned. However, a problem will arise if a class already overrides the <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> method and changes the signature in the process. In <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> , the method head is written in the following way:

```
public class Object {
  …
  protected native Object clone() 
                    throws CloneNotSupportedException;
  …
} 
```

**Listing 11.9**     java/lang/Object.java (Snippet)

The method is <samp class="listingcharacter">native</samp> , which means the method not implemented in Java, but in the system language. The visibility is <samp class="listingcharacter">protected</samp> because only subclasses should see the methods. A subclass overrides <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> and usually omits the <samp class="listingcharacter">throws CloneNotSupportedException</samp>. Visibility is usually raised to <samp class="listingcharacter">public</samp> .

For <samp class="listingcharacter">Point2D</samp> (from which <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> inherits the <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> method), we can write the following:

```
public abstract class Point2D implements Cloneable {
  …

                    public Object clone()
  …
} 
```

**Listing 11.10**     java/awt/geom/Point2D.java (Snippet)

```
public class Point extends Point2D implements java.io.Serializable {
  …
} 
```

**Listing 11.11**     java/awt/Point.java (Snippet)

If a class inherits a <samp class="listingcharacter">clone()</samp> method from which <samp class="listingcharacter">throws CloneNotSupportedException</samp> has been removed, it can’t reintroduce the exception—subclasses can omit <samp class="listingcharacter">throws</samp> clauses but can’t add them. The following code is therefore not possible:

```
public class PointSubclass 
                    extends java.awt.Point {
  @Override // from Point2D
  public Object clone() 
                    throws CloneNotSupportedException // 

                     Compiler error!
  …
} 
```

Since the signature can no longer store an exception clause, you must use a trick and wrap the <samp class="listingcharacter">CloneNotSupportedException</samp> in a runtime exception, as in the following example:

```
public class ColoredPoint extends java.awt.Point {

  public int rgb;

  @Override              // from Point2D
  public Object clone() {

                    throw new RuntimeException( new CloneNotSupportedException() );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 11.12**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/ColoredPoint.java, ColoredPoint

An attempt at cloning leads to something like the following output:

```
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.RuntimeException:
java.lang.CloneNotSupportedException
  at com.tutego.insel.object.ColoredPoint.clone(ColoredPoint.java:10)

                      at …
Caused by: java.lang.CloneNotSupportedException
  ... 2 more 
```

Technically, wrapping the <samp class="listingcharacter">CloneNotSupportedException</samp> in a <samp class="listingcharacter">RuntimeException</samp> solves our problem; however, you should be aware that you’re now “disabling” a behavior that was previously permitted. Subclasses shouldn’t take away any behaviors.

### 11.1.5    Returning Hash Values via hashCode()*

The <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method is supposed to return an integer number (both positive and negative) for each object that is unique and identifies the object. The integer is called a hashcode or a hash value , and <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> is the implementation of a hash function . Hash values are necessary if the objects are placed in special data structures that work according to the hashing procedure. Data structures with hashing algorithms provide efficient access to their elements. The <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.HashMap</samp> class implements such a data structure.

```
class java.lang.
                Object 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int hashCode()</samp>
    Returns the hash value of an object. The base class <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> implements the method natively.

#### Player with Hash Function

In the following example, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Player</samp> class is supposed to override the <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>. To successfully store the objects in an associative memory, <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> is also required, which is also implemented by the <samp class="listingcharacter">Player</samp> class in the following example:

```
package com.tutego.insel.object.hashcode;

public class Player {

  String name;
  int    age;
  double weight;

  /**
   * Returns a hash code value for this {@code Player} object.
   *
   * @return A hash code value for this object.
   *

                       * @see java.lang.Object#equals(java.lang.Object)
   * @see java.util.HashMap
   */

                    @Override public int hashCode() {
    int result = 31 + age;
    result = 31 * result + ((name == null) ? 0 : name.hashCode());
    long temp = Double.doubleToLongBits( weight );
    result = 31 * result + (int) (temp ^ (temp >>> 32));

    return result;
  }

  /**
   * Determines whether two players are equal. Two instances of
   * {@code Player} are equal if the values of their {@code name}, {@code age}
   * and {@code weight} member fields are the same.
   *
   * @param that   an object to be compared with this {@code Player}
   *
   * @return {@code true} if the object to be compared is an instance of
   *         {@code Player} and has the same values; {@code false} otherwise.
   */
  @Override
  public boolean equals( Object that ) {
    if ( this == that )
      return true;

    if ( that == null )
      return false;

    if ( getClass() != that.getClass() )
      return false;

    Player other = (Player) that;

    if ( age != other.age )
      return false;

    if ( Double.compare( weight, other.weight ) != 0 )
      return false;

    if ( ! Objects.equals( name, other.name ) )
      return false;

                        return true;
  }
} 
```

**Listing 11.13**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/hashcode/Player.java

We can test the class with something like the following lines:

```
Player bruceWants = new Player();
bruceWants.name = "Bruce Wants";
bruceWants.age = 32;
bruceWants.weight = 70.3;

Player bruceLii = new Player();
bruceLii.name = "Bruce Lii";
bruceLii.age = 32;
bruceLii.weight = 70.3;

System.out.println( bruceWants.hashCode() );                 // -340931147
System.out.println( bruceLii.hashCode() );                   // 301931244
System.out.println( System.identityHashCode( bruceWants ) ); // 1671711
System.out.println( System.identityHashCode( bruceLii ) );   // 11394033
System.out.println( bruceLii.equals( bruceWants ) );         // false

bruceWants.name = "Bruce Lii";
System.out.println( bruceWants.hashCode() );                 // 301931244
System.out.println( bruceLii.equals( bruceWants ) );         // true 
```

**Listing 11.14**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/hashcode/PlayerHashcodeDemo.java, main()

The static method <samp class="listingcharacter">System.identityHashCode(...)</samp> returns the hashcode for an object as it would be returned by the default implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> if we hadn’t overridden it.

###### [»]  Note

Since the hashcode can be negative, expressions like <samp class="listingcharacter">array[o.hashCode() % array. length()]</samp> are problematic. If <samp class="listingcharacter">o.hashCode()</samp> is negative, the result of the remainder is also negative, and the consequence is an <samp class="listingcharacter">ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException</samp> .

IntelliJ can automatically generate the <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> methods, so you don’t need to write them by hand.

#### Deep or Shallow Comparisons/Hash Values

If an object references subobjects, for example, a person references a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object for the name (no primitive data types), the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> methods pass the comparison and calculation of the hashcode to the referenced subobject (provided the reference isn’t <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> ). The following snippet of our <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method illustrates this point:

```
if ( name == null )
  if ( ((Player)that).name != null )
    return false;
else if ( !
                    name.equals( ((Player)that).name ) )
  return false; 
```

**Listing 11.15**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/hashcode/Player.java, equals() (Snippet)

Accordingly, one task of the <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> class ( <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>) is to perform the equivalence test. Thus, two individuals can be <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>-equal without any problem, even if they reference two non-identical but <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>-equal <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects.

This delegation to the referenced subobject can be read with <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> too, as in the following example:

```
result = 31 * result + ((name == null) ? 0 : 
                    name.hashCode()); 
```

**Listing 11.16**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/hashcode/Player.java, hashCode() (Snippet)

In rare cases, an <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method or <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method of a class doesn’t delegate the comparison or hashcode calculation to the child objects but instead implements the comparison or calculation operation itself.

#### hashCode() Methods of the Wrapper Classes

Each wrapper class declares a static <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode(...)</samp> method that you can use to compute the hash value of a primitive element. ( [Section 11.5](#11_005.html_h11.5) provides further details about this topic.) Consequently, to calculate the hash value of an entire object, all the individual hash values must be calculated and then concatenated to form an integer, in the following way:

```
int h1 = 
                    WrapperClass.hashCode( value1 );
int h2 = 
                    WrapperClass.hashCode( value2 );
int h3 = 
                    WrapperClass.hashCode( value3 );
… 
```

Generators often use the following pattern to link the hash values, which is a good starting point:

```
 int result = h1;
result = 31 * result + h2;
result = 31 * result + h3;
… 
```

If you use the static <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode(...)</samp> methods of the wrapper classes, you only need to work with the data type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and don’t need to know how the hash value is calculated from a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> , for example. However, calculating a hash value may come up, so here’s the implementation:

| Class | Class Method, Static int | Implementation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Boolean</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode(boolean value)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">value ? 1231 : 1237</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode(byte value)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)value</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode(short value)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)value</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode(int value)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode(long value)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)(value ^ (value >>> 32))</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode(float value)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">floatToIntBits(value)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode(double value)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)(doubleToLongBits(value) ^</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">(doubleToLongBits(value) >>> 32));</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Character</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode(char value)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)value</samp> |

**Table 11.1**     Static hashCode(...) Methods and Their Implementations

#### equals(...) and hashCode() Calculation for (Multidimensional) Arrays

Multidimensional arrays represent a special case with regard to <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(…)</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp>. Multidimensional arrays are nothing more than arrays of arrays. The first array for the first dimension references sub-arrays for the second dimension. This implementation becomes important when a question arises as to how these references of the first dimension should be considered with regard to <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>. In this case, the question is whether the sub-arrays of two arrays are only identical or are also the same. (We addressed this issue in more detail in [Chapter 4](#04_001.html_h4), [Section 4.6](#04_006.html_h4.6) .)

If your class contains an array and that should be considered in an <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>, then three variants are possible for handling this array. Comparing arrays yourself via <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> as if they were primitive values is fine if the identity of the arrays is desired in the comparison. While many classes override the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method of <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>, arrays are objects too but they don’t provide their own <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method. The result of an <samp class="listingcharacter">arrays1.equals (arrays2)</samp> call would therefore be an identity comparison. A real content comparison is possible with methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays</samp> utility class. However, two methods could be used in this case:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.equals(Object[] a, Object[] a2)</samp> goes through each element of <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp>. In the case of multidimensional arrays, each reference to a sub-array is considered and tested to determine whether it’s identical to the second array <samp class="listingcharacter">a2</samp>. Thus, if two equal but non-identical main arrays have identical sub-arrays, <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.equals(...)</samp> will return <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>. However, it will retur <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> if the sub-arrays are not identical.

*   If the equality of the sub-arrays plays a role, <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.deepEquals(...)</samp> is the appropriate method because this method always queries the sub-arrays with <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> .

A comparable issue exists when you calculate the hash value. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays</samp> class provides the <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.hashCode(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.deepHashCode(...)</samp> methods to calculate the hash value of an entire array. The first method asks each sub-element for the <samp class="listingcharacter">hash</samp> value via the <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method provided by <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> .

Let’s assume we have a multidimensional array. Then, the sub-element is also an array. <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.hashCode(...)</samp> will then, as mentioned, only call the <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method on the array object, while <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.deepHashCode(...)</samp> will also descend into the sub-array and call <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.deepHashCode(...)</samp> on all sub-arrays until an <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> comparison is possible on a non-array.

What does this mean for our <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(…)</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method? The IntelliJ IDE generates the following code for a two-dimensional <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> array, which uses <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.deep*(...)</samp> :

```
char[][] chessboard = new char[8][8];

  @Override public boolean equals( Object o ) {
    if ( this == o )
      return true;
    if ( !(o instanceof Chess) )
      return false;

    Chess chess = (Chess) o;

    return Arrays.deepEquals( chessboard, chess.chessboard );
  }

  @Override public int hashCode() {
    return Arrays.deepHashCode( chessboard );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 11.17**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/hashcode/Chess.java, Chess

#### Hash Value of a float

Depending on the data types, the calculations always look slightly different. While integers can be put directly into an integer expression for the hash value, in the case of <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, the static conversion methods <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.doubleToLongBits(double)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Float.floatToIntBits(float)</samp> are in use.

The data types <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> have another specialty since <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.NaN</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Float.NaN</samp> and the sign of 0 have to be considered (as described in detail in [Chapter 21](#21_001.html_h21), [Section 21.2.1](#21_002.html_h21.2.1) ).
