In conclusion, if <samp class="listingcharacter">x = +0.0</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">y = –0.0</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp>, but <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.doubleToLongBits(x)</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.doubleToLongBits(y)</samp> .

If <samp class="listingcharacter">x = y = Double.NaN</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">y</samp>, but <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.doubleToLongBits(x)</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.doubleToLongBits(y)</samp> .

If we don’t want to treat the two zeros differently, but instead want to value them as the same, the following is a common idiom:

```
x == 0.0 ? 0L : Double.doubleToLongBits( x ) 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">Double.doubleToLongBits(0.0)</samp> returns “0,” but calling <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.doubleToLongBits(-0.0)</samp> returns “–9.223.372.036.854.775.808.”

#### Equals, the Zero, and Hashing

Objects with equivalent contents according to the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method must get the same hash value.

The two methods <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> are related. Usually when one method is implemented, an implementation of the other method is also necessary because, in the case of equivalence, the hash values must of course also match, which can be written formally in the following way:

```
x.equals( y ) => x.hashCode() == y.hashCode() 
```

This statement captures how the hash value for <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> objects should be calculated from their coordinates. Two point objects that are identical in content have the same coordinates and thus have the same hash value.

If objects have the same hash value but aren’t the same (called a collision ), we have a case where equivalence does not hold in the equation. In other words, don’t assume that, if the hash values of two objects are equal, that the objects are also equal. The probability of equivalence may be high, but this scenario doesn’t necessarily guarantee that the two objects are truly equal.

### 11.1.6    System.identityHashCode(...) and the Problem of Non-Unique Object References*

The equality of objects can be redefined with the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method. If <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> is newly implemented, then this implementation usually also applies to the <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method, which should also be overwritten.

The default implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> now operates in the following way: Different hash values are calculated even for objects that take the same values, which is another reason why you should override <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp>. But what does <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> actually return? This object ID uniquely identifies the object. The original ID is lost when <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> is reimplemented. But if you’re interested in the original <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> value, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">System.identityHashCode(...)</samp> .

###### [»]  Note

Although the hash values for two <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>-equals objects are the same, <samp class="listingcharacter">identityHashCode()</samp> usually returns different values:

```
Point p = new Point( 0, 0 );
Point q = new Point( 0, 0 );
System.out.println( System.identityHashCode(p) ); // e. g. 16032330
System.out.println( System.identityHashCode(q) ); // e. g. 13288040
System.out.println( p.hashCode() );               // 0
System.out.println( q.hashCode() );               // 0
```

If <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> isn’t overridden, then the hash value matches the <samp class="listingcharacter">identityHashCode(...)</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

Some classes don’t override <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp>, and thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">identityHashCode(...)</samp> is equal to the hash value. This scenario arises, for example, with the <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp> class, as shown in the following example:

```
StringBuilder sb1 = new StringBuilder(), sb2 = new StringBuilder();
System.out.printf( "%d %d%n", System.identityHashCode(sb1), sb1.hashCode() );
// for example 1829164700 1829164700
System.out.printf( "%d %d%n", System.identityHashCode(sb2), sb2.hashCode() );
// for example 460141958 460141958
```

This static method <samp class="listingcharacter">identityHashCode(...)</samp> returns the original identifier of the objects. At first glance, these identifiers may look like unique IDs, but may not be. You may indeed have two different objects in the memory for which the result of <samp class="listingcharacter">System.identityHashCode(...)</samp> is the same.

### 11.1.7    Synchronization*

Threads can communicate with each other and share data in the process. Threads can also wait for certain conditions to occur, for example, new input data. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> class declares a total of five versions of the <samp class="listingcharacter">wait(...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">notify()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">notifyAll()</samp> methods for thread termination synchronization.

## 11.2     Weak References and Cleaners

References to objects around us in everyday life are called strong references because automatic garbage collection would never release a used object. However, in addition to strong references, with weak references , the garbage collector will remove the objects. What sounds crazy at first becomes interesting when implementing caching data structures: If an object is in the cache, that’s fine and access is fast; if the object is not in the cache, that’s fine too, but access takes a little longer. Thus, you can use weak references to create cached objects that automatic garbage collection is allowed to clear up when memory is running low.

Thus, weak references interact with automatic garbage collection in a simple way, through a few types for in the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.base</samp> module in the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.ref</samp> package. Special containers can reference an object but still can be emptied by automatic garbage collection, such as the following:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">SoftReference<T></samp>: A container for softly reachable objects. These objects are released late by the garbage collector when the JVM approaches an <samp class="listingcharacter">OutOfMemoryError</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">WeakReference<T></samp>: A container for weakly reachable objects. These objects are released by the garbage collector relatively early in the first garbage collection.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">PhantomReference<T></samp> : A container that’s always empty but is used to keep track of when the garbage collector separates from an object.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Reference<T></samp>: Abstract base class for “reference objects” of <samp class="listingcharacter">PhantomReference</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">SoftReference</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">WeakReference</samp> .

The containers themselves aren’t removed by the garbage collector and end up in a <samp class="listingcharacter">ReferenceQueue<T></samp>. The queue can be used to determine which <samp class="listingcharacter">Reference</samp> containers are empty and can be removed from a data structure, for example. Empty containers are useless and can’t be recycled.

Another type in the package is <samp class="listingcharacter">Cleaner</samp> . An operation (of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Cleaner.Cleanable</samp> ) can be registered to a <samp class="listingcharacter">Cleaner</samp>, which will be called whenever the automatic garbage collection strikes and the object is no longer accessible. Internally, the class uses <samp class="listingcharacter">PhantomReference</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

Let’s create a point and register a <samp class="listingcharacter">Cleaner</samp>. Then, we’ll stimulate the garbage collector by using too much memory space, which will trigger the <samp class="listingcharacter">Cleaner</samp> .

```
Point p = new Point( 1, 2 );
Cleaner.create().register( p, () -> System.out.println( "point is gone" ) );
p = null;
new byte[ (int) Runtime.getRuntime().freeMemory() ].clone();
```

**Listing 11.18**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/lang/ref/CleanerDemo, main()

The <samp class="listingcharacter">register(Object obj, Runnable action)</samp> method receives the object to watch in the first parameter and then a <samp class="listingcharacter">Runnable</samp>, calling the <samp class="listingcharacter">run()</samp> method whenever the <samp class="listingcharacter">Cleaner</samp> cleans up. With our need for memory, therefore, a console output of “Point is gone!” is likely. In no case may the cleanup operation reference <samp class="listingcharacter">p</samp> again. This example also uses a lambda expression (with the arrow) to shorten the code a little. More on this topic will follow in [Chapter 13](#13_001.html_h13) .

## 11.3    The java.util.Objects Utility Class

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects</samp> class contains some static utility functions. These functions primarily perform <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> tests to avoid a subsequent <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> when object methods are called.

### 11.3.1    Built-In Null Tests for equals(...)/hashCode()

For example, if the object variable <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> of a person is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, then <samp class="listingcharacter">name.hashCode()</samp> can’t simply be called without a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> following the call. Three methods of <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects</samp> perform <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> tests before being passed to the <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> method: <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(…)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp>. An additional helper method works with comparators, which you’ll learn more about in [Section 11.4](#11_004.html_h11.4) .

```
class java.util.
                Objects 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static boolean equals(Object a, Object b)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if both arguments are either <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> or if <samp class="listingcharacter">a.equals(b)</samp> also returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>; otherwise, this method returns <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. That <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects.equals(null, null)</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> makes sense, and thus, the method saves you from some manual testing.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int hashCode(Object o)</samp>
    Returns 0 if <samp class="listingcharacter">o</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>; otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter">o.hashCode()</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int hash(Object… values)</samp>
    Calls <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> on each object in the <samp class="listingcharacter">values</samp> collection and concatenates it to a new hash value. The implementation is simply a <samp class="listingcharacter">return Arrays.hashCode(values)</samp> . Using the method is rather expensive due to the construction of the varargs array and possible boxing operations for primitive values.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> int compare(T a, T b, Comparator<? super T> c)</samp>
    Returns 0 if <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> are both either <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> or the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> declares the objects <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> to be equal. If <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> are both not <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, the return is <samp class="listingcharacter">c.compare(a, b)</samp>. If only <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, the result depends on the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> and the order of the parameters.

###### [eg]   Example

Let’s recall the overridden <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method for a player (described in [Section 11.1.5](#11_001.html_h11.1.5) ), where the player name should go into the hash value.

```
result = 31 * result + ((name == null) ? 0 : 
                    name.hashCode());
```

**Listing 11.19**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/object/hashcode/Player.java, hashCode() (Snippet)

With <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects.hashCode(Object)</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> test can be omitted because the static method already performs it. Consider the following example:

```
result = 31 * result + Objects.hashCode( name );
```

### 11.3.2    Objects.toString(…)

Another static method is <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects.toString(Object)</samp>. This method exists in the class for symmetry reasons since <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> is one of the standard methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> class. The method doesn’t need to be used because a corresponding method already exists with <samp class="listingcharacter">String.valueOf(...)</samp> .

```
class java.util.
                Objects 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toString(Object o)</samp>
    Returns the string <samp class="listingcharacter">"null"</samp> if the argument is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>; otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter">o.toString()</samp> .

###### [»]  Note

The <samp class="listingcharacter">String.valueOf(...)</samp> method is overloaded and better suited for primitive arguments than <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects.toString(Object)</samp>, which always requires wrapper objects to be created first. Although <samp class="listingcharacter">String.valueOf(3.14)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects.toString(3.14)</samp> look the same, in the second case, a wrapper <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> object comes into play.

### 11.3.3    null Checks with Built-In Exception Handling

In the preceding methods, <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> is treated as a special case, and exceptions are avoided. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects.toString(null)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects.hashCode(null)</samp> are fine and “work around” <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. This flexibility is not always useful, however, because traditionally you want to avoid <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> as an argument and in returns. Therefore, a good practice is to first test in a method body to determine whether the arguments are non- <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, unless <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> is absolutely desired.

For tests that check whether references are non- <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects</samp> provides a couple of <samp class="listingcharacter">requireNonNull*(...)</samp> methods to carry out <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> checks and throw a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> if an error occurs. These tests are useful for constructors and setters that should initial ize values but want to prevent <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> from being passed through.

###### [eg]  Example

The <samp class="listingcharacter">setName(...)</samp> method is supposed to prohibit a <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> argument equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> . Consider the following example:

```
public void setName( String name ) {
  this.name = 
                    Objects.requireNonNull( name );
}
```

Alternatively, the following error message is possible:

```
public void setName( String name ) {
  this.name = 
                Objects.requireNonNull( name, "Name must not be null" );
}
class java.util.
                Objects 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> T requireNonNull(T obj)</samp>
    Throws a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> if <samp class="listingcharacter">obj</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. Otherwise, the <samp class="listingcharacter">obj</samp> is the return. The declaration is generic and to be understood in such a way that the parameter type is the same as the return type.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> T requireNonNull(T obj, String message)</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter">requireNonNull(obj)</samp>, except that the <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> message is determined.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> T requireNonNull(T obj, Supplier<String> messageSupplier)</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter">requireNonNull(obj, message)</samp>, but the message comes from <samp class="listingcharacter">messageSupplier</samp>. This is useful for messages that are more expensive to build because the <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier</samp> defers the cost of creating the string until a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> actually occurs because only then is the message necessary.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> T requireNonNullElse(T obj, T defaultObj)</samp>
    Returns the first object that’s not <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">defaultObj</samp> must not be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>; otherwise, a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> will follow. Implemented as <samp class="listingcharacter">return (obj != null) ? obj : requireNonNull (defaultObj, "defaultObj");</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> T requireNonNullElseGet(T obj, Supplier<? extends T> supplier)</samp>
    Returns the first object that isn’t <samp class="listingcharacter">null.</samp> If <samp class="listingcharacter">obj</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, the method gets the reference from the <samp class="listingcharacter">supplier</samp>, which then must not return <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>; otherwise, a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> will follow.

### 11.3.4    Tests for null

Behind <samp class="listingcharacter">isNull(Object o)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">nonNull(Object o)</samp>, a simple test is available for <samp class="listingcharacter">o == null</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">o != null</samp> .

```
 class java.util.
                Objects 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static boolean isNull(Object obj)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static boolean nonNull(Object obj)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if <samp class="listingcharacter">obj</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> or non- <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>; otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> .

In normal program code, developers won’t use these methods, but these methods are useful for method references so that, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">stream.filter(Objects::nonNull)</samp> can be read. We’ll return to method references in [Chapter 13](#13_001.html_h13), [Section 13.2](#13_002.html_h13.2), and [Chapter 18](#18_001.html_h18), [Section 18.4](#18_004.html_h18.4) .

### 11.3.5    Checking Index-Related Program Arguments for Correctness

In [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.1.2](#09_001.html_h9.1.2), we highlighted the need to check value ranges and throw exceptions, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">IllegalArgumentException</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">IndexOutOfBoundsException</samp> , in case of errors to prevent incorrect values from sneaking into the object.

Other methods from <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects</samp> check valid value ranges of index-based methods and throw an <samp class="listingcharacter">IndexOutOfBoundsException</samp> in case of an error.

```
class java.util.
                Objects 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int checkIndex(int index, int length)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long checkIndex(long index, long length)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int checkFromToIndex(int fromIndex, int toIndex, int length)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long checkFromToIndex(long fromIndex, long toIndex, long length)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int checkFromIndexSize(int fromIndex, int size, int length)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long checkFromIndexSize(long fromIndex, long size, long length)</samp>

###### [eg]  Example

The following example is an implementation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">get(int)</samp> method in <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.ArrayList</samp> :

```
public E get(int index) {
  Objects.checkIndex(index, size);
  return elementData(index);
}
```

The private <samp class="listingcharacter">elementData(int index)</samp> method directly accesses the internal array with <samp class="listingcharacter">elementData[index]</samp>, which could be larger, however, because the implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">ArrayList</samp> has a certain buffer size. Therefore, prior index-verification is necessary.

## 11.4     Comparing Objects and Establishing Order

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(Object)</samp> provides information about whether two objects have the same state but says nothing about which object is “bigger” or “smaller.” However, in many applications, the order of objects plays a role. This need is obvious in sorting operations, but also in simpler questions, such as finding the largest or smallest item in a collection. If objects are to be compared in Java, these objects must always be arranged in a certain order. The system can never decide on its own, and often, multiple criteria determine a sort order. For example, why is one candy “smaller” than another candy? Perhaps one candy has 20 calories and the other has 600 calories, or maybe because they have different weights?

### 11.4.1    Naturally Ordered or Not?

In Java, two different functional interfaces (in two different packages) for determining the order are available:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp>
    When a class implements <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp>, objects can compare themselves with other objects. Since the classes generally implement only one sorting criterion, natural ordering is implemented in this case.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp>
    An implementing class called <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> takes two objects and compares them. A <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> for candy could, for example, compare according to calories or weight or use a completely different logic. The implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> would not make sense because in this case only one criterion can be implemented (“natural” order), but candies follow no natural order. [[ 174 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn11_03)

To summarize, while <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> usually implements only one ordering criterion, many extra classes of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> type may exist, each defining different orders.

#### Comparable and Comparator in the Java Application Programming Interface

An implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> can be found exactly where a natural ordering is obvious, such as with the following types:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Character</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Date</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Calendar</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">LocalTime</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">LocalDate</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuilder</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">StringBuffer</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">URI</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Enum</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">TimeUnit</samp>

The API documentation contains only a little information on <samp class="listingcharacter">java.text.Collator</samp> and its subclass, <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> .

[![Simplified UML Diagram of Comparator and Comparable](bilderklein/klein11_003.png)](img-f11.3.html)

**Figure 11.3**     Simplified UML Diagram of Comparator and Comparable

###### [»]  Note

Since two ways exist to define an ordering with <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp>, the Java API often provides two methods when an ordering is needed: one with a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> (then no requirement is placed on the elements) and one without a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> (but then the elements must implement the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> interface). If a variant with natural order is missing, a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> can be queried at any time with <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator.naturalOrder()</samp>, which falls back on the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp> .

### 11.4.2    compare*() Method of the Comparable and Comparator Interfaces

The functional interface <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> originates from the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang</samp> package and declares a <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp> method:

```
interface java.lang.
                Comparable<T
                > 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(T o)</samp>
    Compares itself with another object.

The functional interface <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> comes from the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util</samp> package (not from <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang</samp> like <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp>, shown in [Figure 11.3](#11_004.html_f11.3) ) and declares an abstract method:

```
interface java.util.
                Comparator<T> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int compare(T o1, T o2)</samp>
    Compares two arguments for their order.

###### [»]  Note*

In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">compare(...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> also declares the <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean equals (object obj)</samp> known from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>. This method doesn’t need to be implemented because <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> already provides an implementation. The method is in the interface only so that the API documentation explains that <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> only tests whether two <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> objects are equal.

### 11.4.3    Return Values Encode the Order

The return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">compare(...)</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> may be less than 0 (negative), equal to 0, or greater than 0 (positive) and thus determines the order of the objects—referred to as a three-way comparison . Let’s assume you have two objects <samp class="listingcharacter">o1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">o2</samp> whose classes implement <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> . Then, the following agreement rules apply:

| <samp class="listingcharacter">o1.compareTo( o2 ) < 0</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">o1.compareTo( o2 ) == 0</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">o1.compareTo( o2 ) > 0</samp> | ![inline image](bilder/2way-arrow.png)![inline image](bilder/2way-arrow.png)![inline image](bilder/2way-arrow.png) | <samp class="listingcharacter">o1</samp> is “smaller than” <samp class="listingcharacter">o2</samp> .<samp class="listingcharacter">o1</samp> is “equal to” <samp class="listingcharacter">o2</samp> .<samp class="listingcharacter">o1</samp> is “greater than” <samp class="listingcharacter">o2</samp> . |

An external <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> (symbolically called <samp class="listingcharacter">comp</samp> ) behaves similarly:

| <samp class="listingcharacter">comp.compare( o1, o2 ) < 0</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">comp.compare( o1, o2 ) == 0</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">comp.compare( o1, o2 ) > 0</samp> | ![inline image](bilder/2way-arrow.png)![inline image](bilder/2way-arrow.png)![inline image](bilder/2way-arrow.png) | <samp class="listingcharacter">o1</samp> is “smaller than” <samp class="listingcharacter">o2</samp> .<samp class="listingcharacter">o1</samp> is “equal to” <samp class="listingcharacter">o2</samp> .<samp class="listingcharacter">o1</samp> is “greater than” <samp class="listingcharacter">o2</samp> . |

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter">LocalTime</samp> represents time values, and the class implements <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> :

```
LocalTime elevenses = LocalTime.of( 11, 0 );
LocalTime lunchtime = LocalTime.of( 12, 0 );
System.out.println( elevenses.compareTo( lunchtime ) );  //  -1
System.out.println( lunchtime.compareTo( elevenses ) );  //  1
```

### 11.4.4    Sorting Candy by Calories Using a Sample Comparator

Let’s say we need to sort candies by their calories and thus need to write a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> for this purpose—that candies are <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> isn’t appropriate because no natural order exists for candies.

Therefore, an external <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> object should decide which <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp> object is “bigger” by the number of its calories. Fewer calories mean the candy is “smaller.”

The following <samp class="listingcharacter">Candy</samp> record stores calorie values:

```
public record Candy(int calories) {}
```

**numbering_unknown**      Listing 11.20: src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/util/Candy.java, Candy

A candy built by <samp class="listingcharacter">new Candy(100)</samp> should be “smaller” than <samp class="listingcharacter">new Candy(623)</samp>. For this purpose, the candy <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> must use the calories, and no other criteria exist.

```
class CandyCaloriesComparator implements Comparator<Candy> {
  @Override public int compare( Candy candy1, Candy candy2 ) {
    return Integer.compare( candy1.calories(), candy2.calories() );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 11.21**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/util/CandyCaloriesComparator.java, CandyKcalComparator

All wrapper classes have <samp class="listingcharacter">compare(...)</samp> methods for a three-way comparison. This construction is shorter than instructions like the following:

```
int v1 = candy1.calories(), v2 = candy2.calories();
if ( v1 < v2 ) return -1;
else if ( v1 > v2 ) return 1;
return 0; 
```

###### [+]  Design Tip

A comparator can basically have a state, for example for the language, if strings are included in the comparison. A stateless comparator can be programmed with an <samp class="listingcharacter">enum</samp> or written compactly with a lambda expression.

Many places in libraries will require ordering, such as when searching for the maximum element or sorting a list. <samp class="listingcharacter">Collections.max(...)</samp>, for example, finds the largest element of a list, while <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.sort(...)</samp> sorts an array.

Let’s consider an example illustrating how the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> object can do many things, for example, find the largest or smallest element in a collection or sort a data structure. Let’s sort an array of candy. The candy with the fewest calories should be placed in front.

```
Candy[] candies = { new Candy( 100 ), new Candy( 623 ), new Candy( 123 ) };
Arrays.sort( candies, new CandyCaloriesComparator() );
System.out.println( candies[ 0 ].calories() );      // 100 
```

**Listing 11.22**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/util/CandyCaloriesComparatorDemo.java (Snippet)

[![ The Custom Comparator Must Merely Override compare(...) from the Interface](bilderklein/klein11_004.png)](img-f11.4.html)

**Figure 11.4**     The Custom Comparator Must Merely Override compare(...) from the Interface

The sorting method always draws on the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> for the pairs to compare and then asks for the order. If you include a <samp class="listingcharacter">println(...)</samp> in your <samp class="listingcharacter">compare(...)</samp> method, you can watch the sort algorithm at work.

### 11.4.5    Tips for Comparator and Comparable Implementations

If objects should be compared with a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp>, but <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> values should be sorted out beforehand, the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">int compare(T a, T b, Comparator<? super T> c)</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter">Objects</samp> class is useful. The method returns 0 if <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> are both either <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> or the <samp class="listingcharacter">comparator</samp> declares the objects <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> to be equal. If <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> are both not <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, the return is <samp class="listingcharacter">c.compare(a, b)</samp>. If only <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, the return depends on the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> and the order of the parameters.

For implementations of <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp>, in addition to an implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp>, the appropriate implementation in <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> is also important. This implementation consistent only if <samp class="listingcharacter">e1.compareTo(e2) == 0</samp> returns the same result as <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">e1.equals(e2)</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">e1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">e2</samp> have the same type. A violation of this rule can quickly cause problems with sorted sets; the API documentation provides an example. Also, the <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> method should be implemented correctly because, if objects are equal, the hash values must also be equal. Finally, the equivalence is determined by <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(…)</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(…)</samp> .

<samp class="listingcharacter">e.compareTo(null)</samp> should throw a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> even if <samp class="listingcharacter">e.equals(null)</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> is usually not greater than, less than, or equal to another value compared with <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp> so an exception is the only reasonable response.

Java supports serialization, where the states of complex objects are written serially into a data stream. From this data, an object can be reconstructed later, through a process referred to as deserialization. Serializable objects implement the <samp class="listingcharacter">Serializable</samp> interface. If a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> is connected to a data structure—such as a <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap</samp>—and the data structure is to be serialized. However, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> implementation must also implement <samp class="listingcharacter">Serializable</samp> .

### 11.4.6    Static and Default Methods in Comparator

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> interface provides a whole set of static and default methods. (By the way, no static or default methods exist in <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp>.) Particularly interesting are the options for linking several <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> s together.

Let’s start with the methods that are easy to understand:

```
interface java.util.
                Comparator<T> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> Comparator<T> naturalOrder()</samp>
    Returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> that uses the natural order of objects, which means <samp class="listingcharacter">int compare(Comparable<Object> c1, Comparable<Object> c2)</samp> is implemented as <samp class="listingcharacter">return c1.compareTo(c2);</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> Comparator<T> reverseOrder()</samp>
    The static method returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> that uses the natural order like <samp class="listingcharacter">naturalOrder()</samp> but reverses the order and thus corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter">Collections.reverseOrder()</samp>. Basically, this method is a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> with a <samp class="listingcharacter">compare(Comparable<Object> c1, Comparable<Object> c2)</samp> method that returns <samp class="listingcharacter">c2.compareTo(c1)</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default Comparator<T> reversed()</samp>
    Returns a new <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> for this current <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> that reverses the order. Corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter">Collections.reverseOrder(this)</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> Comparator<T> nullsFirst(Comparator<? super T> comparator)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> Comparator<T> nullsLast(Comparator<? super T> comparator)</samp>
    For a given <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp>, these methods return a new <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> for comparisons with <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> and places <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> either before or after the other values in order.

#### Sequence of Comparators

Often, the ordering criterion is composed of several conditions, as the sorting in a phone book shows. First, you might sort by last name, then follows with sorting by first name. To achieve this goal with a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> object, either all individual comparators must be packed into a new <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> object, or individual <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparators</samp> must be bound together to form a “super”- <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp>. The second solution is of course the recommended approach because it increases reusability, and individual <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp>s can then be easily used for other contexts. A useful method is available in <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> for exactly such a stringing:

```
interface java.util.
                    Comparator<T> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default Comparator<T> thenComparing(Comparator<? super T> other)</samp>
    First applies its own <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> and, if it shows states as being equal, then applies the other <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">other</samp>. In other words, if the current <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> returns the result 0, the second passed <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> must answer the question about the order.

Let’s now use these <samp class="listingcharacter">thenComparing(...)</samp> methods from <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> in an example that sorts a list of names by last name and then by first name.

```
public class ComparatorThenComparingDemo {

  record Candy(int calories, String name) {
    @Override public String toString() {
      return name + "/" + calories;
    }
  }

  static final Comparator<Candy> CANDY_CALORIES_COMPARATOR =
      new Comparator<Candy>() {
        public int compare( Candy c1, Candy c2 ) {
          return Integer.compare( c1.calories(), c2.calories() );
        }
      };

  static final Comparator<Candy> CANDY_NAME_COMPARATOR =
      new Comparator<Candy>() {
        public int compare( Candy p1, Candy p2 ) {
          return p1.name.compareTo( p2.name() );
        }
      };

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    List<Candy> candies = Arrays.asList(

                            new Candy( 230, "Special Dark Chocolate" ), new Candy( 230, "Milk 
Chocolate Bar" ),
        new Candy( 60, "Tootsie Pop" ), new Candy( 280, "Snickers Bar" ) );

    candies.sort( CANDY_CALORIES_COMPARATOR );
    System.out.println( candies );

    candies.sort( CANDY_NAME_COMPARATOR );
    System.out.println( candies );

    candies.sort( CANDY_CALORIES_COMPARATOR.thenComparing( CANDY_NAME_COMPARATOR ) );
    System.out.println( candies );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 11.23**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/util/ComparatorThenComparingDemo.java (Snippet)

The result is the following output:

```
[Tootsie Pop/60, Special Dark Chocolate/230, Milk Chocolate Bar/230, Snickers Bar/280]
[Milk Chocolate Bar/230, Snickers Bar/280, Special Dark Chocolate/230, Tootsie Pop/60]
[Tootsie Pop/60, Milk Chocolate Bar/230, Special Dark Chocolate/230, Snickers Bar/280] 
```

With lambda expressions, as described in [Chapter 13](#13_001.html_h13) , the whole thing can be written in a slightly more compact way.

#### Extracting a Comparison Value and Making Comparisons*

The remaining methods in <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> all provide the special capability of taking certain function objects that extract the “key” for the comparisons and then reference the key for the comparison. With the syntax of the method references, you can formulate quite compact <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> objects.

Let’s look the related methods next:

```
interface java.util.
                    Comparator<T> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T,U> Comparator<T> comparing(Function<? super T,? extends U> keyExtractor, Comparator<? super U> keyComparator)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">static <T,U extends Comparable<? super U>> Comparator<T> comparing(Function<? super T, ? extends U> keyExtractor)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> Comparator<T> comparingInt(ToIntFunction<? super T> keyExtractor)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> Comparator<T> comparingLong(ToLongFunction<? super T> keyExtractor)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static<T> Comparator<T> comparingDouble(ToDoubleFunction<? super T> keyExtractor)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default <U extends Comparable<? super U>> Comparator<T> thenComparing(Function<? super T,? extends U> keyExtractor)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default <U> Comparator<T> thenComparing(Function<? super T,? extends U></samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">keyExtractor, Comparator<? super U> keyComparator)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default Comparator<T> thenComparingDouble(ToDoubleFunction<? super T> keyExtractor)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default Comparator<T> thenComparingInt(ToIntFunction<? super T> keyExtractor)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default Comparator<T> thenComparingLong(ToLongFunction<? super T> keyExtractor)</samp>

###### [eg]  Example

Our example to compare candies can be formulated in a different way: You can use lambda expression syntax or alternatively an even more compact method reference; we’ll return to this topic in detail in [Chapter 13](#13_001.html_h13) . Consider the following example:

```
Comparator<Candy> comp = Comparator.comparingInt( candy -> candy.calories() );
// Comparator<Candy> comp = Comparator.comparingInt( Candy::calories );
candies.sort( Comparator.comparingInt( Candy::calories )
                        .thenComparing( Candy::name ) );
```

## 11.5    Wrapper Classes and Autoboxing

The class library provides special classes for each primitive data type like <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>. These wrapper classes (also called envelope classes ) fulfill three important tasks:

*   Wrapper classes provide static helper methods for converting a primitive data type to a string (called formatting) and from the string back to a primitive data type (called parsing ).

*   The data structures such as lists and sets that are used in Java can only store references. Thus, the problem arises of how to add primitive data types to these containers. Wrapper objects encapsulate a simple primitive value in an object so that a reference exists that can be stored in a prebuilt data structure, for example.

*   The wrapper type is important for generics. For example, if a special <samp class="listingcharacter">function</samp> maps an integer to a float, an implementation with <samp class="listingcharacter">Function<</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> isn’t correct—it must be <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">Function<</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> . Primitive data types don’t exist even with generics; wrapper types are always used instead.

Wrapper classes exist for all primitive data types, as listed in [Table 11.2](#11_005.html_t11.2) .

| Wrapper Class | Primitive Type |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Boolean</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Character</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> |

**Table 11.2**     Wrapper Classes and Primitive Data Types

###### [»]  Note

For <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp>, which isn’t a data type, the class <samp class="listingcharacter">Void</samp> exists. This class declares only the constant <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp> of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Class<Void></samp> and is more relevant for reflection (reading properties of a class).

In this section, we’ll first look at creating wrapper objects then explore the methods that appear in all wrapper classes. Finally, we’ll introduce you to individual methods of each wrapper class. (Note that we covered the <samp class="listingcharacter">Character</samp> class in [Chapter 5](#05_001.html_h5), [Section 5.3](#05_003.html_h5.3) , when we talked about characters and strings.)

[![Essential Type Relationships of Wrapper Classes: Character Doesn’t Extend Number](bilderklein/klein11_005.png)](img-f11.5.html)

**Figure 11.5**     Essential Type Relationships of Wrapper Classes: Character Doesn’t Extend Number

### 11.5.1     Creating Wrapper Objects

Wrapper objects can be created in two ways:

*   Via static <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(...)</samp> methods, which are passed a primitive expression or a string.

*   Via boxing: From a primitive value, the compiler automatically generates <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(...)</samp> method calls that return the wrapper object.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example creates some wrapper objects:

```
Integer  int1 = 
                    Integer.valueOf( "
                    30" );  // valueOf()
Long     lng1 = 
                    Long.valueOf( 0xC0B0L );  // valueOf()
Double   dobl = 
                    Double.valueOf( 12.3 );   // valueOf()
Boolean  bool = true;                     // Boxing
Integer  int2 = 42;                       // Boxing
Long     lng2 = 42L;                      // Boxing
```

Let’s compare and contrast these two ways of creating wrapper classes:

*   Boxing is the shortest variant in terms of writing effort, and generally the best, because this option is the most compact. (Boxing isn’t without its problems, however, as [Section 11.5.12](#11_005.html_h11.5.12) describes.) Since boxing accesses the <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(...)</samp> methods, the two variants are semantically identical and differ only in the program code (but are not different in the bytecode).

*   Compared to a constructor, a static <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(...)</samp> method for creating objects has an advantage: Unlike <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> and the constructor, a static method doesn’t always have to create objects anew but can also use preconstructed objects. And that’s exactly what <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(...)</samp> does with the four classes <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp>: If the integers come from the value range –128 to +127, <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(...)</samp> uses prepared objects from a cache. Of course, this approach only works because callers of <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(...)</samp> obtain an immutable object—a wrapper object can’t be changed after its creation.

###### [»]  Note

In the wrapper class <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp>, three static overloaded methods exist: <samp class="listingcharacter">getInteger(String)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">getInteger(String, int)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">getInteger(String, Integer)</samp>. These methods can be easily confused with the <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(String)</samp> method by language novices because of the same return and parameters. However, the <samp class="listingcharacter">getInteger(String)</samp> methods read an environment variable and thus have a completely different task than <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(String)</samp>. In the wrapper class <samp class="listingcharacter">Boolean</samp>, the method <samp class="listingcharacter">getBoolean(String)</samp> has the same feature that it read an environment variable. The other wrapper classes don’t have methods for reading environment variables.

#### Wrapper Objects Are Immutable

Once a wrapper object has been created, the value stored in the wrapper object can’t be changed afterwards. To ensure this immutability, concrete wrapper classes are all final. These wrapper classes are intended only to serve as wrappers and not as complete data types. Since the value can’t be changed (it’s immutable), objects with this property are also called value objects . To increase the content of an <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> object <samp class="listingcharacter">io</samp> by 1, for example, you must reference a new object. Consider the following example:

```
Integer io = Integer.valueOf( 12 );

                    io = Integer.valueOf( io.intValue() + 1 ); 
```

The variable <samp class="listingcharacter">io</samp> references a second <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> object at the end, and the value of the first <samp class="listingcharacter">io</samp> object with <samp class="listingcharacter">12</samp> remains untouched, which is essentially the same as using the data type <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>. When the string <samp class="listingcharacter">s = "Co"; s = s + "ra";</samp> is called, the reference variable <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> is also only assigned a new object, but the string itself doesn’t change.

### 11.5.2    Conversions to a String Representation

All wrapper classes provide static <samp class="listingcharacter">toString(value)</samp> methods for converting the primitive element to a string.

```
String s1 = 
                Integer.toString( 1234567891 ),
       s2 = 
                Long.toString( 123456789123L ),
       s3 = 
                Float.toString( 12.345678912f ),
       s4 = 
                Double.toString( 12.345678912 ),
       s5 = 
                Boolean.toString( true );
System.out.println( s1 );  // 1234567891
System.out.println( s2 );  // 123456789123
System.out.println( s3 );  // 12.345679
System.out.println( s4 );  // 12.345678912
System.out.println( s5 );  // true 
```

**Listing 11.25**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/wrapper/WrapperToString.java, main()

###### [+]  Tip

The following statement is a Java-specific idiom [[ 175 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn11_04) for conversion as well:

```
String s = "" + number;
```

The string always appears in the English written variant. For example, decimal numbers have a period instead of a comma.

###### [»]   Note

When displaying numbers, country-specific formatting is often useful. You can access these formatting options via <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(...)</samp>. Another option is to use a <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> specification for the language as the first parameter. Consider the following examples:

```
System.out.printf( Locale.GERMANY, "%f%n", 1000000\. );  // 1000000,000000
System.out.printf( Locale.ENGLISH, "%f%n", 1234.567 );  // 1234.567000
System.out.printf( Locale.CHINA, "%,.3f%n", 1234.567 ); // 1,234.567 
```

The format specifier for floats is <samp class="listingcharacter">%f</samp>. The additional specification with <samp class="listingcharacter">,.3f</samp> in the last case leads to the thousands separator and three decimal places.

#### toString(...) as Object and Class Method

If a wrapper object is present, the object method <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> returns the string representation of the value stored by the wrapper object. Having identically named <samp class="listingcharacter">toString(...)</samp> static methods and an object method <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> shouldn’t cause confusion; while the class method pulls the working value for conversion from the argument, the object method uses the stored value in the wrapper object.

Statements that go over the wrapper object exclusively for conversion, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.valueOf(v).toString()</samp>, can be easily rewritten as <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">toString(v)</samp>. In addition, the overloaded static method <samp class="listingcharacter">String.valueOf(v)</samp> is also useful, which—precisely because it is overloaded—is declared for all possible data types. However, <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(v)</samp> internally also uses only <samp class="listingcharacter">WrapperClass.toString(v)</samp> .

### 11.5.3    Parsing from a String Representation

Wrapper classes provide static <samp class="listingcharacter">parse*(...)</samp> methods to convert a string to a primitive data type. The string can be preceded by a minus for negative numbers, but a plus for positive numbers is also allowed. These methods were introduced in [Chapter 5](#05_001.html_h5), [Section 5.8.2](#05_008.html_h5.8.2) .

### 11.5.4    The Number Base Class for Numeric Wrapper Objects

All numeric wrapper classes can provide the stored value in any other numeric type. Like <samp class="listingcharacter">doubleValue()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">intValue()</samp>, the method names consist of the name of the desired type and <samp class="listingcharacter">Value</samp>. Technically, the wrapper classes <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Number</samp> [[ 176 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn11_05) class override <samp class="listingcharacter">*Value()</samp> methods. [[ 177 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn11_06)

[![ UML Diagram of Number](bilderklein/klein11_006.png)](img-f11.6.html)

**Figure 11.6**     UML Diagram of Number

```
abstract class java.lang.
                Number
implements Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">byte byteValue()</samp>
    Returns the value of the number as <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">abstract double doubleValue()</samp>
    Returns the value of the number as <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">abstract float floatValue()</samp>
    Returns the value of the number as <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">abstract int intValue()</samp>
    Returns the value of the number as <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">abstract long longValue()</samp>
    Returns the value of the number as <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">short shortValue()</samp>
    Returns the value of the number as <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> .

###### [»]  Note

If the operand types are different in the condition operator, an automatic adjustment will take place, as in the following examples:

```
boolean b = true;
System.out.println(  b ? 1 : 0.1 );  // 1.0
System.out.println( !b ? 1 : 0.1 );  // 0.1 
```

The result type is <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> , so that the integer 1 is output as “1.0” (i.e., a float). The compiler makes the same adjustment for wrapper types that it unboxes and converts, as in the following examples:

```
Integer i = 1;
Double  d = 0.1;

                    System.out.println(  b ? i : d );   // 1.0
System.out.println( !b ? i : d );   // 0.1 
```

While this output is actually clear, misunderstandings can occur if the result isn’t simply output but cached as a reference to the resulting wrapper object. Since the type in the example is either <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp>, the result type can only be the <samp class="listingcharacter">Number</samp> supertype. Consider the following examples:

```
Number n1 = b ? i : d;
System.out.println( n1 );           // 1.0
System.out.println( n1 == i );      // false 
```

The program logic and output are, of course, exactly the same as before, but developers might assume that the compiler doesn’t perform a conversion, but instead references either the original <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> object; however, the compiler doesn’t. The <samp class="listingcharacter">n1</samp> variable in this case references an <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp>-unboxed, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>-converted <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> object, and so the references of <samp class="listingcharacter">n1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> are not identical at all.

If the compiler is really to return the original objects, either the <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> or the <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> object must be explicitly set to <samp class="listingcharacter">Number</samp> , so that unboxing is thus switched off and the condition operator assumes that only arbitrary references exist that aren’t to be interpreted, as in the following examples:

```
Number n2 = b ? (Number) i : d;     // or Number n2 = b ? i : (Number) d;
System.out.println( n2 );           // 1
System.out.println( n2 == i );      // true 
```

### 11.5.5    Performing Comparisons with compare*(...), compareTo(...), equals(...), and Hash Values

If we have two integers 1 and 2 in front of us, saying that 1 is smaller than 2 is a trivial task. With floats, this comparison is a bit more complicated because “special numbers” exist like infinity or a negative 0 and a positive 0\. To ensure that comparing two values always follows the same schema, two kinds of methods in wrapper classes can tell you whether two values are less than, greater than, or equal to each other:

*   On one hand, the object method <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp> is found in the wrapper classes. This method isn’t in the class by chance because wrapper classes implement the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> interface <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp>(as described in [Section 11.4](#11_004.html_h11.4) .)

*   Wrapper classes also have static <samp class="listingcharacter">compare(x, y)</samp> and sometimes <samp class="listingcharacter">compareUnsigned(x, y)</samp> methods.

The return value of these methods is an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> , which encodes whether a value is greater than, less than, or equal to.

###### [eg]   Example

The following example tests several different values:

```
System.out.println( 
                    Integer.compare(1, 2) );         // -1
System.out.println( 
                    Integer.compare(1, 1) );         //  0
System.out.println( 
                    Integer.compare(2, 1) );         //  1

System.out.println( 
                    Double.compare(2.0, 2.1) );      // -1
System.out.println( 
                    Double.compare(Double.NaN, 0) ); //  1

System.out.println( 
                    Boolean.compare(true, false) );  //  1
System.out.println( 
                    Boolean.compare(false, true) );  // -1 
```

**Listing 11.26**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/wrapper/CompareToDemo.java, main()

A <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> is “greater” than a <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> .

[Table 11.3](#11_005.html_t11.3) summarizes the methods of the wrapper classes.

| Class | Method from Comparable | Static Method compare*(...) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(Byte aByte)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compare[Unsigned](byte x, byte y)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(Short aShort)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compare[Unsigned](short x, short y)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(Float aFloat)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compare(float f1, float f2)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(Double aDouble)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compare(double d1, double d2)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(Integer aInteger)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compare(int x, int y)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(Long aLong)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compare(long x, long y)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Character</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(Character aChar)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compare[Unsigned](char x, char y)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Boolean</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(Boolean aBoolean)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int compare(boolean x, boolean y)</samp> |

**Table 11.3**     Methods of Wrapper Classes

The implementation of a static <samp class="listingcharacter">WrapperClass.compare(...)</samp> method is equivalent to <samp class="listingcharacter">WrapperClass.valueOf(x).compareTo(WrapperClass.valueOf(y))</samp> , only the second variant is slower and also longer in spelling.

#### Equal Test via equals(...)

All wrapper classes override the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method from the <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> base class. This scenario allows you to test whether two wrapper objects have the same value, even if the wrapper objects aren’t identical.

###### [eg]  Example

Let’s consider the results of some equal tests:

```
Boolean.TRUE.equals( Boolean.TRUE )                       true
Integer.valueOf( 1 ).equals( Integer.valueOf( 1 ) )       true
Integer.valueOf( 1 ).equals( Integer.valueOf( 2 ) )       false
Integer.valueOf( 1 ).equals( Long.valueOf( 1 ) )          false
Integer.valueOf( 1 ).equals( 1L )                         false
```

Note that the parameter type of <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> is always <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>, but the types must be identical; otherwise, the comparison will automatically return <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. This fact is shown by the penultimate and the final examples. The <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method from lines 4 and 5 rejects any comparison with a non-integer, and a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> is just not an <samp class="listingcharacter">integer</samp> . Boxing is used in the last line, so the program code looks shorter but corresponds to the code from the penultimate line.

The object method <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> of wrapper classes is also a short alternative to <samp class="listingcharacter">wrapperObject.compareTo(anotherWrapperObject) == 0</samp> .

###### [»]  Outlook

The fact that wrapper classes implement <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> is good because, in this way, wrapper objects can be easily placed and retrieved in data structures like an <samp class="listingcharacter">ArrayList</samp>. Furthermore, the fact that wrapper objects are also <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> is also great for data structures like <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp>, which—without externally given <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> classes for comparisons—expect a natural ordering of the elements.

#### Hash Values

The hash value of an object maps the state to a compact integer. If two objects have unequal hash values, the objects must also be unequal (at least if the calculation is correct). To determine the hash value, each class declares the <samp class="listingcharacter">int hashCode()</samp> method via the superclass <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Object</samp> . All wrapper classes override this method. In addition, static methods are available, so you can easily calculate the hash value even without a wrapper object.

###### [eg]   Example

The following example calculates a hashcode via the object method and static method:

```
Double d = 12.12;
System.out.println( d.hashCode() );             // -469813427
System.out.println( Double.hashCode( 12.12 ) ); // -469813427 
```

The value itself is irrelevant.

For the calculation of hash values and their meanings for data structures, [Section 11.1.5](#11_001.html_h11.1.5) .

### 11.5.6    Static Reduction Methods in Wrapper Classes

In the numeric wrapper classes <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp>, you’ll find three methods, <samp class="listingcharacter">sum(</samp>... <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">max(</samp>... <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">min(</samp>... <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> , that do exactly as they promise.

```
final class java.lang.
                Integer|
                Long|
                Float|
                Double
extends Number
implements Comparable<Integer> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">sum(</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">a,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">b)</samp>
    Calculates and returns the total of two values, corresponding to a simple a + b. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> specification stands for the corresponding primitive (type <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>), for example, in <samp class="listingcharacter">int sum(int a, int b)</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">min(</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">a,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">b)</samp>
    Returns the minimum of the two numbers.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">max(</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">a,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">b)</samp>
    Returns the maximum of the two numbers.

Furthermore, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Boolean</samp> classes provide three methods for three Boolean operations:

```
final class java.lang.
                Boolean
implements Comparable<Boolean>, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static boolean logicalAnd(boolean a, boolean b)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">a && b</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static boolean logicalOr(boolean a, boolean b)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">a || b</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static boolean logicalXor(boolean a, boolean b)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">a ^ b.</samp>

These methods aren’t exciting in themselves. For sums (addition), the <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> operator does just as well (and is located behind the <samp class="listingcharacter">sum(...)</samp> methods anyway), and so nobody will get the idea to write <samp class="listingcharacter">i = Integer.sum(i, 1)</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">i++</samp>. For the maximum/minimum values, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class also already provides the corresponding methods <samp class="listingcharacter">min(a, b)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">max(a, b)</samp> . The reason we mention these methods is because they’re quite interesting in the context of functional programming and because they can reduce two values to one.

### 11.5.7    Constants for the Size of a Primitive Type*

All wrapper classes have an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> constant named <samp class="listingcharacter">SIZE</samp> for the number of bits and an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> constant named <samp class="listingcharacter">BYTES</samp> , which is assigned the size of the associated primitive data type.

| Wrapper Class | SIZE Assignment | BYTES Assignment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp> | 8 | 1 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp> | 16 | 2 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> | 32 | 4 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> | 64 | 8 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp> | 32 | 4 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> | 64 | 8 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Character</samp> | 16 | 2 |

The assignments are basically clear to every developer, it’s rather intended for tools or generic libraries.

### 11.5.8    Handling Unsigned Numbers*

All integer data types (except for <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> ) are always signed, and Java is unlikely to ever introduce new data types to distinguish between positive and negative numbers, as C# and C(++) do, for example. Developers must live with the fact that a byte is always between –128 and +127 and not between 0 and 255\. Even if the language doesn’t introduce new types, the Java API helps with methods in wrapper classes.

#### toUnsigned*(...) Methods

The first type of methods interprets a bit pattern as an unsigned number. For example, if a <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> is assigned the bit pattern 11111111, this value doesn’t stand for “255” but instead for “–1.” The static conversion <samp class="listingcharacter">toUnsigned*(...)</samp> methods of the wrapper class can help interpret the bit pattern without a sign bit, thus requiring a change to a next higher data type. This change is obvious because, in the case of 11111111, a <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> can’t store the number 255 because of the restriction to the range of –127 to 128, whereas <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> can.

| <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">static int toUnsignedInt(byte x)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static long toUnsignedLong(byte x)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">static int toUnsignedInt(short x)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static long toUnsignedLong(short x)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">static long toUnsignedLong(int x)</samp> |

**Table 11.5**     toUnsigned*(...) Methods in Byte, Short, and Integer

Obviously, <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> doesn’t provide such a method because no built-in data type exists that is greater than <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> .

#### toUnsignedString(...) and parseUnsignedString(...)

What <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> does provide, however, and also <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> , are conversions to string representations and also parse methods:

| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toUnsignedString(int i)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toUnsignedString(int i, int radix)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static int parseUnsignedInt(String s)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static int parseUnsignedInt(String s, int radix)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toUnsignedString(long i)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toUnsignedString(long i, int radix)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static long parseUnsignedLong(String s)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static long parseUnsignedLong(String s, int radix)</samp> |

**Table 11.6**     Creating and Parsing String Representations of Unsigned Numbers

The <samp class="listingcharacter">parse*(...)</samp> methods throw a <samp class="listingcharacter">NumberFormatException</samp> if the format is wrong.

#### Comparison, Division, and Remainder

Finally, a third group of methods are more mathematical: static methods for comparing, dividing, and residual value creation.

| <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">static int compareUnsigned(int x, int y)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static int divideUnsigned(int dividend, int divisor)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static int remainderUnsigned(int dividend, int divisor)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">static int compareUnsigned(long x, long y)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static long divideUnsigned(long dividend, long divisor)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">static long remainderUnsigned(long dividend, long divisor)</samp> |

### 11.5.9    The Integer and Long Classes

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> class encapsulates the value of an integer of type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> in an object and provides the following elements:

*   Constants

*   Static methods to convert to a string and back

*   Other helper methods of a mathematical nature

To turn the string into a number, you can use <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.parseInt(String)</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

The following example converts the integer 38,317, which is a string, into an integer:

```
String number = "38317";
int integer = 0;
try {
  integer = 
                    Integer.parseInt( number );
}
catch ( NumberFormatException e ) {
  System.err.println( "Error converting " + number );
}
System.out.println( integer );
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">NumberFormatException</samp> is an unchecked exception (see [Chapter 9](#09_001.html_h9), [Section 9.1.3](#09_001.html_h9.1.3), for more details). So, you don’t need to enclose it in a <samp class="listingcharacter">try</samp> block.
