*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger.valueOf( val )</samp> → <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp>

Both constructors and factories can be thought of as special functions that convert from one type to another, making them perfect for transformations. Let’s contrast the following two examples:

| Constructor | Method |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">new BigDecimal( 12.2 )</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal.valueOf( 12.2 )</samp> |

Basically, mapping <samp class="listingcharacter">double → BigDecimal</samp> is performed in two ways: once via <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> and a constructor and once via the <samp class="listingcharacter">valueOf(double)</samp> method.

### 13.3.1     Writing Constructor References

Where method references can specify static methods and object methods, constructor references provide the ability to specify constructors so that they can be passed elsewhere as creators. This feature allows you to elegantly specify constructors as creators, even from a class that doesn’t have any creator methods. As with method references, a functional interface plays a crucial role in this context. But this time the method of the functional interface, when called, causes the constructor call. Where syntactically for method references the method name is placed to the right of the colon, for constructor references, you would use a <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp>. [[ 192 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn13_05)

Constructor references with the library methods of the Stream API are useful.

###### [eg]  Example

The Stream API can build a stream with three <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> numbers, for instance. The floats are converted to <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> objects, then calculated to the power of 20 before the return is output in the following example:

```
Stream.of( 12.5, 11.5, 9.5 )
    .map( BigDecimal::valueOf )
    .map( bigDecimal -> bigDecimal.pow( 20 ) )
    .forEach( System.out::println );
```

This notation is equivalent to the following code:

```
Stream.of( 12.5, 11.5, 9.5 )
    .map( BigDecimal::valueOf )
    .map( bigDecimal -> bigDecimal.pow( 20 ) )
    .forEach( System.out::println );
```

Put simply, the <samp class="listingcharacter">map(...)</samp> method expects a <samp class="listingcharacter">Function<Double,BigDecimal></samp>—exactly the transformation that <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> and constructor perform as well as the method.

###### [eg]  Example

Let’s say we have the following custom functional interface:

```
interface DateFactory { Date 
                    create(); }
```

A constructor reference binds the constructor to the <samp class="listingcharacter">create()</samp> method of the functional interface in the following example:

```
DateFactory factory = 
                    Date::new;
System.out.print( factory.
                    create() );
// for example, Fri Oct 06 22:34:24 CET 2017 
```

The last two lines can also be summarized in the following way:

```
System.out.println( ((DateFactory)Date::new).create() );
```

If only a parameterless constructor is to be called, the functional interface must have only one method that has no parameters and returns something. The return type of the method must of course match the class type. This rule applies to the <samp class="listingcharacter">DateFactory</samp> type from our earlier example. But you can also go a bit more generic, for example, with the existing functional interface <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier</samp>, as we’ll see momentarily in [Section 13.3.2](#13_003.html_h13.3.2) .

The Java API often contains parameters of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> type, which are used as type specification to create objects via the <samp class="listingcharacter">Constructor</samp> of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter">newInstance()</samp> method. The use of <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> can be replaced by a functional interface, and constructor references can be passed instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> objects.

### 13.3.2    Parameterless and Parameterized Constructors

With a parameterless constructor, the method has only one return. In contrast, with a parameterized constructor, the method of the functional interface must of course have a compatible parameter list, as illustrated in the following examples:

| Constructor | <samp class="listingcharacter">Date()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Date(</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter"> t)</samp> |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compatible functional interface | <samp class="listingcharacter">interface DateFactory {</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter"> Date create();</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">interface DateFactory {</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter"> Date create(</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter"> t);</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">}</samp> |
| Constructor reference | <samp class="listingcharacter">DateFactory factory =</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter"> Date::new;</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">DateFactory factory =</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter"> Date::new;</samp> |
| Call | <samp class="listingcharacter">factory.create();</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">factory.create(1);</samp> |

**Table 13.7**     Standard and Parameterized Constructor with Corresponding Functional Interfaces

###### [»]  Note

If the type inference of the compiler reaches its limits, additional type information is required. In this case, the additional information is provided after the colon in square brackets, such as in <samp class="listingcharacter">Class::<Type1, Type2>new</samp> .

### 13.3.3    Useful Predefined Interfaces for Constructor References

The functional interface appropriate for a parameterless constructor must have a return and take no parameter. In contrast, the functional interface for a parameterized constructor must have a corresponding parameter list. Often, a constructor might parameterless or takes exactly one parameter. For these two cases, the Java API provides two practical (generically declared) functional interfaces.

| Functional Interface | Functional Descriptor | Mapping | Matches... |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier<T></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">T get()</samp> | () → T | Parameterless constructor |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Function<T,R></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">R apply(T t)</samp> | (T) → R | Simple parameterized constructor |

**Table 13.8**     Existing Functional Interfaces as Creators

###### [eg]  Example

The functional interface <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier<T></samp> has a <samp class="listingcharacter">T get()</samp> method that you can connect to the parameterless constructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">Date</samp> , as in the following example:

```
Supplier<Date> factory = Date::new;
System.out.print( factory.get() ); 
```

Using <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier</samp> with the type parameter <samp class="listingcharacter">Date</samp> gives the parameterized type <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier<Date></samp>, while <samp class="listingcharacter">get()</samp> consequently returns the type <samp class="listingcharacter">Date</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">factory.get()</samp> call leads to the call of the constructor.

###### [»]  Brain Teaser

A constructor can be a <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier</samp> or a <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp>. Once again, checked exceptions are problematic. You should consider whether the constructor <samp class="listingcharacter">URI(String str) throws URISyntaxException</samp> can be addressed via <samp class="listingcharacter">URI::new</samp> .

## 13.4    Functional Programming

Functional programming makes it possible to parameterize a behavior—a sorting method always works the same, but its behavior during comparisons is different. This parameterization is on a different abstraction level than just passing simple values.

### 13.4.1    Code = Data

When you hear the term data , you might first think of numbers, bytes, strings, or even complex objects with states. In this chapter, we’ll expand this view a little and direct it to program code. Java code, epitomized as a series of bytecodes, also consists of data.

Once you buy into this view that code equals data, then code can also be passed like data and can thus be transferred from one point to another, stored, and later referenced. This ability to transfer code makes customizing the behavior of algorithms easy.

Let’s start with a few examples where program code is passed and accessed later:

*   A thread executes program code in the background. The program code that the Java thread should execute is wrapped into an object of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Runnable</samp> (more precisely, set in a <samp class="listingcharacter">run()</samp> method). When the thread’s turn arrives, the thread calls the <samp class="listingcharacter">run()</samp> method.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Timer</samp> is a <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util</samp> class that can execute program code at specific times. The object method <samp class="listingcharacter">scheduleAtFixedRate(...)</samp> is passed an object of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">TimerTask</samp> , which contains the program code.

*   To sort data, you can define your own sort order, which can be passed to the sorter as a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> declares a comparison method to which the sorter turns to put two objects in the desired order.

*   If the user clicks a button on the interface, an action occurs. For example, in the graphical user interface (GUI) framework Swing—the program code in an object of the type <samp class="listingcharacter">ActionListener</samp> and is attached to the button <samp class="listingcharacter">JButton</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">addActionListener(...)</samp>. If button activation occurs, the UI system processes the program code in the <samp class="listingcharacter">actionPerformed(...)</samp> method of the stored <samp class="listingcharacter">ActionListener</samp> .

To move program code from one place to another, the same mechanism is always used in Java: A class implements a (usually non-static) method that contains the program code to be executed. An object of this class is passed to another location, and the interested party then accesses the program code via the method. The fact that an object can contain more than one implementation, such as variables, constants, and constructors, is not relevant in this context. Let’s now take a closer look at this mechanism by exploring its variants.

### 13.4.2    Programming Paradigms: Imperative or Declarative

In some way, a developer must describe the problem at hand as a program that the computer can eventually execute. In this context, different types of problem description are available, referred to as programming paradigms . So far, we’ve mostly dealt with imperative programming, which focuses on statements. In the English language, verbs have an imperative mood (i.e., the command form), which can be compared quite well with imperative programming because, in both cases, statements capture commands like “do this, do that.” These “commands,” through variables, case distinctions, and jumps, describe the program and the solution path.

While imperative programming is technically the oldest form of describing programs, it’s not the only one. In contrast, declarative programming describes not the how to solve the problem, but the what, (that is, what is actually required), without getting bogged down in exact procedures. At first glance, this kind of programming sounds abstract, but you’re already familiar with the principle if you’ve ever performed the following actions:

*   Made a selection like “*.html” in the command line or in the File Explorer in Windows search field

*   Written a database query with SQL

*   Used an XML selection with XQuery

*   Formulated a build script with Maven

*   Described an XML transformation with Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations (XSLT)

Let’s stay with SQL for a moment to illustrate one point clearly. Of course, in the end, the CPU executes the processing of the tables and the evaluations of the results in a purely imperative way, but declarative programming is about the program description on a higher level of abstraction. Declarative programs are usually much shorter, and thus other advantages come into play, such as easier extensibility and comprehensibility. Since declarative programs often have a mathematical background, formally proving the correctness of the descriptions is also easier.

Declarative programming is a programming style, and a declarative description needs some kind of “runtime environment” because SQL cannot directly control a CPU, for example. But instead of dealing only with special use cases (such as database or XML queries), typical algorithms can also be formulated declaratively, using functional programming. Thus, imperative programs and functional programs are equally powerful in their capabilities.

### 13.4.3    Principles of Functional Programming

While imperative programming focuses on the sequence of statements and object-oriented programming (OOP) focuses on objects with states and behaviors, functional programming is characterized by other things.

#### Pure Functions without Side Effects

In mathematics, a function is a mapping from elements of a definition set to exactly one element of a target set, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">double zero = Math.sin(Math.PI);</samp>. Similarly, <samp class="listingcharacter">string JOHNANDEVE = "johnAndEve".toUpperCase()</samp> is another example from an object-oriented (OO) point of view: A value comes in, and a value comes out.

Functions are called pure functions , if they fulfill the following two prerequisites:

*   They always provide the same outputs for the same inputs.

*   They have no side effects (i.e., don’t modify any external state).

Consequently, <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.sin(...)</samp> is a pure function, but <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.random()</samp> aren’t. That their implementations do change states, for example, on the stack, and thus describe memory cells doesn’t matter—what’s important is the conceptual view. The API documentation should be good enough to name side effects.

An expression built from pure functions is called a pure expression . This kind of expression has a feature called referential transparency in computer sciences, namely, that the result of an expression can be substituted for the expression itself without the program exhibiting any different behavior. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.sin(Math.PI)</samp>, the compiler can substitute the expression with <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> , and the result would be the same. A compiler can perform various optimizations in the presence of referential transparency.

In OOP, you’ll use methods to modify the states of objects. A radio should be louder? We can call <samp class="listingcharacter">volumeUp()</samp>, and the internal state <samp class="listingcharacter">volume</samp> is increased. Having states in objects is natural for OO software development.

OO developers get a funny feeling when they hear “functional programming” because it sounds like no states exist, which is a misconception. Conditions still exist; it’s just that they are “elsewhere.” For this purpose, let’s look at <samp class="listingcharacter">"john&Eve".toUpperCase()</samp>. What is the condition in this case? Does <samp class="listingcharacter">toUpperCase()</samp> modify a state? The <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> method doesn’t change the state of an existing <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object. The basic gist is that the return of <samp class="listingcharacter">toUpperCase()</samp> is a new <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object with the desired states. At the core of functional programming, functions get an object and also return an object, but these objects aren’t changed and can (and even should) be immutable. To summarize, in object orientation, an operation with side effects results in a change to the object; in functional programming, an operation results in a new object with no change to the old object.

Functional libraries can be easily recognized by the fact that they request objects and return objects. For this reason, any method that returns <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp> raises suspicion because the state must be obtained and stored somewhere else. This condition can cause problems when writing, so a backup is necessary for modern parallel access.

#### Nested Calls Instead of Statement Sequences

While imperative programs distinguish between statements and expressions, in functional programming languages, everything is an expression. In the functional world, the focus is on evaluations of expressions rather than on the sequential processing of statements.

Of course, developers of functional programs don’t write everything nested into a single line, but they use several lines. Many functional programming languages provide an operator reminiscent of a variable assignment, but this operator is just a name, a symbol, for the expression—the context is again referential transparency. This approach is quite different from imperative programming languages, where the variable represents a memory area. In functional programming languages, identifiers only make complex nested expressions more readable.

In Java, only a few statements are also expressions, such as method calls with returns or assignments. Case distinctions and loops don’t return a result—one reason why neither exist in these forms in functional programming languages. Even with the condition operator in Java, case distinctions with alternatives can be implemented, which is an expression. Repetitions can be implemented in functional programming languages via recursions. A typical example is the calculation of the factorial. The formula is n! = 1 × 2 × 3 × ... × n , and with loops and variables. In the imperative way, you would write the following code:

```
public static int factorial( int n ) {
  int result = 1;
  for ( int i = 1; i <= n; i++ )
    result *= i;
  return result;
} 
```

Clearly, the many assignments and the case distinction of the loop can be read, which are the typical indicators for imperative programs. The loop counter increases, so state comes into the program because the current index must be kept somewhere in the memory. The recursive variant is quite different. No assignments are made in the program, and the notation is reminiscent of a mathematical definition. Consider the following example:

```
public static int factorial( int n ) {
  return n == 0 ? 1 : n * factorial( n - 1 );
} 
```

Since the number of repetitions can be high and recursions traditionally use up the stack, optimizations are quite important. Many developers therefore look closely at optimizing end-recursive methods —the methods that ultimately call the method itself again. In this case, space can be saved on the stack. (The JVM can’t do this so far and for Oracle engineers it has little priority.)

#### First-Order Functions and Higher-Order Functions

The two points mentioned so far can also be implemented in Java with discipline. However, one thing is not possible with Java that is common in functional programming languages: Functions have a completely different status—they are their own types.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example assigns and executes some functions in JavaScript:

```
function printVodka() { console.log("Vodka"); }
function printWhiskey() { console.log("Whiskey"); }
printDrink = Math.random() > 0.5 ? printVodka : printWhiskey;
printDrink();
```

In Java, only primitive types and reference types exist, and methods as such aren’t types. Functions are values in functional programming languages and thus the following actions are possible:

*   Functions can be assigned to variables.

*   Functions can be passed to other functions.

*   Functions can, in turn, return functions.

Thus, functional programming involves higher-order functions , which allows for the rather flexible composition of functions because functions can be easily passed on.

### 13.4.4    Imperative Programming and Functional Programming

Functional programming is a real alternative to imperative programming. Languages that fall into this paradigm are LISP (first introduced in 1958) and derivatives such as Clojure, Erlang, ML (and OCaml), F#, and Haskell. Java is not a functional programming language because it lacks the ability to use higher-order functions, but you can compensate for this disadvantage with some tricks.

#### Why Functional Programming Has a Hard Time

A list of the most popular programming languages [[ 193 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn13_06) would show that purely functional programming languages aren’t terribly popular. Functional programming is feared by many developers for several reasons:

*   Readability
    Historically, LISP from 1958 represents the beginning of functional programming languages. This language is quite flexible, but awkward to read. Our factorial in LISP would be written as <samp class="listingcharacter">(defun factorial (n) (if (= n 1) 1 (* n (factorial (- n 1)))))</samp>. All those parentheses make a program difficult to read, and the expressions are in the prefix notation <samp class="listingcharacter">- n 1</samp> instead of the usual notation <samp class="listingcharacter">n - 1</samp> . Other functional programming languages are different, but a certain prejudice persists that all functional programming languages are hard to read.

*   Terminology
    Higher-order functions, idempotence, function, functor, predicate, arity, lambda, closure, currying, monoid, and monad—you might think that these terms from functional programming are only for mathematicians and computer scientists. These concepts scare many developers, who consequently don’t engage with the paradigm.

*   Academic and mathematical
    Functional programming also has something academic about it because this programming paradigm is often associated only with mathematical functions in the minds of developers. Only a few will actually need to calculate factorials or Fibonacci numbers in programs, so programmers quickly put functional programming aside. But these prejudices are unfounded, and we recommend mentally detaching functional programming from mathematics because the vast majority of programs have nothing to do with mathematical functions in the true sense, but instead deal much more with formally described methods.

*   Performance and memory consumption
    Without clever optimizations on the part of the compiler and the runtime environment, recursive calls in particular can lead to bulging stacks and poor runtimes.

*   Purely functional
    Some functional programming languages called “pure” don’t permit state changes. The development of input/output operations or simple random numbers is thus a big deal, which is no longer comprehensible for developers.

#### Functional Object-Oriented Languages Are Popular

In recent years, many OOP languages have gained support for functional programming, or new functional programming languages with pragmatic state changes have appeared. From our point of view today, a combination of both concepts looks promising for the future. Functional programming is a way of thinking that has certain advantages, especially in a world of parallel execution where state changes can quickly become a problem. Also, declarative programming shifts more responsibility to the framework, which can get better and better as it progresses through optimizations.

#### How to Program Functionally with Java?

Java doesn’t allow you to pass methods as values—there are no values and no first-class functions . Since we can’t pass functions, we must use a trick. Instead of passing functions, you would perform the following tasks:

1.  Set the functionality into a method.

2.  Set the method into a class.

3.  Create an object of this class.

4.  Pass this object as a kind of wrapper for the function.

To prevent a receiver from getting any object with any method, an interface is added as an intermediary: One side implements the interface and adheres to a contract, and the receiver gets something of the desired type and can call the method.

With this detour Java can also only go far, and the option has existed since Java 1.0\. However, the code size is large, so the path was impractical. Now, however, lambda expressions are the perfect language tool because they make functional programs compact and easy to read, and the JVM has excellent optimization capabilities. Of course, Java can never do 100% of what a functional programming language can do (and enforces), but these capabilities are quite sufficient for practical use.

Thus, Java enables both OOP and functional programming, and developers can choose the path that’s best for solving a problem. Of course, this ambiguity can also create problems because, whenever several possible solutions exist, disputes may arise as to which variant is the best. Indeed, conflicting opinions can prevail from developer to developer. But a functional approach has some undeniable advantages, which we’ll focus on more closely next.

### 13.4.5    Comparator as an Example of Higher-Order Functions

Let’s look again at our example from [Section 13.1](#13_001.html_h13.1), string sorting, but this time from the perspective of a functional programmer. A <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> is a simple “function” with two parameters and one return. This “function” (implemented as a method) is in turn passed to the <samp class="listingcharacter">sort(...)</samp> method. All these tasks are functionally programmed because we’re programming functions and then passing them. [Table 13.9](#13_004.html_t13.9) shows three examples (generics omitted).

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator c1 = (s, t) -> …</samp> | Implements a function via a lambda expression |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.sort(array, c1);</samp> | Takes a “function” as an argument |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator c2 = Collections.reverseOrder(c1);</samp> | Accepts a “function” and also returns a function |

**Table 13.9**     Examples of Functions in Transfer and as a Return

We’ve already established that functions can’t be passed in Java, so we can help ourselves with the possibility of putting the functionality in a method, so that the function becomes an object with a method, which implements the logic. Lambda expressions or method/constructor references provide a compact syntax without the burden of having to write an extra class with a method.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> type is a functional interface and represents a special function with two parameters of the same type and an integer return. Other functional interfaces are a bit more flexible than <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp>, for example, interfaces that allow the return to be <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> or something else (instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> ).

### 13.4.6    Viewing Lambda Expressions as Mappings or Functions

Recall that lambda expressions can be formulated in the following general syntax:

```
( 
                LambdaParameter ) -> { 
                Statements } 
```

The arrow clear shows that we’re dealing with a lambda expression with functions that map something else. In the case of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp>, we have a mapping of two strings to an integer, which can be wrapped in a slightly more mathematical notation: <samp class="listingcharacter">(String, String) → int</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

Methods exist with and without returns and with and without parameters. The same is true with lambda expressions. shows a few examples in Java code with their mappings.

| Lambda Expression | Mapping |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(int a, int b) → a + b</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(int, int) → int</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(int a) → Math.abs( a )</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(int) → int</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(String s) → s.isEmpty()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(String) → boolean</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(Collection c) → c.size()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(Collection) → int</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">() → Math.random()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">() → double</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">(String s) → { System.out.print( s ); }</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(String) → void</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">() → {}</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">() → void</samp> |

**Table 13.10**     Lambda Expressions and How They Map as Functions

###### [»]  Terminology: Function versus Method

The Java language definition doesn’t know the term function and speaks only of methods . Methods are always bound to classes, which means that methods are always bound to a context. This binding is central to object orientation since methods have read and write access to object variables. Lambda expressions, on the other hand, implement functions that first obtain their working values purely from the parameters and don’t depend on classes or objects. The idea behind functional programming languages is to get along without states, that is, to use functions in such a way that they deliver a result. Functions always return the same result for a specific parameter combination, regardless of the state of the surrounding overall program.

## 13.5    Functional Interfaces from the java.util.function Package

Functions implement mappings, and since different types of mappings exist, the Java standard library in the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.function</samp> package provides functional interfaces for the most common cases. [Table 13.11](#13_005.html_t13.11) provides an overview.

| Interface | Mapping |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer<T></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(T) → void</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">DoubleConsumer</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(double) → void</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">BiConsumer<T,U></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(T, U) → void</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier<T></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">() → T</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">BooleanSupplier</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">() → boolean</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate<T></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(T) → boolean</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LongPredicate</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(long) → boolean</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">BiPredicate<T,U></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(T, U) → boolean</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Function<T,R></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">(T) → R</samp> |

**Table 13.11**     Some Predefined Functional Interfaces

### 13.5.1    Blocks with Code and the Functional Interface Consumer

Instructions of code can be put into a method of an object and passed on in this way. This transfer is a common need for which the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.function</samp> package specifies a simple <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer</samp> functional interface that represents a consumer. This consumer accepts and then “consumes” (consumes) data but returns nothing.

```
interface java.util.function.
                Consumer<T> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void accept(T t)</samp>
    Performs operations with the transfer <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default Consumer<T> andThen(Consumer<? super T> after)</samp>
    Returns a new <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer</samp> that first executes the current <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer</samp> and then <samp class="listingcharacter">after</samp> .

The <samp class="listingcharacter">accept(...)</samp> method gets one argument—though of course the implementation doesn’t have to use it—and doesn’t return anything. Transformations aren’t possible with the type because the consumer can only save the results via detours, and the interface isn’t intended for that purpose. <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer</samp> types are intended more as the end link of a chain, where, for example, data is written to a file that has been previously processed. These side effects are intentional, as they come after a chain of side-effect-free operations.

#### Consumer Type in the Application Programming Interface

In the Java API, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer</samp> type usually shows up as an argument of a <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach(Consumer)</samp> method that runs data sources and calls <samp class="listingcharacter">accept(...)</samp> for each element. The method on the <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterable</samp> type is interesting because the important <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection</samp> data structures like <samp class="listingcharacter">ArrayList</samp> implement this interface. Thus, you can easily run over all the data and execute a piece of code for each element. <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator</samp> also has a similar method, the <samp class="listingcharacter">forEachRemaining(Consumer)</samp> method where the word “remaining” clearly indicates that the <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator</samp> may have already experienced a few <samp class="listingcharacter">next()</samp> calls, and therefore, the consumers don’t necessarily catch the first elements.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example outputs each element in a list to the console:

```
Arrays.asList( 1, 2, 3, 4 ).forEach( System.out::println );
```

Compared to a typical iteration, the functional variant is a little shorter in code, but otherwise, no difference exists. Also, <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach(...)</samp> does nothing else on <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterable</samp> other than fetching all elements via the <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator</samp> .

#### Writing a Custom Wrapper Consumer

Consumers always represent code, and an API can now simply accept a block of code along the lines of <samp class="listingcharacter">doSomethingWith(myConsumer)</samp> to, for instance, process it in a background thread or execute it repeatedly. Furthermore, a block of code can be stopped after an allowed maximum duration, after a certain time interval, etc.

Let’s write a <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer</samp> wrapper that logs the execution time of another consumer.

```
class Consumers {
  public static <T> Consumer<T> executionTimeLogger( Consumer<T> block ) {
    return t -> {
      long start = System.nanoTime();
      block.accept( t );
      long duration = System.nanoTime() - start;
      System.getLogger( "executionTime" ).log(
          System.Logger.Level.INFO, "Execution time (ns): {0}", duration );
    };
  }
} 
```

**Listing 13.10**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/lambda/Consumers.java (Snippet)

The following call shows the usage of this method:

```
Arrays.asList( 1, 2, 3, 4 )
      .forEach( 
                    executionTimeLogger( System.out::println ) ); 
```

The result is the following output:

```
1
Jan. 23, 2023 12:16:31 PM c.t.i.l.Consumers lambda$executionTimeLogger$0
INFO: Execution time (ns): 87.800
Jan. 23, 2023 12:16:31 PM c.t.i.l.Consumers lambda$executionTimeLogger$0
INFO: Execution time (ns): 25.100
Jan. 23, 2023 12:16:31 PM c.t.i.l.Consumers lambda$executionTimeLogger$0
INFO: Execution time (ns): 18.100
Jan. 23, 2023 12:16:31 PM c.t.i.l.Consumers lambda$executionTimeLogger$0
INFO: Execution time (ns): 13.200
2
3
4 
```

What we’ve implemented is an example of the execute-around-method pattern , where you put something else around a block of code.

### 13.5.2    Supplier

A supplier (also called provider ) is a factory and provides objects. In Java, the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.function</samp> package declares the <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier</samp> functional interface for object providers:

```
interface java.util.function.
                Supplier<T> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">T get()</samp>
    Performs operations with the transfer <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp> .

<samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier</samp> doesn’t declare any other static or default methods. What’s exactly returned by <samp class="listingcharacter">get()</samp> is a task of the implementation. The result might be new objects, the same objects always (singletons), or objects from a cache.

### 13.5.3    Predicates and java.util.function.Predicate

A predicate is a statement about an object that is true or false. The question <samp class="listingcharacter">"tutego".isEmpty()</samp> asks whether the string “tutego” is empty or not. While the <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp>result is “false”, <samp class="listingcharacter">isEmpty</samp> is therefore a predicate because it can make a truth statement about an object (a string in our case).

Predicates as objects are flexible because objects can be passed to different places. Thus, a predicate can determine what should be deleted from a collection or whether at least one element is in a collection.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.function</samp> package [[ 194 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn13_07) declares a flexible <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate</samp> functional interface in the following way:

```
interface java.util.function.
                Predicate<T> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean test(T t)</samp>
    Performs a test on <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp> and returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the criterion is met; otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, the test of whether a character is a digit can now be performed differently by predicate objects:

```
 Predicate<Character> isDigit = 
   c -> Character.isDigit( c );  // short: Character::isDigit
System.out.println( 
                    isDigit.test('a') );  // false
```

If the <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate</samp> interface had existed earlier in Java 1.0, no need would exist for the <samp class="listingcharacter">Character.isDigit(...)</samp> method. A <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate<Character></samp> could be used as a static variable in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Character</samp> class, so that a test would then be written as <samp class="listingcharacter">Character.IS_DIGIT.test(...)</samp> or as a return from a <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate<Character> isDigit()</samp> method using <samp class="listingcharacter">Character.isDigit().test(...)</samp> . In the future, the API may change so that statements on objects with truth returns will no longer be realized as methods with the classes (but instead will be offered as predicate objects). Fortunately, however, method references give you the flexibility to easily use existing methods as lambda expressions, and so we can return from methods to functions.

#### The Predicate Type in the Application Programming Interface

A few places in the Java API where <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate</samp> objects are used include the following:

*   As an argument for delete methods, to specify elements in collections that should be deleted or filtered

*   In the default methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate</samp> interface itself to link predicates

*   In regular expressions, on a <samp class="listingcharacter">Pattern</samp> ( <samp class="listingcharacter">asPredicate()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">asMatchPredicate()</samp> return a <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate</samp> for tests)

*   In the Stream API, where objects are identified via a predicate as they pass through the stream, for example, to filter them out

###### [eg]  Example

The following example deletes all characters that are digits from a list of arbitrary characters:

```
 Predicate<Character> isDigit = Character::isDigit;
List<Character> list = new ArrayList<>( Arrays.asList( 'a', '1' ) );
list.removeIf( 
                        isDigit );
```

In this way, the focus is not on the loop, but on the deletion.

#### Default Methods of Predicate

A number of default methods are provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate</samp> functional interface:

```
interface java.util.function.
                    Predicate<T> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default Predicate<T> negate()</samp>
    Returns a negation of the current predicate (implemented as <samp class="listingcharacter">return t -> ! test(t);</samp> ).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> Predicate<T> not(Predicate<? super T> target)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">target.negate()</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default Predicate<T> and(Predicate<? super T> p)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default Predicate<T> or(Predicate<? super T> p)</samp>
    Links the current predicate to another predicate with a logical AND/OR.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> Predicate<T> isEqual(Object targetRef)</samp>
    Returns a new predicate that performs an equivalence test with <samp class="listingcharacter">targetRef</samp>, basically <samp class="listingcharacter">return ref -> Objects.equals(ref, targetRef)</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

The following example deletes characters that are not digits from a list of characters:

```
Predicate<Character> isDigit = Character::isDigit;
Predicate<Character> isNotDigit = isDigit.
                        negate();
List<Character> list = new ArrayList<>( Arrays.asList( 'a', '1' ) );
list.removeIf( isNotDigit );
// alternatively: list.removeIf( Predicate.not( isDigit ) ); 
```

### 13.5.4    Functions via the Functional Interface java.util.function.Function

Functions in the sense of functional programming can be of different types: with parameter lists/returns or without. But functions are basically special forms, and the functional interface <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.function.Function</samp> is the most general function that returns a result for an argument.

```
interface java.util.function.
                Function<T,R> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">R apply(T t)</samp>
    Applies a function and provides a return to the input <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

The following example is a function to determine the absolute value:

```
 Function<Double,Double> abs = a -> Math.abs( a );  // alternativ Math::abs
System.out.println( 
                    abs.apply( -12\. ) );           // 12.0 
```

For functions, too, an area of tension arises for the API design. Basically, “functions” now no longer need to be provided as methods at all; classes could also offer them as <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> objects. But since method references easily bridge from method names to objects, developers can work quite well with classic methods.

#### The Function Type in the Application Programming Interface

The Stream API is the biggest beneficiary of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> type. A few examples exist in object comparisons ( <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> ), in the concurrency package, and in associative memories. In the Stream API section, we’ll explore many more examples.

###### [eg]  Example

An associative memory is supposed to be implemented as a cache, which associates the content to file names. If no content for the key (the file name) exists yet, the file content should be read and put into the associative memory. Consider the following example:

```
class FileCache {
  private final Map<String,byte[]> map = new HashMap<>();
  public byte[] getContent( String filename ) {
    return map.computeIfAbsent( filename, file -> {
      try {
        return Files.readAllBytes( Paths.get( file ) );
      } catch ( IOException e ) { throw new UncheckedIOException( e ); }
    } );
  }
}
```

**Listing 13.11**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/lambda/FileCache.java (Snippet)

We’ll return to this method in [Chapter 18](#18_001.html_h18), [Section 18.3](#18_003.html_h18.3); we just wanted to show you passing functions to other functions—in this case, a <samp class="listingcharacter">Function<String,byte[])</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">computeIfAbsent(...)</samp>. As soon as the <samp class="listingcharacter">getContent(String)</samp> call addresses the file cache, the method will ask the <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> for a value, and if it has no value for the key, the lambda expression will return the content for the file name.

#### Getter Methods as Functions via Method References

Method references are among the most syntactically concise tools in the Java language. In combination with getters, a pattern can be read that’s often seen in code. First, let’s review <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> and its use in method references, with the following example:

```
Function<
                    String,String> func1a = (
                    String s) -> s.toUpperCase();
Function<
                    String,String> func1b = 
                    String::toUpperCase;
Function<
                    Point,Double>  func2a = (
                    Point p) -> p.getX();
Function<
                    Point,Double>  func2b = 
                    Point::getX;
System.out.println( func1b.apply( "jocelyn" ) );         // JOCELYN
System.out.println( func2b.apply( new Point( 9, 0 ) ) ); // 9.0 
```

The fact that <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> matches the given method reference is incomprehensible at first glance since the signatures of <samp class="listingcharacter">toUpperCase()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">getX()</samp> don’t declare a parameter. Thus, these methods aren’t functions in the usual sense (into which something goes and out of which something comes). However, we’re dealing with a special case because the methods mentioned in the method reference fulfill the following prerequisites:

*   The methods are non-static (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter">Math::max</samp> ).

*   No reference is being used (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out::print</samp> ).

In this case, however, the compiler will call an object method on exactly the object passed as the first argument of the functional interface. (Please read this sentence twice!)

Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> is a practical type in all scenarios in which states are somehow queried via getters, as is often the case with a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp>, for example. In this scenario, a static method is quite useful, for instance, <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator<...> Comparator.comparing(Function<...> keyExtractor</samp> . (Note that generics are omitted.)

###### [eg]  Example

The following example gets a list of packages accessible from the class loader and sorts them by name:

```
List<Package> list = Arrays.asList( Package.getPackages() );
Collections.sort( list, 
                        Comparator.comparing( Package::getName ) );
System.out.println( list ); // [package java.io, … sun.util.locale … 
```

#### Default Methods in Function

The functional interface prescribes only one <samp class="listingcharacter">apply(...)</samp> method but declares three additional default methods:

```
interface java.util.function.
                    Function<T,R> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> Function<T,T> identity()</samp>
    Returns a function that always returns the input as a result, implemented as <samp class="listingcharacter">return t -> t;</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default <V> Function<T,V> andThen(Function<? super R,? extends V> after)</samp>
    Corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter">t -> after.apply(apply(t))</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default <V> Function<V,R> compose(Function<? super V,? extends T> before)</samp>
    Corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter">v -> apply(before.apply(v))</samp> .

<samp class="listingcharacter">identity()</samp> seems pointless at first glance but serves a purpose if a <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> is required in the API where nothing should change and the input should be the output.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">andThen(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">compose(...)</samp> methods differ in the order in which the functions are called. The good thing is that the parameter names ( <samp class="listingcharacter">before</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">after</samp> ) make it clear what is called here and in what order.

###### [eg]  Example

```
Function<String, String> f1 = s -> "~" + s + "~";
Function<String, String> f2 = s -> "<" + s + ">";
System.out.println( f1.andThen( f2 ).apply( ":)" ) ); // <~:)~>
System.out.println( f2.andThen( f1 ).apply( ":)" ) ); // ~<:)>~
System.out.println( f1.compose( f2 ).apply( ":)" ) ); // ~<:)>~
System.out.println( f2.compose( f1 ).apply( ":)" ) ); // <~:)~> 
```

#### Function versus Consumer/Predicate

Basically, everything can be represented as a <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> because of the following:

*   A <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer<T></samp> can also be understood as <samp class="listingcharacter">Function<T,Void></samp> (something goes in, but nothing comes out).

*   A <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate<T></samp> can also be understood as <samp class="listingcharacter">Function<T,Boolean></samp> .

*   A <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier<T></samp> can also be understood as <samp class="listingcharacter">Function<Void,T></samp> .

Nevertheless, these special types serve their purpose because the more accurate the type, the better.

<samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> is not a base type of <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier</samp> because “no return” or “no parameter” can’t be expressed by a generic type, which would be possible with <samp class="listingcharacter">Function<T,R></samp> .

#### UnaryOperator

Another interface in the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.function package</samp> specializes <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp>, namely, the <samp class="listingcharacter">UnaryOperator</samp>. A <samp class="listingcharacter">UnaryOperator</samp> is a special <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> where the types for “input” and “output” are the same.

```
 interface java.util.function.
                    UnaryOperator<T>
extends Function<T,T> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> UnaryOperator<T> identity()</samp>
    Returns the identity operator that maps all inputs to outputs.

Generic types make it clear that the type of the method parameter is the same as the result type. Except for <samp class="listingcharacter">identity()</samp> , no other functionality exists; the interface is used only for type declaration.

In some places in the Java library, this type also occurs, for example, in the <samp class="listingcharacter">replaceAll(UnaryOperator)</samp> method of <samp class="listingcharacter">List</samp> types.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example doubles each entry in a list:

```
List<Integer> list = Arrays.asList( 1, 2, 3 );
list.replaceAll( 
                        e -> e * 2 );
System.out.println( list );  // [2, 4, 6] 
```

### 13.5.5    I Take Two

“Bi” is a well-known Latin prefix for “two,” which when applied to types from the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.function</samp> package means that two arguments can be passed instead of only one argument.

| Type | Interface | Operation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consumer | <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer<T></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">void accept(T t)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">BiConsumer<T,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">U</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">void accept(T t,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">U u</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> |  |
| Function | <samp class="listingcharacter">Function<T,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">R</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">R apply(T t)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">BiFunction<T,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">U</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">,R></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">R apply(T t,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">U u</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> |  |
| Predicate | <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate<T></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean test(T t)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">BiPredicate<T,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">U</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean test(T t,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">U u</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp> |  |

**Table 13.12**     One- and Two-Argument Methods in Comparison

The “bi” types have no type relationship with non-“bi” types.

#### BiConsumer

The <samp class="listingcharacter">BiConsumer</samp> declares the <samp class="listingcharacter">accept(T, U)</samp> method with two parameters, each of which can carry different types. The main use of the type in the Java standard library is associative memories that pass keys and values to <samp class="listingcharacter">accept(...)</samp>. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> declares the following method:

```
interface java.util.
                    Map<K,V> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default void forEach(BiConsumer<? super K,? super V> action)</samp>
    Runs through the associative memory and calls the <samp class="listingcharacter">accept(...)</samp> method from the passed <samp class="listingcharacter">BiConsumer</samp> on each key-value pair.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example results in an output of temperatures of various cities:

```
Map<String,Integer> map = Map.of( "Manila", 25, "Dortmund", -5 );
map.forEach( (k, v) -> System.out.printf( "%d°C in %s%n", v, k ) );
```

A <samp class="listingcharacter">BiConsumer</samp> has a default method named <samp class="listingcharacter">andThen(...)</samp>, just as the <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer</samp> declares it for chaining.

```
interface java.util.function.
                    BiConsumer<T,U> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default BiConsumer<T,U> andThen(BiConsumer<? super T,? super U> after)</samp>
    Links the current <samp class="listingcharacter">BiConsumer</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">after</samp> to form a new <samp class="listingcharacter">BiConsumer</samp> .

#### BiFunction and BinaryOperator

A <samp class="listingcharacter">BiFunction</samp> is a function with two arguments, while a regular <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> accepts only one argument.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example illustrates the use of <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">BiFunction</samp> with method references:

```
Function<Double,Double> sign = Math::abs;
BiFunction<Double,Double,Double> max = Math::max;
```

The Java library uses <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp> much more often than <samp class="listingcharacter">BiFunction</samp>. The most common use is in the standard library around associative memories, where a key and a value are passed to a <samp class="listingcharacter">BiFunction</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

The following example converts all associated values of a <samp class="listingcharacter">HashMap</samp> to uppercase:

```
 Map<String,String> twitterNames = new HashMap<>();
twitterNames.put( "elonmusk", "Elon Musk" );
twitterNames.put( "jimmyfallon", "Jimmy Fallon" );
BiFunction<String, String, String> uppercaser = (k, v) -> v.toUpperCase();
twitterNames.replaceAll( uppercaser );
System.out.println( twitterNames );  // {elonmusk=ELON MUSK, …} 
```

If the type is the same for a <samp class="listingcharacter">Function</samp>, the Java API provides the more special type <samp class="listingcharacter">UnaryOperator</samp> for these cases. If all three types of a <samp class="listingcharacter">BiFunction</samp> are the same, <samp class="listingcharacter">BinaryOperator</samp> can be used for comparison, in the following ways:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">interface UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T,T></samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">interface BinaryOperator<T> extends BiFunction<T,T,T></samp>

###### [eg]  Example

The following example illustrates the use of <samp class="listingcharacter">BiFunction</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">BinaryOperator</samp> :

```
BiFunction<Double,Double,Double> max1 = Math::max;
BinaryOperator<Double>           max2 = Math::max;
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">BinaryOperator</samp> plays a major role in what’s called reductions, for example, when two values become one, as in <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.max(...)</samp> . We’ll return to this topic when we discuss the Stream API.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">BiFunction</samp> interface declares exactly one default method:

```
interface java.util.function.
                    BiFunction<T,U,R>
extends Function<T,T> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default <V> BiFunction<T,U,V> andThen(Function<? super R,? extends V> after)</samp>

<samp class="listingcharacter">BinaryOperator</samp> , on the other hand, has two static methods:

```
public interface java.util.function.
                    BinaryOperator<T>
extends BiFunction<T,T,T> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> BinaryOperator<T> maxBy(Comparator<? super T> comparator)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> BinaryOperator<T> minBy(Comparator<? super T> comparator)</samp>
    Returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">BinaryOperator</samp> that returns the maximum/minimum with respect to a given <samp class="listingcharacter">comparator</samp> .

#### BiPredicate

A <samp class="listingcharacter">BiPredicate</samp> tests two arguments and condenses them to a truth value. Like <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">BiPredicate</samp> also declares three default methods <samp class="listingcharacter">and(...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">or(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">negate(...)</samp>, although of course <samp class="listingcharacter">BiPredicate</samp> lacks a static <samp class="listingcharacter">isEqual(...)</samp> method like <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate</samp>. For <samp class="listingcharacter">BiPredicate</samp> there’s only one use in the Java standard library in a method for finding files. The use is rare, and besides, a predicate is always a function with <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean</samp> return, so that there’s actually no compelling need for this interface.

###### [eg]  Example

By the way, with <samp class="listingcharacter">Bi*</samp> and two arguments the specialization stop; no types like <samp class="listingcharacter">Tri*</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Quad*</samp>, etc. exist. These types aren’t necessary in practice because, on one hand, a reduction can often take place—for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">max(1, 2, 3)</samp> is equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">max(1, max(2, 3))</samp>. On the other hand, the parameter type can be a collection, as in <samp class="listingcharacter">Function<List<Integer>,Integer> max</samp> .

### 13.5.6    Functional Interfaces with Primitives

The functional interfaces presented so far are quite flexible due to the generic type parameters, but what is missing are signatures with primitives—Java has a “problem” in that generics only work with reference types, but not with primitive types. For this reason, four versions exist of almost all interfaces in the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.function</samp> package: a generic one for arbitrary references and then versions for the types <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> . The designers of the API left wrapper types and support for certain primitive types out for performance reasons, so as to avoid boxing.

[Table 13.13](#13_005.html_t13.13) provides an overview of functional interfaces, all of which have no inheritance relationships to other interfaces.

| Functional Interface | Function Descriptor |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">*Supplier</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">BooleanSupplier</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean getAsBoolean()</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">IntSupplier</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">int getAsInt()</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LongSupplier</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">long getAsLong()</samp> |
