**Table 16.3**     Important Packages in the Java SE

For a developer, you can’t avoid studying the Java API documentation at [https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/index.html](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/index.html).

#### Official Interface (java and javax Packages)

The list provided by the Java documentation represents the permitted access to the library. The types are basically designed to last forever, so developers can count on still being able to run their Java programs in 100 years. But who defines the API? In essence, three sources define APIs:

*   Oracle developers put new packages and types into the API.

*   The Java Community Process (JCP) adopts a new API. Then, Oracle is not acting alone, but instead, a group works out a new API and defines its interfaces.

*   The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) provides an API for XML Document Object Model (DOM), for example.

A good mnemonic is that anything starting with <samp class="listingcharacter">java</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">javax</samp> is a permitted API, and anything else can lead to non-portable Java programs. Some classes are supported that aren’t part of the official API. These classes include, for example, various Swing classes for controlling the appearance of the interface.

#### Standard Extension API (javax Packages)

Some Java packages start with <samp class="listingcharacter">javax</samp> . Originally, these extension packages were intended to complement the core classes. Over time, however, many packages that initially had to be included have now migrated to the standard distribution, so that today, a fairly large proportion start with <samp class="listingcharacter">javax</samp>, but no longer represent extensions that need to be additionally installed. Sun didn’t want to rename the packages at that time, so as not to make migration more difficult. If you notice a package name with <samp class="listingcharacter">javax</samp> in the source code today, therefore, you can no longer easily determine whether an external source must be included or whether the package is already part of the distribution (and since Java version).

Truly external packages include the following packages:

*   The Java Communications API for serial and parallel interfaces

*   The Java Telephony API

*   Speech input/output with the Java Speech API

*   JavaSpaces for shared memory of different runtime environments

*   JXTA for establishing P2P networks

The bottom line is that developers are dealing with the following libraries:

*   With the official Java API

*   With APIs from Java Specification Request (JSR) extensions

*   With unofficial libraries, such as open-source solutions, for example, to access PDF files or control ATMs

An important role is also played by types from the <samp class="listingcharacter">jakarta</samp> package, which is part of Jakarta EE (formerly Java EE) and semi-official.

## 16.2    Simple Time Measurement and Profiling*

In addition to the convenient classes for managing date values, two static methods provide simple ways to measure times for program sections:

```
final class java.lang.
            System 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long currentTimeMillis()</samp>
    Returns the milliseconds elapsed since 1/1/1970, 00:00:00 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long nanoTime()</samp>
    Returns the time from the most accurate system timer. This method has no reference point to any date.

The difference between two time values can be used to roughly estimate the execution times of programs.

###### [+]  Tip

The values of <samp class="listingcharacter">nanoTime()</samp> are always ascending, which isn’t necessarily true for <samp class="listingcharacter">currentTimeMillis()</samp> because Java gets the time from the operating system. System times can change, for example, when a user adjusts the time. Differences of <samp class="listingcharacter">currentTimeMillis()</samp> timestamps are then completely wrong and could even be negative.

### 16.2.1     Profilers

Where the Java virtual machine (JVM) does waste clock cycles in a program is shown by a profiler . Optimization can then begin at those points. Java Mission Control is a powerful program of the JDK and integrates a free profiler. Java VisualVM is another free program that can be obtained from [https://visualvm.github.io/](https://visualvm.github.io/). On the professional and commercial side, JProfiler ([https://www.ej-technologies.com/products/jprofiler/overview.html](https://www.ej-technologies.com/products/jprofiler/overview.html)) and YourKit ([https://www.yourkit.com/java/profiler](https://www.yourkit.com/java/profiler)) are competitors. The Ultimate Version of IntelliJ also includes a profiler.

## 16.3    The Class Class

Let’s suppose we want to write a class browser. This program should display all classes belonging to the running program and furthermore additional information, such as variable assignment, declared methods, constructors, and some information about the inheritance hierarchy. For this purpose, you’ll need the library class, <samp class="listingcharacter">class</samp> . Instances of <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> are objects that, for example, represent a Java class, record or a Java interface.

In this respect, Java differs from many conventional programming languages because the members of classes can be queried by the currently running program using the <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> objects. The instances of <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> are a restricted kind of meta-object [[ 208 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn16_02)—containing the description of a Java type but revealing only selected information. Besides normal classes, interfaces are also represented by a <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object, and even arrays and primitive data types—instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp>, the class name <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> would probably have been more appropriate.

### 16.3.1    Obtaining a Class Object

First, for a given class, you must identify the associated <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object. <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> objects themselves can only be created by the JVM. (We can’t create instances because the constructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> is private.) To obtain a reference to a <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object, the following solutions are available:

*   If an instance of the class is available, you can call the <samp class="listingcharacter">getClass()</samp> method of the object and get the <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> instance of the associated class.

*   Each type contains a static variable named <samp class="listingcharacter">.class</samp> of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp>, which references the associated <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> instance.

*   The ending <samp class="listingcharacter">.class</samp> is also permitted for primitive data types. The same <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object returns the static variable <samp class="listingcharacter">TYPE</samp> of the wrapper classes. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">int.class == Integer.TYPE</samp> is true.

*   The class method <samp class="listingcharacter">Class.forName(String)</samp> can query a class, and you’ll obtain the associated <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> instance as a result. If the type hasn’t been loaded yet, <samp class="listingcharacter">forName(String)</samp> searches for and binds the class. Because searching can go wrong, a <samp class="listingcharacter">ClassNotFoundException</samp> is possible.

*   If you already have a <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object but are interested in its ancestors instead, you can simply get a <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object for the superclass via <samp class="listingcharacter">getSuperclass()</samp> .

The following example shows three ways to obtain a <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object for <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.Date</samp> :

```
Class<Date> c1 = java.util.Date
                .class;
System.out.println( c1 );        // class java.util.Date
Class<?> c2 = new java.util.Date()
                .getClass();
 // or Class<? extends Date> c2 = …

System.out.println( c2 );        // class java.util.Date
try {
  Class<?> c3 = 
                Class.forName( "java.util.Date" );
  System.out.println( c3 );      // class java.util.Date
}
catch ( ClassNotFoundException e ) { e.printStackTrace(); } 
```

**Listing 16.1**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/meta/GetClassObject.java, main()

The variant with <samp class="listingcharacter">forName(String)</samp> is useful if the name of the desired class wasn’t determined when the program was translated.

Otherwise, the previous technique is more catchy, and the compiler can check if the type exists. A full qualification is needed: <samp class="listingcharacter">Class.forName("Date")</samp> would only search for <samp class="listingcharacter">Date</samp> in the default package, and the return isn’t a collection after all.

###### [eg]  Example

Note that class objects for primitive elements aren’t returned by <samp class="listingcharacter">forName(String)</samp>. The two expressions <samp class="listingcharacter">Class.forName("boolean")</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Class.forName(boolean.class.getName())</samp> lead to a <samp class="listingcharacter">ClassNotFoundException</samp> .

```
class java.lang.
                Object 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final Class<? extends Object> getClass()</samp>
    Returns the <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> instance at runtime which represents the class of the object.

```
final class java.lang.
                Class<T>
implements Serializable, GenericDeclaration, Type, AnnotatedElement 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">static Class<?> forName(String className) throws ClassNotFoundException</samp>
    Returns the <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> instance for the class, record or interface with the specified fully qualified name. If the type hasn’t yet been required by the program, the class loader searches for and loads the class. The method never returns <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. If the class couldn’t be loaded and included, a <samp class="listingcharacter">ClassNotFoundException</samp> will occur. The alternative method, <samp class="listingcharacter">forName(String name, boolean initialize, ClassLoader loader)</samp> , also allows loading with a desired class loader. The class name must always be fully qualified.

#### ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError*

A <samp class="listingcharacter">ClassNotFoundException</samp> can be thrown by any of the following methods:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">forName(...)</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">loadClass(String name [, boolean resolve])</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">ClassLoader</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">findSystemClass(String name)</samp> from <samp class="listingcharacter">ClassLoader</samp>

An exception occurs whenever the class loader can’t find the class by its class name. Thus, the trigger is when an application wants to load types dynamically, but those types aren’t present.

In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">ClassNotFoundException</samp> , the <samp class="listingcharacter">NoClassDefFoundError</samp> is a hard <samp class="listingcharacter">LinkageError</samp> that the JVM raises whenever it can’t load a class referenced in the bytecode. For example, let’s consider an expression like <samp class="listingcharacter">new MyClass()</samp>. When the JVM executes this code, it attempts to load the bytecode from <samp class="listingcharacter">MyClass</samp>. If the bytecode for <samp class="listingcharacter">MyClass</samp> has been removed after compilation, the JVM raises the <samp class="listingcharacter">NoClassDefFoundError</samp> due to the unsuccessful load attempt. Also, the error occurs if the <samp class="listingcharacter">MyClass</samp> class was found when loading the bytecode, but <samp class="listingcharacter">MyClass</samp> has a static initialization block that in turn references a class for which no class file exists.

While <samp class="listingcharacter">ClassNotFoundException</samp> is more common than <samp class="listingcharacter">NoClassDefFoundError</samp> , the exception is generally an indication that a Java Archive file (JAR file) is missing in the module path.

#### Problems after Applying an Obfuscator*

The fact that the compiler automatically generates bytecode according to this modified source code only leads to unexpected problems if you run an obfuscator over the program text, which subsequently modifies the bytecode and thus obscures the meaning of the program or the bytecode and renames types in the process. Obviously, an obfuscator must not rename types whose <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> instances are requested.

Otherwise, the obfuscator must correctly replace the corresponding strings as well (but of course not replace all strings that happen to match class names).

### 16.3.2     A Class Is a Type

In Java, different types exist, and classes, records, interfaces, and enumeration types are represented by the JVM as <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> objects. In the Reflection API, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> interface represents all types and the only implementing class is Class. Below Type there are some subinterfaces:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">ParameterizedType</samp> represents generic types like <samp class="listingcharacter">List<T></samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">TypeVariable<D></samp> represents, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">T extends Comparable<? super T></samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">WildcardType</samp> represents <samp class="listingcharacter">? super T</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">GenericArrayType</samp> represents something like <samp class="listingcharacter">T[]</samp> .

The only method of <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">getTypeName()</samp>, and this method is just a default method that calls <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">Type</samp> is the return of various methods in the Reflection API, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">getGenericSuperclass()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">getGenericInterfaces()</samp> of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> class, and many other methods listed in the Javadoc under USE .

## 16.4    The Utility Classes System and Members

In the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.System</samp> class, methods exist for requesting and changing system variables, for redirecting the standard data streams, for determining the current time, for terminating the application, and for several other tasks. All methods are exclusively static, and an instance of <samp class="listingcharacter">System</samp> can’t be created. In the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Runtime</samp> class, additional helper methods are available, such as for starting external programs or for requesting memory requirements. Unlike <samp class="listingcharacter">System</samp>, only one method is static in this class, namely, the singleton method <samp class="listingcharacter">getRuntime()</samp>, which returns the instance of <samp class="listingcharacter">Runtime</samp> .

[![Members of the System and Runtime Classes](bilderklein/klein16_004.png)](img-f16.4.html)

**Figure 16.4**     Members of the System and Runtime Classes

###### [»]   Remark

All in all, the <samp class="listingcharacter">System</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Runtime</samp> classes don’t seem particularly orderly, as shown in [Figure 16.4](#16_004.html_f16.4) ; you may think everything that doesn’t fit elsewhere can be found in these two classes. Also, some methods of one class would be just as good in the other class.

The fact that the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">System.arraycopy(...)</samp> for copying arrays isn’t located in <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.Arrays</samp> can only be explained historically. Furthermore, <samp class="listingcharacter">System.exit(int)</samp> redirects to <samp class="listingcharacter">Runtime.getRuntime().exit(int)</samp>. Some methods are obsolete and distributed differently: The <samp class="listingcharacter">exec(...)</samp> of <samp class="listingcharacter">Runtime</samp> to start external processes is handled by a new class ( <samp class="listingcharacter">ProcessBuilder</samp>), and the question about the memory state or the number of processors is answered by MBeans, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">ManagementFactory.getOperatingSystemMXBean().getAvailableProcessors()</samp> . But API design is like gambling: One rash action, and you've lost the farm.

### 16.4.1    Memory of the Java Virtual Machine

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Runtime</samp> object includes the following three methods that provide information about the memory of the JVM:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">maxMemory()</samp> returns the maximum number of bytes available for the JVM. The value can be set when calling the JVM with <samp class="listingcharacter">-Xmx</samp> in the command line.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">totalMemory()</samp> is what is currently used and can grow to <samp class="listingcharacter">maxMemory()</samp>. Basically, this memory limit can also shrink again. The following applies: <samp class="listingcharacter">maxMemory()</samp> > <samp class="listingcharacter">totalMemory()</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">freeMemory()</samp> indicates the memory that is free for new objects and also provokes the automatic garbage collection process. The following applies: <samp class="listingcharacter">totalMemory()</samp> > <samp class="listingcharacter">freeMemory()</samp>. However, <samp class="listingcharacter">freeMemory()</samp> isn’t the entire freely available memory area because the “share” of <samp class="listingcharacter">maxMemory()</samp> is still missing.

Two pieces of information are missing and therefore must be calculated:

*   Used memory: <samp class="listingcharacter">long usedMemory = Runtime.getRuntime().totalMemory() -</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">Runtime.getRuntime().freeMemory();</samp>

*   Free total memory: <samp class="listingcharacter">long totalFreeMemory = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() - usedMemory;</samp>

###### [eg]  Example

The following example outputs information about the memory on a computer:

```
long totalMemory     = Runtime.getRuntime().totalMemory();
long freeMemory      = Runtime.getRuntime().freeMemory();
long maxMemory       = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory();
long usedMemory      = totalMemory - freeMemory;

                    long totalFreeMemory = maxMemory - usedMemory;

System.out.printf(
  "total=%d MiB, free=%d MiB, max=%d MiB, used=%d MiB, total free=%d MiB%n",
  totalMemory >> 20, freeMemory >> 20, maxMemory >> 20,
  usedMemory >> 20, totalFreeMemory >> 20 );
```

The result is the following output:

```
total=126 MiB, free=124 MiB, max=2016 MiB, used=1 MiB, total free=2014 MiB
```

### 16.4.2    Number of CPUs or Cores

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Runtime</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">availableProcessors()</samp> returns the number of logical processors or cores.

###### [eg]  Example

Print the number of processors/cores:

```
System.out.println( Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() );  // 4
```

### 16.4.3    System Properties of the Java Environment

The Java environment manages system properties, such as path separators or virtual machine versions in the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.Properties</samp> object. The static method <samp class="listingcharacter">System.getProperties()</samp> queries these system properties and returns the filled <samp class="listingcharacter">Properties</samp> object. However, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Properties</samp> object isn’t absolutely necessary for querying individual properties: <samp class="listingcharacter">System.getProperty(...)</samp> directly queries a property.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example outputs the name of the operating system:

```
System.out.println( System.getProperty( "os.name" ) );  // e.g., Windows 10
```

The following example outputs all system properties on the screen:

```
System.getProperties().list( System.out );
```

An excerpt of the result is shown in the following output:

```
-- listing properties --
sun.desktop=windows
awt.toolkit=sun.awt.windows.WToolkit
java.specification.version=9
file.encoding.pkg=sun.io
sun.cpu.isalist=amd64
…
```

[Table 16.4](#16_004.html_t16.4) shows a list of the important standard system properties.

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">java.version</samp> | Version of the Java Runtime Environment (JRE) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">java.class.path</samp> | The current classpath |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">java.library.path</samp> | Path for native libraries |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">java.io.tmpdir</samp> | Path for temporary files |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">os.name</samp> | Name of the operating system |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">file.separator</samp> | Separator of the path segments, for example / (Unix) or \ (Windows) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">path.separator</samp> | Separator for path specifications, such as : (Unix) or ; (Windows) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">line.separator</samp> | Newline character (string) |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">user.name</samp> | Name of the logged-on user |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">user.home</samp> | Home directory of the user |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">user.dir</samp> | Current directory of the user |

**Table 16.4**     Standard System Properties

#### Application Programming Interface Documentation

A few more keys are listed in the API documentation at <samp class="listingcharacter">System.getProperties()</samp>. Some variables are also accessible in other ways, such as through the <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> class.

```
final class java.lang.
                    System 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String getProperty(String key)</samp>
    Returns the assignment of a system property. If the key is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> or empty, a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> or an <samp class="listingcharacter">IllegalArgumentException</samp> , respectively, will occur.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String getProperty(String key, String def)</samp>
    Returns the assignment of a system property. If the property isn’t present, the method returns the string <samp class="listingcharacter">def</samp>, which is the default value. For the exceptions, the same applies as for <samp class="listingcharacter">getProperty(String)</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String setProperty(String key, String value)</samp>
    Reassigns a system property. The return is the previous assignment or <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> if no previous assignment exists.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String clearProperty(String key)</samp>
    Deletes a system property from the list. The return is the previous assignment or <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> if no previous assignment exists.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">static Properties getProperties()</samp>
    Returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">Properties</samp> object filled with the current system assignments.

### 16.4.4    Setting Custom Properties from the Console*

Properties can also be set from the console during the program startup. This approach is convenient for a configuration that controls, for example, the behavior of a program. On the command line, <samp class="listingcharacter">-D</samp> specifies the name of the property and, after an equal sign (without whitespace), its value. Consider the following example:

```
$ java 
                -DLOG –DUSER=Chris -DSIZE=100
             com.tutego.insel.lang.SetProperty 
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">LOG</samp> property is “simply exists” but with no assigned value. The next two properties, <samp class="listingcharacter">USER</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">SIZE</samp>, are associated with values that are first of type <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> and must be further processed by the program. This information doesn’t appear with the argument list in the static <samp class="listingcharacter">main(String[])</samp> method because it precedes the name of the class and is already processed by the JRE.

To read the properties, we’ll use the familiar <samp class="listingcharacter">System.getProperty(...)</samp> method in the following example:

```
Optional<String> logProperty = ofNullable( System.getProperty( "LOG" ) );
Optional<String> user nameProperty = ofNullable( System.getProperty( "USER" ) );
Optional<String> sizeProperty = ofNullable( System.getProperty( "SIZE" ) );

System.out.println( logProperty.isPresent() );                          // true
user nameProperty.ifPresent( System.out::println );                      // Chris
sizeProperty.map( Integer::parseInt ).ifPresent( System.out::println ); // 100
System.out.println( System.getProperty( "DEBUG", "false" ) );           // false 
```

**Listing 16.2**     com/tutego/insel/lang/SetProperty.java, main()

In return, you’ll receive a string indicating the value via <samp class="listingcharacter">getProperty(String)</samp>. If no property of that name exists at all, you’ll get <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> instead. In this way, we can know if this value was set at all. So, a simple <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> test tells us whether <samp class="listingcharacter">logProperty</samp> is present or not. Instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">-DLOG</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">-DLOG=</samp> also returns the same result because the associated value is the empty string. Since all properties are of type <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> to begin with, <samp class="listingcharacter">user nameProperty</samp> is easy to output, and you’ll get either <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> or the string specified after <samp class="listingcharacter">=</samp>. If the types aren’t strings, they must be processed further, for example, with <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.parseInt()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.parseDouble()</samp>, and so on. The <samp class="listingcharacter">System.getProperty(String, String)</samp> method, which is passed two arguments, is pretty useful in this case because the second argument represents a default value. Thus, a default value can always be assumed.

#### Boolean.getBoolean(String)

In the case of properties that are assigned truth values, the following statement can be written:

```
boolean b = Boolean.parseBoolean( System.getProperty( property ) );  // (*) 
```

There’s another variant for the truth values. The static method <samp class="listingcharacter">Boolean.getBoolean(String)</samp> searches for a property with the specified name in the system properties. Thus, the following is analogous to the line <samp class="listingcharacter">(*)</samp> :

```
boolean b = Boolean.getBoolean( property ); 
```

You might be surprised to find this static method in the wrapper class <samp class="listingcharacter">Boolean</samp> because property access has nothing to do with wrapper objects and the class actually goes beyond its area of responsibility in this case.

Compared to a separate, direct <samp class="listingcharacter">System</samp> query, <samp class="listingcharacter">getBoolean(String)</samp> also has a disadvantage in that, when it returns <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>, you can’t distinguish whether the property simply doesn’t exist or whether the property is assigned the value <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. Also, incorrectly set values like <samp class="listingcharacter">-DP=fa1se</samp> always result in <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. [[ 209 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn16_03)

```
final class java.lang.
                    Boolean
implements Serializable, Comparable<Boolean> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static boolean getBoolean(String name)</samp>
    Reads a system property named <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp> and returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the value of the property is equal to the string <samp class="listingcharacter">"true"</samp>. The return value is <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> if the value of the system property is <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>, if the property doesn’t exist, or if the property is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> .

### 16.4.5    Newline Characters and line.separator

To move from the end of one line to the beginning of the next, a newline is inserted. The character for a new line doesn’t have to be a single character; several characters may also be necessary. Unfortunately for programmers, the number of characters for a newline sequence depends on the architecture, for instance:

*   Unix, macOS: Line feed (LF for short), <samp class="listingcharacter">\n</samp>

*   Windows: Carriage return (CR for short) and line feed

The control code for a carriage return is 13 (0x0D); the control code for a line feed is 10 (0x0A). Java also assigns its own escape sequences for these characters: <samp class="listingcharacter">\r</samp> for carriage returns and <samp class="listingcharacter">\n</samp> for line feeds. (The <samp class="listingcharacter">\f</samp> sequence is for a form feed, also called a “page feed,” which doesn’t play any role in line breaks).

In Java, you can obtain a newline character or a newline string from the system in one of the following three ways:

*   By calling <samp class="listingcharacter">System.getProperty("line.separator")</samp>

*   By calling <samp class="listingcharacter">System.lineSeparator()</samp>

*   You don’t always have to query the character (or, strictly speaking, a possible string of characters) individually. If the character is part of a formatted output at the <samp class="listingcharacter">formatter</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">String.format(...)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(...)</samp>, the format specifier <samp class="listingcharacter">%n</samp> stands for exactly the newline string stored in the system.

### 16.4.6    Environment Variables of the Operating System

Almost every operating system uses the concept of environment variables ; for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp> is known for the search path for applications on Windows and Unix. Java enables access to these system environment variables. Two static methods are used for this purpose:

```
final class java.lang.
                System 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Map<String, String> getEnv()</samp>
    Reads a set of <samp class="listingcharacter"><string, string></samp> pairs with all system properties.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String getEnv(String name)</samp>
    Reads a system property named <samp class="listingcharacter">name</samp>. If the property doesn’t exist, the return will be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> .

| Variable Name | Description | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">COMPUTERNAME</samp> | Name of the computer | MOE |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">HOMEDRIVE</samp> | Drive of the user directory | C: |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">HOMEPATH</samp> | Path of the user directory | \Users\Christian |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">OS</samp> | Name of the operating system* | Windows_NT |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">PATH</samp> | Search path | C:\windows\SYSTEM32; C:\windows … |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">PATHEXT</samp> | File extensions that represent executable programs | .COM;.EXE;.BAT;.CMD;.VBS;.VBE;.JS;.JSE;.WSF;.WSH;.MSC |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">SYSTEMDRIVE</samp> | Drive of the operating system | C: |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">TEMP</samp> and also <samp class="listingcharacter">TMP</samp> | Temporary directory | C:\Users\CHRIST~1\AppData\Local\Temp |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">USERDOMAIN</samp> | Domain of the user | MOE |
| <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">USERNAME</samp> | Name of the user | Christian |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">USERPROFILE</samp> | Profile directory | C:\Users\Christian |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">WINDIR</samp> | Directory of the operating system | C:\windows |
| * The result differs from <samp class="listingcharacter">System.getProperty("os.name")</samp> , which already returns “Windows 10” for Windows 10. |

**Table 16.5**     Selection of Some Environment Variables Available in Windows

Some variables are also accessible via the system properties, for instance, with <samp class="listingcharacter">System.getProperties()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">System.getProperty(.</samp> ..), and so on.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example outputs the environment variables of the system:

```
Map<String,String> map = System.getenv();
map.forEach( (k, v) -> System.out.printf( "%s=%s%n", k, v ) );
```

## 16.5    The Languages of Different Countries

When developers start with console or GUI output, they often hardwire the output to a local language. If the language changes, the software can’t handle other country-specific rules, for example, when formatting floats. Developing “multilingual” programs that provide localized outputs in different languages is not too difficult. Basically, you’ll replace all language-dependent strings and formatting of data with code that takes into account country-specific output formats and rules. Java offers a solution for these cases: on one hand, you can define a language that then specifies rules according to which the Java API can automatically format data, and on the other hand, you can allow language-dependent parts to be swapped out to resource files.

### 16.5.1    Regional Languages via Locale Objects

In Java, <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> objects represent languages in geographic, political, or cultural regions. The language and the region must be separated because a region or a country doesn’t always clearly specify the language. For Canada, in the province of Quebec, the French edition is relevant, which, of course, differs from the English edition. Each of these language-specific properties can be encapsulated in a special object. These <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> objects are then passed to a <samp class="listingcharacter">Formatter</samp> that’s located behind <samp class="listingcharacter">String.format(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(...)</samp> or passed to a <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp>. These outputs are referred to as locale sensitive .

#### Building Locale Objects

<samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> objects are always created with the name of the language and optionally with the name of the country or a region and variant. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> class provides three ways to build the objects:

*   Using the <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> constructor (deprecated in Java 19)

*   Using the nested <samp class="listingcharacter">Builder</samp> class of <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> uses the builder pattern to build new <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> objects

*   Using the <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">forLanguageTag(...)</samp> and a string identifier

###### [eg]  Example

Country abbreviations are specified in the constructor of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> class, for example, for a language object for Great Britain or France. Consider the following examples:

```
Locale greatBritain = new Locale( "en", "GB" );
Locale french       = new Locale( "fr" );
```

In the second example, we don’t care about the country. We’re simply choosing French as the language, no matter what part of the world.

Languages are identified by 2-letter abbreviations from the ISO 639 code [[ 210 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn16_04) ( ISO Language Code ), and country names are 2-letter abbreviations described in ISO 3166 [[ 211 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn16_05) ( ISO Country Code ).

###### [eg]  Example

Three variants for building <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale.JAPANESE</samp> are found in the following example:

```
Locale loc1 = new Locale( "ja" );
Locale loc2 = new Locale.Builder().setLanguage( "ja" ).build();
Locale loc3 = Locale.forLanguageTag( "ja" );
final class java.util.
                    Locale
implements Cloneable, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale(String language)</samp>
    Creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> object for the <samp class="listingcharacter">language</samp> given by the ISO-693 standard. Invalid identifiers aren’t recognized.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale(String language, String country)</samp>
    Creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> object for a <samp class="listingcharacter">language</samp> according to ISO 693 and a <samp class="listingcharacter">country</samp> according to the ISO 3166 standard.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">Locale(String language, String country, String variant)</samp>
    Creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> object for a language, a country, and a variant. <samp class="listingcharacter">variant</samp> is a vendor-dependent specification like “WIN” or “MAC.”

The static <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale.getDefault()</samp> method returns the currently set language. For the running JVM, <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale.setDefault(Locale)</samp> can change the language.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> class has more methods; developers should study the Javadoc for the <samp class="listingcharacter">Builder</samp>, for <samp class="listingcharacter">forLanguageTag(...)</samp> and the new extensions and filter methods. [[ 212 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn16_06)

#### Constants for Some Languages

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> class has constants for commonly occurring languages, with an option for specifying countries. The constants for countries and languages include, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">CANADA</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">CHINA</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">FRENCH</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">GERMAN</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">ITALIAN</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">KOREAN</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">TAIWAN</samp> , <samp class="listingcharacter">UK</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">US</samp> . Behind an abbreviation like <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale.UK</samp>, nothing else exists except for the initialization with <samp class="listingcharacter">new Locale("en", "GB")</samp> .

#### Methods That Accept Instances of Locale

<samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> objects are actually not interesting as objects—they do have methods, but more exciting is its use as a type for the identification of a language. Dozens of methods in the Java library accept <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> objects and adjust their behaviors based on them. Examples include <samp class="listingcharacter">printf(Locale, ...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">format(Locale, ...)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">toLowerCase(Locale)</samp> .

###### [+]  Tip

If no variant of a format or parse method exists with a <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> object; the method usually doesn’t support language-dependent behavior. The same limitation applies to objects that don’t accept a <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> via a constructor or setter. <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.toString(...)</samp> is one such example, as is <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.parseDouble(...)</samp>. In internationalized applications, these methods will rarely be found. Also, string concatenation with, for example, a float isn’t permitted (because a <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> method is called internally), and using <samp class="listingcharacter">String.format(...)</samp> is definitely a better option.

#### Methods of Locale*

<samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> objects provide a number of methods that reveal the ISO-639 code of the country, for example.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example outputs the <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> information accessible for languages in selected countries. The objects <samp class="listingcharacter">System</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">out</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale.*</samp> are imported statically:

```
 out.println(GERMANY.getCountry());           // DE
out.println(GERMANY.getLanguage());          // de
out.println(GERMANY.getVariant());           //
out.println(GERMANY.getISO3Country());       // DEU
out.println(GERMANY.getISO3Language());      // deu
out.println(CANADA.getDisplayCountry());     // Canada
out.println(GERMANY.getDisplayLanguage());   // German
out.println(GERMANY.getDisplayName());       // German (Germany)
out.println(CANADA.getDisplayName());        // English (Canada)
out.println(GERMANY.getDisplayName(FRENCH)); // allemand (Allemagne)
out.println(CANADA.getDisplayName(FRENCH));  // anglais (Canada) 
```

**Listing 16.3**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/locale/GermanyLocal.java, main()

Static methods also exist for querying <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> objects:

```
final class java.util.
                    Locale
implements Cloneable, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Locale getDefault()</samp>
    Returns the language preset by the JVM, which defaults to the operating system.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Locale[] getAvailableLocales()</samp>
    Returns a list of all installed <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> objects. The field contains at least <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale.US</samp> and about 160 entries.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String[] getISOCountries()</samp>
    Returns an array of all 2-letter ISO-3166 country codes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Set<String> getISOCountries(Locale.IsoCountryCode type)</samp>
    Returns a set with all ISO-3166 country codes, where the <samp class="listingcharacter">IsoCountryCode</samp> list determines the following: <samp class="listingcharacter">PART1_ALPHA2</samp> returns the code of 2 letters, <samp class="listingcharacter">PART1_ALPHA3</samp> of 3 letters, <samp class="listingcharacter">PART3</samp> of 4 letters.

On the other hand, other methods provide abbreviations according to ISO standards:

```
final class java.util.
                    Locale
implements Cloneable, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String getCountry()</samp>
    Returns the country abbreviation according to the ISO-3166 2-letter code.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String getLanguage()</samp>
    Returns the abbreviation of the language in ISO-639 code.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String getISO3Country()</samp>
    Returns the ISO abbreviation of the country of these settings and throws a <samp class="listingcharacter">MissingResourceException</samp> if the ISO abbreviation isn’t available.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">String getISO3Language()</samp>
    Returns the ISO abbreviation of the language of these settings and throws a <samp class="listingcharacter">MissingResourceException</samp> if the ISO abbreviation isn’t available.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String getVariant()</samp>
    Returns the abbreviation of the variant or an empty string.

These methods provide abbreviations, but they aren’t intended for human-readable output. For various <samp class="listingcharacter">get*()</samp> methods, therefore, corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">getDisplay*()</samp> methods exist:

```
final class java.util.
                    Locale
implements Cloneable, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String getDisplayCountry(Locale inLocale)</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">final String getDisplayCountry()</samp>
    Returns the name of the country for screen outputs for a language or <samp class="listingcharacter">Loacale.getDefault()</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String getDisplayLanguage(Locale inLocale)</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">String getDisplayLanguage()</samp>
    Returns the name of the screen output language for a given <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale.getDefault()</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String getDisplayName(Locale inLocale)</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">final String getDisplayName()</samp>
    Returns the name of the settings for a language or <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale.getDefault()</samp> .
