The return of <samp class="listingcharacter">asList(...)</samp> isn’t a concrete class type like <samp class="listingcharacter">ArrayList</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">LinkedList</samp>, but something unknown, which <samp class="listingcharacter">asList(...)</samp> returns as <samp class="listingcharacter">List</samp> . This list is just another view of the array.

Now, however, some room for interpretation about what exactly is possible with the return remains. In addition, we might need to know whether the list allows fast point access ( <samp class="listingcharacter">RandomAccess</samp> implemented) or whether optional operations such as changes or even total reorganizations are conceivable. A look at the implementation reveals more. The result is an adapter that redirects list methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">get(index)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">set(index, element)</samp> directly to the array. Since array lengths are final, modification methods such as <samp class="listingcharacter">remove(...)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">add(...)</samp> result in an <samp class="listingcharacter">UnsupportedOperationException</samp> .

###### [»]  Note

If changes to the <samp class="listingcharacter">asList(...)</samp> return are desired, the result must be copied into a new data structure, in the following way:

```
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>( Arrays.asList( "A", "B" ) );
list.add( "C" );
```

#### List.of(…)

An alternative to <samp class="listingcharacter">asList(...)</samp> are various static overloaded <samp class="listingcharacter">of(...)</samp> methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">List</samp> interface. In these methods, too, any number of arguments can be passed. With <samp class="listingcharacter">asList(...)</samp>, however, the underlying array may change, so that the list changes automatically. With <samp class="listingcharacter">List.of(...)</samp>, the references passed will be copied. Also, no elements can be written back to the <samp class="listingcharacter">List.of(...)</samp> list, but they can be written to the <samp class="listingcharacter">asList(...)</samp> list.

### 18.1.7    ListIterator*

The <samp class="listingcharacter">ListIterator</samp> interface is an extension of <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator</samp>. This interface adds other methods so that elements can also be inserted at the current position. The location is also called the cursor. You should conceive of the location of the cursor as always between the elements; at the start, the cursor is located before the first element. The <samp class="listingcharacter">remove()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">set(e)</samp> methods aren’t associated with cursor positions; they operate on the last element that was provided by <samp class="listingcharacter">next()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">previous()</samp> .

```
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
Collections.addAll( list, "b", "c", "d" );

                ListIterator<String> it = list.listIterator();

it.add( "a" );                     // Add in front
System.out.println( list );        // [a, b, c, d]

                it.next();                         // Position before

                it.remove();                       // Delete element
System.out.println( list );        // [a, c, d]

                it.next();                         // Position before

                it.set( "C" );                     // Replace element
System.out.println( list );        // [a, C, d]

                it = list.listIterator( 1 );       // New iterator with start pos. 1

                it.add( "B" );                     // Add B
System.out.println( list );        // [a, B, C, d]

                it = list.listIterator( list.size() );

it.previous();                     // One place forward

                it.remove();                       // Delete last element
System.out.println( list );        // [a, B, C] 
```

**Listing 18.6**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/util/list/ListIteratorDemo.java, main()

###### [+]   Tip

As shown in the following example, <samp class="listingcharacter">ListIterator</samp> can also process the elements backwards:

```
List<String> list = new ArrayList<String>();
Collections.addAll( list, "1", "2", "3", "4" );
for ( ListIterator<String> it = list.listIterator( list.size() );
      it.hasPrevious(); )
  System.out.print( 
                it.previous() + " " ); // 4 3 2 1
interface 
                ListIterator<E>
extends Iterator<E> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean hasPrevious()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean hasNext()</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if a preceding or following element exists.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">E previous()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">E next()</samp>
    Returns the previous or next element of the list or issues <samp class="listingcharacter">NoSuchElementException</samp> if the element doesn’t exist. Then, the method sets the cursor position back or forward.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int previousIndex()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int nextIndex()</samp>
    Returns the index of the preceding or following element. If <samp class="listingcharacter">previousIndex()</samp> goes before the list, the method will return <samp class="listingcharacter">-1</samp>. If <samp class="listingcharacter">nextIndex()</samp> goes after the list, the method will return the length of the entire list.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void remove()</samp>
    Removes the last element returned by <samp class="listingcharacter">next()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">previous()</samp> (an optional operation).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void add(E o)</samp>
    Inserts a new object in front of the current position in the list (an optional operation).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void set(E o)</samp>
    Replaces the element returned last by <samp class="listingcharacter">next()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">previous()</samp> (an optional operation).

### 18.1.8    Understanding toArray(...) of Collection: Recognizing Traps

The <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray()</samp> method of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection</samp> interface returns an array of objects by definition. You must understand both the type of the entries and the type of the array itself.

###### [eg]  Example

The following application of <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray()</samp> transfers all the points of a collection into a new array:

```
 ArrayList<Point> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add( new Point(13, 43) );
list.add( new Point(9, 4) );
Object[] points = list
                    .toArray();
```

With <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray()</samp> , we get an array with references to <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> objects, but we can’t simply write <samp class="listingcharacter">points[1].x</samp> to access the <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> object variable because the <samp class="listingcharacter">points</samp> array has the declared element type <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>. The explicit type conversion is missing, and only <samp class="listingcharacter">((Point)points[1]).x</samp> is correct.

You might consider simply changing the type of the array from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[]</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">Point[]</samp> since are <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> instances in the array, after all, and then try the following incorrect code:

```
Point[] points = list.toArray();             // 

                 Compiler error 
```

The compiler reports the error “Type mismatch: cannot convert from Object[] to Point[]” because the return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray()</samp> is an <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[]</samp> and not a <samp class="listingcharacter">Point[]</samp>. Now, maybe we could fix this type problem with a typecasting to a <samp class="listingcharacter">Point[]</samp> , perhaps in the following way:

```
Point[] points = (Point[]) list.toArray();   // 

                 Problem at runtime 
```

While we no longer have a problem at compile time, at runtime, we’ll get the message “java.lang.ClassCastException: class [Ljava.lang.Object; cannot be cast to class [Ljava.awt.Point;” even if only <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> objects actually existed in the array.

Let’s examine this programming error. What we did wrong is simple: We confused the type of the array with the types of the array elements. In the following code, we can assign anything to an array of object references:

```
Object[] os = new Object[ 3 ];
os[0] = new Point();
os[1] = "Which seat can I take?";
os[2] = LocalDate.now(); 
```

Notice that the type of the array is <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[]</samp>, and the array elements are also of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>. Behind the keyword <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp>, which creates the array object, is the common supertype for allowed array elements. For <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[]</samp> arrays, the elements may be references for any objects. Clearly, an array can only hold object references that are compatible with the type for the array itself, that is, that refer to instances of the specified class or to copies of subclasses of that class. Consider the following example:

```
/* 1 */  Object[] os = new Point[ 3 ];
/* 2 */  os[0] = new Point();
/* 3 */  os[1] = LocalDate.now();              // 

                 ArrayStoreException 
/* 4 */  os[2] = "Which seat can I take?";     // 

                 ArrayStoreException 
```

Lines 3 and 4 are permitted by the compiler but lead to an <samp class="listingcharacter">ArrayStoreException</samp> at runtime .

Let’s return to the <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray()</samp> method. Because the data structure to be read might contain anything, the type of the elements must be <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>. We’ve just established that the element type of the array object returned as a result by the <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray()</samp> method must be at least as comprehensive. Since there’s no more general (more comprehensive) type than <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>, the type of the array is also <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[]</samp>.This rule must be true, even if the elements of a data structure have a more special type in individual cases. A general implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray()</samp> has no choice but to create the array of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[]</samp> and the elements of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> .

To summarize, we previously wrote <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[] os = new Point[3];</samp> and saw that <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[]</samp> is a base type of <samp class="listingcharacter">Point[]</samp>. This fact is possible because <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> is also a basic type of <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp>. The inheritance relationship of types carries over to the inheritance relationship of the arrays of those types, which is called covariance . However, if only an <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[]</samp> array is created—as by the parameterless <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray()</samp>—the result can’t be casted to the <samp class="listingcharacter">Point[]</samp> type, even if each element is a <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> .

#### The Solution to the Problem

Now, before we write a loop with a type conversion for every single array element or do a typecasting every time we access elements, we should consider the second <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray(T[])</samp> method, which accepts a predefined array for the result as a parameter. With this method, the result array is of a more special type than <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[]</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

The following example requests an array of type <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray()</samp> method:

```
List<Point> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add( new Point(13,43) );
list.add( new Point(9,4) );
Point[] points = (Point[]) list.
                        toArray( new Point[0] );
```

You’ll get list items copied into an array, and the type of the array is <samp class="listingcharacter">Point[]</samp>, matching the list items currently present. The parameter indicates the desired type, which in this case is the <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> array.

###### [+]  Performance Tip

A best practice is to specify the size of the result array, that is, as large as the list, for <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray(T[])</samp>. Then, <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray(T[])</samp> fills exactly this array and returns it instead of building a new array. Consider the following example:

```
ArrayList<Point> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add( new Point(13,43) );

                        list.add( new Point(9,4) );
Point[] points = list.toArray( 
                        new Point[list.size()] );
// alternative Point[] points = list.toArray( Point[]::new );
```

#### Creating Arrays with Reflection*

Internally, the <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray(T[])</samp> method uses reflection to dynamically create an array of the same type as the passed array. A method from <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.reflect.Array</samp> is used for this task:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">public static Object newInstance(Class<?> componentType, int length)</samp>

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, we’ll create a new array that has the same type as <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>. The new empty field should have space for <samp class="listingcharacter">len</samp> elements:

```
Object[] array = { new Point(-1, -1), new Point( 1, 1 ) };
int len = 100;
Object[] b = (Object[]) Array.newInstance(
                         array.getClass().getComponentType(), len);
```

The <samp class="listingcharacter">array.getClass()</samp> call returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object for the <samp class="listingcharacter">array</samp>, such as an object representing the <samp class="listingcharacter">Point[]</samp> type. With <samp class="listingcharacter">array.getClass().getComponentType()</samp>, you’ll get a <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object for the element type of the array (i.e., <samp class="listingcharacter">Point</samp> ).

So, we dynamically do what <samp class="listingcharacter">new TYP[len]</samp> does, where <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> must have the element type set at compile time. Since the return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">newInstance()</samp> is a general <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> , the conversion to a suitable array must finally take place.

If the passed array is large enough to store all the elements of the collection, <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray(T[])</samp> copies the elements from the collection into the array. Incidentally, <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray(new Object[0])</samp> is equivalent to calling <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray()</samp> .

### 18.1.9    Managing Primitive Elements in Data Structures

Each Collection API data structure, even if used generically, accepts only references. Primitive data types don’t accept the collections, which has the consequence that wrapper objects are necessary. (Via boxing, Java seems to insert primitive elements, but in reality, Java inserts wrapper objects.)

For instance, in the following code, two new <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> objects are created and then moved into the list:

```
 List<Double> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add( 
                1.1 );
list.add( 
                2.2 ); 
```

When written differently and more clearly, you can truly see what is really happening:

```
List<Double> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add( Double.valueOf(
                1.1) );
list.add( new Double(
                2.2) ); 
```

From the call of <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.valueOf(...)</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> usage can’t be read, but the method is implemented as <samp class="listingcharacter">Double valueOf(double d){ return</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">new Double(d)</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">; }</samp> .

#### Special Libraries

For performant applications and large amounts of primitive elements, using a class for the special data type makes sense. Instead of programming these special classes on their own, developers can use two implementations:

*   Eclipse Collections ([https://www.eclipse.org/collections/](https://www.eclipse.org/collections/)) include primitive collections and a comprehensive API.

*   fastutil ([https://fastutil.di.unimi.it/](https://fastutil.di.unimi.it/)) provides extensions with data structures for numerous primitive elements and high-performance input/output classes.

## 18.2    Sets

A set is an (initially) unordered collection of elements. Each element may occur only once. For sets, the Java library provides the interface <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.Set</samp> . Popular implementing classes include the following:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp>: For fast set implementation by hashing method (based on <samp class="listingcharacter">HashMap</samp> ).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> : Sets are implemented by balanced binary trees that allow sorting.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">LinkedHashSet</samp> : Fast set implementation while maintaining insertion order.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">EnumSet</samp> : A special set exclusively for enumerations.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">CopyOnWriteArraySet</samp> : For fast, thread-safe data structures, optimized for many read operations but few write operations.

### 18.2.1    A First Example of a Set

Our next example program analyzes a text and recognizes cities that were previously entered into a data structure. All cities that appear in the text are collected and subsequently output.

```
 package com.tutego.insel.util.set;

import java.text.BreakIterator;
import java.util.*;

public class WhereHaveYouBeen {
  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    // Build set with cities

                Set<String> allCities = new HashSet<>();
    allCities.add( "Seattle" );
    allCities.add( "Denver" );
    allCities.add( "Manila" );
    allCities.add( "Seoul" );
    allCities.add( "Siquijor" );

    // Build set for visited cities

                Set<String> visitedCities = new TreeSet<>();

    // Parse sentence and break it into words. All cities found
    // include in new data structure
    String sentence = "From Seattle I drive to Denver and fly to Manila.";
    BreakIterator iter = BreakIterator.getWordInstance();
    iter.setText( sentence );

    for ( int first = iter.first(), last = iter.next();
          last != BreakIterator.DONE;
          first = last, last = iter.next() ) {
      String word = sentence.substring( first, last );
      if ( 
                allCities.contains( word ) )

                visitedCities.add( word );
    }

    // Some statistics

    System.out.println( "Number of visited cities: " + visitedCities.size() );
    System.out.println( "Number of unvisited cities: " +
                        (
                allCities.size() - visitedCities.size()) );
    System.out.println( "Visited cities: " + String.join( ", ", visitedCities ) );

                Set<String> unvisitedCities = new TreeSet<>( allCities );
    unvisitedCities.removeAll( visitedCities );
    System.out.println( "Unvisited cities: " + String.join( ", ", unvisitedCitie

                s ) );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 18.7**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/util/set/WhereHaveYouBeen.java

A total of three sets occur in this program:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">allCities</samp> stores all possible cities. The choice falls on the <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp> type because the set doesn’t need to be sorted, concurrency is not an issue, and <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp> provides a good access time.

*   A <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet visitedCities</samp> memorizes the visited cities. This <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> is also fast but has the advantage of keeping the elements sorted, which will help our later output.

*   To determine all unvisited cities, the program calculates the difference set between all cities and visited cities. No method in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> interface does this directly—in fact, no operation in <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> has the return type <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection</samp>. So, you can only use a method like <samp class="listingcharacter">removeAll(...)</samp>, which removes the visited cities from the set of all cities to determine which cities haven’t been visited yet. But a “problem” with the <samp class="listingcharacter">removeAll(...)</samp> method is its destructive nature: The elements are deleted from the set. However, because the original set shouldn’t be changed, we’ll copy all cities to a cache ( <samp class="listingcharacter">unvisitedCities</samp> ) and delete elements from this cache, leaving the original set untouched.

###### [»]  Note

Regular expressions are an option for decomposing sentences and occur elsewhere in the book as well. However, the <samp class="listingcharacter">BreakIterator</samp> has an advantage in that it can correctly classify every single Unicode character.

### 18.2.2    Methods of the Set Interface

In addition to operations for requesting and inserting elements, a set class declares methods for intersecting and joining sets.

```
interface java.util.
                Set<E>
extends Collection<E> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean add(E o)</samp>
    Places <samp class="listingcharacter">o</samp> in the set if no <samp class="listingcharacter">equals</samp>-equals object exists in the set yet. Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> on successful insertion.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c)</samp>
    Inserts all elements of <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> into the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp>. If <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> is a different <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">addAll(...)</samp> stands for the set union. In essence, this method is similar to <samp class="listingcharacter">for (E e : c) add(e);</samp>. The return is <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the collection has changed in any way.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void clear()</samp>
    Deletes the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean contains(Object o)</samp>
    Determines if the element <samp class="listingcharacter">o</samp> is included in the set.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean containsAll(Collection<?> c)</samp>
    Determines if <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> a subset of <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <E> Set<E> copyOf (Collection<? extends E> coll)</samp>
    Creates an unmodifiable copy.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean isEmpty()</samp>
    Determines if the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> empty.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator<E> iterator()</samp>
    Returns an iterator for the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean remove(Object o)</samp>
    Deletes <samp class="listingcharacter">o</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> and returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the deletion was successful; otherwise, returns <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> if no <samp class="listingcharacter">equals</samp> -like object exists in the set.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean removeAll(Collection<?> c)</samp>
    Deletes all elements of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> and returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> on successful deletion.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean retainAll(Collection<?> c)</samp>
    The set retains all elements that are also contained in <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp>—in other words, all elements of the current set that aren’t also present in <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> are deleted. No change occurs to the data structure <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp>. The own set is then the intersection with <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp>, but <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> may contain many more elements.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int size()</samp>
    Returns the number of elements in the set.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[] toArray()</samp>
    First creates a new array to store all the elements of the set and then copies the elements into the array.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><T> T[] toArray(T[] a)</samp>
    If the passed array is large enough for all elements of the set, then all elements of the set are copied into the array, and <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> is returned. If the array is too small, a new array of type <samp class="listingcharacter">T</samp> is created, and all elements are copied from the set to the array and returned.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default <T> T[] toArray(IntFunction<T[]> generator)</samp>
    As documented in <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection</samp> .

In the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> interface, the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> methods originating from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> are specified with their functionalities related to sets in the API documentation.

In addition, several static methods for creating immutable sets are available:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <E> Set<E> copyOf(Collection<? extends E> coll)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <E> Set<E> of()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <E> Set<E> of(E... elements)</samp>

###### [»]  Note

Elements stored in a <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> must remain immutable. On one hand, they may not be retrievable after a change; on the other hand, elements may appear twice in the set in this way, which contradicts the philosophy of the interface.

#### Adding Another Element

If an element isn’t yet contained in a set, <samp class="listingcharacter">add(...)</samp> inserts the element and returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>. If already present, <samp class="listingcharacter">add(...)</samp> does nothing and returns <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp>. (This scenario is different for a <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> because in that case <samp class="listingcharacter">put(...)</samp> overrides the key.) Whether an element to be added matches an existing element already in the set is determined by the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method, in which case equivalence matters instead of identity.

```
Set<Point> set = new HashSet<>();
Point p1 = new Point(), p2 = new Point();
System.out.println( set.add(p1) );      // true
System.out.println( set.add(p1) );      // false
System.out.println( set.add(p2) );      // false
System.out.println( set.contains(p1) ); // true
System.out.println( set.contains(p2) ); // true 
```

### 18.2.3    HashSet

A <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.HashSet</samp> class manages elements in a fast hash-based data structure. As a result, elements are quickly sorted and easily found. If sorting the elements in the <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp> is necessary, elements must be copied into a <samp class="listingcharacter">List</samp> or a <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> and then sorted.

```
class java.util.
                HashSet<E>
extends AbstractSet<E>
implements Set<E>, Cloneable, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet()</samp>
    Creates an empty <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp> object.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet(Collection<? extends E> c)</samp>
    Creates a new unsorted <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp> from the collection <samp class="listingcharacter">c</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet(int initialCapacity)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet(int initialCapacity, float loadFactor)</samp>
    These two constructors are meant for optimization. <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp> is internally based on the <samp class="listingcharacter">HashMap</samp> .

### 18.2.4    TreeSet: The Sorted Set

The <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.TreeSet</samp> class also implements the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> interface like <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp> but follows a different implementation strategy. A <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> always manages the items sorted. [[ 221 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn18_03) If <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> saves a new element, <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> automatically inserts the element sorted into the data structure. This operation costs a little more time than a <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp>, but this kind of sorting is permanent. For this reason, outputting all elements in an orderly fashion later isn’t time consuming. However, searching for a single element is somewhat slower than in the <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp> . But the term “slower” must be put into perspective: The search is logarithmic in time and therefore not really “slow.” When inserting and deleting, a reorganization of the tree must be accepted for certain constellations, which worsens the insertion or deletion time. However, these costs also exist in re-hashing, but these costs can be avoided by using the appropriate starting size.

```
class java.util.
                TreeSet<E>
extends AbstractSet<E>
implements NavigableSet<E>, Cloneable, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet()</samp>
    Creates a new, empty <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet(Collection<? extends E> c)</samp>
    Creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> from the given <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet(Comparator<? super E> c)</samp>
    Creates an empty <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> with a given <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> that does the comparisons for sorting the internal data structure.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet(SortedSet<E> s)</samp>
    Creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> and takes over all elements of <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> and also the sorting of <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>. (No constructor is available with <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableSet</samp> .)

###### [eg]  Example

The following code tests whether a list of date values, each of which can occur only once in the list, is sorted in ascending order:

```
 List<Instant> dates = List.of( Instant.ofEpochMilli( 2L ),
                               Instant.ofEpochMilli( 3L ) );
boolean isSorted = new ArrayList<>( new TreeSet<>( dates ) ).equals( dates );
```

If the constructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> accepts another collection, the result is a sorted collection of all elements. This collection can in turn be passed into another constructor that accepts arbitrary <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection</samp> objects. Our example compares two <samp class="listingcharacter">List</samp> instances via <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> , where lists have an order. If the order after sorting matches the order before sorting, the list was already sorted.

Of course, better implementations can be conceived. For example, you could use an iterator to run the collection and see if the next element is always greater than or equal to.

#### Significance of Sorting

Due to internal sorted storage, two particularly important conditions should be kept in mind:

*   Comparing the elements must be possible. For example, if <samp class="listingcharacter">Player</samp> objects come into the <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp>, but <samp class="listingcharacter">Player</samp> doesn’t implement the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> interface, <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> throws an exception because <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> doesn’t know what order the players should be in.

*   The elements must be of the same type. How can a church object be compared with a vacuum cleaner object?

###### [eg]  Example

In this example, words should be considered the same even if they differ in capitalization or have whitespace at the beginning and end. The following code sorts strings into a set (case-insensitive) and ignores whether the word was preceded or followed by whitespace:

```
Comparator<String> comparator = 
  (s1, s2) -> String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER.compare( s1.trim(), s2.trim() );
Set<String> set = new TreeSet<>( comparator );
Collections.addAll( set, "xxx ", " 
                        XXX", "tang", " xXx", " QUEEN " );
System.out.println( set ); // [ QUEEN , tang, xxx ]
```

#### The equals(...) Method and the Comparison Methods

The <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method plays a major role in many data structures. The <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> is different because it uses an external <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> or the <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp> method for classification if the elements are <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp>. If the compare method returns 0, the elements are equal, and equal elements aren’t permitted in the set. <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> isn’t used in this case, although of course the <samp class="listingcharacter">equals</samp> implementation should return <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if <samp class="listingcharacter">compare(...)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(...)</samp> returns 0.

For example, let’s use the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> from our previous example for <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> objects, which makes case-insensitive comparisons and ignores whitespace. Then, according to <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> the strings “ <samp class="listingcharacter">xxx</samp>” and “ <samp class="listingcharacter">XXX</samp>” are certainly not equal, but our own <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> would indicate equivalence:

```
Comparator<String> comparator = 
  (s1, s2) -> String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER.compare( s1.trim(), s2.trim() );
Set<String> set = new TreeSet<>( comparator );
set.add( "xxx " );
set.add( "XXX" );
System.out.println( set );                        // [xxx ]
System.out.println( set.contains( "  XXX   " ) ); // true 
```

### 18.2.5    The Interfaces NavigableSet and SortedSet

<samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> implements the interface <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableSet</samp> and provides methods that return the next higher or next lower element for a given element. Thus, not only are the usual queries about set affiliation conceivable on sets, but also queries like “Give me the element that is greater than or equal to a given element.”

The following example queues up three <samp class="listingcharacter">LocalDate</samp> objects in a <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">LocalDate</samp> class implements <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable<LocalDate></samp> because these objects have a natural order. The methods <samp class="listingcharacter">lower(…)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">ceiling(…)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">floor(…)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">higher(…)</samp> select the requested object from the set.

```
NavigableSet<LocalDate> set = new TreeSet<>();
set.add( LocalDate.of( 2018, Month.MARCH, 10 ) );
set.add( LocalDate.of( 2018, Month.MARCH, 12 ) );
set.add( LocalDate.of( 2018, Month.MARCH, 14 ) );

LocalDate cal1 = set.
                lower( LocalDate.of( 2018, Month.MARCH, 12 ) );
System.out.printf( "%tF%n", cal1 );   // 2018-03-10

LocalDate cal2 = set.
                ceiling( LocalDate.of( 2018, Month.MARCH, 12 ) );
System.out.printf( "%tF%n", cal2 );   // 2018-03-12

LocalDate cal3 = set.
                floor( LocalDate.of( 2018, Month.MARCH, 12 ) );
System.out.printf( "%tF%n", cal3 );   // 2018-03-12

LocalDate cal4 = set.
                higher( LocalDate.of( 2018, Month.MARCH, 12 ) );
System.out.printf( "%tF%n", cal4 );   // 2018-03-14 
```

**Listing 18.9**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/util/set/SortedSetDemo.java

A method like <samp class="listingcharacter">tailSet(...)</samp> is useful especially for date objects because it can return all time points after a specified start date.

<samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> implements the <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableSet</samp> interface, which in turn extends <samp class="listingcharacter">SortedSet</samp>—a historical legacy. In total, <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableSet</samp> provides 15 operations, adding from <samp class="listingcharacter">SortedSet</samp> the methods <samp class="listingcharacter">headSet(…)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">tailSet(…)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">subSet(…)</samp> with overloaded version of methods that allow the bounds to be exclusive or inclusive.

```
interface java.util.
                NavigableSet<E>
extends SortedSet<E> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableSet<E> headSet(E toElement)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableSet<E> tailSet(E fromElement)</samp>
    Return a subset of elements that are genuinely smaller/larger than <samp class="listingcharacter">toElement/fromElement</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableSet<E> headSet(E toElement, boolean inclusive)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableSet<E> tailSet(E fromElement, boolean inclusive)</samp>
    Compared to the upper methods, additionally determine whether the output element may belong to the result set.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableSet<E> subSet(E fromElement, E toElement)</samp>
    Returns a subset in the desired range.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">E pollFirst()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">E pollLast()</samp>
    Retrieves and removes the first or last element. The return is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> if the <samp class="listingcharacter">set</samp> is empty.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">E higher(E e)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">E lower(E e)</samp>
    Returns the subsequent or preceding element in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> that’s genuinely greater or less than <samp class="listingcharacter">E</samp>, respectively; otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> is returned if no such element exists.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">E ceiling(E e)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">E floor(E e)</samp>
    Returns the subsequent or preceding element in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> that’s greater than or less than or equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">E</samp>; otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> is returned if no such element exists.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator<E> descendingIterator()</samp>
    Returns the elements in reverse order.

From the <samp class="listingcharacter">SortedSet</samp> interface, <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableSet</samp> basically inherits only three operations because <samp class="listingcharacter">subSet(…)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">headSet(…)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">tailSet(…)</samp> are redefined with covariant return type in <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableSet</samp> .

```
interface java.util.
                SortedSet<E>
extends Set<E> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">E first()</samp>
    Returns the smallest element in the list.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">E last()</samp>
    Returns the largest element.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator<? super E> comparator()</samp>
    Returns the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> associated with the set. The return can be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> if the objects can compare themselves via <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">SortedSet<E> subSet(E fromElement, E toElement)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">SortedSet<E> headSet(E toElement)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">SortedSet<E> tailSet(E fromElement)</samp>
    Returns subsets as live views.

Unlike <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp> iterator returns the elements sorted in ascending order. The two <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray(...)</samp> methods also benefit from this feature since they use the iterator to return a sorted array.

### 18.2.6    LinkedHashSet

A <samp class="listingcharacter">LinkedHashSet</samp> combines the order fidelity of a list with the high performance of set operations of <samp class="listingcharacter">HashSet</samp>. This class doesn’t provide list methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">first()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">get(int index)</samp> but is an implementation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> interface only, where the iterator returns the elements in the insertion order. Consider the following example:

```
 Set<Integer> set = new 
                LinkedHashSet<>(
  Arrays.asList( 9, 8, 7, 6, 9, 8 )
);

for ( Integer i : set )
  System.out.print( i + " " );      // 9 8 7 6

System.out.printf( "%n%s", set );   // [9, 8, 7, 6] 
```

**Listing 18.10**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/util/set/LinkedHashSetDemo.java, main()

Since a <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> can contain each element only once, as a result, you’ll get each element only once, but at the same time, the order of insertion isn’t lost. The iterator returns the elements according to the exact insertion order.

###### [eg]  Example

The fact that a <samp class="listingcharacter">LinkedHashSet</samp> is a set that contains elements only once but behaves like a list when inserted is useful for deleting duplicate elements from a list, as in the following example code:

```
 public static <T> List<T> removeDuplicate( List<T> list ) {
  return new ArrayList<>( new LinkedHashSet<>( list ) );
}
```

The result is a new list, and <samp class="listingcharacter">list</samp> itself isn’t modified. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">removeDuplicate( Arrays.asList( 1,2,1,3,1,2,4 ) )</samp> results in the list <samp class="listingcharacter">[1, 2, 3, 4]</samp> .

#### LinkedHashSet and Iterator

An iterator can be used to list each element of <samp class="listingcharacter">LinkedHashSet</samp> by order of insertion. The iterator of <samp class="listingcharacter">LinkedHashSet</samp> also supports the <samp class="listingcharacter">remove()</samp> method. You can use this method to delete the oldest entries and keep only the newest two elements in the following way:

```
LinkedHashSet<Integer> set = new LinkedHashSet<>();
set.addAll( Arrays.asList( 3, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4 ) );
System.out.println( set );  // [3, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4]
for ( Iterator<Integer> iter = set.iterator(); iter.hasNext(); ) {
  iter.next();
  if ( set.size() > 2 )
    iter.remove();
}
System.out.println( set );  // [5, 4] 
```

## 18.3    Associative Memory

An associative memory associates a key with a value. Java provides the general interface <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> for data structures of this kind with important operations like <samp class="listingcharacter">put(key, value)</samp> to create an association and <samp class="listingcharacter">get(key)</samp> to get an associated value.

### 18.3.1    The HashMap and TreeMap Classes and Static Map Methods

The Java library implements associative memory with a few classes, and we’ll focus our attention on two important classes first:

*   A quick implementation is the hashtable, which is implemented in Java by <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.HashMap</samp> . [[ 222 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn18_04) The key objects must be “hashable” (i.e., must implement <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> concretely). A special interface for the elements isn’t necessary.

*   In addition, the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.TreeMap</samp> class is somewhat slower in access but keeps all key objects always sorted. Elements are sorted into an internal binary tree. Keys can be put in order, which requires some preparation.

###### [eg]  Example

Let’s start with an associative memory to which we can add values, as in the following example:

```
 Map<String,String> twitterNames = new 
                    HashMap<>();
twitterNames
                    .put( "katyperry", "Katy Perry" );
twitterNames
                    .put( "taylorswift13", "Taylor Swift" );
twitterNames
                    .put( "Cristiano", "Cristiano Ronaldo" );
twitterNames
                    .put( "ddlovato", " Demi Lovato" );
twitterNames
                    .put( "KingJames", "LeBron James" );
```

The second <samp class="listingcharacter">HashMap</samp> is supposed to associate strings with numbers:

```
 Map<String,Number> num = new 
                    HashMap<>();
num
                    .put( "two", 2 );      // Boxing via Integer.valueOf(2)
num
                    .put( "three", 3.0 );  // Boxing via Double.valueOf(3.0) 
```

[![UML Class Diagram of the Map Interface](bilderklein/klein18_002.png)](img-f18.2.html)

**Figure 18.2**     UML Class Diagram of the Map Interface

While <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> methods are essential for the key objects of the hashed associative memory but aren’t necessary for tree-oriented methods—in these cases, only an order between the elements must be established, either with <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> .

An associative memory works fast only in one direction. For example, in the case of a phone directory, if a name has been associated with a number, the data structure can quickly answer the question of which phone number. The other direction takes much longer because no link exists in the other direction. The association is always one-sided. These classes are not prepared for reciprocal relationships.

#### The HashMap Class

The <samp class="listingcharacter">HashMap</samp> class is ideal for storing many elements unsorted and making them quickly available again via the keys. The internal hashing process is fast, but sorting the keys by a given criterion isn’t possible. An iterator will also provide an arbitrary order for us.

```
class java.util.
                    HashMap<K,V>
extends AbstractMap<K,V>
implements Map<K,V>, Cloneable, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">HashMap()</samp>
    Creates a new hash table.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">HashMap(Map<? extends K,? extends V> m)</samp>
    Creates a new hash table from another <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> .

#### The TreeMap Class and the SortedMap/NavigableMap Interface

A <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap</samp> implements the <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableMap</samp> interface , which in turn inherits from the <samp class="listingcharacter">SortedMap</samp> interface , which in turn extends <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp>. A <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableMap</samp> sorts the elements of an associative memory by key and provides access to the smallest or largest element.

*   Some methods from <samp class="listingcharacter">SortedMap</samp> like <samp class="listingcharacter">firstKey()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">lastKey()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">subMap(fromKey, toKey)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">tailMap(fromKey, toKey)</samp> form partial views of the associative memory.

*   Additional methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">NavigableMap</samp>: <samp class="listingcharacter">pollFirstEntry()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">pollLastEntry()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">descendingMap()</samp> are available.

To sort the keys in a <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap</samp>, the same applies as for the <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeSet</samp>: The elements must have a natural order, or an external <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> must specify the order.

```
class java.util.
                    TreeMap<K,V>
extends AbstractMap<K,V>
implements NavigableMap<K,V>, Cloneable, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap()</samp>
    Creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap</samp> that expects a natural order from its elements.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap(Comparator<? super K> comparator)</samp>
    Creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap</samp> with a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> so that the elements don’t need to have a natural order.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap(Map<? extends K,? extends V> m)</samp>
    Creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap</samp> with sorted elements from <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> , which must have a natural order.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap(SortedMap<K,? extends V> m)</samp>
    Creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap</samp> with sorted elements from <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> and also adopts the order from <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> .

To allow sorting, access is slightly slower than via <samp class="listingcharacter">HashMap</samp> , but hashing doesn’t permit elements to be sorted.

#### Static Map Methods

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> interface declares some static methods for building immutable <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> objects:

```
interface java.util.
                    Map<K, V> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> copyOf(Map<? extends K,? extends V> map)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> of()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1, K k2, V v2)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1, K k2, V v2, K k3, V v3)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1, K k2, V v2, K k3, V v3, K k4, V v4)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1, K k2, V v2, K k3, V v3, K k4, V v4, K k5, V v5)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1, K k2, V v2, K k3, V v3, K k4, V v4, K k5, V v5, K k6, V v6)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1, K k2, V v2, K k3, V v3, K k4, V v4, K k5, V v5, K k6, V v6, K k7, V v7)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1, K k2, V v2, K k3, V v3, K k4, V v4, K k5, V v5, K k6, V v6, K k7, V v7, K k8, V v8)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1, K k2, V v2, K k3, V v3, K k4, V v4, K k5, V v5, K k6, V v6, K k7, V v7, K k8, V v8, K k9, V v9)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> of(K k1, V v1, K k2, V v2, K k3, V v3, K k4, V v4, K k5, V v5, K k6, V v6, K k7, V v7, K k8, V v8, K k9, V v9, K k10, V v10)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map.Entry<K,V> entry(K k, V v)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <K, V> Map<K,V> ofEntries(Map.Entry<? extends K,? extends V>... entries)</samp>

### 18.3.2     Inserting and Querying the Associative Memory

We’ve said that the elements of the associative memory are pairs consisting of keys and their associated values. The retrieval of values is efficiently possible only via keys.

#### Inserting Data

To add key-value pairs, the <samp class="listingcharacter">put(key, value)</samp> method can be used. The first argument is the key, and the second argument is the value to be associated with the key.

###### [+]  Note Regarding null

In some implementations of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> interface, the key or value can be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. In these cases, we recommend looking at the Javadoc of the individual classes. For <samp class="listingcharacter">HashMap</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> is explicitly allowed as a key and a value; for <samp class="listingcharacter">ConcurrentHashMap</samp>, neither key nor value may be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> .

```
interface java.util.
                    Map<K, V> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">V put(K key, V value)</samp>
    Stores the key and the value in the associative memory. If already an entry exists in the associative memory for this key, the old value will be overridden, and the previous value for the key will be returned (unlike from <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp>, where the operation would do nothing in this case). If the key is new, <samp class="listingcharacter">put(...)</samp> will return <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. Thus, with <samp class="listingcharacter">put(key, value) == null</samp>, you can’t clearly determine if <samp class="listingcharacter">put(...)</samp> overrides a value and the old value was <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> or if there wasn’t any key-value pair in the associative memory in the first place.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void putAll(Map<? extends K,? extends V> m)</samp>
    Inserts all key-value pairs from <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> into the current <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> . This method also overrides existing keys under certain circumstances.

#### Traversing All Values

The default method <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach(java.util.function.BiConsumer)</samp> traverses all key-value pairs and calls a <samp class="listingcharacter">BiConsumer</samp> , which is a functional interface with a method that gets two parameters—key and value. The consumer can then evaluate the data.

###### [eg]  Example

The following code creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> with two pairs and outputs them:

```
Map<String, Integer> numbers = Map.of( "two", 2, "three", 3 );

                        BiConsumer<String, Integer> action =

                            (key, value) -> System.out.println( key + "=" + value );

                        numbers.forEach( action );
```

The result could be the following output:

```
three=3
two=2
```

or

```
two=2
three=3
```

The fact that the order is different might seem odd but is desired by design; <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> isn’t supposed to have a particular order. Incidentally, the same rule applies to <samp class="listingcharacter">Set</samp> .

#### Querying an Associated Value

To read an element again, <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> declares the <samp class="listingcharacter">get(key)</samp> operation. The argument identifies the object to be found via the key by picking out the object from the data structure that’s equal to the query object in the sense of <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>. If the object doesn’t exist, the return will be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. However, <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> can also be the value associated with a key since <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> is perfectly permitted as a value.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example queries the associative memory after “two”:

```
Map<String, Integer> numbers = Map.of( "two", 2, "three", 3 );
Integer number = numbers.get( "two" );
if ( number != null )
  System.out.println( number.intValue() );
```

The result will be a <samp class="listingcharacter">Number</samp> object. With generics, typecasting can be omitted if—as in our example— <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> objects were associated with the string. If the type hasn’t been specified previously, typecasting is necessary.

```
interface java.util.
                    Map<K,V> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">V get(Object key)</samp>
    Returns the object associated with the corresponding key. If no object matches, the method will return <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default V getOrDefault(Object key, V defaultValue)</samp>
    If an associated value exists for the <samp class="listingcharacter">key</samp>, that value will be returned; otherwise, the default <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> will be returned.

#### Does the Key Exist? Does the Value Exist?

With <samp class="listingcharacter">get(...)</samp>, the presence of a key can’t really be tested for sure because <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> can be associated with a key. This rule applies, for example, to <samp class="listingcharacter">HashMap</samp>, where <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> is permitted both as key and value. A safe alternative is provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter">containsKey(...)</samp> method, which returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if a key occurs in the table.

In contrast to <samp class="listingcharacter">get(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">containsKey(...)</samp>, which allow finding a value given a key, you can also search only for values without a certain key. However, this search operation is much slower because all values must be traversed. The class provides <samp class="listingcharacter">containsValue(...)</samp> for this purpose. We can also get all associated values from the <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> without the keys.

```
interface java.util.
                    Map<K,V> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean containsKey(Object key)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the key occurs in the associative memory. <samp class="listingcharacter">HashMap</samp> performs the comparison for equivalence with <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>. Accordingly, the object to be compared should suitably override this method from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> must be consistent with each other. The equivalence of two objects under <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> must also follow the equality of <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> in each case.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean containsValue(Object value)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the associative memory contains one or more values that match the contents of the <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp> object (i.e., via <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> ).

## 18.4    The Stream API

Together with lambda expressions on the language side, an entire new library was implemented in Java 8 that makes processing datasets easy called the Stream API . At the core of the Stream API are operations to filter, map, and reduce the data in collections.

### 18.4.1    Declarative Programming

The Stream API is used in a functional style, and programs can thus be quite compact. The individual methods of the Stream API are all presented in detail in this section, each shown in the following example:

```
Object[] words = { " ", '3', null, "2", 1, "" };
Arrays.stream( words )              // Creates new stream
      .filter( Objects::nonNull )   // Leave non-null references in the stream
      .map( Objects::toString )     // Convert objects to strings
      .map( String::trim )          // Truncate whitespace
      .filter( s -> ! s.isEmpty() ) // Leave non-empty elements in the stream
      .map( Integer::parseInt )     // Convert strings to integers
      .sorted()                     // Sort the integers
      .forEach( System.out::println );  // 1 2 3 
```

While the classes from the Collection API implement optimal storage forms for data, the task of the Stream API is to conveniently query and aggregate the data. The Stream API emphasizes the what, not the how . Traversals and iterations don’t occur in the code; instead, the Fluent API declaratively describes what the result should look like. The library ultimately implements the how. For example, an implementation can decide whether processing is sequential or parallel, whether the order is important, whether all data must be cached for sorting purposes, and so on.

[![The Pipeline Principle for Streams from the Previous Example](bilderklein/klein18_003.png)](img-f18.3.html)

**Figure 18.3**     The Pipeline Principle for Streams from the Previous Example

### 18.4.2    Internal versus External Iteration

The first thing you notice about the Stream API is that the classic loop is missing. Usually, you would use loops to run through data and make queries on the elements. Traditional loops are always sequential and run from element to element, from beginning to end. The same rule is true for an iterator. The Stream API takes a different approach. With its help, the external iteration (controlled by loops from the developer) can be replaced by an internal iteration (the Stream API fetches data). For example, when <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach(...)</samp> requests data, the data source is tapped and the data retrieved, but not before.

One advantage is that we specify which data structure should be run through, but how this task is done internally can be determined and optimized by the implementation itself. If you write the loop yourself, the processing always runs element by element, while an internal iteration can also parallelize on its own and have partial problems computed by multiple execution units.

###### [»]  Note

Appended to various collections is a <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach(...)</samp> method that runs over all elements and calls a method on a passed consumer. However, the classic <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop (or even the extended <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop) isn’t now obsolete. Besides being easy to write and debug, the usual loop still has some advantages. <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach(...)</samp> usually gets the executable code via a lambda expression, which has its limitations. For example, a lambda expression may not describe local variables (all local variables addressed by the lambda expression are effectively final) and may not throw checked exceptions. Inside a loop, neither is an issue. Incidentally, a <samp class="listingcharacter">break</samp> can be used for loop terminations, which doesn’t exist in lambda expressions either ( <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> in lambda corresponds to <samp class="listingcharacter">continue</samp> ).

### 18.4.3     What Is a Stream?

A stream is a sequence of data (but not a data source per se) that stores data like a data structure. The data from the stream is processed through a chain of the following downstream processing steps:

*   Filter

*   Map

*   Reduce

Processing along a chain is referred to as a pipeline and consists of three components:

*   The pipeline starts with a data source, such as an array, a data structure, or a generator.

*   Various processing steps follow, such as filtering (elements disappear from the stream) or mapping (a data type can also be converted into another data type). These changes along the way are called intermediate operations . The result of an intermediate operation is again a stream.

*   At the end, the result is collected, and the result is no longer a stream. For example, a reduction would be the formation of a maximum or the concatenation of strings.

The actual data structure isn’t changed; rather, at the end of the intermediate operations, a terminal operation asks for the result. An example terminal operation is <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach(...)</samp> , which is located at the end of the chain and for which the stream stops.

Many terminal operations reduce the passing data to a value, unlike <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach(...)</samp>, for example. This reduction occurs in methods for simply counting elements or for calculating totals and are called reducing operations . In the API, ready-made methods are available for standard reductions—for instance, calculating a total, maximum, or average—but general reductions are possible via your own functions, for example, calculating a product instead of the total.

#### Lazy Love

All intermediary operations are “lazy” because they postpone computations until they are needed. As shown in the first example, when the elements are taken from the array, they are passed to the next processing step in order. If the filter removes elements from the stream, they are gone and don’t need to be considered in a later step. It is therefore not the case that the data physically exists multiple times in a data structure with all elements, for example.

In contrast to continuing operations, in terminal operations, a result must be present: These operations are “eager.” Basically, everything is deferred until a value is needed, that is, until a terminal operation really wants to access the result.

#### State: Yes or No?

Intermediary operations may or may not have states. A filter operation, for example, has no state because, to accomplish its task, the program must look only at the current element, not at preceding ones. A sort operation, on the other hand, has a state: It “wants” all other elements to be saved because only knowing the current element isn’t sufficient for sorting; knowledge of all preceding ones is needed too.

## 18.5    Creating a Stream

The <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.stream</samp> package declares various types related to streams. At the center is a generically declared <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> interface for object streams. A copy is always generated from a data source. Numerous stream generators are available.

| Type | Method | Return |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection<E></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">stream()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<E></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">stream(T[] array)</samp> (static) | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">stream(T[] array, int start, int end)</samp> (static) | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">empty()</samp> (static) | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">of(T… values)</samp> (static) | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">of(T value)</samp> (static) | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">generate(Supplier<T> s)</samp> (static) | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">iterate(T seed,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">UnaryOperator<T> f)</samp> (static) | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">iterate(T seed, Predicate<? super T> hasNext, UnaryOperator<T> next)</samp> (static) | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">ofNullable(T t)</samp> (static) | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Optional<T></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">tokens()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<String></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">lines()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<String></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Files</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">lines(Path path)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<String></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">lines(Path path, Charset cs)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<String></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">list(Path dir)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<Path></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">walk(Path start, FileVisitOption… options)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<Path></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">walk(Path start, int maxDepth, FileVisitOption… options)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<Path></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">find(Path start, int maxDepth, BiPredicate<Path,BasicFileAttributes> matcher, FileVisitOption… options)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<Path></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">BufferedReader</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">lines()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<String></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Pattern</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">splitAsStream(CharSequence input)</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<String></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ZipFile</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">stream()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<? extends ZipEntry></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">JarFile</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">stream()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<JarEntry></samp> |
|  | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<JarEntry></samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">versionedStream()</samp> |

**Table 18.1**     Methods That Provide Stream Instances

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream.empty()</samp> method returns a stream without elements, as expected.

### 18.5.1    Stream.of*(…)

<samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> has some factory methods for new streams, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">of(...)</samp>. Several instance methods of other classes may also provide streams. The <samp class="listingcharacter">of(...)</samp> methods are implemented as static interface methods of <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">of(T... values)</samp> is just a facade for <samp class="listingcharacter">Arrays.stream(values)</samp>. The method <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> Stream<T> ofNullable(T t)</samp>, if <samp class="listingcharacter">t == null</samp>, returns an empty stream, and if <samp class="listingcharacter">t != null</samp>, it returns a stream with exactly the element <samp class="listingcharacter">t</samp> . This method is useful for partial streams that are to be integrated.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example produces a stream from the given integers, removes their signs, sorts the result, and then outputs the result:

```
 Stream.of( -4, 1, -2, 3 )
      .map( Math::abs )
      .sorted()
      .forEach( System.out::println ); // 1 2 3 4
```

### 18.5.2     Stream.generate(…)

<samp class="listingcharacter">generate(...)</samp> produces elements from a <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier</samp> ; the stream is infinite.

###### [eg]  Examples

The following example creates a stream of Fibonacci numbers [[ 223 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn18_05) :

```
class FibSupplier implements Supplier<BigInteger> {
  private final Queue<BigInteger> fibs =
      new LinkedList<>( Arrays.asList( BigInteger.ZERO, BigInteger.ONE ) );
  @Override public BigInteger get() {
    fibs.offer( fibs.remove().add( fibs.peek() ) );
    return fibs.peek();
  }
};
Stream.
                    generate( new FibSupplier() )
      .limit( 1000 ).forEach( System.out::println );
```

This implementation doesn’t use a lambda expression but instead an old-fashioned class implementation since we need to remember the last two elements to determine the next element in the Fibonacci sequences. Thus, the implementation stores a <samp class="listingcharacter">LinkedList</samp> that’s used as a <samp class="listingcharacter">Queue</samp>. When requesting a new Fibonacci number, we delete the first element from the queue (the head element) so that the second one slips in, and add the value to the remembered head element, resulting in the new Fibonacci number. We append the new element to the end in the second step and return it. Parallel access isn’t allowed. The stream is initially infinitely large but is then limited to 1,000 elements via <samp class="listingcharacter">limit(...)</samp> .

### 18.5.3    Stream.iterate(…)

The two static <samp class="listingcharacter">iterate(...)</samp> methods generate a stream from a start value and a function that produces the next element. In <samp class="listingcharacter">iterate(T seed, UnaryOperator<T> f)</samp> the stream is infinite; in the second method <samp class="listingcharacter">iterate(..., Predicate<? super T> hasNext, ...)</samp>, a satisfied predicate terminates the stream and is reminiscent of a classic <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> loop. Termination via a predicate is quite flexible because, with the first <samp class="listingcharacter">iterate(...)</samp> method, the stream is infinite and thus is often followed by <samp class="listingcharacter">limit(...)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">takeWhile(</samp> ...) to limit the elements.

###### [eg]  Example 1

The following example produces several permutations of a string:

```
UnaryOperator<String> shuffleOp = s -> {
  char[] chars = s.toCharArray();
  for ( int index = chars.length - 1; index > 0; index-- ) {

                        int rndIndex = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt( index + 1 );
    if ( index == rndIndex ) continue;
    char c = chars[ rndIndex ];
    chars[ rndIndex ] = chars[ index ];
    chars[ index ] = c;
  }
  return new String( chars );
};
String text = "He's a very naughty boy! Now, go away!";
Stream.
                    iterate( text, shuffleOp ).limit( 10 ).forEach( System.out::println );
```

The random integers don’t come from a <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> object this time, but from <samp class="listingcharacter">ThreadLocalRandom</samp> . This special class is connected to the current thread and can also provide single random numbers or a stream. With concurrency, this variant provides better performance.

###### [eg]  Example 2

The following example creates an infinite stream of <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> objects starting at 10,000,000 and continues in units until, with high probability, a prime number appears. Then, the stream ends at that point:

```
Predicate<BigInteger> isNotPrime = i -> ! i.isProbablePrime( 10 );
UnaryOperator<BigInteger> incBigInt = i -> i.add( BigInteger.ONE );
Stream.
                    iterate( BigInteger.valueOf( 10_000_000 ), isNotPrime, incBigInt )
      .forEach( System.out::println );
```

### 18.5.4    Parallel or Sequential Streams

A stream can be parallel or sequential. In other words, threads can perform certain operations concurrently, such as searching for an item. <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> via <samp class="listingcharacter">isParallel()</samp> if a stream performs operations concurrently.

All <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection</samp> data structures can provide a potentially concurrent stream using the <samp class="listingcharacter">parallelStream()</samp> method.

| Type | Method | Return |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">parallelStream()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<E></samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">stream()</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<E></samp> |

**Table 18.2**     Querying Parallel and Non-Parallel Streams from Each Collection

Any parallel stream can be converted to a sequential stream using the <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> method, <samp class="listingcharacter">sequential()</samp>. Parallel streams use the fork-and-join framework internally, but not every stream should automatically be parallel. (Parallelization doesn’t necessarily lead to performance improvements.) For example, if parallelization isn’t possible, using threads serves little purpose.

## 18.6    Terminal Operations

As mentioned earlier in [Section 18.4.3](#18_004.html_h18.4.3), operations can be intermediary or terminal. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> interface provides a total of 18 terminal operations, and the returns of these methods might be something like <samp class="listingcharacter">void</samp> or an array. For intermediary operations, returns are all new <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> instances. Let’s look at the available terminal operations one by one.

###### [»]  Note

Once a stream has been consumed, it can’t be reused!

### 18.6.1    Number of Elements

Perhaps the simplest terminal operation is <samp class="listingcharacter">count()</samp>. This operation provides a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> with the number of elements that exist in the stream.

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T,Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">long count()</samp>

###### [eg]  Example

The following example determines how many elements an array of references has, apart from <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> :

```
Object[] array = { null, 1, null, 2, 3 };
long size = Stream.of( array )
                  .filter( Objects::nonNull ).
                    count();
System.out.println( size );  // 3
```

### 18.6.2    And Now All: forEach*(…)

The Stream API provides two <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach*(...)</samp> methods to run the results:

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T,Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">void forEach(Consumer<? super T> action)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void forEachOrdered(Consumer<? super T> action)</samp>
