A code block of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer</samp> type is always passed. The functional interface <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer</samp> has one parameter, and <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach*(...)</samp> passes element by element to the <samp class="listingcharacter">Consumer</samp> as it runs.

Running with <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach(...)</samp> is an implementation detail. The order isn’t necessarily deterministic, which is especially noticeable in parallel streams. <samp class="listingcharacter">forEachOrdered(...)</samp> behaves differently, respecting the order of the stream source even if the stream is processed in parallel in between. However, sometimes, the stream framework doesn’t use internal parallelization when <samp class="listingcharacter">forEachOrdered(...)</samp> queries the elements.

###### [eg]  Example

In the first case, the output of the values is unordered (for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">rfAni</samp>); in the second case, ordered ( <samp class="listingcharacter">Afrin</samp> ):

```
"Afrin".chars().parallel().
                    forEach( c -> System.out.print( (char) c ) );
System.out.println();
"Afrin".chars().parallel().
                    forEachOrdered(  c -> System.out.print( (char) c ) );
```

### 18.6.3    Getting Individual Elements from the Stream

If the stream produces multiple data points in order, <samp class="listingcharacter">findFirst()</samp> returns the first element in the stream, whereas <samp class="listingcharacter">findAny()</samp> can return any element from the stream. The latter method is especially interesting for parallel operations, although which element is returned is completely open. Both methods have an advantage in that they are abbreviating operations and thus save you some work.

Since a stream of elements can be empty, the return of the following methods is always an <samp class="listingcharacter">Optional</samp> :

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T,Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Optional<T> findFirst()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Optional<T> findAny()</samp>

###### [eg]  Example

Example for both <samp class="listingcharacter">find*(…)</samp> -methods:

```
Consumer<Character> print = System.out::println;
List<Character> chars = List.of( '1', 'a', '2', 'b', '3', 'c' );

                    chars.parallelStream().findFirst().ifPresent( print ); // 1
chars.parallelStream().findAny().ifPresent( print );   // b
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">findFirst()</samp> always returns the first element <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp>, but <samp class="listingcharacter">findAny()</samp> could return any. In the output that result could be <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> , for example.

If other stateful operations are in between, an optimization with <samp class="listingcharacter">findAny()</samp> is sometimes invalid. So, <samp class="listingcharacter">stream.sorted().findAny()</samp> won’t be able to bypass sorting.

### 18.6.4    Existence Tests with Predicates

Three methods determine whether the elements of a stream fulfill a condition:

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T, Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean anyMatch(Predicate<? super T> predicate)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean allMatch(Predicate<? super T> predicate)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean noneMatch(Predicate<? super T> predicate)</samp>

The condition is always formulated as a <samp class="listingcharacter">Predicate</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

For a stream with two strings, the following code tests whether either all, any, or none of the elements are empty:

```
System.out.println( Stream.of("", "").
                    allMatch( String::isEmpty ) );   // true
System.out.println( Stream.of("", "a").
                    anyMatch( String::isEmpty ) );  // true
System.out.println( Stream.of("", "a").
                    noneMatch( String::isEmpty ) ); // false
```

### 18.6.5    Reducing a Stream to Its Smallest or Largest Element

A stream can consist of any number of elements, which can be reduced to one value by means of reduction functions. A well-known example is the <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.max(a, b)</samp> method, which maps two values to the maximum. These maximum/minimum methods also exist in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> :

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T, Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Optional<T> min(Comparator<? super T> comparator)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Optional<T> max(Comparator<? super T> comparator)</samp>

Note that a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> must always be passed, and the methods never draw on the natural order. Helpful in this regard is a <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp> utility method that returns a natural <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparator</samp>. The methods return an <samp class="listingcharacter">Optional.empty()</samp> if the stream is empty.

###### [eg]  Example

What’s the largest number in the stream?

```
System.out.println( Stream.of( 9, 3, 4, 11 ).max( Comparator.naturalOrder() ). 
get() );
```

Determining the minimum and maximum are just two examples of reduction. In general, each pair of values can be reduced to one value, for instance, with a minimum function.

| Stream (4, 2, 3, 1) | Function Application | Result (Minimum) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | - | 4 |
| 2 | min (4, 2) | 2 |
| 3 | min (2, 3) | 2 |
| 1 | min (2, 1) | 1 |

**Table 18.3**     Minimum Calculation for the Stream via Reduction

In the first case, no function is applied, and the stream is not reduced. The individual element thus remains present.

### 18.6.6    Reducing a Stream with Its Own Functions

Java uses the functional interfaces <samp class="listingcharacter">BiFunction<T,U,R></samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">BinaryOperator<T></samp> for reductions. ( <samp class="listingcharacter">BinaryOperator<T></samp> is a <samp class="listingcharacter">BiFunction<T,T,T></samp> by inheritance.)

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> type declares three <samp class="listingcharacter">reduce(...)</samp> methods that use these functional interfaces. Note that this reduction function is associative, that is, f(a, f(b, c)) = f(f(a, b), c ) holds because arbitrary pairs can be formed and reduced, especially in concurrent processing.

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T,Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Optional<T> reduce(BinaryOperator<T> accumulator)</samp>
    Gradually reduces all pairs of values to one value using the <samp class="listingcharacter">accumulator</samp>. If the <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> is empty, the <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">Optional.empty()</samp> method returns. If only one element exists, that element forms the return.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">T reduce(T identity, BinaryOperator<T> accumulator)</samp>
    Reduces the values, reducing the first element with <samp class="listingcharacter">identity</samp> over the <samp class="listingcharacter">accumulator</samp>. If the stream is empty, <samp class="listingcharacter">identity</samp> forms the return.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><U> U reduce(U identity, BiFunction<U,? super T,U> accumulator, BinaryOperator<U> combiner)</samp>
    The first two methods always return the element type <samp class="listingcharacter">T</samp> of the stream as the result type. With this method, the result type is not <samp class="listingcharacter">T</samp>, but <samp class="listingcharacter">U</samp>, since the <samp class="listingcharacter">accumulator</samp> maps the types <samp class="listingcharacter">(U, T)</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">U</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">combiner</samp> is only necessary if two results are merged in parallel processing; otherwise, the <samp class="listingcharacter">combiner</samp> is superfluous. However, because the value must not be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> ; unfortunately, you must pass something, even if that value is unnecessary in later processing. The combiner is always invoked after the function.

###### [eg]  Example

The following code tries to determine the largest element in a stream of positive numbers:

```
System.out.println( Stream.of( 9, 3, 4, 11 ).reduce( 0, Math::max ) );  // 11
```

Unlike the <samp class="listingcharacter">max(...)</samp> method of <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">reduce(...)</samp> directly returns an <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> and not an <samp class="listingcharacter">Optional</samp> because if <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> is empty, <samp class="listingcharacter">0</samp> (the identity, here the neutral element) will be returned. This result is problematic because 0 is not the largest element of an empty stream.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example reduces a stream of <samp class="listingcharacter">Dimension</samp> objects to the sum of their areas:

```
Dimension[] dims = { new Dimension( 10, 10 ), new Dimension( 100, 100 ) };
BiFunction<Integer, Dimension, Integer> accumulator =
    (area, dim) -> area + dim.height * dim.width;
BinaryOperator<Integer> combiner = Integer::sum;
System.out.println(
  Arrays.stream( dims ).
                    reduce( 0, accumulator, combiner )
); // 10100
```

The result of a reduction is always a new value, where “value” can of course be anything: a number, a string, a date, and so on.

### 18.6.7     Writing Results to a Container, Part 1: collect(...)

While the <samp class="listingcharacter">reduce(...)</samp> methods always produce new values in each processing step due to the accumulator, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">collect(...)</samp> can work somewhat differently. Simply put, <samp class="listingcharacter">collect(...)</samp> allows you to put data from a stream into a container (a data structure or even a string) and return that container.

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T,Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><R> R collect(Supplier<R> resultFactory, BiConsumer<R,? super T> accumulator,</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">BiConsumer<R,R> combiner)</samp>
    Collects the elements in a container. These three parameters all have different tasks:

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter">resultFactory</samp>: The <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier</samp> sets up the container. This value is also the return type.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter">Accumulator</samp>: The <samp class="listingcharacter">BiConsumer</samp> gets two arguments (the container and the element) and then must add the element to the container.

    *   <samp class="listingcharacter">combiner</samp> : The container is only necessary for parallel processing and is responsible for merging two containers.

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, four numbers of a stream should end up in the <samp class="listingcharacter">LinkedHashSet</samp> :

```
LinkedHashSet<Integer> set = Stream.of( 2, 3, 1, 4 )
          .collect(LinkedHashSet::new, LinkedHashSet::add, LinkedHashSet::addAll);
System.out.println( set );  // [2, 3, 1, 4]
```

For the general initialization of a <samp class="listingcharacter">LinkedHashSet</samp>, we still have a bit too much code. An easier approach is to add the elements with <samp class="listingcharacter">Collection.addAll(...)</samp> .

As with <samp class="listingcharacter">reduce(...)</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">collect(...)</samp> method gets each element, but the latter method doesn’t combine that element into a combination but set the elements usually in a container. For this reason, the used types aren’t <samp class="listingcharacter">BinaryOperator</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">BiFunction</samp> (get something and return something) but <samp class="listingcharacter">BiConsumer</samp> (get something but return nothing). The condition is thus located in the container and not in the intermediate processing steps.

###### [eg]  Example

A separate class makes this state keeping necessary, for example, when a stream of integers is queried for how many numbers were positive, negative, or zero. You could thus write the following collector:

```
 class NegZeroPosCollector {
  public long neg, zero, pos;
  public void accept( int i ) {
    if ( i > 0 ) pos++; else if ( i < 0 ) neg++; else zero++;
  }

  public void combine( NegZeroPosCollector other ) {
    neg += other.neg; zero += other.zero; pos += other.pos;
  }
}
```

During usage, the collector must be built, and the accumulator and combiner must be specified in the following way:

```
 NegZeroPosCollector col = Stream.of( 1, -2, 4, 0, 4 )
                                .collect( NegZeroPosCollector::new,
                                          NegZeroPosCollector::accept,
                                          NegZeroPosCollector::combine );
System.out.printf( "-:%d, 0:%d, +:%d", col.neg, col.zero, col.pos );  
// -:1, 0:1, +:3
```

### 18.6.8    Writing Results to a Container, Part 2: Collector and Collectors

Two variants of the <samp class="listingcharacter">collect(...)</samp> method exist, and the second variant is defined in the following way:

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T,Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><R> R collect(Collector<? super T,R> collector)</samp>

A <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector</samp> combines supplier, accumulator, and combiner. The static <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector.of(...)</samp> method builds a <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector</samp>, which you can also pass to <samp class="listingcharacter">collect(Collector)</samp> . Returning to our earlier example, you could write the following identical code:

```
 .collect( 
                Collector.of( LinkedHashSet::new,
                         LinkedHashSet::add, LinkedHashSet::addAll) ); 
```

The advantage of using <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector</samp> is that it combines three objects (actually, also a fourth one, <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector.Characteristics</samp>). This interface declares two static <samp class="listingcharacter">of(...)</samp> methods, as well as other methods, each of which queries the functions from the <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector</samp>. Some relevant methods include the <samp class="listingcharacter">accumulator()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">characteristics()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">combiner()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">finisher()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">supplier()</samp> methods.

<samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">Collector.Characteristics</samp> is an enumeration type with three elements ( <samp class="listingcharacter">CONCURRENT</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">IDENTITY_FINISH</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">UNORDERED</samp>) that describe the properties of a <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector</samp> .

#### The Collectors Utility Class

For standard cases, you won’t need to assemble a <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector.of(...)</samp>. Instead, you can use a utility class, <samp class="listingcharacter">Collectors</samp>, with almost 40 static methods, each of which returns <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector</samp> instances. These methods can be roughly grouped in the following way:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">toSet()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">toList()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">to*Map(...)</samp> , etc. for collections

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">toUnmodifiable*()</samp> for unmodifiable collections where elements can’t be added, deleted, or replaced.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">groupingBy*(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">partitioningBy(...)</samp> for creating groups

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">averagingLong(...)</samp> , among others, for simple returns

*   String <samp class="listingcharacter">Collectors</samp> like <samp class="listingcharacter">joining(...)</samp> , which concatenate strings in a stream

###### [eg]  Example

The following example combines several strings in a stream to create a single string:

```
String s = Stream.of( "192", "0", "0", "1" )
                 .collect( 
                        Collectors.joining("."
                        ) );
System.out.println( s );  // 192.0.0.1
```

The following example builds a <samp class="listingcharacter">set<string></samp> with two start values:

```
Set<String> set = Stream.of( "a", "b" ).collect( 
                        Collectors.toSet() );
```

The following example builds a <samp class="listingcharacter">Map<Integer, String></samp> consisting of two key-value pairs:

```
Map<Integer,String> map =
  Stream.of( "1=one", "2=two" )
        .collect( Collectors.toMap( k -> Integer.parseInt(k.split("=")[0]),
                                    v -> v.split("=")[1] ) );
final class java.util.stream.
                    Collectors 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> Collector<T,?,List<T>> toList()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T> Collector<T,?,Set<T>> toSet()</samp>

We recommend closely studying the other methods in the Javadoc.

###### [»]  Note

A <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector</samp> is the only reasonable means to transfer stream elements into a container. Developers should avoid the side effects of any intermediary or terminal operations for two reasons: First, you would lose the advantage of functional programming (where operations have no side effects), and second, chaos could break out from the parallel processing of non-synchronized data structures. So, no alternative to the charming <samp class="listingcharacter">Collectors.joining(".")</samp> can be written in the following way:

```
StringBuilder 
                        res = new StringBuilder();
Stream.of( "192", "0", "0", "1" )
      .forEach( s ->

                        res.append( 
                        res.length() == 0 ? "" : "." ).append( s ) );
System.out.print( 
                        res );
```

If a lambda expression requires write access to external variables, alarm bells should ring. Incidentally, the same rule applies to reductions. Although basically <samp class="listingcharacter">forEach(...)</samp> can write anything in a, for example, thread-safe atomic data type, a call to <samp class="listingcharacter">reduce(...)</samp> is very much preferred because this the functional style of programing.

###### [+]  Tip

Since data of a stream is often written to a list at the end, the default method <samp class="listingcharacter">toList()</samp> can be used directly on the <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> type. Even though you might imagine an implementation using a <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector</samp> , the OpenJDK implementation is different, as shown in the following example:

```
default List<T> toList() {
  return (List<T>) Collections.unmodifiableList(
      new ArrayList<>( Arrays.asList( this.toArray() ) )
  );
}
```

### 18.6.9    Writing Results to a Container, Part 3: Groupings

Objects can often be divided into groups by the fact that referenced subobjects determine a category. Since this concept sounds terribly abstract, let’s consider a few examples:

*   Accounts have an account type, and we want to search for a listing of all accounts by account type. So, n accounts associated with an account type, all of which have the same account type.

*   People may have a profession, and we want to search a list of all people by profession.

*   Threads can be in different states (waiting, sleeping, etc.); what you’re searching for is an association between a state and threads in that state.

To solve these problems with the Stream API, <samp class="listingcharacter">collect(...)</samp> can be used with a special <samp class="listingcharacter">Collector</samp> provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter">groupingBy*(...)</samp> methods of <samp class="listingcharacter">Collectors</samp> . We’ll deal only with the simplest variant.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example outputs all running threads:

```
Map<Thread.State, List<Thread>> map =
  Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet().stream()
        .collect( Collectors.groupingBy( Thread::getState ) );
System.out.println( map.get( Thread.State.RUNNABLE ) );
```

First, <samp class="listingcharacter">Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet()</samp> returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">set<threads></samp> with all active threads. From this set, you can derive a stream and use a collector that groups by thread status. The result is an association between <samp class="listingcharacter">Thread.State</samp> and a <samp class="listingcharacter">List<Threads></samp> .

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Collectors</samp> class uses a lot of Generics:

```
final class java.util.stream.
                Collectors 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T,K> Collector<T,?,Map<K,List<T>>> groupingBy(Function<? super T,? extends K> classifier)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T,K,A,D> Collector<T,?,Map<K,D>> groupingBy(Function<? super T,? extends K> classifier, Collector<? super T,A,D> downstream)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T,K,D,A,M extends Map<K,D>> Collector<T,?,M> groupingBy(Function<? super T,?</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">extends K> classifier, Supplier<M> mapFactory, Collector<? super T,A,D> downstream)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T,K> Collector<T,?,ConcurrentMap<K,List<T>>> groupingByConcurrent(Function<? super T,? extends K> classifier)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T,K,A,D> Collector<T,?,ConcurrentMap<K,D>> groupingByConcurrent(Function<? super T,? extends K> classifier, Collector<? super T,A,D> downstream)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static <T,K,A,D,M extends ConcurrentMap<K,D>> Collector<T,?,M></samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">groupingByConcurrent(Function<? super T,? extends K> classifier, Supplier<M></samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">mapFactory, Collector<? super T,A,D> downstream)</samp>

The function that extracts the key for the associative memory is the <samp class="listingcharacter">classifier</samp> in the API. This function must always be specified. We’ve looked at the simplest method—the first one—in an example; it always returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> of lists. The other methods can also return a <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> with other data structures (or simple accumulated values instead of lists), which is the intention of <samp class="listingcharacter">downstream</samp>. Also, concrete <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> implementations can be specified (such as <samp class="listingcharacter">TreeMap</samp>), as in the <samp class="listingcharacter">mapFactory</samp>. Otherwise, <samp class="listingcharacter">groupingBy(Function)</samp> would select a <samp class="listingcharacter">Map</samp> class for you.

###### [eg]   Example

The following example collects the names of all threads by status:

```
Map<Thread.State, List<String>> map =
  Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet().stream()
        .collect( Collectors.groupingBy(
             Thread::getState,
             Collectors.mapping( Thread::getName, Collectors.toList() ) ) );
System.out.println( map.get( Thread.State.RUNNABLE ) ); 
```

The following example builds an associative memory that doesn’t associate the thread state with the threads themselves, but simply with the number of threads:

```
Map<Thread.State, Long> map =
  Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet().stream()
         .collect( Collectors.groupingBy( Thread::getState,
                                          Collectors.counting() ) );
System.out.println( map.get( Thread.State.RUNNABLE ) );    /3 3
```

The following example associates each thread status with an average value of the priorities of threads of the same status:

```
Map<Thread.State,Double> map =
  Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet().stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy( Thread::getState,
                           Collectors.averagingInt(Thread::getPriority) ) );
        System.out.println( map.get( Thread.State.RUNNABLE ) ); // 7.25
        System.out.println( map.get( Thread.State.WAITING ) );  // 8.0
```

### 18.6.10    Transferring Stream Elements to an Array or an Iterator

Finally, let’s consider the last three aggregating methods. Two <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray(...)</samp> methods of <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> transfer the stream’s data into an array. <samp class="listingcharacter">iterator()</samp> on <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> in turn returns an <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator</samp> with all the data (the method comes from the <samp class="listingcharacter">BaseStream</samp> supertype).

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T,Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[] toArray()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><A> A[] toArray(IntFunction<A[]> generator)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator<T> iterator()</samp>

The two <samp class="listingcharacter">toArray(...)</samp> methods are necessary because, in the first case, the type the array is unclear—only <samp class="listingcharacter">Object[]</samp> is known to be true by default. The <samp class="listingcharacter">IntFunction</samp> is passed the size of the stream, and the result is usually an array of that size. Constructor references can come in handy in this context. Primitive arrays can never form a return—for this scenario, you would need to use special primitive stream classes.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example puts all elements of a stream into a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> array:

```
String[] strings = Stream.of( "well", "Hmm", "Like" ).
                    toArray( String[]::new );
```

## 18.7    Intermediary Operations

Not all terminal operations result in a new modified stream but instead may simply terminate the current stream. The situation is different for intermediary operations, which modify the stream, for example, by removing elements, mapping them to other values and types, or sorting elements. Each intermediary method returns a new stream object, as seen in [Table 18.4](#18_007.html_t18.4) .

| Full Notation | Cascaded Notation |
| --- | --- |
|  
```
Stream<Object> a =
 Stream.of(" ",'3',null,"2",1,"");
Stream<Object> b = a.filter(Objects::nonNull);
Stream<String> c = b.map(Objects::toString );
Stream<String> d = c.map(String::trim);
Stream<String> e = d.filter(s -> !s.isEmpty());
Stream<Integer> f = e.map(Integer::parseInt);
Stream<Integer> g = f.sorted();
g.forEach(System.out::println);
```

 |  
```
Stream
 .of(" ",'3',null,"2",1,"")
 .filter(Objects::nonNull)
 .map(Objects::toString)
 .map(String::trim)
 .filter(s -> ! s.isEmpty())
 .map(Integer::parseInt)
 .sorted()
 .forEach(System.out::println);
```

 |

**Table 18.4**     Detailed and Compact Writing in Comparison

###### [»]  Note

No current method may modify the current source; otherwise, the result is indeterminate. Changes occur only along the chain from one stream to the next, as discussed earlier in [Section 18.6.8](#18_006.html_h18.6.8) .

### 18.7.1     Element Previews

A simple intermediary operation is <samp class="listingcharacter">peek(...)</samp> , which may view the current element during a pass.

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T,Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T> peek(Consumer<? super T> action)</samp>

###### [eg]  Example

The following example looks in a stream before and after a sort:

```
System.out.println( Stream.of( 9, 4, 3 )
                          .
                    peek( System.out::println ) // 9 4 3
                          .sorted()

                    .peek( System.out::println ) // 3 4 9
                          .collect( Collectors.toList() ) );
```

### 18.7.2    Filtering Elements

One of the most important stream methods is <samp class="listingcharacter">filter(...)</samp> , which returns all elements in the stream that satisfy a criterion and ignores all others that don’t satisfy that criterion.

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T,Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T> filter(Predicate<? super T> predicate)</samp>

###### [eg]  Example

The following example outputs all the words that have any two vowels in a row:

```
Stream.of( "boot", "aha", "mouse" )
      .filter( Pattern.compile( "[aeiou]{2}" ).asPredicate() )
      .forEach( System.out::println );      // boot mouse
```

### 18.7.3    Stateful Intermediary Operations

The vast majority of intermediary operations can evaluate and modify elements directly on the fly, eliminating the need for memory-intensive intermediate storage. However, some intermediary operations have a state, such as the following operations:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">limit(long)</samp> : Limits the stream to a certain number of maximum elements

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">skip(long)</samp> : Skips a number of elements

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">distinct()</samp> : Deletes all duplicate elements

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">sorted(...)</samp> : Sorts the stream

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T,Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T> limit(long maxSize)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T> skip(long n)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T> distinct()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T> sorted()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<T> sorted(Comparator<? super T> comparator)</samp>

###### [eg]  Example 1

The following example determines which word is the longest word in the list:

```
Stream.of( "Blessed", "are", "the", "cheesemakers" )
    .sorted( 
                    Comparator.comparing( String::length ).reversed() )
    .findFirst().ifPresent( System.out::println ); // cheesemakers
```

Alternatively, with <samp class="listingcharacter">max(...)</samp> , you could write the following code:

```
 .max( Comparator.comparing( String::length ) )
```

###### [eg]  Example 2

The following example splits a string into substrings, maps each substring to the first character, and deletes duplicate elements from the stream:

```
List<String> list = Pattern.compile( " " ).splitAsStream( "Pu Po Aha La" )
    .map( s -> s.substring(0, 1) )
    .peek( System.out::println ) // P P A L

                    .distinct()                  // \/\/\/
    .peek( System.out::println ) //  P A L
    .collect( Collectors.toList() );
System.out.print( list );                       // [P, A, L]
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">peek(...)</samp> makes it clear what the elements look like before and after applying <samp class="listingcharacter">distinct()</samp> .

###### [»]   Note

A method like <samp class="listingcharacter">skip(...)</samp> looks innocent at first glance, but its use can be quite heavy on memory usage and performance when parallel streams with order (such as sorting) come into play. With <samp class="listingcharacter">stream.parallel().sorted().skip(10000)</samp>, all elements must still be sorted first so that the first 10,000 can be skipped. Sequential streams or streams without order (which are provided by the <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">unordered()</samp> ) are incomparably faster, but of course not possible in every case.

### 18.7.4    Prefix Operations

By a prefix, we mean a subsequence of a stream that starts at the first element. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">limit(long)</samp> to generate a prefix yourself, but in general, the idea is to have a condition that all elements of a prefix stream must satisfy and to terminate the stream when the condition no longer applies to an element. Java declares the two methods <samp class="listingcharacter">takeWhile(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">dropWhile(</samp> ...) for this purpose, used in the following ways:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default Stream<T> takeWhile(Predicate<? super T> predicate)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">default Stream<T> dropWhile(Predicate<? super T> predicate)</samp>

<samp class="listingcharacter">takeWhile(...)</samp> could be paraphrased as “take as long as <samp class="listingcharacter">predicate</samp> applies,” while <samp class="listingcharacter">dropWhile(...)</samp> means “drop as long as <samp class="listingcharacter">predicate</samp> applies.”

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, the stream should end immediately upon arriving at the word “Tesla”:

```
new Scanner( "Am considering taking Tesla private at $420\. Funding secured." )
    .useDelimiter( "\\P{Alpha}+" ).tokens()
    .takeWhile( s -> ! s.equalsIgnoreCase( "tesla" ) )
    .forEach( System.out::println );  // Am considering taking
```

###### [eg]  Example

In the following example, all empty strings or strings with whitespace should be skipped at the beginning:

```
Stream.of( " ", "", "a", "", "b" )
    .dropWhile( s -> s.trim().isEmpty() )
    .forEach( System.out::println ); // "a", "", "b"
```

<samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">takeWhile(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">dropWhile(...)</samp> can be used together: Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream.of( 1, 2, -1, 3, 4, -1, 5, 6 ).dropWhile( i -> i > 0 ).skip( 1 ).takeWhile( i -> i > 0 ).forEach( System.out::println );</samp> returns the output <samp class="listingcharacter">3 4</samp>. The element that satisfies the predicate is itself the first element in the new stream. We can skip this element using <samp class="listingcharacter">skip(1)</samp> .

###### [»]  Note

Prefixes are only useful for ordered streams. If streams are parallel, they must be put back in the right order for the prefix calculation, which can be a rather expensive operation.

### 18.7.5    Images

The ability to map elements in a stream to new elements is one of the most powerful tools of the Stream API. Three types of mapping methods can be distinguished in this context:

*   The simplest variant is <samp class="listingcharacter">map(Function)</samp> . The function gets the stream element as an argument and returns a result, which then goes into the stream. In this case, the type may change if the function doesn’t give the same type as it takes. The function is applied to each element one by one, and the order of results follows the order of the stream.

*   The three methods <samp class="listingcharacter">mapTo[Int|Long|Double]([int|long|double]Function)</samp> work like <samp class="listingcharacter">map(Function)</samp> , except that the functions return a primitive value, and the result is a primitive stream.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">flatMap*(*Function)</samp> methods also replace elements in the stream, with the difference that the functions all return <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> objects themselves whose elements are then placed in the result stream. The term flat comes from the fact that the “inner” streams do not themselves all come as elements in the source stream (so to speak, a <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<Stream></samp>) but are “knocked flat.” Application examples are usually scenarios like “ n players associate m items; we search a stream of all items of all players.” The function can return <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> if nothing is to be placed in the stream.

```
interface java.util.stream.
                Stream<T>
extends BaseStream<T,Stream<T>> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><R> Stream<R> map(Function<? super T,? extends R> mapper)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">IntStream mapToInt(ToIntFunction<? super T> mapper)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">LongStream mapToLong(ToLongFunction<? super T> mapper)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">DoubleStream mapToDouble(ToDoubleFunction<? super T> mapper)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"><R> Stream<R> flatMap(Function<? super T,? extends Stream<? extends R>> mapper)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">IntStream flatMapToInt(Function<? super T,? extends IntStream> mapper)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">LongStream flatMapToLong(Function<? super T,? extends LongStream> mapper)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">DoubleStream flatMapToDouble(Function<? super T,? extends DoubleStream> mapper)</samp>

###### [eg]  Example

The following example converts a string array with numbers into a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> array:

```
String[] numbers = { "1", "2", "3" };
long[] parseInts = Stream.of( numbers )
                    .mapToLong( Long::parseLong ).toArray();
```

###### [eg]  Example

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale.getAvailableLocales()</samp> method returns an array of <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> objects supported by a system. In the following example, we’re interested in all country codes:

```
Stream.of( Locale.getAvailableLocales() )
      .map( Locale::getCountry )
      .distinct()
      .forEach( System.out::println );
```

Via a <samp class="listingcharacter">Locale</samp> object, <samp class="listingcharacter">DateFormatSymbols.getInstance(locale).getWeekdays()</samp> retrieves the names of the weekdays. In the following example, we want all the days of the week of all installed areas as the result:

```
Stream.of( Locale.getAvailableLocales() )
      .flatMap( l -> Stream.of( DateFormatSymbols.getInstance( l ).getWeekdays() ) )
      .filter( s -> ! s.isEmpty() )
      .distinct()
      .forEach( System.out::println );
```

###### [+]  Tip

The function passed to <samp class="listingcharacter">flatMap(...)</samp> must return a stream as a result or <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> if nothing should happen. Always supplying a stream is never wrong, and thus instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>, you would have the function return an empty stream with <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream.empty()</samp>. Applications for these empty streams can be seen in the following scenario: In the API, let’s say some methods return only <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> instead of arrays or collections, and we assume <samp class="listingcharacter">result</samp> is such a return (which can be <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> or an array). Then, you would use the <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream</samp> in the following way:

```
Stream<…> flatStream = Optional.ofNullable( result )
                               .map( Stream::of ).orElse( Stream.empty() );
```

The case distinction is whether the collection is <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> should be solved here functionally with <samp class="listingcharacter">Optional</samp> or with <samp class="listingcharacter">result != null ? result</samp>: <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream.empty()</samp>. The static <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream.of(...)</samp> is used in this case via a method reference and works for an array; for a stream from a collection, you must use <samp class="listingcharacter">result.stream()</samp> .

Let’s summarize with an example. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> method <samp class="listingcharacter">getEnumConstants()</samp> returns an array of constants if the <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object represents an enumeration—otherwise, the array isn’t empty, but <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp>. (In this way, you can distinguish between whether <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> object has no elements or isn’t an enumeration type at all.) In the following example, we’ll collect and output all constants from three <samp class="listingcharacter">Class</samp> objects:

```
Stream.of( Object.class, Thread.State.class, DayOfWeek.class )
      .flatMap( clazz -> Optional.ofNullable( clazz.getEnumConstants() )
                                 .map( Stream::of ).orElse( Stream.empty() ) )
      .forEach( System.out::println );
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> is often an uninvited guest, and the stream method <samp class="listingcharacter">ofNullable(...)</samp> can help you avoid errors. The following code gets all the coordinates into one stream:

```
Stream.of( null, new Point( 1, 2 ), null, new Point( 3, 4 ) )
      .flatMap( q -> Stream.of( q.x, q.y ) )
      .forEach( System.out::println );
```

With <samp class="listingcharacter">flatMap(...)</samp>, a <samp class="listingcharacter">NullPointerException</samp> will be thrown. With <samp class="listingcharacter">filter(...)</samp>, you could hide any <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> in advance, but another solution would be to write the following code:

```
Stream.of( null, new Point( 1, 2 ), null, new Point( 3, 4 ) )
      .flatMap( p -> Stream.ofNullable( p ).flatMap( q -> Stream.of( q.x, q.y ) ) )
      .forEach( System.out::println );
```

## 18.8    Further Reading

Every programmer should know the basic data structures and their performance and memory characteristics. A good book to dive deeper into this topic is Data Structures and Algorithms in Java by Robert LaFore (Sams Publishing, 2002). The Stream API doesn’t have many methods, but like SQL, the possible combinations are vast. Practice is the name of the game. But be careful! If an expression is no longer readable, simplify it, for example, by using classic loops. For practice, try to create separate tasks for each method of the Stream API. The book Java 8 in Action: Lambdas, Streams, and functional-style Programming by Raoul-Gariel Urma, Mario Fusco, and Alan Mycroft (Manning Publications, 2014) sheds light on functional programming and the Stream API.

# 19     Files and Data Streams

“Quick-wittedness is any answer that is so clever
that the listener wishes he had given it.”
—Elbert Green Hubbard (1856–1915)

Computers are so useful to us because they process data. The processing cycle begins with the reading of the data, includes processing, and ends with the output of the data. This is called the IPO model (input-process-output) in data processing systems. In the early days of IPO, inputs consisted of punch cards entered by system operators. Fortunately, those days are over. Nowadays, we store our data in files [[ 224 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn19_01) and databases. Note that a file is only interesting in its context; otherwise, it contains no information, and therefore, the view of a file is important. A program also consists of data and is often represented as a file.

## 19.1    Old and New Worlds in java.io and java.nio

Whenever an application programming interface (API) doesn’t behave as desired, we often say that it’s “historically grown.” This characterization is exactly what can be seen in file operations.

### 19.1.1    java.io Package with the File Class

The <samp class="listingcharacter">java.io package</samp> declares a central <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> class since Java 1.0, which stands for a file or directory in the current file system. <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> offers numerous file-oriented operations, such as creating, deleting, and renaming files; listing directories; and more.

#### File Problems

With <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> , everything is focused on one class, and that class can’t really solve everyday problems. The following questions will remain:

*   How can we copy a file easily and quickly?

*   How can we move a file while keeping the semantics the same on different platforms?

*   How can we respond to a change in the file system so that a callback informs us immediately that file has changed?

*   How can we simply traverse a directory recursively?

*   How can we create and track a symbolic link?

*   The <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> class has become a catch-all for all possible query methods like readability, modification dates, and so on. One problem with this development is that certain things aren’t really identical on every system, such as file permissions, for example.

*   How can we implement <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> operations that are abstracted and not only based on the local file system? Abstraction is desirable so that the same API also addresses a virtual file system in the main memory, addresses remote file systems such as FTP, or addresses a repository.

### 19.1.2    NIO.2 and the java.nio Package

An alternative to the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.io</samp> package, with its <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> class, is the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.nio.file</samp> package with further types, like the <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Paths</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Files</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">FileSystem</samp> types. Those types are called NIO.2 types.

#### java.io.File or java.nio.* Types?

The <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> class is needed in only a few places these days and actually only for two reasons:

*   Old APIs expect <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> objects as parameters. Bridges are available for linking APIs in this case, but the new NIO.2 types basically replace the <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> class entirely. In the long run, the <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> object should no longer be expected.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> objects are still necessary if files are really to be represented on your own local file system and not independently of the file system like a ZIP file. A good example is <samp class="listingcharacter">Desktop</samp> with the <samp class="listingcharacter">open(File)</samp> method.

## 19.2    File Systems and Paths

At the center of NIO.2 are the <samp class="listingcharacter">FileSystem</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> types:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">FileSystem</samp> describes a data system and is an abstract class. This type is implemented by concrete file systems, such as the local file system or a ZIP archive. To access the current file system, the <samp class="listingcharacter">FileSystems</samp> class declares a static method: <samp class="listingcharacter">FileSystems.getDefault()</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> represents a path to a file or directory, where paths can be relative or absolute. These methods are somewhat reminiscent of the old <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> class, but one big difference is that <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> itself represents the file or directory and declares query methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">isDirectory()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">lastModified()</samp>. In contrast, <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> represents only the path and provides only path-related methods. Modification methods aren’t included; extra types like <samp class="listingcharacter">BasicFileAttributes</samp> for attributes must be used in these cases.

### 19.2.1    FileSystem and Path

A <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> object can’t be created via a constructor like <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> because the class is abstract. However, <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> have a few things in common, for example, being immutable. The <samp class="listingcharacter">FileSystem</samp> object provides the corresponding <samp class="listingcharacter">getPath(...)</samp> method, and a <samp class="listingcharacter">FileSystem</samp> is retrieved from <samp class="listingcharacter">FileSystems</samp> via a factory method.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> object:

```
FileSystem fs = FileSystems.getDefault();
Path p = 
                    fs.getPath( "C:/Windows/Fonts/" );
```

With a shortcut, you can write the following code:

```
Path p = 
                    Paths.get( "C:/Windows/Fonts/" );
```

Since the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">FileSystems.getDefault().getPath(...)</samp> is a bit clumsy, three shorter options are available:

*   Using the utility class <samp class="listingcharacter">Paths</samp>. A call of <samp class="listingcharacter">Paths.get(...)</samp> returns the <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> (see [Chapter 7](#07_001.html_h7), [Section 7.1.2](#07_001.html_h7.1.2) ).

*   Using the two static <samp class="listingcharacter">of(...)</samp> methods that exist in <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> .

*   A <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> can also be derived from a <samp class="listingcharacter">File object</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">toPath()</samp> .

```
final class java.nio.file.
                Paths 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Path get(String first, String… more)</samp>
    Creates a path from segments. For example, if the backslash <samp class="listingcharacter">\</samp> is the path separator on your file system, then <samp class="listingcharacter">Paths.get("a", "b", "c ")</samp> is equal to <samp class="listingcharacter">Paths.get("a\b\c")</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Path get(URI uri)</samp>
    Creates a path from a URI.

```
final class java.nio.file
                .Path 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Path of(String first, String... more)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Path of(URI uri)</samp>

Each <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> object also has a <samp class="listingcharacter">getFileSystem()</samp> method, which you can use to get back to the <samp class="listingcharacter">FileSystem</samp> .

[![ Dependencies of the Paths and Path Types](bilderklein/klein19_001.png)](img-f19.1.html)

**Figure 19.1**     Dependencies of the Paths and Path Types

###### [»]  Note

The path string must not contain <samp class="listingcharacter">\u0000</samp> in Java; otherwise, an exception will be thrown. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">Paths.get("my.php\u0000.jpg")</samp> leads to the exception “java.nio.file.InvalidPathException: Illegal char < > at index 6: my.php.” This exception is an important security feature, for example, to protect a web server from accepting false files. The filename looks like a JPG file via <samp class="listingcharacter">"my.php\u0000.jpg".endsWith(".jpg")</samp>, but if everything after the null string were truncated (which some file systems do), a my.php file would suddenly be created.

#### Features of a Path

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> type declares various <samp class="listingcharacter">get*(...)</samp> methods and an <samp class="listingcharacter">isAbsolute()</samp> method, which have some similarity to the methods from <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp>, as shown in [Figure 19.2](#19_002.html_f19.2). [Listing 19.1](#19_002.html_l19.1) shows a few examples of usage.

```
Path p = Paths.get( "C:/Windows/Fonts/" );
System.out.println( 
                    p.toString() );                  // C:\Windows\Fonts
System.out.println( 
                    p.isAbsolute() );                // true
System.out.println( 
                    p.getRoot() );                   // C:\
System.out.println( 
                    p.getParent() );                 // C:\Windows
System.out.println( 
                    p.getNameCount() );              // 2
System.out.println( p.getName(
                    p.getNameCount()-1) ); // Fonts 
```

**Listing 19.1**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nio2/FileSystemPathFileDemo1.java, main()

Methods such as <samp class="listingcharacter">getPath()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">getRoot()</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">getParent()</samp> all return <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> objects from the components of a given path. Three methods will not result in a <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> :

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">toString()</samp> returns a string representation.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">toUri()</samp> returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">URI</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">toFile()</samp> returns a traditional <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> object.

Because <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> stores a hierarchical list of names for the path, each segment of the path can be queried. This task of <samp class="listingcharacter">getName(int n)</samp> in turn returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">subpath(int beginIndex, int endIndex)</samp> method returns a <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> with the segments of the specified range. <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> implements the <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterable</samp> interface, which imposes an <samp class="listingcharacter">iterator()</samp> method, which in turn means that <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> can appear to the right of the colon in the extended <samp class="listingcharacter">for</samp> .

[![The Class Diagram of Path](bilderklein/klein19_002.png)](img-f19.2.html)

**Figure 19.2**     The Class Diagram of Path

The check methods <samp class="listingcharacter">startsWith(Path other)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">endsWith(Path other)</samp>, which determine whether the path starts or ends with a certain other path, are quite convenient. <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> is overridden from within <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp>. Since <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> implements the <samp class="listingcharacter">Comparable<Path></samp> interface, <samp class="listingcharacter">compareTo(Path)</samp> is implemented as well. The <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> method doesn’t resolve the paths, but only looks at their names; the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">isSameFile(Path, Path)</samp> of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Files</samp> class performs this test and resolves relative references. Besides <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> also overrides <samp class="listingcharacter">hashCode()</samp> .

```
interface java.nio.file.
                    Path
extends Comparable<Path>, Iterable<Path>, Watchable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String toString()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">File toFile()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">URI toUri()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path getFileName()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path getParent()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">Path getRoot()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean isAbsolute()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int getNameCount()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path getName(int index)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterator<Path> iterator()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path subpath(int beginIndex, int endIndex)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean endsWith(Path other)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean endsWith(String other)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean startsWith(Path other)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean startsWith(String other)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean equals(Object other)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(Path other)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int hashCode()</samp>

[![The Inheritance Relationship of Path](bilderklein/klein19_003.png)](img-f19.3.html)

**Figure 19.3**     The Inheritance Relationship of Path

###### [»]  Note

The <samp class="listingcharacter">getFileName()</samp> method doesn’t return a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> but instead a <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> object with only the file name with <samp class="listingcharacter">getNameCount() == 1</samp>. Therefore, using <samp class="listingcharacter">path.getFileName().endsWith(".xml")</samp> to check whether a filename like trainings.xml ends in “.xml” isn’t helpful because <samp class="listingcharacter">endsWith(...)</samp> tests whether the last segment in the path (in this case, the complete filename without directory specification) has exactly this name. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">path.getFileName().toString().endsWith(".xml")</samp> is valid as a solution.

###### [»]  Note

Different file systems have their own limitations and notations. Sometimes, the folder separator character is a “/” and sometimes a “\.” Wikipedia [[ 225 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn19_02) provides an overview of how different operating systems define separators or define the root directory. Java also accepts the slash as a folder separator on Windows.

#### Creating New Paths

The <samp class="listingcharacter">resolve*(...)</samp> methods create new paths from existing ones. These methods accept the parameter types <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

The following example joins a user directory with an image directory:

```
Path picturePath = Paths.get( System.getProperty("user.home") )
                        .
                        resolve( "Pictures" )
                        .resolve( "Squid Game" );
System.out.println( picturePath ); // e.g., C:\Users\Chris\Pictures\Squid Game
```

The subdirectories can also be entered directly in <samp class="listingcharacter">get(...)</samp> .

In the same folder as Haldeman.jpg, a new path for the file nixon.tar is requested:

```
Path haldeman = Paths.get( "d:/smoking gun tapes/Haldeman.jpg" );
Path nixon    = haldeman.resolveSibling( "nixon.tar" );
System.out.println( nixon );  // d:\smoking gun tapes\nixon.tar 
```

An interesting method is also <samp class="listingcharacter">relativize(Path)</samp> , which returns a relative path from a base specification that leads to another path.

###### [eg]  Example

As shown in the following example, the relative path <samp class="listingcharacter">..\Cursors</samp> leads from c:/Windows/Fonts to c:/Windows/Cursors :

```
System.out.println( Paths.get( "C:/Windows/Fonts" )
                         .
                    relativize( Paths.get("C:/Windows/Cursors") )
); // ..\Cursors
interface java.nio.file.
                    Path
extends Comparable<Path>, Iterable<Path>, Watchable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path relativize(Path other)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path resolve(Path other)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path resolve(String other)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path resolveSibling(Path other)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path resolveSibling(String other)</samp>

#### Normalization and Path Resolution

As with the <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> class, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> class symbolizes a path but doesn’t have to point to a concrete file or directory. For this reason, the methods we’ve described so far only provide information that can be inferred from the given name without resorting to the file system. Thus, for relative paths, the query methods provide little that’s exciting. Consider the following example:

```
Path p = Paths.get( "../.." );
System.out.println( p.toString() );                  // ..\..
System.out.println( p.isAbsolute() );                // false
System.out.println( p.getRoot() );                   // null
System.out.println( p.getParent() );                 // ..
System.out.println( p.getNameCount() );              // 2
System.out.println( p.getName(p.getNameCount()-1) ); // .. 
```

**Listing 19.2**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nio2/FileSystemPathFileDemo2.java, main()

To bring some order into relative path specifications, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> class provides the <samp class="listingcharacter">normalize()</samp> method, which removes the references “.” and “..” without accessing the file system. To resolve the relative addressing with access to the file system, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> class provides the two methods, <samp class="listingcharacter">toAbsolutePath()</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">toRealPath(...)</samp> , as shown in the following example:

```
Path dotDotSlashDotDot = Paths.get( "../.." );
System.out.println( 
                    dotDotSlashDotDot.toAbsolutePath() );
// e.g., C:\Users\Christian\Dropbox\workspace\..\..

try {
  System.out.println( 
                    dotDotSlashDotDot.toRealPath( LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS ) );
// e.g., C:\Users\Christian\

  System.out.println( Paths.get( "../♡" ).toRealPath( LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS ) );
}
catch ( IOException e ) {
  e.printStackTrace();
} 
```

**Listing 19.3**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nio2/RealAndAbsolutePath.java, main()

The first method <samp class="listingcharacter">toAbsolutePath()</samp> doesn’t normalize; the method simply resolves the relative path to an absolute path. The resolution of <samp class="listingcharacter">../..</samp> is performed by <samp class="listingcharacter">toRealPath(LinkOption...)</samp> , where the (optional) argument expresses whether links should be followed or not.

###### [»]   Note

The <samp class="listingcharacter">toRealPath(...)</samp> method raises an exception when trying to resolve a path to a file that doesn’t exist. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">Paths.get("../♡").toRealPath(…)</samp> links to “java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException,” whether with or without <samp class="listingcharacter">LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS</samp>. In contrast, <samp class="listingcharacter">Paths.get( "../0x" ).toAbsolutePath()</samp> doesn’t result in an error.

```
interface java.nio.file.
                    Path
extends Comparable<Path>, Iterable<Path>, Watchable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path normalize()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path toAbsolutePath()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Path toRealPath(LinkOption… options)</samp>

Two other <samp class="listingcharacter">register(...)</samp> methods are available in <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> , but these methods relate to registering a listener that reacts to changes in the file system.

### 19.2.2    The Files Utility Class

Since the <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> class represents only paths (and not file information such as length or modification time) and since <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> also doesn’t provide a way to create and delete files, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Files</samp> class takes over these tasks.

A simple method is <samp class="listingcharacter">size(...)</samp>, which returns the length of the file. Unlike <samp class="listingcharacter">java.io.File</samp>, almost all <samp class="listingcharacter">Files</samp> methods result in an <samp class="listingcharacter">IOException</samp> if problems occur with the input/output operations.

```
final class java.nio.file.
                Files 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long size(Path path) throws IOException</samp>
    Returns the size of the file.

#### Easy Reading and Writing of Files

Through the methods <samp class="listingcharacter">readAllBytes(...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">readAllLines(...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">readString(...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">lines(...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">write(...)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">writeString(...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Files</samp> can simply read a file’s content or write strings or a byte field. Consider the following example:

```
URI uri = ListAllLines.class.getResource( "/lyrics.txt" ).toURI();
Path p = Paths.get( uri );
System.out.printf( "File '%s' with size of %d byte(s) with lines:%n",
                   p.getFileName(), 
                    Files.size( p ) );
int lineCnt = 1;

                    for ( String line : 
                    Files.readAllLines( p ) )
  System.out.println( lineCnt++ + ": " + line ); 
```

**Listing 19.4**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/nio2/ListAllLines.java, main()

```
final class java.nio.file.
                    Files 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static byte[] readAllBytes(Path path) throws IOException</samp>
    Reads the file completely into a byte field.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static List<String> readAllLines(Path path) throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static List<String> readAllLines(Path path, Charset cs) throws IOException</samp>
    Reads the file line by line and provides a list of these lines. The specification of an encoding is optional; by default, the encoding is <samp class="listingcharacter">StandardCharsets.UTF_8</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String readString(Path path) throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String readString(Path path, Charset cs) throws IOException</samp>
    Reads a file completely and returns the contents as a string. Without encoding, UTF-8 applies by default.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Path write(Path path, byte[] bytes, OpenOption… options) throws IOException</samp>
    Writes a byte array to a file.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Path write(Path path, Iterable<? extends CharSequence> lines, OpenOption…</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">options) throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Path write(Path path, Iterable<? extends CharSequence> lines, Charset cs,</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">OpenOption… options) throws IOException</samp>
    Writes all lines from the <samp class="listingcharacter">Iterable</samp> to a file. The encoding is optional but is <samp class="listingcharacter">StandardCharsets.UTF_8</samp> unless otherwise specified.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Path writeString(Path path, CharSequence csq, OpenOption… options) throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Path writeString(Path path, CharSequence csq, Charset cs, OpenOption… options) throws IOException</samp>
    Writes a string to the named file. The passed <samp class="listingcharacter">path</samp> is returned. Without encoding, UTF-8 applies by default.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">OpenOption</samp> enumeration is a vararg, and therefore, arguments aren’t mandatory. <samp class="listingcharacter">StandardOpenOption</samp> is an enumeration of type <samp class="listingcharacter">OpenOption</samp> with constants like <samp class="listingcharacter">APPEND</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">CREATE</samp> , and so on.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example reads a UTF-8 encoded file:

```
String s = Files.readString( path );
```

###### [»]   Note

Even though an obvious choice might be to feed the <samp class="listingcharacter">Files</samp> method with a <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> object representing an HTTP URI, this approach won’t work. Thus, already the first line of the program returns an exception of the type “java.nio.file.FileSystemNotFoundException: Provider 'http' not installed.” You can not treat a HTTP-URI as a <samp class="listingcharacter">Path</samp> object.

```
URI uri = new URI( "http://tutego.de/javabuch/aufgaben/bond.txt" );
Path path = Paths.get( uri );     // 

List<String> content = Files.readAllLines( path );
System.out.println( content ); 
```

#### A Stream of Lines

The previous <samp class="listingcharacter">Files</samp> methods read and write the complete content, which can become a memory problem. If the reading should be done line by line, <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<String></samp> is a good alternative instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">readAllLines()</samp>, in which each line is a <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp> object, thus all lines are kept in the memory. Two methods provide a stream of lines:

```
final class java.nio.file.
                    Files 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static Stream<String> lines(Path path)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Stream<String> lines(Path path, Charset cs)</samp>
    Returns a stream of lines from a file. The specification of the encoding is optional, which is <samp class="listingcharacter">StandardCharsets.UTF_8</samp> by default.

#### Copying Data Streams

In some cases, the data should not go directly from a file into a byte array or string list (or from a byte array or string collection into a file). Instead, you want data to move from a file into a data stream. In this case, two <samp class="listingcharacter">copy(...)</samp> methods are useful:

```
final class java.nio.file.
                    Files 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long copy(InputStream in, Path target, CopyOption… options)</samp>
    Empties the input stream and copies the data to the file. The number of bytes copied is the return value.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long copy(Path source, OutputStream out)</samp>
    Copies all data from the file to the output stream. The number of bytes copied is the return value.

## 19.3     Random Access Files

Files can be read and modified in two different ways: first, via a data stream that processes bytes as in a media stream and, second, via random access. While the data stream enforces a strict sequence, random access doesn’t care because it can jump back and forth arbitrarily within a file and maintains a file pointer that you can set. Since we’re dealing with files, the whole thing is then called a random access file, and the class that provides random access is <samp class="listingcharacter">java.io.RandomAccessFile</samp> .

### 19.3.1    Opening a RandomAccessFile for Reading and Writing

The class declares two constructors that use a file name or <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> object to create a <samp class="listingcharacter">RandomAccessFile</samp> object. In the constructor, the second parameter specifies a string for the access mode; this parameterized constructor can be used to open a file in read or write mode, as shown in [Table 19.1](#19_003.html_t19.1) . The specification avoids errors because a file opened for reading can’t be overwritten by mistake.

| Mode | Function |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp> | The file will be opened for reading. Attempting to write to this file is penalized with an exception. If the file doesn’t exist, an error will be triggered. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">rw</samp> | The file is opened for reading and writing. An existing file is opened, and the data can be appended without deleting the file. If the file doesn’t exist, the file will be (re-)created, and its start size will be zero. If the file should be deleted, you must do so explicitly by using <samp class="listingcharacter">delete()</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter">File</samp> class itself. |

**Table 19.1**     Two Modes for the Constructor of RandomAccessFile

In addition, an <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> can be appended to <samp class="listingcharacter">rw</samp> ; these additions represent options for synchronizing the data with the file system when writing.

```
class java.io.
                RandomAccessFile
implements DataOutput, DataInput, Closeable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">RandomAccessFile(String name, String mode) throws FileNotFoundException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">RandomAccessFile(File file, String mode) throws FileNotFoundException</samp>
    Opens the file. Whether the file is prepared for reading or writing is determined by the <samp class="listingcharacter">mode</samp> string with the valid assignments <samp class="listingcharacter">r</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">rw</samp>. If the mode is set incorrectly, an <samp class="listingcharacter">IllegalArgumentException</samp> will be raised. A <samp class="listingcharacter">FileNotFoundException</samp> will be raised if the file can’t be opened.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void close()</samp>
    Closes an open file.

### 19.3.2     Reading from RandomAccessFile

To retrieve data from a file managed with <samp class="listingcharacter">RandomAccessFile</samp>, you can use one of the <samp class="listingcharacter">read*(...)</samp> methods. These methods directly read the byte field from the file or read several bytes combined to a primitive data type. <samp class="listingcharacter">readChar()</samp>, for example, reads 2 bytes in a row and combines them into a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> .

```
class java.io.
                RandomAccessFile
implements DataOutput, DataInput, Closeable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int read() throws IOException</samp>
    Reads exactly 1 byte and returns this byte as <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int read(byte[] b) throws IOException</samp>
    Reads the amount of <samp class="listingcharacter">b.length()</samp> bytes and stores this value in the <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> field.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int read(byte[] b, int off, int len) throws IOException</samp>
    Reads <samp class="listingcharacter">len</samp> bytes from the file and writes them to the <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> array starting at the position <samp class="listingcharacter">off</samp> in the array. The read size is always returned, even if less than <samp class="listingcharacter">len</samp> bytes were read.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final boolean readBoolean() throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final byte readByte() throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final short readShort() throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final int readInt() throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final long readLong() throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final char readChar() throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final double readDouble() throws IOException</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final float readFloat() throws IOException</samp>
    Reads a primitive data type.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final int readUnsignedByte() throws IOException</samp>
    Reads a byte interpreted as unsigned.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final int readUnsignedShort() throws IOException</samp>
    Reads two bytes interpreted as unsigned.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final void readFully(byte[] b) throws IOException</samp>
    Attempts to fill the entire buffer <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final void readFully(byte[] b, int off, int len) throws IOException</samp>
    Reads <samp class="listingcharacter">len</samp> bytes and stores them in buffer <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> starting at index <samp class="listingcharacter">off</samp> .

Finally, the following two methods return a string:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final String readLine() throws IOException</samp>
    Reads a line of text terminated by the end-of-line character <samp class="listingcharacter">\r</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">\n</samp> or a combination <samp class="listingcharacter">\r\n</samp>. The last line doesn’t need to be terminated in this way because an end of file counts as an end of line. <samp class="listingcharacter">readLine()</samp> doesn’t interpret characters as Unicode, but simply takes the characters as ASCII bytes. (Without converting various code pages, such as from a file in an unfamiliar IBM format, <samp class="listingcharacter">readLine()</samp> won’t read the correct corresponding Unicode lines. This byte-in-char conversion would have to be done manually.) Also, because <samp class="listingcharacter">RandomAccessFile</samp> doesn’t buffer, line-by-line processing of ASCII files via <samp class="listingcharacter">readLine()</samp> isn’t suitable for speed reasons, and the appropriate <samp class="listingcharacter">Scanner</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">BufferedReader</samp> class should be used.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">final String readUTF()</samp>
    Reads a modified UTF-encoded string and returns a Unicode string. A UTF string combines either 1, 2, or 3 bytes into a Unicode character. Later in this section, we’ll describe UTF encoding in more detail.

#### Return -1 and EOFException*

The methods do not all return an error if the file has already been processed and no more data is present. In the case of <samp class="listingcharacter">int read()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int read(byte[])</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">int read(byte[], int, int)</samp>, a return value of <samp class="listingcharacter">-1</samp> is the result, and no exception arises. The same behavior is true for <samp class="listingcharacter">readLine()</samp>. The method returns <samp class="listingcharacter">null</samp> at the end of the file. Other read methods may enforce a certain number of bytes, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">readLong()</samp> with 8 bytes or <samp class="listingcharacter">readByte()</samp> for only 1 byte. Thus, in case of an end of file, an <samp class="listingcharacter">EOFException</samp> will follow. You’ll rarely see other uses of <samp class="listingcharacter">EOFException</samp> in the Java library.

#### UTF-8 Encoding*

<samp class="listingcharacter">writeUTF(String)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">readUTF()</samp> are two operations prescribed by the <samp class="listingcharacter">DataOutput</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">DataInput</samp> interfaces. In addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">RandomAccessFile</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">DataOutputStream</samp> implements the <samp class="listingcharacter">DataOutput</samp> interface, and <samp class="listingcharacter">DataInputStream</samp> implements the <samp class="listingcharacter">DataInput</samp> interface.

Java manages Unicode characters via the <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> data type, which is only 16 bits long. [[ 226 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn19_03) In many regions, most characters come from the conventional 8 bits of the Latin-1 character set. If the characters were sent as Unicode (i.e., 2 bytes), half of the 16-bit data stream would essentially consist of zeros.
