In Java programs, octal numbers should be used with caution. If you fill a number left-justified with the 0 for reasons of readability, you’ll experience a surprise:

```
int i = 118;
int j = 012;                        // Octal 012 is decimal 10 
```

### 21.1.4     Effect of Typecasting on Bit Patterns

Typecasting sometimes results in the upper bits of integers being simply cut off. When adjusting floats to integers, rounding is performed. This section will demonstrate what exactly happens.

#### Explicit Typecasting for Integers

When converting a larger integer type to a smaller one, the upper bits are truncated. An adjustment of the sign does not take place. The representation in bits shows this scenario clearly:

```
int   ii = 123456789;     // 0000011101011011_
                    11001101_00010101
int   ij =   -123456;     // 1111111111111110_
                    00011101_11000000

short si = (short) ii;    //                  
                    11001101_00010101
short sj = (short) ij;    //                  
                    00011101_11000000

System.out.println( si ); // -13035
System.out.println( sj ); //   7616 
```

**Listing 21.1**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/math/TypecastDemo.java, main()

<samp class="listingcharacter">si</samp> becomes a negative number because the 16th bit at <samp class="listingcharacter">int ii</samp> was set and now shows the negative sign at <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>. The number after <samp class="listingcharacter">ij</samp> doesn’t have a 16th bit set, and so, the <samp class="listingcharacter">short sj</samp> becomes positive.

#### Converting short and char

Like <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> has a length of 16 bits. But this conversion is not possible without explicit casting. because of the sign of <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>. Characters are by definition always unsigned. If a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> with a last set bit of the highest value were converted to a <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, the result would be a negative number. Likewise, if a <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> denotes a negative number, the top bit in the <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> would be set, which is undesirable. The explicit conversion always produces only positive numbers.

The loss in typecasting from <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> occurs, for example, in the character encodings for Chinese, Japanese, or Korean characters because, in these cases, the first bit is set in Unicode, which must give way to the unset sign bit when converting to a <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp> .

#### Typecastings of int and char

The <samp class="listingcharacter">print*(...)</samp> method is overloaded with the types <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> , and typecasting results in the desired output, as shown in the following examples:

```
int  c1 = 65;
char c2 = 'A';

                    System.out.println( c1 );              // 65
System.out.println( (int)c2 );         // 65
System.out.println( (char)c1 );        // A
System.out.println( c2 );              // A
System.out.println( (char)(c1 + 1) );  // B
System.out.println( c2 + 1 );          // 66 
```

You can output an integer value in an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> as a character, just as you can output a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> variable as a numeric value. Note that an arithmetic operation on <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp> types results in an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. For this reason, the following expression doesn’t work for <samp class="listingcharacter">char c</samp> :

```
c = c + 1; 
```

The correct version would be the following example:

```
c = (char)(c + 1) 
```

#### Different Value Ranges for Floats and Integers

Of course, the conversion between <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> ![inline image](bilder/2way-arrow.png) <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> can’t be without loss of information. How could that be possible? While both a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> and a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> have 64 bits for data storage, a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> can’t store an integer as efficiently as a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> and has some “overhead” for large exponents. When implicitly converting a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> to a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> , some information-carrying bits may be missed, as illustrated by the following example:

```
long   l = 1111111111111111111L; // 1111111111111111111
double 
                    d = l;                    // 1111111111111111170 (1.11111111111111117E18)
long   m = (long) d;             // 1111111111111111168 
```

Java permits the conversion of a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> into a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> without explicit adaptation and also into an even smaller <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, which is perhaps even stranger since <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> has a precision of only 6 to 7 digits, while <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> has 18 digits. Consider the following example:

```
long  l = 1000000000000000000L;
float 
                    f = l;
System.out.printf( "%f", f );    // 999999984306749440,000000 
```

#### Loss of Material Due to Overflows*

Overflows in calculations can lead to serious errors, as in the crash of Ariane 5 on June 4, 1996, exactly 36.7 seconds after launch. The European Space Agency (ESA) had launched the unmanned rocket, which carried four satellites, from French Guiana. Fortunately, no lives were lost, but the material damage amounted to about $500 million. The project also involved development costs of around $7 billion. The reason for the crash was a rounding error in the Ada program when converting a 64-bit float (the horizontal velocity) to a signed 16-bit integer. Unfortunately, the number was larger than 2 ^(15) – 1 and the conversion wasn’t secured because the programmers hadn’t assumed this range of numbers. An exception occurred, and, as a consequence, the guidance system broke down, and the self-destruct mechanism was triggered as the engines threatened to stall. The really stupid thing about this story is that the software wasn’t essential for the flight and only served for launch preparations. In the event of an interruption during the countdown, the program could have been quickly terminated. Some program parts had been copied, unchanged, from the Ariane 4 software via copy/paste , but the Ariane 5 flew faster.

### 21.1.5    Working without Signs

Except for <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>, all integral data types in Java are signed and encoded in the two’s complement. With a <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> , 8 bits are available for the coding of a value; however, actually only 7 bits are available because 1 bit is used for encoding the sign. The value range is from –128 to +127\. A workaround enables you to exhaust the full range of values and pretend that Java has unsigned data types.

#### Using Byte as an Unsigned Data Type

An important property of explicit typecasting for integer types is that the excess bytes are simply truncated. Let’s look at typecasting in this case with an example:

```
int  l =        0xABCD6F;
byte b = (byte) 0xABCD
                    6F;
System.out.println( Integer.toBinaryString( l ) ); // 101010111100110101101111
System.out.println( Integer.toBinaryString( b ) ); //                  1101111 
```

If a number is in the range from 0 to 255, a <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> can basically store it by its 8 bits. However, Java must be forced, by explicit typecasting, to ignore the sign bit. Only then will the number 255 correspond to 8 set bits because assigning it with <samp class="listingcharacter">byte b = 255;</samp> doesn’t work.

For further processing to be successful, another property must be taken into account. Let’s look at the following example:

```
byte b1 = (byte) 255;
byte b2 = -1;
System.out.println( b1 );  // -1
System.out.println( b2 );  // -1 
```

The bit pattern is the same in both cases, and all bits are set. But the fact that the console output is negative involves another Java feature: Java converts the signed byte to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> during further processing (the parameter type in the method is <samp class="listingcharacter">toBinaryString(int)</samp>). In this conversion process, the sign moves on from the <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> to the <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> . The following example illustrates this conversion process with a binary output:

```
byte b = (byte) 255;
int  i = 255;
System.out.printf( "%d %s%n", b, Integer.toBinaryString(b) );
// -1  11111111111111111111111111111111
System.out.printf( "%d %s%n", i, Integer.toBinaryString(i) );
// 255                         11111111 
```

The assignment of the lower 8 bits of <samp class="listingcharacter">byte b</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">int i</samp> is identical. But whereas with <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> the top 3 bytes are really zero, Java also fills up the top 3 bytes with 255 by automatically adjusting the sign when converting from <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> in the two’s complement. If the calculation is to be continued without a sign, this conversion is disruptive. Java always makes this automatic adjustment when calculating with <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, not just when a method requires the data type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> , in our example.

To get a data value between 0 and 255 during further processing (i.e., to see the byte of an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> unsigned), we’ll cut out the lower 8 bits with the AND operation—all other bits thus remain excluded:

```
byte b = (byte) 255;
System.out.println( b );          // -1
System.out.println( b & 0xff );   // 255 
```

Note that the AND operation leads to the target type <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> .

#### Library Methods for Unsigned Treatments

Always putting a <samp class="listingcharacter">& 0xff</samp> to an expression to hide the top bytes isn’t much work, but it’s not pretty either. Methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">toUnsignedInt(byte)</samp> are much nicer since their names clearly document what’s actually happening.

The following methods in <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp> may be useful:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int toUnsignedInt(byte x)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long toUnsignedLong(byte x)</samp>

Similarly, the following methods in <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> may be useful:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long toUnsignedLong(int x)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toUnsignedString(int i, int radix)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toUnsignedString(int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int parseUnsignedInt(String s, int radix)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int compareUnsigned(int x, int y)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int divideUnsigned(int dividend, int divisor)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int remainderUnsigned(int dividend, int divisor)</samp>

The following methods in <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> may be useful:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String toUnsignedString(long i, int radix)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static String toUnsignedString(long i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long parseUnsignedLong(String s, int radix)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int compareUnsigned(long x, long y)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long divideUnsigned(long dividend, long divisor)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long remainderUnsigned(long dividend, long divisor)</samp>

Finally, the following methods in <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp> may be useful:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int toUnsignedInt(short x)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long toUnsignedLong(short x)</samp>

In addition to simple <samp class="listingcharacter">toUnsigned*(...)</samp> methods in wrapper classes, methods can be added that also allow the conversion of numbers to a string and the parsing of a string. New methods can also be read for <samp class="listingcharacter">integer</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> , which perform unsigned comparisons, division, and residual value calculation.

#### Conversions from byte to char

With a similar way of working, you can also solve the question of how to convert a byte whose <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> value is in the minus range into a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>. The first approach via typecasting <samp class="listingcharacter">(char) byte</samp> is wrong, and only a rectangular box or a question mark will appear in the output, as shown in the following example:

```
byte b = (byte) 'ß';
System.out.println( (char) b );         // Output is  ? 
```

Again, the dilemma is the incorrect sign matching. When the byte is used, it’s first converted to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. The character <samp class="listingcharacter">ß</samp> then becomes –33\. In the next step, this –33 is then converted into a <samp class="listingcharacter">char</samp>. That results in 65,503 and is beyond what we wanted. The problem can be solved by considering only the lower 8 bits of <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> , performed again by hiding some bits via the AND operator. The following notation is correct:

```
char c = (char) (b & 0x00ff);
System.out.println( c );                // Output is ß 
```

As a rule, such an explicit adaptation will rarely occur in the code because Java provides extra classes for the conversion of character encodings.

### 21.1.6    The Shift Operators

In Java, three shift operators can be used to shift the bits of a value by a certain number of positions:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">n << s</samp>: Left shifting of the bits of <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> by <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> positions

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">n >> s</samp>: Arithmetic right shifting by <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> positions with signs

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">n >>> s</samp>: Logical right shifting by <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> positions without signs

These binary shift operators move all bits of a data word (the bit pattern) to the right or left. In the case of the shift, the number of positions by which the shift takes place is written after the binary operator (i.e., in the right operand). Although only two directions are possible, you still must consider whether or not the sign is observed when shifting to the right. This decision is referred to as arithmetic shift (sign remains) or logical shift (sign is filled with 0).

#### n << s

The bits of the operand <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> are shifted <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp> times to the left, taking the sign into account (multiplied by 2 at each step), which results in <samp class="listingcharacter">2</samp> to the power of <samp class="listingcharacter">s</samp>. The bit space that becomes free on the right is always filled with 0\. However, the sign changes as soon as a 1 is shifted from position MSB – 1 to MSB. (MSB stands for Most Significant Bit , that is, the bit with the highest significance in the binary representation.)

###### [»]  Note

Although the data type of the right operand is first an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> with full value range, only values up to 31 are meaningful for <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and up to 63 bits for <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> as shift positions (width) because only the last 5 or 6 bits are considered. Otherwise, the shift is always performed by the value that results from dividing by 32 or 64 as the remainder, so that <samp class="listingcharacter">x << 32</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">x << 0</samp> are also equal. Consider the following examples:

```
System.out.println( 1 << 30 );  // 1073741824
System.out.println( 1 << 31 );  // -2147483648
System.out.println( 1 << 32 );  // 1 
```

#### n >> s (Arithmetic Right Shift)

When shifting to the right, a 1 or a 0 is inserted from the left, depending on whether the sign bit is set or not. So, the left sign bit remains untouched.

###### [eg]  Example

Observe how the bits are shifted to the right:

```
Consumer<Integer> printBinary = value -> {
  String s = String.format( "%32s", Integer.toBinaryString( value ) );
  System.out.println( s.replace( ' ', '0' ) );
};
printBinary.accept( 0b10000000_00000000__00000000_00000000 >> 0 );
printBinary.accept( 0b10000000_00000000__00000000_00000000 >> 1 );
printBinary.accept( 0b10000000_00000000__00000000_00000000 >> 2 );

printBinary.accept( 0b10000000_00000000__00000000_00000000 >>> 0 );
printBinary.accept( 0b10000000_00000000__00000000_00000000 >>> 1 );
printBinary.accept( 0b10000000_00000000__00000000_00000000 >>> 2 );
```

The result is the following output:

```
10000000000000000000000000000000
11000000000000000000000000000000
11100000000000000000000000000000
10000000000000000000000000000000
01000000000000000000000000000000
00100000000000000000000000000000
```

###### [»]  Note

A bit that has been pushed out is lost forever! Consider the following examples:

```
System.out.println( 65535 >> 8 );  // 255
System.out.println(   255 << 8 );  // 65280 
```

In this case, 65,535 = 0xFFFF, but after right shifting 65,535 >> 8, we get 0x00FF = 255\. If we now shift to the left again (i.e., 0x00FF << 8), the result is 0xFF00 = 65,280.

For the integer data types, taking into account the always present sign, a signed integer division by 2 follows for normal right-shifts.

#### n >>> s (Logical Right Shift)

The <samp class="listingcharacter">>>></samp> operator doesn’t take into account the sign of the variable, so an unsigned right-shift is performed. Thus, only zeros are inserted on the left, at the place of the most significant bit; the sign is also shifted.

###### [eg]   Example

You can use shift operators to easily extract the individual bytes of a larger data type, such as a 4-byte <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> , as in the following example:

```
byte b1 = (byte)(v >>> 24),
     b2 = (byte)(v >>> 16),
     b3 = (byte)(v >>>  8),
     b4 = (byte)(v       );
```

For a positive number, this shift has no effect, and the behavior is the same as for the <samp class="listingcharacter">>></samp> operator.

###### [eg]  Example

For negative operands, the following output is particularly exciting:

```
System.out.println(  64 >>> 1 );  // 32
System.out.println( -64 >>> 1 );  // 2147483616 
```

A <samp class="listingcharacter"><<<</samp> operator makes no sense since the left-shift only inserts zeros to the right anyway.

### 21.1.7    Setting, Clearing, Reversing, and Testing a Bit

You can use bit operators together with shift operators to set a bit or to determine whether a bit has been set. Let’s consider the following methods that set, query, invert, and clear a particular bit:

```
static int setBit( int n, int pos ) {
  return n | (1 << pos);
}

static int clearBit( int n, int pos ) {
  return n & ~(1 << pos);
}

static int flipBit( int n, int pos ) {
  return n ^ (1 << pos);
}

static boolean testBit( int n, int pos ) {
  int mask = 1 << pos;

                  return (n & mask) == mask;
  // alternativ: return (n & 1<<pos) != 0;
} 
```

### 21.1.8    Bit Methods of the Integer and Long Classes

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> classes provide a set of static methods for bit manipulation and for querying various bit states of integers. The notation <samp class="listingcharacter">int|long</samp> indicates by <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> the static methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> class and by <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> the static methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> class.

```
final class java.lang.
                Integer|
                Long
extends Number
implements Comparable<Integer|Long> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int Integer.bitCount(long i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int Long.bitCount(long i)</samp>
    Returns the number of set bits.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int Integer.reverse(int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long Long.reverse(long i)</samp>
    Reverses the order of the bits.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int Integer.reverseBytes(int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long Long.reverseBytes(long i)</samp>
    Sets the bytes in the reverse order (i.e., the first byte to the last position, the second byte to the penultimate position, and so on).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int Integer.rotateLeft(int i, int distance)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long Long.rotateLeft(long i, int distance)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int Integer.rotateRight(int i, int distance)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long Long.rotateRight(long i, int distance)</samp>
    Rotates the bits by <samp class="listingcharacter">distance</samp> positions to the left or to the right.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int Integer.highestOneBit(int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long Long.highestOneBit(long i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int Integer.lowestOneBit(int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long lowestOneBit(long i)</samp>
    The result is <samp class="listingcharacter">i</samp> , where all bits are cleared except the bit with the highest/lowest value. In other words, they return a value where only the highest (leftmost) or lowest (rightmost) bit is set. So, only 1 bit is set at most; of course, no bit is set with argument 0, and the result is also 0.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long Long.numberOfLeadingZeros(long i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">static int Integer.numberOfTrailingZeros(int i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long Long.numberOfTrailingZeros(long i)</samp>
    Returns the number of zero bits before the highest or after the lowest set bit.

As an example, [Table 21.7](#21_001.html_t21.7) shows some applications of the static bit methods on the <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> class.

| Static Method of the Long Class | Method Result |
| --- | --- |

| <samp class="listingcharacter">lowestOneBit(0b00011000)</samp> | 8 |

| <samp class="listingcharacter">numberOfLeadingZeros( Long.MIN_VALUE )</samp> | 0 |

## 21.2    Floating Point Arithmetic in Java

Numbers with periods are called floating points , floats, or fractions (fraction numbers) . The term “float” originates from the fact that sliding (shifting) the decimal point represents a change in the number defined as a product of a digit and a power of 10\. Let’s consider the speed of light at 299,792.458 kilometers per second as an example: 299.792,458 = 29.979,2458 × 10 ¹ = 2.997,92458 × 10 ² = 299,792458 × 10 ³ = 29,9792458 × 10 ⁴ = 2,99792458 × 10 ⁵ .

For floats, Java supports the types <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> , which follow the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 754 specification . This standard has been in existence since the mid-1980s. A <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> has a length of 32 bits, while a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> has a length of 64 bits. Related arithmetic operations are defined in the IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic .

###### [»]   Note

Be aware that the accuracy of <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> is actually not that great. Inaccuracy can quickly grow, as shown in the following example:

```
System.out.println( 234567
                8.88f );   //  234567
                9.0 
```

### 21.2.1    Special Values for Infinity, Zero, and Not a Number

The <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> data types can store not only “standard numbers,” but they can also accept a positive or negative zero. Furthermore, Java defines special values for the following numbers:

*   Both positive and negative infinity

*   Not a number (NaN)

#### Positive and Negative Zeros

A positive zero (+0.0) and a negative zero (–0.0) appear with an underflow (the result of a calculation is too small to be represented).

###### [eg]  Example

The following example generates underflows:

```
System.out.println( 1E-322 *  0.0001 );  //  0.0
System.out.println( 1E-322 * -0.0001 );  // -0.0 
```

With the comparison operator <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp>, positive zero is equal to negative zero, so <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0 ==</samp> - <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0</samp> returns the result <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp>. As a result, <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0 > -0.0</samp> is also wrong. However, the bit mask is distinguishable, as shown by the comparison <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.doubleToLongBits(0.0) != Double.doubleToLongBits (-0.0)</samp> .

Another small difference is evident when calculating <samp class="listingcharacter">1.0 /</samp> - <samp class="listingcharacter">0.0</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">1.0 / 0.0</samp> . Due to the limit value, the result goes towards negative infinity and towards positive infinity, respectively.

#### Infinity

The overflow of a mathematical operation results in a positive or negative infinity.

###### [eg]  Example

The following examples multiple two really large values and divide some values by zero:

```
 System.out.println(  1E300 * 1E20 );    //  Infinity
System.out.println( -1E300 * 1E20 );    // -Infinity
System.out.println( 1\. /  0\. );         //  Infinity
System.out.println( 1\. / -0\. );         // -Infinity
```

For these values, the Java library declares two constants in <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp> . Together with the largest and smallest representable floats, these values can be represented by the following constants:

| Value for | Float | Double |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positive infinity | <samp class="listingcharacter">Float.POSITIVE_INFINITY</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY</samp> |
| Negative infinity | <samp class="listingcharacter">Float.NEGATIVE_INFINITY</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY</samp> |
| Smallest value | <samp class="listingcharacter">Float.MIN_VALUE</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.MIN_VALUE</samp> |
| Greatest value | <samp class="listingcharacter">Float.MAX_VALUE</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.MAX_VALUE</samp> |

**Table 21.8**     Special Values and Their Constants

The minimum for <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> values is about 10 ^(–324), and the maximum is about 10 ^(308). In addition, <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp> declare constants for <samp class="listingcharacter">MAX_EXPONENT/MIN_EXPONENT</samp> .

###### [»]  Note

The display of overflow/underflow and of undefined results is only available for floats, not for integers.

```
public final class java.lang.
                    Float|
                    Double
extends Number
implements Comparable<Float|Double> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static boolean isInfinite(float|double v)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if <samp class="listingcharacter">v</samp> is either <samp class="listingcharacter">POSITIVE_INFINITY</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">NEGATIVE_INFINITY</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static boolean isFinite(float|double d)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> is a finite number.

#### The Number That’s Not a Number

NaN is often an error indicator for the result of undefined arithmetic operations, such as 0/0.

###### [eg]   Example

The following examples result in NaN when calculating the root of a negative number and performing a division by zero:

```
System.out.println( Math.sqrt(-4) );     // NaN
System.out.println( 0.0 / 0.0);          // NaN 
```

<samp class="listingcharacter">NaN</samp> is declared as a constant in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> classes. The static method <samp class="listingcharacter">isNaN(...)</samp> tests whether a number is NaN.

```
public final class java.lang.
                    Float|
                    Double
extends Number
implements Comparable<Float|Double> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static final float|double NaN = 0.0 / 0.0;</samp>
    Declaration of NaN for <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static boolean isNaN(float|double v)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the passed number is <samp class="listingcharacter">v</samp> NaN.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean isNaN()</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the current <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp>| <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> object is NaN.

The implementation of <samp class="listingcharacter">isNan(float|double v)</samp> is simple: <samp class="listingcharacter">return v != v</samp> .

#### Everything in Order*

Except for the value NaN, a total order is defined on all floats; that is, they can be enumerated from the smallest number to the largest. At the edge is negative infinity, followed by negative numbers, negative zero, positive zero, positive numbers, and positive infinity. The only thing remaining is the single unsorted number, <samp class="listingcharacter">NaN</samp>. All numerical comparisons, such as <samp class="listingcharacter"><</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter"><=</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">></samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">>=</samp> return <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> with <samp class="listingcharacter">NaN</samp>. A comparison with <samp class="listingcharacter">==</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">false</samp> if one of the operands is <samp class="listingcharacter">NaN</samp>. <samp class="listingcharacter">!=</samp> behaves the other way round; <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> is returned if one of the operands is <samp class="listingcharacter">NaN</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

The following example puts NaN through some equality tests:

```
System.out.println( Double.NaN == Double.NaN );     // false
System.out.println( Double.NaN != Double.NaN );     // true 
```

Since NaN isn’t equal to itself, the following construction, which is usually an infinite loop, is simply skipped with <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> as <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.NaN</samp> :

```
while ( d == d ) { /* Never executed */ } 
```

A NaN value adjusted to an integer, such as <samp class="listingcharacter">(int) Double.NaN</samp>, results in 0, and no exception is thrown. [[ 230 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn21_03)

#### Quiet NaNs*

A problem in floating point arithmetic is that no exceptions indicate errors. NaNs of this kind are also called quiet NaNs ( qNaNs). Thus, as a developer, you must always determine yourself if the result is correct during a calculation. An average numerical processor distinguishes between a qNaN and a signaling NaN ( sNaN ).

### 21.2.2    Standard Notation and Scientific Notation for Floats*

Two notations exist for representing floating point literals: standard and scientific. The scientific notation is an extension of the standard notation. In scientific notation, the decimal places are followed by an <samp class="listingcharacter">E</samp> (or <samp class="listingcharacter">e</samp>) with an exponent to the base 10\. The part before the separator may be introduced by a <samp class="listingcharacter">+</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">-</samp> sign. Also, the exponent can be positive or negative [[ 231 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn21_04) but must be an integer. [Table 21.9](#21_002.html_t21.9) contains three examples.

| Standard | Scientific |
| --- | --- |
| 123450.0 | 1.2345E5 |
| 123450.0 | 1.2345E+5 |
| 0.000012345 | 1.2345E–5 |

**Table 21.9**     Notations of Floats

###### [eg]  Example

Scientific notation is used in the following examples:

```
double x = 3.00e+8;
float  y = 3.00E+8F;
```

### 21.2.3    Mantissas and Exponents*

Internally, floats consist of three parts: a sign, an integer exponent, and a mantissa . While the mantissa determines accuracy, the exponent indicates the magnitude of the number.

The calculation for floats from the three elements looks basically as follows: Sign × Mantissa × 2 ^ Exponent, where the sign can be –1 or +1\. The mantissa m is not a number with an arbitrary value range but is normalized, which means the value is in the range of 1 ⩽ m < 2\. Therefore, a float that starts with 1 is therefore also called 1-plus-form. [[ 232 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn21_05) The initially signed exponent is also not stored directly, but as a biased exponent in an IEEE-encoded representation. Depending on the accuracy, +127 (for <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>) and +1,023 (for <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>) gets added to the exponent. After the calculation, an integer always exists in the representation. The values 127 and 1,023 are referred to as bias .

The sign always costs 1 bit, and the number of bits for exponents and mantissas depends on the data type, as listed in [Table 21.10](#21_002.html_t21.10) .

| Data Type | Number of Bits for the Exponent | Number of Bits for the Mantissa |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> | 8 | 23 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> | 11 | 52 |

**Table 21.10**     Number of Bits for Exponents and Mantissas

###### [eg]  Example

The following examples are encodings for the number 123,456.789 as a <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> and as a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">#</samp> separates sign, exponent, and mantissa:

```
0#10001111#11100010010000001100101
0#10000001111#1110001001000000110010011111101111100111011011001001
```

To get from this representation to the number, you can write the following:

```
BigInteger biasedExponent = new BigInteger( "10001111", 2 );
BigInteger mantissa = new BigInteger( "11100010010000001100101", 2 );
int exponent = (int) Math.pow( 2, biasedExponent.longValue() - 127 );
double m = 1\. + (mantissa.longValue() / Math.pow( 2, 23 ));
System.out.println( exponent * m );  // 123456.7890625 
```

The exponent (without bias) of a float is returned by <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.getExponent(...)</samp> ; thus, applied to our number, the result is 16.

Access to the bit pattern is provided by the methods <samp class="listingcharacter">long doubleToLongBits(double)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">int Float.floatToIntBits(float)</samp>. The reverse methods are <samp class="listingcharacter">double Double.longBitsToDouble(long)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">float Float.intBitsToFloat(int)</samp> .

###### [eg]   Example

Print an alternative representation of <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> floating point numbers:

```
double x = 123456.789;
float  y = 123456.789f;
out.printf( "%016x%n", 
                    Double.doubleToLongBits( x ) ); // 40fe240c9fbe76c9
out.printf( "%08x%n", 
                    Float.floatToIntBits( y ) );     // 47f12065
out.println( Long.toBinaryString( 
                    Double.doubleToLongBits( x ) ) );
out.println( Integer.toBinaryString( 
                    Float.floatToIntBits( y ) ) );
```

###### [»]  Note

Since floats can only be represented as approximations for periodic binary fractions, the result is often not “precise.” Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">0.1</samp> corresponds to a periodic mantissa in IEEE format.

## 21.3    The Members of the Math Class

The <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Math</samp> class is a typical utility class that declares only static methods and class variables for constants. The private constructor can’t be used to create instances of <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> . All operations take place strictly according to the IEEE-754 specification.

###### [»]  History Lesson

Between Java 1.2 and Java 16, the Java compiler supported the <samp class="listingcharacter">strictfp</samp> keyword. The distinction was supposed to allow the JVM to not strictly follow the IEEE-754 specification and thus execute Java programs more quickly on local hardware. However, for the last 20 years, all processors have supported IEEE-754, and the distinction has become irrelevant—all mathematical operations performed by the JVM are as described in the IEEE-754 standard. With the removal of <samp class="listingcharacter">strictfp</samp>, the <samp class="listingcharacter">StrictMath</samp> class also became irrelevant.

### 21.3.1    Object Variables of the Math Class

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class has two public class variables:

```
class java.lang.
                Math 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static final double E</samp>
    The Euler number [[ 233 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn21_06) e = 2.7182818284590452354.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static final double PI</samp>
    The number pi [[ 234 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn21_07) = 3.14159265358979323846.

### 21.3.2     Absolute Values and Signs

The two static <samp class="listingcharacter">abs(...)</samp> methods return the amount of the argument (mathematical amount function: y = | x|). If a negative value is passed as an argument, <samp class="listingcharacter">abs(...)</samp> converts it to a positive value.

A special method is also <samp class="listingcharacter">copySign(double, double)</samp> . It determines the sign of a float and transfers it to another number.

```
class java.lang.
                Math 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int abs(int x)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long abs(long x)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static float abs(float x)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static double abs(double x)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static double copySign(double magnitude, double sign)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static float copySign(float magnitude, float sign)</samp>
    Returns <samp class="listingcharacter">magnitude</samp>, but with the sign of <samp class="listingcharacter">sign</samp> .

###### [»]  Note

For exactly one value, <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.abs(int)</samp> can’t return a positive, and the result is truly negative: –2,147,483,648\. This number is the smallest representable <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> number ( <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.MIN_VALUE</samp>), while +2,147,483,648 doesn’t fit into an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> at all! The largest <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> number that can be represented is 2,147,483,647 ( <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.MAX_VALUE</samp>). What should <samp class="listingcharacter">abs(-2147483648)</samp> actually result in?

#### Querying Signs

The static method <samp class="listingcharacter">signum(value)</samp> returns a numeric return for the sign of <samp class="listingcharacter">value</samp>, namely, “+1” for positive, “–1” for negative numbers, and “0” for 0\. The method isn’t quite logically distributed between the classes <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> for floats and <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp>/ <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> for integers. Consider the following examples:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">.signum(int i), java.lang.</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">.signum(long i)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">.signum(double d), java.lang.</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">.signum(float f)</samp>

The static <samp class="listingcharacter">max(...)</samp> methods return the larger of the passed values. The static <samp class="listingcharacter">min(...)</samp> methods return the smaller of two values.

```
class java.lang.
                Math
```

### 21.3.4    Rounding Values

To round values, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class provides five static methods:

```
class java.lang.
                Math 
```

#### Rounding Up and Down with ceil(double) and floor(double)

The static method <samp class="listingcharacter">ceil(double)</samp> rounds a value up and returns the next higher integer (but as a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, not a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>) if the number isn’t already an integer. The static method <samp class="listingcharacter">floor(double)</samp> rounds down to the next lower integer. Consider the following examples:

```
System.out.println( Math.
                    ceil(-99.1) );    //  -99.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    floor(-99.1) );   // -100.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    ceil(-99) );      //  -99.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    floor(-99) );     //  -99.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    ceil(-.5) );      //   -0.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    floor(-.5) );     //   -1.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    ceil(-.01) );     //   -0.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    floor(-.01) );    //   -1.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    ceil(0.1) );      //    1.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    floor(0.1) );     //    0.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    ceil(.5) );       //    1.0

                    System.out.println( Math.
                    floor(.5) );      //    0.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    ceil(99) );       //   99.0
System.out.println( Math.
                    floor(99) );      //   99.0 
```

#### Commercial Rounding via round(...)

The static methods <samp class="listingcharacter">round(double)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">round(float)</samp> round to the nearest integer of type <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> . Whole numbers aren’t rounded up. This is called commercial rounding. You can use <samp class="listingcharacter">round(...)</samp> as a counterpart to the typecasting <samp class="listingcharacter">(long) doublevalue</samp> , as in the following examples:

```
System.out.println( Math.round(1.01) );     //  1
System.out.println( Math.round(1.4) );      //  1
System.out.println( Math.round(1.5) );      //  2
System.out.println( Math.round(1.6) );      //  2
System.out.println( (int) 1.6 );            //  1
System.out.println( Math.round(30) );       // 30
System.out.println( Math.round(-2.1) );     // -2
System.out.println( Math.round(-2.9) );     // -3
System.out.println( (int) -2.9 );           // -2 
```

###### [»]  Internal Affairs

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.round(int)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.round(long)</samp> methods are programmed into Java. They add 0.5 to the current parameter and pass the result to the static <samp class="listingcharacter">floor( double)</samp> method.

```
public static long round( double a ) {
  return (long) floor( a + 0.5 );
}
```

**Listing 21.4**     java.lang.Math, round(double) (Slightly Shortened)

#### Fair Rounding with rint(double)

<samp class="listingcharacter">rint(double)</samp> is comparable to <samp class="listingcharacter">round(...)</samp>, except that <samp class="listingcharacter">rint(double)</samp> is “fair,” meaning that <samp class="listingcharacter">rint(double)</samp> rounds up or down at 0.5 depending on whether the adjacent number is odd or even.

```
System.out.println( Math.round(-1.5) );     //   -1
System.out.println( Math.rint( -1.5) );     // -2.0

                    System.out.println( Math.round(-2.5) );     //   -2
System.out.println( Math.rint( -2.5) );     // -2.0
System.out.println( Math.round( 1.5) );     //    2
System.out.println( Math.rint(  1.5) );     //  2.0
System.out.println( Math.round( 2.5) );     //    3
System.out.println( Math.rint(  2.5) );     //  2.0 
```

**Listing 21.5**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/math/Rounding3Demo.java, main()

With a consistent rounding up or down, errors naturally propagate more awkwardly than with this 50/50 strategy.

###### [eg]  Example

The static <samp class="listingcharacter">rint(double)</samp> method can also be used when numbers should be rounded to two decimal places. If <samp class="listingcharacter">d</samp> is of type <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, the expression <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.rint(d*100.0)/100.0</samp> returns the rounded number.

```
class Round2Scales {
  public static double roundScale2( double d ) {
    return Math.rint( d * 100 ) / 100.;
  }

  public static void main( String[] args ) {
    System.out.println( roundScale2(+1.341 ) );    //  1.34
    System.out.println( roundScale2(-1.341 ) );    // -1.34
    System.out.println( roundScale2(+1.345 ) );    //  1.34
    System.out.println( roundScale2(-1.345 ) );    // -1.34

    System.out.println( roundScale2(+1.347 ) );    //  1.35
    System.out.println( roundScale2(-1.347 ) );    // -1.35
  }
} 
```

### 21.3.5    Remainder of an Integer Division*

Besides the remainder operator <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp> , which calculates the remainder of the division, a static method named <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.IEEEremainder(double, double)</samp> can also calculate the remainder.

```
 double a = 44.0;
double b = 2.2;
System.out.println( a / b );                      // 20.0
System.out.println( 
                a % b );                      // 2.1999999999999966
System.out.println( 
                Math.IEEEremainder( a, b ) ); // -3.552713678800501E-15 
```

**Listing 21.7**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/math/IEEEremainder.java, main()

The second result is almost 2.2 with the mathematical inaccuracy, but slightly smaller, so the algorithm couldn’t subtract another 2.2\. The static method <samp class="listingcharacter">IEEEremainder(double, double)</samp> returns a result close to zero (–0.0000000000000035527136788005), which is better because 44.0 can be divided by 2.2 without a remainder, so the remainder would actually be 0.

```
class java.lang.
                Math 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static double IEEEremainder(double dividend, double divisor)</samp>
    Returns the remainder of the division of the dividend and divisor, as required by the IEEE-754 standard.

A separate static method that sometimes returns better results—with the values 44 and 2.2 being actually 0.0—is shown in the following example:

```
public static double remainder( double a, double b ) {
  return Math.signum(a) *
         (Math.abs(a) - Math.abs(b) * Math.floor(Math.abs(a)/Math.abs(b)));
} 
```

### 21.3.6    Division with Rounding toward Negative Infinity and Alternative Remainders*

Integer division in Java is simple: convert the integers to floats, perform the division, and truncate everything after the decimal point. For example, <samp class="listingcharacter">3 / 2</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">9 / 2</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">4</samp>. If the result is negative, either because of a negative dividend or because of a negative divisor, the same thing happens: <samp class="listingcharacter">-9 / 2</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">-4</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">9 / -2</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">-4</samp> . Let’s look at rounding these numbers.

If the result of a division is positive and has a decimal part, the result is made a little smaller by truncating the decimal places (i.e., by rounding down). If <samp class="listingcharacter">3 / 2</samp> would be 1.5 for floats, it’s <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> for an integer division rounded down. With negative results of a division, the reverse is true because, by truncating the decimal places, the number becomes slightly greater. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">-3 / 2</samp> is, strictly speaking, –1.5, but in integer division, it is <samp class="listingcharacter">-1</samp>. But <samp class="listingcharacter">-1</samp> is greater than –1.5, and therefore, Java applies a procedure that rounds to zero.

#### The floorDiv(...) Method to Round to Negative Infinity

Three methods don’t round to zero if the result of a division is negative but instead round to negative infinity (i.e., also in the direction of the smaller number, as is the case with positive results).

```
class java.lang.
                    Math 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int floorDiv(int x, int y)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long floorDiv(long x, long y)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long floorDiv(long x, int y)</samp>

In practical terms, <samp class="listingcharacter">4/3</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.floorDiv(4, 3)</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp>, but where <samp class="listingcharacter">-4 / 3</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">-1</samp>, in contrast, <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.floorDiv(-4, 3)</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">-2</samp> .

#### The floorMod(...) Method to Round to Negative Infinity

The division also appears indirectly in the calculation of the remainder. Remember: The relationship between the division <samp class="listingcharacter">a/b</samp> and the remainder <samp class="listingcharacter">a%b</samp> ( <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> is called dividend , <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> divisor ) is <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)(a/b) * b + (a%b) = a</samp>. A division exists in the equation, but with two kinds of divisions ( <samp class="listingcharacter">a / b</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">floorDiv(a, b)</samp>), consequently, two kinds of remainders must also exist, which differ if the signs are different. For this reason, besides <samp class="listingcharacter">a % b</samp>, the library method <samp class="listingcharacter">floorMod(a, b)</samp> is available, and the relationship between <samp class="listingcharacter">floorMod(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">floorDiv(...)</samp> is <samp class="listingcharacter">floorDiv(a, b) * b + floorMod(a, b) == b</samp>. A transformation of the equation is followed by <samp class="listingcharacter">floorMod(a, b) = a - (floorDiv(a, b) * b)</samp>. The result is in the range <samp class="listingcharacter">-abs(b)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">abs(b)</samp>, and the sign of the result is determined by the divisor <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> (for the <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp> operator, the dividend <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> ).

The Javadoc for <samp class="listingcharacter">floorMod(…)</samp> shows an example with the values 4 and 3 with different signs.

| floorMod(…) Method | % Operator |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">floorMod(+4, +3) == +1</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">+4 % +3 == +1</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">floorMod(+4, -3) == -2</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">+4 % -3 == +1</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">floorMod(-4, +3) == +2</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">-4 % +3 == -1</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">floorMod(-4, -3) == -1</samp> | <samp class="listingcharacter">-4 % -3 == -1</samp> |

**Table 21.11**     Results of Different Ways to Calculate a Remainder

If the signs for <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> are identical, the results of <samp class="listingcharacter">floorMod(a, b)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">a % b</samp> will also be the same. The examples in the table also demonstrate the difference in the result sign, which comes once from the dividend ( <samp class="listingcharacter">%</samp>) and once from the divisor ( <samp class="listingcharacter">floorMod(...)</samp>). The completely different events (apart from the sign) in the pairs (+4, –3) and (–4, +3) simply result from different results of the division.

```
class java.lang.
```

The mathematical operation a × b + c occurs frequently in calculations, so that processors today can perform this calculation in an optimized way, that is, faster and with a higher accuracy. <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> has the <samp class="listingcharacter">fma(...)</samp> method for the fused multiply-accumulate function from the IEEE-754 standard.

### 21.3.8    Square Root and Exponential Methods

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class also provides methods for calculating the square root and other exponential methods:


*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static double sqrt(double x)</samp>
    Returns the square root of <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp>; <samp class="listingcharacter">sqrt</samp> stands for square root .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static double cbrt(double a)</samp>
    Calculates the cube root of <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static double hypot(double x, double y)</samp>
    Calculates the square root of x ² + y ², also called Euclidean distance. Could be rewritten as <samp class="listingcharacter">sqrt(x*x + y*y)</samp>, but <samp class="listingcharacter">hypot(...)</samp> provides better accuracy and performance.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static double scalb(double d, double scaleFactor)</samp>

Can in principle also be written as <samp class="listingcharacter">d * Math.pow(2, scaleFactor)</samp>, but <samp class="listingcharacter">scalb(...)</samp> provides better performance.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">static double exp(double x)</samp>
    Returns the exponential value of <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> to the base e (of the Euler number e = 2.71828...), for instance, e ^x .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static double expm1(double x)</samp>
    Returns the exponential value of <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> to the base e minus 1 (i.e., e ^x – 1). Calculations near zero can express <samp class="listingcharacter">expm1(x) + 1</samp> more precisely than <samp class="listingcharacter">exp(x)</samp> .

#### The Question of 0.0/0.0 and 0.0^0.0*

As you’ve learned, 0.0/0.0 results in a straightforward NaN. In contrast to the integer values, however, we don’t get an exception in this case because the special number NaN has been introduced especially for this purpose. You might ask what exactly results in <samp class="listingcharacter">(long)(double)(0.0/0.0)</samp>. The Java Language Specification (JLS) states [[ 235 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn21_08) that converting a floating point value NaN to an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> 0 or to a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> results in 0.

Another exciting question concerns the result of 0.0 ^(0.0). To calculate general powers, the static function <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.pow(double a, double b)</samp> is used. From your school days, you may recall that we take the square root of a number when the exponent <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> is exactly ½. But now we want to know what happens if <samp class="listingcharacter">a = b = 0</samp>. The JLS requires that the result is always 1.0 if the exponent <samp class="listingcharacter">b</samp> is equal to –0.0 or 0.0\. Thus, in this case, base <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> doesn’t matter at all. In some algebra books, 0 ⁰ is treated as undefined. However, it makes perfect sense to define 0 ⁰ as 1 since otherwise numerous special treatments for 0 would be required. [[ 236 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn21_09)

### 21.3.9    The Logarithm*

The logarithm is the inverse function of the exponential function. The exponential function and the logarithm are related by the following relationship: If y = a ^x, then x = log [a]( y). The logarithm calculated by <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.log(double)</samp> is the natural logarithm to base e. In mathematics, this relationship is indicated by ln ( logarithmus naturalis, natural logarithm). Logarithms with base 10 are referred to as common logarithm or Briggsian logarithm and are abbreviated as lg, while logarithms with base 2 ( binary logarithm, dual logarithm) are abbreviated as lb. In Java, the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">log10(double)</samp> exists for the brig logarithm lg, but not for the binary logarithm lb, which must still be emulated. In general, the following conversion applies: log [b]( x) = log [a]( x) ÷ log [a]( b ).

###### [eg]   Example

In the following example, a custom static method calculates the logarithm for base 2:

```
public static double lb( double x ) {
  return Math.log( x ) / Math.log( 2.0 );
}
class java.lang.
                Math 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static double log(double a)</samp>
    Calculates the logarithm of <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> to the base e .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static double log10(double a)</samp>
    Returns the logarithm of <samp class="listingcharacter">a</samp> to the base 10.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static double log1p(double x)</samp>
    Returns log ( x ) + 1.

### 21.3.11    Random Numbers

Positive random floats between greater than or equal to 0.0 and truly less than 1.0 are returned by the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.random()</samp> . The return value is <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and a type conversion to <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> always leads to the result 0.

To have values in a different range of values, a simple solution is to expand the random numbers from <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.random()</samp> to the desired range of values by multiplication (scaling) and shift them appropriately by addition (an offset). To obtain random integer numbers between <samp class="listingcharacter">min</samp> (inclusive) and <samp class="listingcharacter">max</samp> (inclusive), you can write the following code:

```
public static long random( long min, long max ) {
  return min + Math.round( Math.random() * (max - min) );
} 
```
