A custom implementation isn’t necessary because the <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> class—and its subclasses—provide several useful object methods like <samp class="listingcharacter">nextInt(n)</samp>. The implementation is not in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class itself, but in <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp>, which we’ll take a closer look at in [Section 21.5](#21_005.html_h21.5) .

## 21.4     Accuracy and the Value Range of Type and Overflow Control*

Data types in Java always have a certain number of bytes, and thus the value range is known. However, an operation can run beyond this range of values.

### 21.4.1    The Largest and Smallest Values

For each primitive data type, a separate class in Java is available with various methods and constants. The classes <samp class="listingcharacter">Byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> have the constants <samp class="listingcharacter">MIN_VALUE</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">MAX_VALUE</samp> for their minimum and maximum value ranges. The <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> classes also have the important constants <samp class="listingcharacter">NEGATIVE_INFINITY</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">POSITIVE_INFINITY</samp> for negative and positive infinity as well as <samp class="listingcharacter">NaN</samp> (undefined).

###### [»]  Note

<samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.MIN_VALUE</samp> represents the smallest value the integer can assume: –2,147,483,648\. However, <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.MIN_VALUE</samp> represents the smallest positive number (best approximation to 0) that a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> can represent (4.9E-324).

When we speak of “double precision,” especially when hearing the word <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> as opposed to <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, you must be careful because <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> provides more than twice as precise a mantissa, at least according to the number of bits. However, this precision doesn’t say anything about the number of decimal places.

###### [eg]  Craft Task

Ask yourself the question, “Why are the expenses the way they are?” when considering the following example:

```
double d1 = 0.02d;
float  f1 = 0.02f;
System.out.println( 
                    d1 == f1 );         // false
System.out.println( 
                    (float) d1 == f1 ); // true

double d2 = 0.02f;
float  f2 = 0.02f;
System.out.println( 
                    d2 == f2 );         // true 
```

### 21.4.2    Overflow and Everything Entirely Exact

For some mathematical questions, you must determine whether operations (such as addition, subtraction, or multiplication) may go beyond the valid number range (i.e., leave the integer range of an integer of 32 bits, for example). If the result of a calculation doesn’t fit into the value range of a number, this error won’t be displayed by Java by default; neither the compiler nor the runtime environment will report this problem. Also, no exception is raised since no built-in overflow control is available in Java.

###### [eg]  Example

Mathematically, a × a ÷ a = a is correct, so, for example, 100,000 × 100,000 ÷ 100,000 = 100,000\. In Java, the result is different because overflow occurs in <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> at 100,000 × 100,000\. Consider the following example:

```
System.out.println( 100_000 * 100_000 / 100_000 );     // 14100 
```

This statement prints <samp class="listingcharacter">14100</samp>. If we increase the data type to <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> by placing an <samp class="listingcharacter">L</samp> after <samp class="listingcharacter">100_000</samp>, we’re still safe with this multiplication since a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> can store the result, as in the following example:

```
System.out.println( 100_000
                    L * 100_000 / 100_000 );    // 100000 
```

#### Multiplying int Integers

The <samp class="listingcharacter">*</samp> operator doesn’t perform any data type matching on <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, so multiplying two <samp class="listingcharacter">ints</samp> again returns <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. But the product can quickly run beyond the acceptable value range, thus causing an overflow. Even if the product is written to a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> variable, the conversion from <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> doesn’t occur until after the multiplication. Consider the following examples:

```
int  i = Integer.MAX_VALUE * Integer.MAX_VALUE;
long l = Integer.MAX_VALUE * Integer.MAX_VALUE;
System.out.println( i );     // 1
System.out.println( l );     // 1 
```

If two <samp class="listingcharacter">ints</samp> must be multiplied without overflow, one of the two factors must be adjusted to <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> so that the calculation leads to the correct result ( <samp class="listingcharacter">4611686014132420609</samp> ), as in the following example:

```
System.out.println( Integer.MAX_VALUE * (long) Integer.MAX_VALUE );
System.out.println( (long) Integer.MAX_VALUE * Integer.MAX_VALUE ); 
```

Because this typecasting can be quickly forgotten and isn’t particularly explicit, the <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class provides the static method <samp class="listingcharacter">long multiplyFull(int x, int y)</samp>, which performs the typecasting for you using <samp class="listingcharacter">(long)x * (long)y</samp> .

#### Multiplying Long Integers

No primitive data type has more than 64 bits (8 bytes), so the result of <samp class="listingcharacter">long * long</samp> with its 128 bits only fits completely into a <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp>. However, one method allows you to query the upper 64 bits of a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> multiplication separately, using the <samp class="listingcharacter">multiplyHigh(long x, long y)</samp> method in <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> .

###### [eg]   Example

Example of multiplying large numbers:

```
BigInteger v = BigInteger.valueOf( Long.MAX_VALUE )
                         .multiply( BigInteger.valueOf( Long.MAX_VALUE ) );
System.out.println( v );  // 85070591730234615847396907784232501249

long lowLong = Long.MAX_VALUE * Long.MAX_VALUE;
long highLong = 
                        Math.multiplyHigh( Long.MAX_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE );
BigInteger w = BigInteger.valueOf( highLong )
                         .shiftLeft( 64 )
                         .add( BigInteger.valueOf( lowLong ) );
System.out.println( w );  // 85070591730234615847396907784232501249 
```

#### Detecting an Overflow

All the methods listed below in <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> provide overflow detection:

```
class java.lang.
                    Math 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int addExact(int x, int y)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long addExact(long x, long y)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int subtractExact(int x, int y)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long subtractExact(long x, long y)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int multiplyExact(int x, int y)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int multiplyExact(long x, int y)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long multiplyExact(long x, long y)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int toIntExact(long value)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int incrementExact(int a)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long incrementExact(long a)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int decrementExact(int a)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long decrementExact(long a)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static int negateExact(int a)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static long negateExact(long a)</samp>

All methods throw an <samp class="listingcharacter">ArithmeticException</samp> if the operation isn’t feasible—the last one, for example, if <samp class="listingcharacter">(int)value != value</samp>. Unfortunately, Java doesn’t declare subclasses like <samp class="listingcharacter">UnderflowException</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">OverflowException</samp> and only reports anything of type <samp class="listingcharacter">ArithmeticException</samp> with the error message “xxx overflow,” even if it’s actually an underflow.

###### [eg]   Example

As shown in the following example, subtracting 1 from the smallest integer using <samp class="listingcharacter">subtractExact(...)</samp> leads to an exception:

```
subtractExact( Integer.MIN_VALUE, 1 );    // 

                         ArithmeticException 
```

###### [»]  Comparison with C#

C# behaves the same way as Java and doesn’t respond to an overflow by default. However, special <samp class="listingcharacter">checked</samp> blocks can report an <samp class="listingcharacter">OverflowException</samp> when an overflow occurs in basic arithmetic operations. The following code raises this exception: <samp class="listingcharacter">checked { int val = int.MaxValue; val++; }</samp>. Such <samp class="listingcharacter">checked</samp> blocks don’t exist in Java. If you require this special overflow control, you must use the methods and then also rewrite a <samp class="listingcharacter">val++</samp> to <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.addExact(val, 1)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.incrementExact(val)</samp> .

### 21.4.3    What in the World Does the ulp Method Do?

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class provides special methods if you’re concerned about computational (im)precision and may work with numerical approximations.

The distance from one float to the next isn’t always the same due to the internal structure. The exact distance of a number to the next possible one is shown by <samp class="listingcharacter">ulp(double)</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">ulp(float)</samp>. This funny method name is an abbreviation for “unit in the last place.” The exact next higher/lower number is determined by the methods <samp class="listingcharacter">nextUp(float|double)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">nextDown(float|double)</samp>, which use <samp class="listingcharacter">nextAfter(...)</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

Ask yourself the question, “What comes after and before 1?” when considering the following example:

```
System.out.printf( "%.16f%n", Math.
                    nextUp( 1 ) );
System.out.printf( "%.16f%n", Math.
                    nextDown( 1 ) );
System.out.printf( "%.16f%n", Math.
                    nextAfter( 1, Double.
                    POSITIVE_INFINITY ) );
System.out.printf( "%.16f%n", Math.
                    nextAfter( 1, Double.
                    NEGATIVE_INFINITY ) );
```

The result is the following output:

```
1.000000119209289
0.9999999403953552
1.0000001192092896
0.9999999403953552
```

<samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">next</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Up</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">(d)</samp> is an abbreviation for <samp class="listingcharacter">nextAfter(d, Double.</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">POSITIVE_INFINITY</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">next</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">Down</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">(d)</samp> is an abbreviation for <samp class="listingcharacter">nextAfter(d, Double.</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">NEGATIVE_INFINITY</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">)</samp>. If the second argument of <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.nextAfter(...)</samp> is larger than the first, then the next larger number will be returned; if the second argument is smaller, then the next smaller number will be returned. In case of equality, the same number comes back.

| Method | Return |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.ulp( 0.00001 )</samp> | 0.000000000000000000001694065895 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.ulp( –1 )</samp> | 0.00000011920928955078125 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.ulp( 1 )</samp> | 0.00000011920928955078125 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.ulp( 2 )</samp> | 0.0000002384185791015625 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.ulp( 10E30 )</samp> | 1125899906842624 |

**Table 21.12**     As the Numbers Get Bigger, the Jumps Also Get Bigger

#### A Quantum of Inaccuracy

The usual mathematical floating point operations have a ulp of ½, which is as accurate as possible. The Javadoc will indicate how much in ulps <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> methods can deviate from the real result. Calculation errors can’t be avoided, especially with complex methods. Thus, <samp class="listingcharacter">sin(double)</samp> may have a possible inaccuracy of 1 ulp; <samp class="listingcharacter">atan2(double, double)</samp>, an inaccuracy of at most 2 ulps; and <samp class="listingcharacter">sinh(double)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">cosh(double)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">tanh(double)</samp> , inaccuracies of 2.5 ulp.

The <samp class="listingcharacter">ulp(...)</samp> method is interesting for testing because you can always implement deviations in the appropriate order of magnitude. For small numbers, a difference of perhaps 0.001 makes sense; for larger numbers, the tolerance may be larger.

Java declares three special constants in the <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Float</samp> classes, which can be illustrated via <samp class="listingcharacter">nextAfter(...)</samp>. Let’s look at some examples using <samp class="listingcharacter">Double</samp> :

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">MIN_VALUE</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">nextUp(0.0)</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.longBitsToDouble(0x0010000000000000L)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">MIN_NORMAL</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">MIN_VALUE/(nextUp(1.0)-1.0)</samp> = <samp class="listingcharacter">Double.longBitsToDouble(0x1L)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">MAX_VALUE = nextAfter(POSITIVE_INFINITY, 0.0) =</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">   Double.longBitsToDouble(0x7fefffffffffffffL)</samp>

## 21.5    Random Numbers: Random, ThreadLocalRandom, and SecureRandom

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class provides a simple method for random numbers: <samp class="listingcharacter">random()</samp> . Internally, however, this method based on a different class that you can also use directly, thus enabling you to ask for more than just random numbers between 0 and 1.

The usual random numbers of Java are actually pseudo-random numbers because they are generated by a mathematical algorithm. Good “random values” are repeated only after exceedingly long sequences, have no obvious context, and are generated quickly. Perfect random numbers would never be predictable: The probability for each number would always be the same—regardless of the preceding values—and the sequences would never be repeated.

### 21.5.1    The Random Class

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> class in the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util</samp> package implements a generator for pseudo-random numbers. Unlike <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.random()</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> doesn’t provide any static functions but does provide a set of <samp class="listingcharacter">next*(...)</samp> methods. The static function <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.random()</samp> uses a <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> object internally.

#### Creating Random Objects with a Seed

Every <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> object needs an initial value for the calculation. The initial value for each random number is a 48-bit seed. “Seed ” indicates that, in the generation of random numbers, as with plants, a seed leads to offspring. From this initial value, the random number generator then determines the following numbers by linear congruences. (Thus, the numbers aren’t really random but instead obey a mathematical procedure.)

At the beginning, you’ll need an instance of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> class. This instance is initialized with a random value (data type <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>), which is then used for the subsequent calculations. This initial value shapes the entire sequence of generated random numbers, although how the sequence behaves isn’t obvious. One thing is certain: Two <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> objects created with the same initial values also return the same sequence of random numbers, namely: If the seed is the same, of course, the sequence of random numbers is always the same. For testing, this similarity isn’t bad at all. The parameterless constructor of <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> initializes the start value with the sum of a magic start value and <samp class="listingcharacter">System.nanoTime()</samp> .

```
class 
                    Random
implements RandomGenerator, Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Random()</samp>
    Creates a new random number generator.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">Random(long seed)</samp>
    Creates a new random number generator and uses the <samp class="listingcharacter">seed</samp> parameter as a start value.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void setSeed(long seed)</samp>
    Resets the seed. The generator subsequently behaves in the same way as a generator freshly created with this seed value.

#### Generating Single Random Numbers

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> class generates random numbers for four different data types: <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> (32 bit), <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> (64 bit), <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> . Four methods are available for this purpose:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int nextInt()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">long nextLong()</samp>
    Returns the next pseudo-random number from the entire value range (i.e., between <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.MIN_VALUE</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer.MAX_VALUE</samp> or between <samp class="listingcharacter">Long.MIN_VALUE</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">Long.MAX_VALUE</samp> ).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">float nextFloat()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">double nextDouble()</samp>
    Returns the next pseudo-random number between 0.0 and 1.0.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int nextInt(int range)</samp>
    Returns an <samp class="listingcharacter">int pseudo-random number</samp> in the range 0 to <samp class="listingcharacter">range</samp> .

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> class has a special method for generating a series of random numbers all at once: the <samp class="listingcharacter">nextBytes(byte[])</samp> method. The parameter is a byte array, which is completely filled with random numbers.

All methods for generating random numbers are based on the <samp class="listingcharacter">next(int bits)</samp> method. This method is implemented in <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp>, but due to its <samp class="listingcharacter">protected</samp> visibility, the method is only visible from an inheriting class. Subclasses are possible because <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> is a normal public non-final class.

#### Pseudo-Random Numbers in the Normal Distribution*

Via a special method, you can obtain random numbers that satisfy a normal distribution : <samp class="listingcharacter">nextGaussian()</samp>. This method works internally according to the polar method and generates two normally distributed numbers from two independent pseudo-random numbers. The midpoint is 0, and the standard deviation is 1\. The values returned by <samp class="listingcharacter">nextGaussian()</samp> are <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> numbers and often approximate 0. Larger numbers are rather rare.

```
class java.util.
                    Random
implements Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">double nextGaussian()</samp>
    Returns the nearest random number in a Gaussian normal distribution with 0.0 as the midpoint and a standard deviation of 1.0.

#### Generating a Stream of Random Numbers*

If several random numbers are required, a loop with repeated calls of <samp class="listingcharacter">next*()</samp> isn’t necessary. Instead, two varieties of methods in <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> return a bunch of random numbers.

The first approach uses an array:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">void nextBytes(byte[] bytes)</samp>
    Fills the <samp class="listingcharacter">bytes</samp> array with random bytes.

Other methods provide a stream of random numbers:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">IntStream ints(…)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">LongStream longs(…)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">DoubleStream doubles(…)</samp>

###### [eg]  Example

The following example returns ten random numbers that are probably prime numbers:

```
LongStream stream = new Random().longs()
                       .filter( v -> BigInteger.valueOf( v ).isProbablePrime(5) );
stream.limit( 10 ).forEach( System.out::println );
```

The methods <samp class="listingcharacter">ints(...)</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">longs(...)</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">doubles(...)</samp> come in four flavors, as shown in [Table 21.13](#21_005.html_t21.13) .

| Parameterization | Explanation |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">IntStream ints()</samp> | Returns an infinite stream of random numbers in the entire range of values of the primitives. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">LongStream longs()</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">DoubleStream doubles()</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ints(long streamSize)</samp> | Returns a stream with <samp class="listingcharacter">streamSize</samp> random numbers. |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">longs(long streamSize)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">doubles(long streamSize)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ints(int randomNumberOrigin,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">int randomNumberBound)</samp> | Returns an infinite stream of random numbers with values in the range from <samp class="listingcharacter">randomNumberOrigin</samp> (inclusive) to <samp class="listingcharacter">randomNumberBound</samp> (exclusive). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">longs(long randomNumberOrigin,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">long randomNumberBound)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">doubles(double randomNumberOrigin,</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">double randomNumberBound)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">ints(long streamSize, int</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">randomNumberOrigin, int</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">randomNumberBound)</samp> | Returns a stream with <samp class="listingcharacter">streamSize</samp> random numbers with values in the range from <samp class="listingcharacter">randomNumberOrigin</samp> (inclusive) to <samp class="listingcharacter">randomNumberBound</samp> (exclusive). |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">longs(long streamSize, long</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">randomNumberOrigin, long</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">randomNumberBound)</samp> |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">doubles(long streamSize, double</samp> <samp class="listingcharacter">randomNumberOrigin, double</samp>
<samp class="listingcharacter">randomNumberBound)</samp> |

**Table 21.13**     Stream Methods of the Random Class

###### [eg]  Example

The following example outputs five random floats in the range from 10 to 20:

```
new Random().doubles(5, 10, 20).forEach( System.out::println );
```

### 21.5.2    ThreadLocalRandom

The <samp class="listingcharacter">ThreadLocalRandom</samp> class is a subclass of <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> and overrides central methods because <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> has a safeguard against concurrent access that <samp class="listingcharacter">ThreadLocalRandom</samp> doesn’t have—an object of this class should only ever be used in the same thread. For this reason, a <samp class="listingcharacter">ThreadLocalRandom</samp> isn’t created via <samp class="listingcharacter">new</samp> , but a static factory method returns the object associated with the respective thread.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example determines two random numbers between 1 and 10:

```
Random threadLocalRandom = ThreadLocalRandom.current();
System.out.println( threadLocalRandom.nextInt( 1, 10 + 1 ) );
System.out.println( threadLocalRandom.nextInt( 1, 10 + 1 ) );
```

### 21.5.3    The SecureRandom Class*

The <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> class is in a dilemma: producing good and random numbers, on one hand, but also calculating quickly on the other hand. <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp> doesn’t generate cryptographically decent numbers; for this scenario, the implementation would need more effort (which costs more time). Still, such advanced random numbers are not generally necessary in everyday life.

Random numbers that are cryptographically more sound are provided by <samp class="listingcharacter">java.security.SecureRandom</samp>, a subclass of <samp class="listingcharacter">Random</samp>. This subclass provides the same set of <samp class="listingcharacter">next*(...)</samp> methods, but the quality of the random numbers is better. This isn’t due to <samp class="listingcharacter">SecureRandom</samp> itself because the class doesn’t implement any algorithms, but to the referenced replaceable random number providers. An implementation is provided by <samp class="listingcharacter">SecureRandom.getInstanceStrong()</samp> or by the parameterless constructor as well. In this case, however, the <samp class="listingcharacter">SecureRandom</samp> object doesn’t necessarily have to be “strong,” that is, it doesn’t have to meet the highest cryptographic standards. The difference exists because <samp class="listingcharacter">new SecureRandom().getAlgorithm().toString()</samp> returns SHA1PRNG, and <samp class="listingcharacter">SecureRandom.getInstanceStrong().getAlgorithm().toString()</samp> returns Windows PRNG.

## 21.6    Large Numbers*

The fixed length of the primitive data types <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> for integer values, and <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> for floating point values, isn’t sufficient for various numerical calculations. Arbitrarily large numbers in cryptography and precise resolutions in financial mathematics are particularly desirable. For such applications, two classes in the <samp class="listingcharacter">math</samp> package are available: <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> for integers and <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> for floats, as shown in [Figure 21.1](#21_006.html_f21.1) .

[![The Inheritance Relationship of BigInteger and BigDecimal](bilderklein/klein21_001.png)](img-f21.1.html)

**Figure 21.1**     The Inheritance Relationship of BigInteger and BigDecimal

### 21.6.1    The BigInteger Class

The <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> class enables you to create and manage integers of any accuracy for use in calculations. <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> objects are always as long internally as the corresponding results take up space ( infinite word size). The calculation options go far beyond options using primitive types and furthermore offer many static methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> class. Extensions include modular arithmetic, the determination of the greatest common divisor (GCD ), pseudo-prime tests , bit manipulation, and more.

###### [eg]   Example

The square of a number consisting only of 1s yields an interesting result, namely, a number that is both a palindrome [[ 237 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn21_10) and also counts up (to the middle) in the manner of 1234, etc. Consider the following example:

```
BigInteger ones = BigInteger.ONE;
for ( int i = 0; i < 20; i++ ) {
  System.out.println( ones + "^2 = " + ones.pow( 2 ) );
  ones = ones.multiply( BigInteger.TEN ).add( BigInteger.ONE );
}
```

**Listing 21.9**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/math/BigIntegerDemo.java, main()

The result of the loop is the following output:

```
1^2 = 1
11^2 = 121
111^2 = 12321
1111^2 = 1234321
11111^2 = 123454321
…
11111111111111111111^2 = 123456790123456790120987654320987654321
```

Like strings, <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> objects are always immutable. The same rule is true for <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> . Thus, mathematical operations on these objects always return new objects.

#### Constants for Selected BigInteger Objects

In our small example, we used some existing <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> objects to create new objects with their help. In total, the class provides four constants:

```
class java.math.
                    BigInteger
extends Number
implements Comparable<BigInteger> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static final BigInteger ZERO</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static final BigInteger ONE</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static final BigInteger TWO</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static final BigInteger TEN</samp>

#### Creating BigInteger Objects

For creation, several constructors and a factory method are available. No parameterless constructor exists because an empty immutable <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> object isn’t especially useful.

```
class java.math.
                    BigInteger
extends Number
implements Comparable<BigInteger> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static BigInteger valueOf(long val)</samp>
    A static factory method that constructs a <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> from a <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger(String val)</samp>
    Creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> from a string of digits with an optional sign.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger(String val, int radix)</samp>
    A string with an optional sign is translated into a <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> object. The constructor uses the specified base <samp class="listingcharacter">radix</samp> to interpret the characters of the string as digits. For <samp class="listingcharacter">radix</samp> > 10, the letters A-Z or a-z are used as additional “digits.”

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger(byte[] val)</samp>
    A byte array with a two’s complement representation of a <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> number in big-endian format (array element with index 0, contains the bits with the highest values) initializes the new <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> object.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger(byte[] val, int off, int len)</samp>
    Like <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger(byte[] val)</samp> , only a subfield is considered.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger(int signum, byte[] magnitude)</samp>
    Creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> object from a big-endian amount or sign representation. <samp class="listingcharacter">signum</samp> specifies the sign and can be assigned –1 (negative numbers), 0 (zero), and 1 (positive numbers).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger(int signum, byte[] magnitude, int off, int len)</samp>
    As the previous constructor, but with a subfield.

In addition to constructors that initialize the object with values from a byte array or string, an object can also be created with a random assignment. The class <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> uses the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.Random</samp> class. Likewise, <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> objects can be created that are pseudo-primes.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger(int numbits, Random rnd)</samp>
    Returns a random number from the value range 0 to 2 ^(numBits –1) . All values are equally probable.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger(int bitLength, int certainty, Random rnd)</samp>
    Creates a <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> number with bit length <samp class="listingcharacter">bitLength</samp> (>1), which is a prime number with some probability. The <samp class="listingcharacter">certainty</samp> value determines how probable an incorrect judgment might be. With probability 1/(2 ^(certainty)), the generated number is not a prime number after all. The larger <samp class="listingcharacter">certainty</samp> is (and the less probable a misjudgment), the more time the constructor takes.

In case of incorrect strings, the constructor with a string parameter will throw a <samp class="listingcharacter">NumberFormatException</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

Let’s say we have a string that encodes a binary sequence of zeros and ones. Then, an object of the <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> class can be used to convert this string into a byte array. In a second step of the following example, an output is made:

```
String s = "11011101 10101010 0010101 00010101".replace( " ", "" );
byte[] bytes = 
                        new BigInteger( s, 2 ).toByteArray(); // [158,261,69,69]
System.out.println( Long.toBinaryString( ByteBuffer.wrap( bytes ).getInt() ) );
// 1101110110101010001010100010101
System.out.printf( "%04X", 
                        new BigInteger( 1, bytes ) ); // 6ED51515
```

The first output uses <samp class="listingcharacter">ByteBuffer.wrap(bytes).getInt()</samp> as a trick to assemble the bytes of a (small) array into an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>. However, the call only works if the array for an <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> is exactly 4 bytes in size—in addition to <samp class="listingcharacter">getInt()</samp>, you can also use <samp class="listingcharacter">getShort()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">getLong()</samp> for arrays of size 2 and 8. For our example, <samp class="listingcharacter">getInt()</samp> is OK because we actually have 4 bytes. The second output shows yet another use case for <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp>, namely, to produce hex outputs; the byte array can be of any length. The fact that it’s called <samp class="listingcharacter">new BigInteger(1, bytes)</samp> instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">new BigInteger(bytes)</samp> is important because we don’t want a sign for the hexadecimal output if the first bit in the byte array is set and usually indicates a negative number. The format string <samp class="listingcharacter">%4X</samp> fills the output on the left with zeros if necessary.

#### Internal Representation*

The implementation represents a <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> object internally as well as the primitive data types <samp class="listingcharacter">byte</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">short</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> in the two’s complement. The other operations also correspond to the integer operations of the primitive data types, such as division by zero, which throws an <samp class="listingcharacter">ArithmeticException</samp> .

Internally, a <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> increases the range of values, if necessary, so that some operations aren’t transferable. For example, the shift operator <samp class="listingcharacter">>>></samp> can’t be taken over because, in a right-shift, we have no sign bit in the <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> . Since the size of the data type is always expanded if necessary and no overflow is possible due to this internal adjustment of the internal buffer, users may have to include their own overflow test in their programs if they need to limit the value range.

An interpretation of the values must also be made for logical operators. For operations on two <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> objects with different bit lengths, the smaller value is matched to the larger one by replication (repetition) of the sign bit. You can use special bit operators to set individual bits. As with the <samp class="listingcharacter">BitSet</samp> class, the “infinite” size allows bits to be set even if the number doesn’t require that many bits. Bit operations can’t change the sign of a number; if necessary, a new sign bit with the original value is added before the number.

#### Methods of BigInteger

The first category of methods replicates arithmetic operations for which there would otherwise be an operator character or method from <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp> :

```
class java.math.
                    BigInteger
extends Number
implements Comparable<BigInteger> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger abs()</samp>
    Returns the absolute value, similar to <samp class="listingcharacter">Math.abs(...)</samp> for primitive data types.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger add(BigInteger val)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger and(BigInteger val)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger andNot(BigInteger val)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger divide(BigInteger val)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger mod(BigInteger m)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger multiply(BigInteger val)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger or(BigInteger val)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger remainder(BigInteger val)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger subtract(BigInteger val)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger xor(BigInteger val)</samp>
    Creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> object with the sum, AND-operation, AND-NOT-operation, division, modulo, product, OR-operation, remainder, difference, and XOR-operation of this object and the other one.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger[] divideAndRemainder(BigInteger val)</samp>
    Returns an array with two <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> objects. In the array, the return object, position 0 contains the value for <samp class="listingcharacter">this / val</samp>, followed by <samp class="listingcharacter">this % val</samp> at position 1.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger modInverse(BigInteger m)</samp>
    Creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> by inverting the current <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> (equivalent to <samp class="listingcharacter">1/this</samp>) and then taking it modulo <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger modPow(BigInteger exponent, BigInteger m)</samp>
    Takes the current <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> to the power of <samp class="listingcharacter">exponent</samp> modulo <samp class="listingcharacter">m</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger negate()</samp>
    Negates the object and thus returns a new <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> with reversed sign.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger not()</samp>
    Returns a new <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> whose bits are negated.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger pow(int exponent)</samp>
    Creates <samp class="listingcharacter">this</samp> to the power of <samp class="listingcharacter">exponent</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int signum()</samp>
    Returns the sign of the custom <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> object.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger sqrt()</samp>
    Returns the square root and <samp class="listingcharacter">ArithmeticException</samp> if the number is negative.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger[] sqrtAndRemainder()</samp>
    Returns an array with two elements. In the first position is the square root ( <samp class="listingcharacter">see sqrt()</samp>); in the second position is the difference between the current value and the product of <samp class="listingcharacter">sqrt()</samp> .

###### [eg]  Example

The wrapper classes <samp class="listingcharacter">Integer</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">Long</samp> don’t provide methods for determining a greatest common divisor or for checking for a prime number. Using <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> in this case may pay off. For example, what is the GCD of 855 and 99? Answers will be <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger.valueOf( 855 ).gcd( BigInteger.valueOf( 99 ) ).longValsueExact()</samp> with 9.

The next category of methods is closely related to the bits of the number:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int bitCount()</samp>
    Counts the number of set bits of the number that’s in the two’s complement.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int bitLength()</samp>
    Returns the number of bits necessary to represent the number in the two’s complement without a sign bit.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger clearBit(int n)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger flipBit(int n)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger setBit(int n)</samp>
    Returns a new <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> object with the n th bit deleted, flipped, or set, respectively.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger shiftLeft(int n)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger shiftRight(int n)</samp>
    Shifts the bits by <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> places to the left or right.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int getLowestSetBit()</samp>
    Returns the position of the bit that is set furthest to the right in the representation of the number.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter"></samp><samp class="listingcharacter">boolean testBit(int n)</samp>
    <samp class="listingcharacter">true</samp> if the bit <samp class="listingcharacter">n</samp> is set.

The following methods are of particular interest for cryptographic procedures:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger gcd(BigInteger val)</samp>
    Returns the greatest common divisor from the current object and <samp class="listingcharacter">val</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean isProbablePrime(int certainty)</samp>
    Determines if the <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> object with probability <samp class="listingcharacter">certainty</samp> is a prime number.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger nextProbablePrime()</samp>
    Returns the next integer after the current <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> , which is probably a prime number.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static BigInteger probablePrime(int bitLength, Random rnd)</samp>
    Returns a prime number of length <samp class="listingcharacter">bitLength</samp> with a certain probability.

Furthermore, several extraction and conversion methods are available:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">double doubleValue()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">float floatValue()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int intValue()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">long longValue()</samp>
    Converts <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> to a <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp>, or <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>. These methods are implemented methods of the abstract superclass <samp class="listingcharacter">Number</samp>. If the value ranges don’t fit, they’ll be made to fit. Conversion errors due to lack of accuracy aren’t noticed by mistake. [[ 238 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn21_11)

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">long longValueExact()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int intValueExact()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">short shortValueExact()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">byte byteValueExact()</samp>
    Converts the value of <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> to the desired primitive data type. If the accuracy isn’t sufficient, an <samp class="listingcharacter">ArithmeticException</samp> will follow. The <samp class="listingcharacter">*ValueExact()</samp> methods follow the construction of the <samp class="listingcharacter">*Exact()</samp> methods from <samp class="listingcharacter">Math</samp>, which throw an <samp class="listingcharacter">ArithmeticException</samp> if the value range is exceeded during operations (addition, multiplication...).

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">byte[] toByteArray()</samp>
    Returns a byte array with <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> as two’s complement.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String toString()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">String toString(int radix)</samp>
    Return the string representation from this <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> to base 10 or to any base.

###### [eg]   Example

The following example uses <samp class="listingcharacter">byteValue()</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">byteValueExact()</samp> in comparison:

```
System.out.println( BigInteger.TEN.pow( 3 ).byteValue() );
BigInteger.TEN.pow( 3 ).byteValueExact();
```

While the former returns the output –24, the latter is followed by a “java.lang.ArithmeticException: BigInteger out of int range” because of course 1,000 doesn’t fit into a byte.

The last group of methods are comparison methods:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger max(BigInteger val)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger min(BigInteger val)</samp>
    Returns the larger or smaller of the <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> objects.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">boolean equals(Object x)</samp>
    Compares whether <samp class="listingcharacter">x</samp> and the current <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> object take on the same value. Overrides the method from <samp class="listingcharacter">Object</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int compareTo(BigInteger o)</samp>
    Since the <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> class implements the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Comparable</samp> interface, any <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> object can be compared to another <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp>. This method is useful because, in this way, <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> objects can be easily placed into sortable data structures.

### 21.6.2    Example: Quite Long Factorials with BigInteger

In our next example, the program should calculate the factorial of a natural number. The number must be positive:

```
import java.math.*;

public class Factorial {
  static BigInteger factorial( int n ) {
    BigInteger result = BigInteger.ONE;

    if ( n > 1 )
      for ( int i = 1; i <= n; i++ )
        result = result.multiply( BigInteger.valueOf(i) );

    return result;
  }

  public static void main( String[] args ) {

                    System.out.println( factorial(100) );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 21.10**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/math/Factorial.java

In addition to this iterative variant, a recursive variant is also conceivable. However, two reasons warn against its use. First, memory requirements are high because, for the calculation of n!, n objects are necessary. Unlike the iterative variant, however, all intermediate objects must be kept in the memory until the recursion is resolved. This memory requirement results in the second weakness: a longer runtime. For academic reasons, however, this path should be mentioned because it’s interesting to observe how this recursive implementation can eat up memory. The problem wouldn’t be so bad if the heap could no longer store new objects, but unfortunately, the stack of the current thread is impacted:

```
public static BigInteger 
                factorial2( int i ) {
  if ( i <= 1 )
    return BigInteger.ONE;

  return BigInteger.valueOf( i ).multiply( 
                factorial2( i - 1 ) );
} 
```

**Listing 21.11**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/math/Factorial.java, factorial2()

### 21.6.3    Large Floats with BigDecimal

While <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> takes care of the integers of arbitrary accuracy, <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> takes care of the floats. Again, these objects are immutable, and three constants exist: <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal.ZERO</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal.ONE</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal.TEN</samp> .

#### Creating BigDecimal

<samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> provides parameterized constructors for various types, including <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">String</samp>, and initializes a <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> object with them.

###### [»]  Note

Care must be taken with <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> . Consider the following example:

```
new BigDecimal( 1.00000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000001 )
```

The compiler takes the literal to the range valid for <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> ( <samp class="listingcharacter">1</samp> ), as in the following example:

```
new BigDecimal( "1.00000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000001" )
```

This number is precise. The same phenomenon can be observed with <samp class="listingcharacter">System.out.println(new BigDecimal(Math.PI));</samp> , which outputs the following value:

```
3.141592653589793
                        115997963468544185161590576171875 
```

The output suggests high accuracy; however, the correct version is the following value:

```
3.141592653589793
                        238462643383279502884197169399375 
```

#### Methods instead of Operators

With the <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> objects, you can now perform calculations known from <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> . The main methods are the following:

```
class java.math.
                    BigDecimal
extends Number
implements Comparable<BigDecimal> 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal add(BigDecimal augend)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal subtract(BigDecimal subtrahend)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal divide(BigDecimal divisor)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal multiply(BigDecimal multiplicand)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal remainder(BigDecimal divisor)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal abs()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal negate()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal plus()</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal max(BigDecimal val)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal min(BigDecimal val)</samp>

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal pow(int n)</samp>

#### Rounding Mode

A special feature is the <samp class="listingcharacter">divide(...)</samp> method, which can additionally get a rounding mode and optionally a number of valid decimal places. Let’s first look at the method without a rounding mode indicated, as in the following example:

```
BigDecimal ten = new BigDecimal( "10" );
BigDecimal two = new BigDecimal( "2" );
System.out.println( ten.divide( two ) );          // 5 
```

If the result is an integer or the result is exact, the lack of rounding isn’t a problem:

```
System.out.println( BigDecimal.ONE.divide(b) );  // 0.5 
```

However, if the result isn’t exact, <samp class="listingcharacter">divide(...)</samp> can’t be used. The expression <samp class="listingcharacter">new BigDecimal(1).divide( new BigDecimal(3) )</samp> results in the runtime error “java.lang.ArithmeticException: Non-terminating decimal expansion; no exact representable decimal result.”

At this point, various rounding modes specify how the last digit of a rounding should be determined. A rounding mode can be specified via an enumeration, <samp class="listingcharacter">java.math.Submit RoundingMode</samp> . The following constants exist:

| Constant in RoundingMode | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">DOWN</samp> | Rounding toward 0 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">UP</samp> | Rounding away from 0 |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">FLOOR</samp> | Rounding toward negative infinity |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">CEILING</samp> | Rounding toward positive infinity |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">HALF_UP</samp> | Rounding to nearest neighbor and away from 0 if both neighbors are equidistant |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">HALF_DOWN</samp> | Rounding to nearest neighbor and towards 0 if both neighbors are equidistant |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">HALF_EVEN</samp> | Rounding to the nearest neighbor and to the even neighbor if both neighbors are equidistant |
| <samp class="listingcharacter">UNNECESSARY</samp> | No rounding; operation must be exact |

**Table 21.14**     The Meanings of RoundingMode Constants

<samp class="listingcharacter">ROUND_UNNECESSARY</samp> may only be used if the division is exact; otherwise, an <samp class="listingcharacter">ArithmeticException</samp> will be thrown.

```
BigDecimal one   = BigDecimal.ONE;
BigDecimal three = new BigDecimal( "3" );

System.out.println( one.divide( three, 
                    RoundingMode.UP ) );      // 1
System.out.println( one.divide( three, 
                    RoundingMode.DOWN ) );    // 0 
```

**Listing 21.12**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/math/DivideRoundingMode.java, main()

Now, the number of decimal places can be determined, as shown in the following examples:

```
System.out.println( one.divide( three, 6, RoundingMode.UP ) );   // 0.333334
System.out.println( one.divide( three, 6, RoundingMode.DOWN ) ); // 0.333333 
```

###### [eg]   Example

<samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> provides the useful <samp class="listingcharacter">setScale(...)</samp> method, which can you can use to set the number of decimal places, which is quite useful for rounding. In our example, 45 liters of gasoline are supposed to be paid at 1.399:

```
BigDecimal petrol = new BigDecimal( "1.399" ).multiply( new BigDecimal(45) );
System.out.println( petrol.
                        setScale( 3, RoundingMode.HALF_UP ) );
System.out.println( petrol.
                        setScale( 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP ) );
```

**Listing 21.13**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/math/RoundWithSetScale.java, main()

The expenses are 62.955 and 62.96.

```
extends Number
implements Comparable<BigDecimal> 
```

### 21.6.4    Conveniently Setting the Calculation Accuracy via MathContext

An object of type <samp class="listingcharacter">java.math.MathContext</samp> conveniently specifies the calculation accuracy (not the decimal places) and the rounding mode for <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> . As the previous example showed, this information was given to the individual calculation methods. Now, this one object can be easily passed to all calculation methods.

The state is set with the constructors because <samp class="listingcharacter">MathContext</samp> objects will be immutable afterwards.

```
class java.math.
                MathContext
implements Serializable 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">MathContext(int setPrecision)</samp>
    Creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">MathContext</samp> object with specified precision as rounding mode <samp class="listingcharacter">HALF_UP</samp> .

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">MathContext(int setPrecision, RoundingMode setRoundingMode)</samp>
    Creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">MathContext</samp> with specified precision and a given rounding mode of type <samp class="listingcharacter">RoundingMode</samp> . The declared constants of the enumeration are <samp class="listingcharacter">CEILING</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">DOWN</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">FLOOR</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">HALF_DOWN</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">HALF_EVEN</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">HALF_UP</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">UNNECESSARY</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">UP</samp> .

    Creates a new <samp class="listingcharacter">MathContext</samp> object from a string. The structure of the string corresponds to the formatting of <samp class="listingcharacter">MathContext toString()</samp> .

    Returns a string representation, for example, <samp class="listingcharacter">precision=34 roundingMode=HALF_EVEN</samp> for <samp class="listingcharacter">MathContext.DECIMAL128</samp> .

For the usual cases, four ready-made <samp class="listingcharacter">MathContext</samp> objects are available as constants of the class: <samp class="listingcharacter">DECIMAL128</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">DECIMAL32</samp>, <samp class="listingcharacter">DECIMAL64</samp>, and <samp class="listingcharacter">UNLIMITED</samp> .

### 21.6.5     Calculating even Faster with Mutable Implementations

The two data types <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> are immutable, which leads to runtime losses in many calculations. Alternatives are available in the open-source world, such as [https://github.com/bwakell/Huldra](https://github.com/bwakell/Huldra), which implements other algorithms in addition to changeability. However, <samp class="listingcharacter">BigInteger</samp> is also continuously optimized by Oracle.

## 21.7    Money and Currency

Numbers require context. A number alone without a unit and without context isn’t usable. Numbers always must describe something: an age, a tree height, a turnover, or more generally “life, the universe, and everything.”

### 21.7.1    Representing Amounts of Money

For money amounts, no specific data type exists in Java, and so the storage of money values can look different, depending on the program. The following data types are suitable:

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">BigDecimal</samp> : Its advantages are precise calculations and selectable roundings.

*   A pair of <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> : Enables separate storage of the digits before and after the decimal point.

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">int</samp> or <samp class="listingcharacter">long</samp> : Instead of separate dollar and cent amounts, everything is stored in cents.

###### [»]  Note

The primitive data types <samp class="listingcharacter">double</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">float</samp> aren’t recommended because of their inability to correctly represent multiples of 0.01—rounding errors can quickly occur.

#### Money and Currency API

In Java Specification Request (JSR) 354 “Money and Currency API ,” a separate data type for amounts of money is defined. Originally, the types were supposed to be included in Java Platform, Standard Edition (Java SE), but this inclusion hasn’t happened yet. Nevertheless, these types are interesting, and the reference implementation Moneta is worth a look: [http://javamoney.github.io/ri.html](http://javamoney.github.io/ri.html). Besides monetary amounts, this small library permits conversions, formatting, and custom currencies.

### 21.7.2    ISO 4217

Currencies are described by currency codes, and their definitions can be found in the ISO 4217 standard.

| ISO-4217 Code | Currency/Unit | Country |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EUR | Euro | Countries of the Economic and Monetary Union of the European Union |
| CNY | Renminbi | China |
| DKK | Crown | Denmark |
| GBP | Pound | United Kingdom |
| INR | Rupee | India |
| USD | Dollar | USA, Ecuador, etc. |
| XAU | Troy ounce of gold |  |

**Table 21.15**     Some ISO 4217 Codes

The last entry in the table reveals that there are also ISO codes for precious metals and even funds. A numeric code is defined for each abbreviation.

### 21.7.3    Representing Currencies in Java

Java represents currencies through the <samp class="listingcharacter">java.util.Currency</samp> class. Instances of the class are requested by the factory method <samp class="listingcharacter">getInstance(String currencyCode)</samp> or selected from an enumeration.

###### [eg]  Example

The following example outputs all the currencies registered in the system with some additional information:

```
 Currency.getAvailableCurrencies().stream()
        .sorted( Comparator.comparing( Currency::getCurrencyCode ) )
        .forEach( c -> System.out.printf( “%s, %s, %s, %s%n”,

                    c.getCurrencyCode(), 
                    c.getSymbol(),

                    c.getDisplayName(), 
                    c.getNumericCode() ) );
```

The result is the following output:

```
ADP, ADP, Andorran Peseta, 20
AED, AED, VAE Dirham, 784
AFA, AFA, Afghan Afghani (1927-2002), 4
AFN, AFN, Afghan Afghani, 971
ALL, ALL, Albanian Lek, 8
…
```

## 21.8     Further Reading

Apart from classes to support large ranges of values, the Java library doesn’t provide many other algorithms often needed for mathematical problems. The few available methods include <samp class="listingcharacter">solveCubic(...)</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">solveQuadratic(...)</samp> from the <samp class="listingcharacter">CubicCurve2D</samp> and <samp class="listingcharacter">QuadCurve2D</samp> classes, and even those aren’t without errors. [[ 239 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn21_12)

On the (free) market, however, a large number of extensions are available, for example, for fractions, polynomials, and matrices. Let’s briefly look at a small selection of extensions:

*   Eclipse January ([https://projects.eclipse.org/projects/science.january](https://projects.eclipse.org/projects/science.january)): an Eclipse Foundation project for large n -dimensional fields and matrices. Emulates the NumPy library known in Python. The goal is to define standard interfaces.

*   Commons Math: The Apache Commons Mathematics Library ([https://commons.apache.org/proper/commons-math/](https://commons.apache.org/proper/commons-math/)): includes statistics, linear algebra , complex numbers , and fractions, among others.

Another problem area is dealing with calculation inaccuracies, but these problems are simply in the nature of things. Other problems exist as well, which the paper “How Java’s Floating-Point Hurts Everyone Everywhere” ([https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~wkahan/JAVAhurt.pdf](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~wkahan/JAVAhurt.pdf)) covers in great detail.

# 22     Testing with JUnit

“There’s no reason why you should have a computer at home.”
—Ken Olson , President of Digital Equipment Corporation, 1977

In this chapter you’ll learn to write unit tests for Java applications with the JUnit testing framework.

## 22.1    Software Tests

To gain as much confidence as possible in one’s own codebase, software tests are a good idea. Tests are small programs that run automatically over the codebase without user control and use rules to show that sections of the code behave as specified. Of course, software can’t show the absence of errors, but a test case always shows whether a program meets the requirements of the specification.

[![Test, Test, Test, but Please Have a Plan!](bilderklein/klein22_001.png)](img-f22.1.html)

**Figure 22.1**     Test, Test, Test, but Please Have a Plan!

Although software testing is extremely important, it’s not terribly popular among software developers. One reason is that tests cost time, which must be spent in instead of pursuing actual development work. If the actual software needs changing, test cases often must be modified as well, so ultimately, you’re managing two construction sites at once. Since developers should always complete a feature as soon as possible, testing is often dropped from the agenda. Another reason is that some developers think they are infallible coding gods, who consider all their program code (after a few hours of debugging) to be absolutely correct, performant, and delightful.

How can such a skeptical group now be convinced to write tests after all? A big advantage of automated testing is that, when major changes are made to the source codebase (i.e., refactoring), your test cases automatically tell you if everything has been changed correctly. After refactoring, for example, for a performance optimization, the tests report an error, something has probably been “optimized” in the wrong way. Software is subject to permanent change and is never finished, a sufficiently compelling argument for testing because, when software has reached a certain size, what effects changes to the source codebase will have is unpredictable. In addition, another reason exists for dealing with tests: One positive side effect of testing is that the generated software is significantly better by design because writing testable software, although tricky, almost inevitably results in better design. And a better design is always desirable because it increases comprehensibility and makes customizing the software later much easier.

### 22.1.1    Procedure for Writing Test Cases

The focus of software testing is on three characteristics: automatic, repeatable, and traceable. These characteristics require a library that must support two things:

*   Test cases always look the same and consist of three steps. First, a scenario is developed, then the method or a combination of methods to be tested is called, and finally the specific application programming interface (API) of the testing framework determines whether the executed program has shown exactly the desired behavior. This process is taken over by some sort of “is it true that” methods that match the desired state with the actual state and throw an exception if a conflict exists. In the event of an error, the tests should document exactly what went wrong.

*   The testing framework must run the tests and issue a message in the event of an error. This part of the testing framework is referred to as the test runner .

In the following sections, we’ll focus on the description of unit tests . These tests examine individual units . In addition, other tests will be required, such as load tests, performance tests, and integration tests, but these topics don’t play a major role for the purposes of our book.

## 22.2    The JUnit Testing Framework

Oracle doesn’t define a general standard framework for defining unit test cases, nor does it provide a runtime environment for test cases. Testing frameworks fill this gap; the most popular in the Java area is the free open-source JUnit ([https://junit.org/junit5/](https://junit.org/junit5/)). More than 60% of all open-source projects on GitHub reference this library.

### 22.2.1    JUnit Versions

Kent Beck and Erich Gamma started developing the JUnit framework in 2000\. Its current state is the result of contributions from various developers. The original JUnit 3 branch doesn’t use any annotations. This lack of annotations changed in 2006 with the release of JUnit 4, which currently has the largest user base. Because JUnit 4 is a monolithic library, JUnit 5 was written, and modularization was implemented. JUnit 5 consists of three parts: JUnit Platform, JUnit Jupiter, and JUnit Vintage . For the remainder of our discussion about JUnit, we’re always referring JUnit 5.

### 22.2.2    Integrating JUnit

Since JUnit isn’t part of Java Platform, Standard Edition (Java SE), you’ll need to integrate libraries in the classpath. You can, of course, download the JAR files manually and include them in the classpath, but an easier and faster approach uses Maven and an integrated development environment (IDE). First, we’ll add the following dependency to the Project Object Model (POM) file:

```
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
  <artifactId>junit-jupiter-engine</artifactId>
  <version>5.8.2</version>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency> 
```

**numbering_unknown**      pom.xml (Supplement)

Most standard IDEs provide wizards that you can use to easily create test cases from existing classes. Test cases can be processed at the touch of a button, and a colored bar instantly shows whether or not our job has been done well.

### 22.2.3    Test-Driven Development and the Test-First Approach

Let’s develop our JUnit example using a specific approach called the test-first approach . In this case, the test case is written before the actual implementation. The sequence with the test-first approach (somewhat extended) can be described in the following way:

1.  Consider which class and method to write. Create source code for the class and for the variables, methods, or constructors so that the compilation unit can be compiled. The code blocks are empty, but sometimes contain a <samp class="listingcharacter">return</samp> statement with return, so the types and methods or constructors are “there” but have no functionality.

2.  Write the API documentation and document the function and meaning of parameters, returns, and exceptions.

3.  Test the API on an example that shows whether the class feels “natural” with its members. If necessary, go back to step 1 and adjust the properties.

4.  Implement a test class.

5.  Implement the logic of the actual program.

6.  Determine if the implementation introduces new things that a test case should test. If yes, extend the test case.

7.  Run the tests and repeat from step 5 until everything runs error free.

The test-first approach has a great advantage of forcing overly hasty developers to start thinking again. These developers, without thinking much, may grab the keyboard and implement and change everything again in 20 minutes. Major changes cost time and therefore money, and the test-first approach reduces the need for later changes. Because when developers invest time in API documentation and write test cases, they already have a clear idea of how the class works, and major changes are less likely.

The test-first approach is an application of test-driven development (TDD) , which is a matter of defining testability right away as a goal in software development. This omission of testing was a problem with earlier development models, such as the well-known waterfall model , which placed testing at the end (i.e., after analysis, design, and implementation). A consequence of this old sequence was often a large chunk of program code that was impossible to test, which with TDD should no longer happen. Today, for every architecture, design, and class, developers should think about how to test the result right from the start. Research has shown that, with TDD, designs are significantly better.

On the question of when to test, only one thing can be said: as often as possible. This recommendation is sound because, the sooner a test fails due to an incorrect program change, the sooner the error can be corrected. Therefore, the best times for testing are before and after major design changes and definitely before committing to version control. In the modern development process, a computer may run continuous integration software. These systems integrate a build server that automatically checks out sources from a version control system, compiles them, and then runs test cases and other metrics. This software then carries out an integration test , which is where all the modules of the software are assembled into a whole, highlighting problems that may not show up in isolated tests on the developer machines.

### 22.2.4    Test, Implement, Test, Implement, Test, Rejoice

So far, Java doesn’t provide a simple function that reverses strings. Our first JUnit example is therefore wrapped around a new <samp class="listingcharacter">Strings</samp> class with a static <samp class="listingcharacter">reverse(String)</samp> method.

#### Writing a Class to Be Tested

Based on the TDD approach, you can implement a class with a method so that a correct interpretation is possible, but everything is initially without functionality. (The example doesn’t include the complete API documentation.)

```
public class Strings {

  /** 
```

```
 * @param string input. 
```

```
 * @return reversed string 
```

```
 */ 
```

```
 public static String reverse( String string ) {
    return null;
  }
} 
```

**Listing 22.2**     src/main/java/com/tutego/insel/junit/util/Strings.java, Strings

The name and parameter type “feel” right, and against this custom API, a test case can now be written.

#### Writing a JUnit Test Case

Now, you may think that an empty reversed string also results in an empty string and that the string “abc” therefore results in “cba.” Our goal is to get the best possible coverage of all cases. If you suspect case distinctions in the program code, you should try to find enough test cases that all these case distinctions are covered. Special cases or limits in value ranges are always interesting to test. (Our method doesn’t offer much in this context, but for a substring functionality, for instance, you can quickly find many tests that could be interesting.)

```
package com.tutego.insel.junit.util;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

                    import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class StringsTest {

                    @Test
  void 
                    reverse_non_null_string() {
    // given
    String emptyString = 
                    "";

                        // when
    String reversed = 
                    Strings.reverse( emptyString );

    // then

                    assertEquals( "", reversed ); 
    assertEquals( "cba", Strings.reverse( "abc" ) );
  }
} 
```

**Listing 22.3**     src/test/java/com/tutego/insel/junit/util/StringsTest.java

The class reveals five code patterns:

*   The test class ends with the suffix <samp class="listingcharacter">Test</samp> , but this rule is only a convention and is not mandatory. Usually, the classes are package-visible.

*   The methods that take on individual scenarios and test the classes or methods have the annotation <samp class="listingcharacter">@Test</samp> . Usually, the test methods are package-visible.

*   Different authors use different naming practices for test methods, and no mandatory naming convention exists. In our case, we chose a notation where the prefix names the method to be tested, followed by what the test actually checks, which is the reversal of non-empty strings. To improve readability, an underscore separates the segments, thus leading to the method name <samp class="listingcharacter">reverse_non_null_string()</samp>. A traditional naming convention is that the method containing the test begins with the prefix <samp class="listingcharacter">test</samp> and ends with the name of the method it tests. Following this blueprint, our method could be called <samp class="listingcharacter">testReverse()</samp> .

*   JUnit provides a set of <samp class="listingcharacter">assert*(...)</samp> methods that compare the expected state with the actual state. If discrepancies are found, an exception will be thrown. <samp class="listingcharacter">assertEquals(...)</samp> internally performs an <samp class="listingcharacter">equals(...)</samp> comparison of two objects. Accordingly, if <samp class="listingcharacter">Strings.reverse("")</samp> returns the empty string <samp class="listingcharacter">""</samp> , all is well, and the test continues.

*   The static import of all static members of the class <samp class="listingcharacter">org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions</samp> shortens the notation, so that instead of <samp class="listingcharacter">Assertions.assertEquals(...)</samp>, only <samp class="listingcharacter">assertEquals(...)</samp> can be written in the program.

### 22.2.5    Running JUnit Tests

You can execute test cases in several different ways, including the following:

1.  In a development environment, the tests can be easily executed. Eclipse or IntelliJ, for example, displays the results in a JUnit view and provides direct visual feedback through a green or red bar.

2.  JUnit can run the tests from the command line via the Console Launcher. [[ 240 ]](footnotes.html_ftn-fn22_01)

3.  A test run in the IDE is useful in development. However, in a professional build infrastructure, tests are triggered using Maven or Gradle. In Maven, the test run is part of a phase in the lifecycle.

#### Revising a Custom Implementation

In our example, the test run will fail because we lack a working implementation of the <samp class="listingcharacter">reverse(...)</samp> method. So far, the body reads:

```
public static String reverse( String string ) {

                    return null;
} 
```

Let’s change this method body with the following code:

```
public static String reverse( String string ) {

                    return new StringBuilder( string ).reverse().toString();
} 
```

No error will occur in the next test run.

### 22.2.6    assert*(...) Methods of the Assertions Class

<samp class="listingcharacter">Assertions</samp> is a class with various <samp class="listingcharacter">assert*(...)</samp> methods that raise an <samp class="listingcharacter">AssertionFailedError</samp> whenever a current value doesn’t meet expectations. The JUnit Runner catches all <samp class="listingcharacter">AssertionFailedError</samp>s and stores them for statistics. With three exceptions, all methods of the <samp class="listingcharacter">Assertions</samp> class start with the prefix <samp class="listingcharacter">assert</samp>: two are called <samp class="listingcharacter">fail(...)</samp>, and one is called <samp class="listingcharacter">isArray(...)</samp>. The <samp class="listingcharacter">assert*(...)</samp> methods are available either with a test message, which appears when JUnit is to specify an extra message, or without, when no extra message is requested. The messages can also be supplied via a <samp class="listingcharacter">Supplier<String></samp> , but this string isn’t included in the following documentation.

#### Is Something True or False?

Actually, the <samp class="listingcharacter">assertTrue(boolean condition)</samp> method should be sufficient for testing. If the condition is true, then everything is fine. If not, an internal <samp class="listingcharacter">AssertionFailedError</samp> will occur, which is a subclass of <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.AssertionError</samp>, which is itself a subclass of <samp class="listingcharacter">java.lang.Error</samp> .

```
class org.junit.jupiter.api.
                    Assertions 
```

*   <samp class="listingcharacter">static void assertTrue(boolean condition)</samp>
